document.title: Physical Setting/Earth Science Core Curriculum

DF7F89E4725643469E0F1964923BDE80.description:
Rocks are usually composed of one or more minerals.
• Rocks are classified by their origin, mineral content, and texture.
• Conditions that existed when a rock formed can be inferred from the rock’s mineral
content and texture.
• The properties of rocks determine how they are used and also influence land usage
by humans.

137C6D6BCD50449691CC02018003897D.description:
Minerals are formed inorganically by the process of crystallization as a result of specific environmental conditions. These include:
• cooling and solidification of magma
• precipitation from water caused by such processes as evaporation, chemical reactions,
and temperature changes
• rearrangement of atoms in existing minerals subjected to conditions of high
temperature and pressure.

78E6BA5500D5439399E7AF144E50B83B.description:
Minerals have physical properties determined by their chemical composition and crystal structure.• Minerals can be identified by well-defined physical and chemical properties, such as cleavage, fracture, color, density, hardness, streak, luster, crystal shape, and reaction with acid.
•Chemical composition and physical properties determine how minerals are used by humans.

2001ED4E4A4A4A5A819F5EFDC6E23450.description: Explain the properties of materials in terms of the arrangement and properties of the atoms that compose them.

E8A32EAA1C774565BFA91E9EA78BA06E.description: Matter is made up of particles whose properties determine the observable characteristics of matter and its reactivity.

99748599BA824FA8BE14C05EEDDE034F.description:
Temperature and precipitation patterns are altered by:
• natural events such as El Niño and volcanic eruptions
• human influences including deforestation, urbanization, and the production of green-
house gases such as carbon dioxide and methane.

0D60CD68E6734C81BB00D217CC97B8BC.description: A location’s climate is influenced by latitude, proximity to large bodies of water, ocean currents, prevailing winds, vegetative cover, elevation, and mountain ranges.

7993E66C3E4244CD8AE5AD494D462736.description:
The transfer of heat energy within the atmosphere, the hydrosphere, and Earth’s surface occurs as the result of radiation, convection, and conduction.
• Heating of Earth’s surface and atmosphere by the Sun drives convection within the
atmosphere and oceans, producing winds and ocean currents.

0A7A2B3FC02149D98EDD285A0B3C1F70.description:
Insolation (solar radiation) heats Earth’s surface and atmosphere unequally due to variations in:
• the intensity caused by differences in atmospheric transparency and angle of inci-
dence which vary with time of day, latitude, and season
• characteristics of the materials absorbing the energy such as color, texture, trans-
parency, state of matter, and specific heat
• duration, which varies with seasons and latitude.

2D910AE1F06E48598E56B390D7E3C408.description: Explain how incoming solar radiation, ocean currents, and land masses affect weather and climate.

ABED162702154F62BD6475EB6053E626.description: Sediments of inorganic and organic origin often accumulate in depositional envi- ronments. Sedimentary rocks form when sediments are compacted and/or cemented after burial or as the result of chemical precipitation from seawater.

F7010FE85C9445619EA1CF54563721B7.description:
Patterns of deposition result from a loss of energy within the transporting system
and are influenced by the size, shape, and density of the transported particles. Sediment deposits may be sorted or unsorted.

A833EBBBF62341CBA2579086B3694C40.description:
The natural agents of erosion include:
• Streams (running water): Gradient, discharge, and channel shape influence a
stream’s velocity and the erosion and deposition of sediments. Sediments trans- ported by streams tend to become rounded as a result of abrasion. Stream fea- tures include V-shaped valleys, deltas, flood plains, and meanders. A watershed is the area drained by a stream and its tributaries.
• Glaciers (moving ice): Glacial erosional processes include the formation of U-shaped valleys, parallel scratches, and grooves in bedrock. Glacial features include moraines, drumlins, kettle lakes, finger lakes, and outwash plains.
• Wave Action: Erosion and deposition cause changes in shoreline features, includ- ing beaches, sandbars, and barrier islands. Wave action rounds sediments as a result of abrasion. Waves approaching a shoreline move sand parallel to the shore within the zone of breaking waves.
• Wind: Erosion of sediments by wind is most common in arid climates and along shorelines. Wind-generated features include dunes and sand-blasted bedrock.
• Mass Movement: Earth materials move downslope under the influence of gravity.

9BD34F839CB94F28B818A036C13EDCCB.description: Natural agents of erosion, generally driven by gravity, remove, transport, and deposit weathered rock particles. Each agent of erosion produces distinctive changes in the material that it transports and creates characteristic surface features and land- scapes. In certain erosional situations, loss of property, personal injury, and loss of life can be reduced by effective emergency preparedness.

902DE6C6FF8546989EDDFB8871AB5669.description: Weathering is the physical and chemical breakdown of rocks at or near Earth’s sur- face. Soils are the result of weathering and biological activity over long periods of time.

ED81ED1CB947418D86FFCEDFD9516B77.description: Climate variations, structure, and characteristics of bedrock influence the develop- ment of landscape features including mountains, plateaus, plains, valleys, ridges, escarpments, and stream drainage patterns.

95B0E578D6FC497790F8D43AABB3E370.description: Topographic maps represent landforms through the use of contour lines that are isolines connecting points of equal elevation. Gradients and profiles can be determined from changes in elevation over a given distance.

0C6460197ED94AAD964768D01AB1680E.description: Landforms are the result of the interaction of tectonic forces and the processes of weathering, erosion, and deposition.

8FA36422679342A89CAC3D4043F1AF99.description: Plate motions have resulted in global changes in geography, climate, and the pat- terns of organic evolution.

A91B33D4352241C6A836EE930D3B8F3C.description: Many of Earth’s surface features such as mid-ocean ridges/rifts, trenches/subduc- tion zones/island arcs, mountain ranges (folded, faulted, and volcanic), hot spots, and the magnetic and age patterns in surface bedrock are a consequence of forces associated with plate motion and interaction.

3A8556AE94F54BA5BDE231BCC0DB8C65.description: Many processes of the rock cycle are consequences of plate dynamics. These include the production of magma (and subsequent igneous rock formation and contact metamor- phism) at both subduction and rifting regions, regional metamorphism within subduction zones, and the creation of major depositional basins through down-warping of the crust.

55E021F5CE764ACDB5C6ED319DF041B3.description:
The lithosphere consists of separate plates that ride on the more fluid asthenosphere and move slowly in relationship to one another, creating convergent, divergent, and trans- form plate boundaries. These motions indicate Earth is a dynamic geologic system.
• These plate boundaries are the sites of most earthquakes, volcanoes, and young
mountain ranges.
• Compared to continental crust, ocean crust is thinner and denser. New ocean crust
continues to form at mid-ocean ridges.
• Earthquakes and volcanoes present geologic hazards to humans. Loss of property,
personal injury, and loss of life can be reduced by effective emergency preparedness.

103C7FED462242D9BF309A996621AD41.description: The outward transfer of Earth’s internal heat drives convective circulation in the mantle that moves the lithospheric plates comprising Earth’s surface.

BB3ACF87F6524355B07361C32E557DA7.description:
Properties of Earth’s internal structure (crust, mantle, inner core, and outer core) can be inferred from the analysis of the behavior of seismic waves (including velocity and refraction).
• Analysisofseismicwavesallowsthedeterminationofthelocationofearthquakeepicen-
ters, and the measurement of earthquake magnitude; this analysis leads to the inference that Earth’s interior is composed of layers that differ in composition and states of matter.

50033DE92E9B4A23B97012DE6A9B3091.description: Seasonal changes can be explained using concepts of density and heat energy. These changes include the shifting of global temperature zones, the shifting of planetary wind and ocean current patterns, the occurrence of monsoons, hurricanes, flooding, and severe weather.

26213CB2B4D84C069805E7C4EBC9F2B6.description: Atmospheric moisture, temperature and pressure distributions; jet streams, wind; air masses and frontal boundaries; and the movement of cyclonic systems and associ- ated tornadoes, thunderstorms, and hurricanes occur in observable patterns. Loss of property, personal injury, and loss of life can be reduced by effective emergency preparedness.

1E8D0A27B8764DE283A9D5AE3E1EF68F.description: Weather variables can be represented in a variety of formats including radar and satellite images, weather maps (including station models, isobars, and fronts), atmos- pheric cross-sections, and computer models.

830FA3FDDD1D4F7086AEB7EF94DC5870.description: Air temperature, dewpoint, cloud formation, and precipitation are affected by the expansion and contraction of air due to vertical atmospheric movement.

ADB5F1FD7DF1401799FCF069124B7EDE.description:
Weather variables are interrelated. For example:
• temperature and humidity affect air pressure and probability of precipitation
• air pressure gradient controls wind velocity

EE7FDA675AAA4FE289CF4BEF6EAB8603.description: Weather variables are measured using instruments such as thermometers, barometers, psychrometers, precipitation gauges, anemometers, and wind vanes.

D9081E8C74DA49B693DF2E3F8B477C83.description: Weather patterns become evident when weather variables are observed, measured, and recorded. These variables include air temperature, air pressure, moisture (relative humidity and dewpoint), precipitation (rain, snow, hail, sleet, etc.), wind speed and direction, and cloud cover.

9D35C137D6DA44ADBF2A63FF4DA8EF4E.description: The transfer of heat energy within the atmosphere, the hydrosphere, and Earth’s interior results in the formation of regions of different densities. These density differences result in motion.

ACFE137F790F4BBD8A5D238B0C88D763.description: Earth systems have internal and external sources of energy, both of which create heat.

D3D24313C4704572BA405C821B916ED4.description: Use the concepts of density and heat energy to explain observations of weather patterns, seasonal changes, and the movements of Earth’s plates.

C6EFB9CED0234B71B2EA9F17387B21F6.description: Many of the phenomena that we observe on Earth involve interactions among components of air, water, and land.

D26CF6A8C8C2435ABD373D0B141FEF8A.description:
Geologic history can be reconstructed by observing sequences of rock types and fossils to correlate bedrock at various locations.  •
The characteristics of rocks indicate the processes by which they formed and the envi- ronments in which these processes took place.
• Fossils preserved in rocks provide information about past environmental
conditions.
• Geologists have divided Earth history into time units based upon the fossil
record.
•Age relationships among bodies of rocks can be determined using principles of origi- nal horizontality, superposition, inclusions, cross-cutting relationships, contact meta- morphism, and unconformities. •The presence of volcanic ash layers, index fossils, and meteoritic debris can provide additional information.
The regular rate of nuclear decay (half-life time period) of radioactive isotopes allows geologists to determine the absolute age of materials found in some rocks.

EF5B2FD47C3D4877B11DDDCF97942F80.description:
The pattern of evolution of life-forms on Earth is at least partially preserved in the rock record.
• Fossil evidence indicates that a wide variety of life-forms has existed in the past and
that most of these forms have become extinct.
• Human existence has been very brief compared to the expanse of geologic time.

55B9799716534975BC83538402178D39.description: The evolution of life caused dramatic changes in the composition of Earth’s atmosphere. Free oxygen did not form in the atmosphere until oxygen-producing organisms evolved.

1E0888AECBE64DE08BFF28A001BF5159.description:
Earth has continuously been recycling water since the outgassing of water early in its history. This constant recirculation of water at and near Earth’s surface is described by the hydrologic (water) cycle.
• Water is returned from the atmosphere to Earth’s surface by precipitation. Water
returns to the atmosphere by evaporation or transpiration from plants. A portion of the precipitation becomes runoff over the land or infiltrates into the ground to become stored in the soil or groundwater below the water table. Soil capillarity influences these processes.
• The amount of precipitation that seeps into the ground or runs off is influenced by climate, slope of the land, soil, rock type, vegetation, land use, and degree of saturation.
• Porosity, permeability, and water retention affect runoff and infiltration.

DA425C39C93F4B03A14AC5041C95E213.description: Earth’s oceans formed as a result of precipitation over millions of years. The pres- ence of an early ocean is indicated by sedimentary rocks of marine origin, dating back about four billion years.

D7CC30D2F1994FF69158D9B99C73D231.description: Earth’s early atmosphere formed as a result of the outgassing of water vapor, carbon dioxide, nitrogen, and lesser amounts of other gases from its interior.

AD5DFAA7D95D4A1BB22F20370A7A993F.description:
Asteroids, comets, and meteors are components of our solar system.
• Impact events have been correlated with mass extinction and global climatic change.
• Impact craters can be identified in Earth’s crust.

AFCD6D9B5D704EE4AB29EB6B23DB6391.description:
Our solar system formed about five billion years ago from a giant cloud of gas and debris. Gravity caused Earth and the other planets to become layered according to density differences in their materials.
• The characteristics of the planets of the solar system are affected by each planet’s
location in relationship to the Sun.
• The terrestrial planets are small, rocky, and dense. The Jovian planets are large,
gaseous, and of low density.

02F2B5AD1AB440DB9F95D97837C977D3.description:
Stars form when gravity causes clouds of molecules to contract until nuclear fusion of light elements into heavier ones occurs. Fusion releases great amounts of energy over millions of years.
• The stars differ from each other in size, temperature, and age.
• Our Sun is a medium-sized star within a spiral galaxy of stars known as the Milky Way. Our galaxy contains billions of stars, and the universe contains billions of such galaxies.

DD68323B23CC486F9CCC5741876AA882.description:
The universe is vast and estimated to be over ten billion years old. The current the- ory is that the universe was created from an explosion called the Big Bang. Evidence for this theory includes:
• cosmic background radiation
• a red-shift (the Doppler effect) in the light from very distant galaxies.

FA7396DAF73B4503BDA046CF9B0D9403.description: Describe current theories about the origin of the universe and solar system.

F7CB19B1927F4BCAB6187248F3AEC729.description:
Approximately 70 percent of Earth’s surface is covered by a relatively thin layer of
water, which responds to the gravitational attraction of the moon and the Sun with a daily cycle of high and low tides.

91E9A21E187E49E1B7BFDA579FF4D3F0.description: The Sun’s apparent path through the sky varies with latitude and season.

52B2CB95E6FE424283AA99D09DE2504C.description: Seasonal changes in the apparent positions of constellations provide evidence of Earth’s revolution.

EC63A0ED2DF441AF9BAA04F059957796.description:
Earth’s changing position with regard to the Sun and the moon has noticeable effects.
• Earth revolves around the Sun with its rotational axis tilted at 23.5 degrees to a line
perpendicular to the plane of its orbit, with the North Pole aligned with Polaris. • During Earth’s one-year period of revolution, the tilt of its axis results in changes in the angle of incidence of the Sun’s rays at a given latitude; these changes cause varia- tion in the heating of the surface. This produces seasonal variation in weather.

CAD44A26723441E8AB2A4B30D09D0E57.description: The Foucault pendulum and the Coriolis effect provide evidence of Earth’s rotation.

E2AA05B147404CD8A5A81D470BBF58F6.description: Earth rotates on an imaginary axis at a rate of 15 degrees per hour. To people on Earth, this turning of the planet makes it seem as though the Sun, the moon, and the stars are moving around Earth once a day. Rotation provides a basis for our system of local time; meridians of longitude are the basis for time zones.

98AEBE61DA9F48199EF71225E6FA29A2.description: Earth’s coordinate system of latitude and longitude, with the equator and prime meridian as reference lines, is based upon Earth’s rotation and our observation of the Sun and stars.

DD8059C34A944074BBD96DFBE339CD3B.description:
Nine planets move around the Sun in nearly circular orbits.
• The orbit of each planet is an ellipse with the Sun located at one of the foci.
• Earth is orbited by one moon and many artificial satellites.

BE4D868749F940139C7EACD1D4BA2C28.description:
Most objects in the solar system are in regular and predictable motion.
• These motions explain such phenomena as the day, the year, seasons, phases of the
moon, eclipses, and tides.
• Gravity influences the motions of celestial objects. The force of gravity between two
objects in the universe depends on their masses and the distance between them.

2703E24C70E1476EB5E438BBAB157779.description: Explain complex phenomena, such as tides, variations in day length, solar insolation, apparent motion of the planets, and annual traverse of the constellations.

E2E745F2E0A34EFFA9555BBBFF65FF27.description: The Earth and celestial phenomena can be described by principles of relative motion and perspective.

document.title: Elementary Science Core Curriculum Grades K-4

35ACA9463B2045BCA64157ADBC4F5691.description: Humans, as individuals or communities, change environments in ways that can be either helpful or harmful for themselves and other organisms.

8EC7A043DD6846F08B0402EA2EB9E44E.description: Over time humans have changed their environment by cultivating crops and raising animals, creating shelter, using energy, manufacturing goods, developing means of transportation, changing populations, and carrying out other activities.

FD5388EC788040C48DDD9FAECE9C6394.description: Humans depend on their natural and constructed environments.

BE0C80BA2E9E47D48BBEC7F8B56FB5E2.description: Identify ways in which humans have changed their environment and the effects of those changes.

4C8210C00C0246D78954AB9FFEA81966.description: Human decisions and activities have had a profound impact on the physical and living environments.

7266C6E4A7E54EB987456904C26ECA25.description: Heat energy from the Sun powers the water cycle (see Physical Science Key Idea 2).

8D3E4A4F136B4731985574B59B9A9978.description: The Sun’s energy is transferred on Earth from plants to animals through the food chain.

EFD2FD0AC3814FE6B6BF145EB1C1A8E5.description: Plants manufacture food by utilizing air, water, and energy from the Sun.

B728769710D740D28047BC805A2ABCE0.description: Describe the relationship of the Sun as an energy source for living and nonliving cycles.

2CE400940311426CBD340CD721C470E8.description: Plants and animals depend on each other and their physical environment.

D4B96E664BFE499782B95DE818F65D7E.description: When the environment changes, some plants and animals survive and reproduce, and others die or move to new locations.

ED40898FDED14980A4302372FC7AFFF3.description: An organism’s pattern of behavior is related to the nature of that organism’s environment, including the kinds and numbers of other organisms present, the availability of food and other resources, and the physical characteristics of the environment.

EDECEA4222CD4791B689767313719871.description: Decomposers are living things that play a vital role in recycling nutrients.

59DE7C5E74AD4D33BE3FB9B686A226DD.description: Animals that eat plants for food may in turn become food for other animals. This sequence is called a food chain.

BFE537A959AC4C41B4F105DDD4EAC4C8.description: All animals depend on plants. Some animals (predators) eat other animals (prey).

D4932FB6E4594A0CAD72E86258618D1D.description:
Green plants are producers because they provide the basic food supply for themselves
and animals.

801DB43ECE8B46F982BB32A2ECB46038.description: Describe how plants and animals, including humans, depend upon each other and the nonliving environment.

61B610BB55BF4D8CB169F4A0394F5F7C.description: Plants and animals depend on each other and their physical environment.

E885725BA576428E89C7D665DA7F37EA.description: Good health habits include hand washing and personal cleanliness; avoiding harmful substances (including alcohol, tobacco, illicit drugs); eating a balanced diet; engaging in regular exercise.

9722D4A0774A4F188C8480F13359CA45.description:
Humans need a variety of healthy foods, exercise, and rest in order to grow and
maintain good health.

9D83AA927BD94580B8692784A719DD62.description: Describe the factors that help promote good health and growth in humans.

95530CECF5BC4B1ABA801112A6C50D6E.description: Organisms maintain a dynamic equilibrium that sustains life.

9090477CA6B0426E946EE0F7597FA85E.description: The health, growth, and development of organisms are affected by environmental conditions such as the availability of food, air, water, space, shelter, heat, and sunlight.

3D8F700AD56B4D5699BD88F6BEB70F06.description: Some animal behaviors are influenced by environmental conditions. These behaviors may include: nest building, hibernating, hunting, migrating, and communicating.

42CB6BC3C1034EEF83A2197D9BB6B099.description: Particular animal characteristics are influenced by changing environmental conditions including: fat storage in winter, coat thickness in winter, camouflage, shedding of fur.

980D5CA970064060A866B020002DEC00.description: Some animals, including humans, move from place to place to meet their needs.

A3DF09EFADAE406E9504D50A04607E2F.description: Senses can provide essential information (regarding danger, food, mates, etc.) to animals about their environment.

DBA4EBBEE8EC4037AC411E3901E5935F.description: Animals respond to change in their environment, (e.g., perspiration, heart rate, breathing rate, eye blinking, shivering, and salivating).

57458662FB194EA084E31D85F4A20525.description:
Plants respond to changes in their environment. For example, the leaves of some
green plants change position as the direction of light changes; the parts of some plants
undergo seasonal changes that enable the plant to grow; seeds germinate, and leaves
form and grow.

7D2AC9E3823B47D9818983C64A6AB4E9.description: Describe some survival behaviors of common living specimens.

2479FECC10F04DA683FC89BEAA08EF64.description: Organisms maintain a dynamic equilibrium that sustains life.

9F64431229B04869A09DD272A1F0B852.description: An organism’s external physical features can enable it to carry out life functions in its particular environment.

324E08374B884CE5954FB8F58A342EDC.description: All living things grow, take in nutrients, breathe, reproduce, and eliminate waste.

0FADBDB1CEEA4DCFB5D34F1857C67C4C.description: Describe basic life functions of common living specimens (e.g., guppies, mealworms, gerbils).

20706F68FD5B4A199685690E9E43DB4A.description: Organisms maintain a dynamic equilibrium that sustains life.

D1F521E152404BD38D03347E5DD824F9.description: Food supplies the energy and materials necessary for growth and repair

F660932E5A6842BEB46EB8CD77CF1C7F.description: Growth is the process by which plants and animals increase in size.

04DAFB733855498F81F1B5548D7CB681.description: Describe evidence of growth, repair, and maintenance, such as nails, hair, and bone, and the healing of cuts and bruises.

59A2A85C829F400EB3DE732A36E61D04.description: The continuity of life is sustained through reproduction and development.

16C1B5E69E7B4EB5ADB587E9EF46DCF1.description: The length of time from an animal’s birth to its death is called its life span. Life spans of different animals vary.

3E029A7A142A47ED8CC379F7CEC39F29.description: Each kind of animal goes through its own stages of growth and development during its life span.

CBE904412E7749D183BBCA358CE67592.description: Each generation of animals goes through changes in form from young to adult. This completed sequence of changes in form is called a life cycle. Some insects change from egg to larva to pupa to adult.

1071A250657342DAB7C1F4C9566A416A.description: Life cycles of some plants include changes from seed to mature plant.

1C9D08812E604FE0A5E597993A8EBFB0.description: The length of time from beginning of development to death of the plant is called its life span

F36FA5EF5C144637A586F0900D41213B.description: Each kind of plant goes through its own stages of growth and development that may include seed, young plant, and mature plant.

202226AB1FF24A1995EDFAAA82F5BA24.description:
Plants and animals have life cycles. These may include beginning of a life, development
into an adult, reproduction as an adult, and eventually death.

DD5BC06054EA45DFA2CD84E57BDBB6F9.description: Describe the major stages in the life cycles of selected plants and animals.

2AF9F1A9AB7941A5820430E51F4F7365.description: The continuity of life is sustained through reproduction and development.

542622B2206B498C8ED86D7AC723B87C.description: All individuals have variations, and because of these variations, individuals of a species may have an advantage in surviving and reproducing.

4E6E661088EC4D869EB933726A25445E.description:
Individuals within a species may compete with each other for food, mates, space,
water, and shelter in their environment.

82B019C2E6084006998AF86BD525A723.description: Observe that differences within a species may give individuals an advantage in surviving and reproducing.

3846159FF6F547AEB224275988DB0438.description: Individual organisms and species change over time.

66A1C503C5A04A83A9C6B12D86D79890.description:
In order to survive in their environment, plants and animals must be adapted to
that environment.

CA86EDDBF5D04089B13F482B73582B92.description:
Each plant has different structures that serve different functions in growth,
survival, and reproduction

ED210CDB267746D5BED244ECD53C7242.description:
Each animal has different structures that serve different functions in growth,
survival, and reproduction.

260BC50943DB47E08B6D750AD3F117EF.description: Describe how the structures of plants and animals complement the environment of the plant or animal.

654DB36ECDEF4792A83C583D84E505BF.description: Individual organisms and species change over time.

7DC7E20B70D247ADB9F7AD32C446A2AC.description: Plants and animals can transfer specific traits to their offspring when they reproduce.

F870594A61D04D7DA25271ACD1705494.description:
Plants and animals closely resemble their parents and other individuals in their
species.

AE5A6071E6EA407495AB993A40E0FB40.description: Recognize that for humans and other living things there is genetic continuity between generations

09461103F46445BFA6AACB2453F70AC3.description: Organisms inherit genetic information in a variety of ways that result in continuity of structure and function between parents and offspring.

202BCEB5BC864A869842B39725A54941.description: Some characteristics result from an individual’s interactions with the environment and cannot be inherited by the next generation (e.g., having scars; riding a bicycle).

B568BB58142A44EFBE8F2A6EE7C1264D.description:
Some traits of living things have been inherited (e.g., color of flowers and number
of limbs of animals).

2F6B476B5FA342CDA18478EF74AEF629.description: Recognize that traits of living things are both inherited and acquired or learned

0576231E40794A30BC61E699AD497290.description: Organisms inherit genetic information in a variety of ways that result in continuity of structure and function between parents and offspring.

B694DDFC47A140F780580BCE9B060A72.description: Living things grow, take in nutrients, breathe, reproduce, eliminate waste, and die.

E19AA527D866402591AF4CE3E678D414.description: Describe the life processes common to all living things.

76B9352C586141479A48E5101962C037.description: Living things are both similar to and different from each other and from nonliving things.

540201C291CD4E25B9F6FAFAA826E767.description: Nonliving things can be human-created or naturally occurring.

6522FE8840A94FE4BFE686A597E5A030.description: Nonliving things do not live and thrive.

C96A31B091DF434EB619ED6F193987B0.description: Plants require air, water, nutrients, and light in order to live and thrive.

28DAF82039D142F4BE2BD96D16E25E7E.description: Animals need air, water, and food in order to live and thrive.

9BE4BF04F92B4F84B18F643A33688DB6.description: Describe the characteristics of and variations between living and nonliving things.

76D5A6704B8E4160834E7C42215D4554.description: Living things are both similar to and different from each other and from nonliving things.

045FFA1C410E48E2B6506AB292D9523A.description:
Students will understand and apply scientific concepts, principles, and theories pertaining to the physical
setting and living environment and recognize the historical development of ideas in science.

EAA15B3DD3CA44AE9918EDBA132887FD.description: The force of magnetism on objects decreases as distance increases.

4282CB0B2DDB44B5AEEEA8D3BD82FCE3.description:
The forces of gravity and magnetism can affect objects through gases, liquids, and
solids.

DBEE87566BD94DA1948FF9EDEA4DC53F.description: Describe how forces can operate across distances.

81D57E00FA5444F19A45C59DBA2B3717.description: Energy and matter interact through forces that result in changes in motion.

C4F0B604953449FC976443F97C316615.description:
Mechanical energy may cause change in motion through the application of force and
through the use of simple machines such as pulleys, levers, and inclined planes.

42EB36AB6712479BAEBFAC12F21B0E41.description: Magnetism is a force that may attract or repel certain materials.

93BB3A69340244D08B6EE4B10AD3054B.description: The amount of change in the motion of an object is affected by friction.

E652FEF6CF434C669C6EDDB725A4D878.description: The force of gravity pulls objects toward the center of Earth.

A0F4F429FA974E4BAC9B4079EDD4DBBD.description:
The position or direction of motion of an object can be changed by pushing or
pulling.

0806F5547CA4491180EBAD23476370C7.description:
The position of an object can be described by locating it relative to another object
or the background (e.g., on top of, next to, over, under, etc.).

CB123FA7F6204A6381CEA054312D97F0.description: Describe the effects of common forces (pushes and pulls) of objects, such as those caused by gravity, magnetism, and mechanical forces.

AB5B1847DAEF4BD9B4CB3AB0F94FCFF9.description: Energy and matter interact through forces that result in changes in motion.

4D7C28BFD6104E79BA320502DCE0A713.description:
Humans utilize interactions between matter and energy.
• chemical to electrical, light, and heat: battery and bulb
• electrical to sound (e.g., doorbell buzzer)
• mechanical to sound (e.g., musical instruments, clapping)
• light to electrical (e.g., solar-powered calculator)

73BE3F4461C24305815AF8F006301B43.description:
Everyday events involve one form of energy being changed to another.
• animals convert food to heat and motion
• the Sun’s energy warms the air and water

AF4DF5C3CF0A46779370F2FF2EE8FC20.description: Observe the way one form of energy can be transferred into another form of energy present in common situations (e.g., mechanical to heat energy, mechanical to electrical energy, chemical to heat energy).

FDEC1D000D3E439DA86B7B9EFCEDEBBC.description: Energy exists in many forms, and when these forms change energy is conserved

13386D98D6EC4D5FBFE91F85915EBF0D.description: Interactions with forms of energy can be either helpful or harmful.

29726C21F06942558E61F12AE1B36F98.description: Heat can be released in many ways, for example, by burning, rubbing (friction), or combining one substance with another.

E25FF142FFCA426EACD483E02A746696.description: Electricity travels in a closed circuit.

22E508EA925E4138ADA52E0709F5CC45.description: Energy and matter interact: water is evaporated by the Sun’s heat; a bulb is lighted by means of electrical current; a musical instrument is played to produce sound; dark colors may absorb light, light colors may reflect light.

9431925986524AECA61D2D41BB82FA73.description: Some materials transfer energy better than others (heat and electricity).

D5588C2566DB44C0827DE683E76549BD.description: Energy can be transferred from one place to another.

62671761577E46DF8B0D212452E30841.description: Energy exists in various forms: heat, electric, sound, chemical, mechanical, light.

D5D6CB27EB084C089A239C6C5465FD08.description: Describe a variety of forms of energy (e.g., heat, chemical, light) and the changes that occur in objects when they interact with those forms of energy.

7F7841B0292D4BEF9610FC40ED9033D1.description: Energy exists in many forms, and when these forms change energy is conserved.

19757F97F63B432DB2C67FE0DFB4EB33.description: Changes in the properties or materials of objects can be observed and described.

C79E58130EC148779429DD0F8BE93C78.description: Temperature can affect the state of matter of a substance.

204ECB703A12486383E50C19A6B146BD.description:
Matter exists in three states: solid, liquid, gas.
• solids have a definite shape and volume
• liquids do not have a definite shape but have a definite volume
• gases do not hold their shape or volume

891EDBA6969B4F9BA7B58B3920F435B7.description: Describe chemical and physical changes, including changes in states of matter.

DD17EBADEE6C41069598D10FF0CDACAD.description: Matter is made up of particles whose properties determine the observable characteristics of matter and its reactivity

2416D08FE2F14DEB92DAB9C4F9563C09.description: Some properties of an object are dependent on the conditions of the present surroundings in which the object exists. For example: • temperature - hot or cold • lighting - shadows, color • moisture - wet or dry

45A04A7D46524F5BB9AC4D6DF64399B9.description: Objects and/or materials can be sorted or classified according to their properties.

15824B93A6734DD7A350FA4EAAF1EFDD.description: The material(s) an object is made up of determine some specific properties of the object (sink/float, conductivity, magnetism). Properties can be observed or measured with tools such as hand lenses, metric rulers, thermometers, balances, magnets, circuit testers, and graduated cylinders.

159532892AFA488DBE36BDE076BB1B0C.description: Measurements can be made with standard metric units and nonstandard units. (Note: Exceptions to the metric system usage are found in meteorology.)

0C93F4B04CA64C3F9DF22E7F72607991.description: Objects have properties that can be observed, described, and/or measured: length, width, volume, size, shape, mass or weight, temperature, texture, flexibility, reflectiveness of light.

09BDE077C8D0411D978F7D2F583DF6C0.description: Matter has properties (color, hardness, odor, sound, taste, etc.) that can be observed through the senses.

6687BECEA67C4C228F93E984B6F6C5EB.description:
Matter takes up space and has mass. Two objects cannot occupy the same place at
the same time.

6F56A9DFD8654D1C984FA7917D188161.description: Observe and describe properties of materials, using appropriate tools.

803030FCE20942C7BD331FE95061D9A5.description: Matter is made up of particles whose properties determine the observable characteristics of matter and its reactivity

38F2F1FB97F1466287EF17C35DDC0F27.description:
Extreme natural events (floods, fires, earthquakes,volcanic eruptions, hurricanes,
tornadoes, and other severe storms) may have positive or negative impacts on living
things.

3322AB7FA2AE49CEB763A5867B2623D2.description:
Erosion and deposition result from the interaction among air, water, and land.
• interaction between air and water breaks down earth materials
• pieces of earth material may be moved by air, water, wind, and gravity
• pieces of earth material will settle or deposit on land or in the water in different
places
• soil is composed of broken-down pieces of living and nonliving earth material

134E57FB588548CEA0FF27672F19FC2C.description:
Water is recycled by natural processes on Earth.
• evaporation: changing of water (liquid) into water vapor (gas)
• condensation: changing of water vapor (gas) into water (liquid)
• precipitation: rain, sleet, snow, hail
• runoff: water flowing on Earth’s surface
• groundwater: water that moves downward into the ground

365BFBC604B24F919D835B8B320A0F0C.description:
Weather can be described and measured by:
• temperature
• wind speed and direction
• form and amount of precipitation
• general sky conditions (cloudy, sunny, partly cloudy)

9EDFA1DCAE4247B683D922E34A920841.description: Weather is the condition of the outside air at a particular moment.

B85FFA095E684E3498F0D8C42511C8E3.description: Describe the relationship among air, water, and land on Earth.

3A65F69A6443481186BDD5E83A9AC2A6.description: Many of the phenomena that we observe on Earth involve interactions among components of air, water, and land.

1301E0624A084F1AB8258B9E28400AF2.description:
The Sun and other stars appear to move in a recognizable pattern both daily and
seasonally.

ED95C10B4D9F4EE588F5989511BD4C68.description:
Humans organize time into units based on natural motions of Earth:
• second, minute, hour
• week, month

4DADCB64F27047E382C230E61B765614.description:
Natural cycles and patterns include:
• Earth spinning around once every 24 hours (rotation), resulting in day and
night
• Earth moving in a path around the Sun (revolution), resulting in one Earth year
• the length of daylight and darkness varying with the seasons
• weather changing from day to day and through the seasons
• the appearance of the Moon changing as it moves in a path around Earth to
complete a single cycle

A80CC5488D1C477DB8AACFF0C1F3BACE.description: Describe patterns of daily, monthly, and seasonal changes in their environment.

9B0FA1D18C514AEA953504579C8F9DF2.description: The Earth and celestial phenomena can be described by principles of relative motion and perspective: Describe patterns of daily, monthly, and seasonal changes in their environment.

C167F6FFFD954C858C0F7357C85A2C2A.description: Energy released during nuclear reactions is much greater than the energy released during chemical reactions.

01CDB3AE61AB4A3CAD4E1C8662DB9558.description: Energy released in a nuclear reaction (fission or fusion) comes from the fractional amount of mass that is converted into energy. Nuclear changes convert matter into energy.

6E87FDBEA99B4884B634FB1F75562D84.description: A change in the nucleus of an atom that converts it from one element to another is called transmutation. This can occur naturally or can be induced by the bombardment of the nucleus with high-energy particles.

98544F22523A408B9A3B70C3D0185DC0.description: Performance Indicator:  Compare energy relationships within an atom's nucleus to those outside the nucleus.

862B74D698B043FFA506E9D48B075378.description: Physical properties of substances can be explained in terms of chemical bonds and intermolecular forces. These properties include conductivity, malleability, solubility, hardness, melting point, and boiling point.

8063D90F1641462BA74A30C5B67EB3E6.description: Intermolecular forces created by the unequal distribution of charge result in varying degrees of attraction between molecules. Hydrogen bonding is an example of a strong intermolecular force.

457CD8C9F0FA45F98932CD65BF57B710.description: Molecular polarity can be determined by the shape of the molecule and distribution of charge. Symmetrical (nonpolar) molecules include CO2, CH4, and diatomic elements. Asymmetrical (polar) molecules include HCl, NH3, and H2O.

9F9D35249E374A38B808A213D83240CB.description: The electronegativity difference between two bonded atoms is used to assess the degree of polarity in the bond.

117FA205AAC045C8A7ED128BEDBBFCE4.description: Electronegativity indicates how strongly an atom of an element attracts electrons in a chemical bond. Electronegativity values are assigned according to arbitrary scales.

5746D291BB3E4A46A112AA9C2C3D8EE0.description: When a bond is broken, energy is absorbed. When a bond is formed, energy is released.

589878D1F47849F984321E1DDF0798FB.description: Metals tend to react with nonmetals to form ionic compounds. Nonmetals tend to react with other nonmetals to form molecular (covalent) compounds. Ionic compounds containing polyatomic ions have both ionic and covalent bonding.

CA0C8A51C51C41D584A47C4EDE9512DC.description: Two major categories of compounds are ionic and molecular (covalent) compounds.

52B254D79CA44BAB93A837252631CB36.description: Some elements exist in two or more forms in the same phase. These forms differ in their molecular or crystal structure, and hence in their properties.

7DB9759A24CD426FA6CC9AD28EA9D0B8.description: In a multiple covalent bond, more than one pair of electrons are shared between two atoms. Unsaturated organic compounds contain at least one double or triple bond.

BC07BBD9495B42CE8E85224F7CC05F85.description: Electron-dot diagrams (Lewis structures) can represent the valence electron arrangement in elements, compounds, and ions.

7719AF85F187474FB66049D6D522501F.description: When an atom gains one or more electrons, it becomes a negative ion and its radius increases. When an atom loses one or more electrons, it becomes a positive ion and its radius decreases.

B8BC01E05A5F41C29F26CEADC162EC37.description: Atoms attain a stable valence electron configuration by bonding with other atoms. Noble gases have stable valence configurations and tend not to bond.

F60995EA367F41CC8492D7CC26BAA906.description:
Chemical bonds are formed when valence electrons are: 
• transferred from one atom to another (ionic) 
• shared between atoms (covalent) 
• mobile within a metal (metallic)

96AAF44CA87C4EDBA2016F7244DD10C2.description: Performance Indicator:  Explain chemical bonding in terms of the behavior of electrons.

4AD2F6F3BB674F3D933210358F8EBE3D.description: Energy and matter interact through forces that result in changes in motion

FC96CBDFA40D47D9B02D5336A2AA6845.description: There are benefits and risks associated with fission and fusion reactions

C6A7DC23AFB549CAAB53FBEF60CDACF7.description: There are inherent risks associated with radioactivity and the use of radioactive isotopes. Risks can include biological exposure, long-term storage and disposal, and nuclear accidents.

8E7CC0ED651F4DC7B0F69E8BE53FB468.description: Radioactive isotopes have many beneficial uses. Radioactive isotopes are used in medicine and industrial chemistry for radioactive dating, tracing chemical and biological processes, industrial measurement, nuclear power, and detection and treatment of diseases.

845AA7E428AB4C0EB7E6D0945BD769D5.description: Nuclear reactions can be represented by equations that include symbols which represent atomic nuclei (with mass number and atomic number), subatomic particles (with mass number and charge), and/or emissions such as gamma radiation.

21574A27E65C495FBCAB4D8B434A4803.description: Nuclear reactions include natural and artificial transmutation, fission, and fusion.

0C4698FF67F6488E8227C17D91F901F6.description: Each radioactive isotope has a specific mode and rate of decay (half-life).

90B9FCB74F4E430194F7680F60C3090F.description: Performance Indicator:  Explain the benefits and risks of radioactivity.

EA56715FDDAF41EDACA2EFD6C0DB23F6.description: The concepts of kinetic and potential energy can be used to explain physical processes that include: fusion (melting), solidification (freezing), vaporization (boiling, evaporation), condensation, sublimation, and deposition.

A167D65C9B3542948867A6A785E02696.description: Temperature is a measurement of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a sample of material. Temperature is not a form of energy.

BE2BF37F7621437593325DA3AB4C2BC0.description: Heat is a transfer of energy (usually thermal energy) from a body of higher temperature to a body of lower temperature. Thermal energy is the energy associated with the random motion of atoms and molecules.

A83D986D090340E2B9718673579CFA85.description: Performance Indicator:  Explain heat in terms of kinetic molecular theory.

F348105F681F456F8F8A4D639E70C4D7.description: Energy released or absorbed during a chemical reaction (heat of reaction) is equal to the difference between the potential energy of the products and potential energy of the reactants.

EA423933BB6F49CEB2293575C95E8F13.description: Energy released or absorbed during a chemical reaction can be represented by a potential energy diagram.

A21E02BEE1124C6B915F2E801FCD63C5.description: Chemical and physical changes can be exothermic or endothermic.

14434F98841A4C40BB45EF94E8F2786A.description: Energy can exist in different forms, such as chemical, electrical, electromagnetic, thermal, mechanical, nuclear.

354E372D656749958B642E2A56A7ECDC.description: Performance Indicator:  Observe and describe transmission of various forms of energy.

CA7B805C05C24DD5A1A9E8D0BBAA746E.description: Energy exists in many forms, and when these forms change energy is conserved.

ADEEB9643D4A48F6A849E5D0C9DF1EA4.description: LeChatelier's principle can be used to predict the effect of stress (change in pressure, volume, concentration, and temperature) on a system at equilibrium.

D5304639D41540E9804F2167D0A78196.description: At equilibrium the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction. The measurable quantities of reactants and products remain constant at equilibrium.

314B49A5CE7F423BA875357B4024067F.description: Some chemical and physical changes can reach equilibrium.

28BAE033DAFC49CFACBE63E3EE6899FF.description: A catalyst provides an alternate reaction pathway, which has a lower activation energy than an uncatalyzed reaction.

2D36E36C63F04FFBAA67E6B3D477F775.description: The rate of a chemical reaction depends on several factors: temperature, concentration, nature of the reactants, surface area, and the presence of a catalyst.

81D8009017A044F5901335EE5F60321C.description: Equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain an equal number of particles.

74823B393BD849C389297CBA6BADF43E.description: Collision theory states that a reaction is most likely to occur if reactant particles collide with the proper energy and orientation.

009B4D078FDA4676966C76FA50305303.description: Kinetic molecular theory describes the relationships of pressure, volume, temperature, velocity, and frequency and force of collisions among gas molecules.

38006C7C93F04907AA5C593E2F0F6B22.description:
Kinetic molecular theory (KMT) for an ideal gas states that all gas particles: 
• are in random, constant, straight-line motion. 
• are separated by great distances relative to their size; the volume of the gas particles is considered negligible. 
• have no attractive forces between them. 
• have collisions that may result in a transfer of energy between gas particles, but the total energy of the system remains constant.

6C4370C233E94A3BB37BAAB6370A4E09.description: The concept of an ideal gas is a model to explain the behavior of gases. A real gas is most like an ideal gas when the real gas is at low pressure and high temperature.

4177F1C401C64E9EAE09129210485FDB.description: Performance Indicator:  Use kinetic molecular theory (KMT) to explain rates of reactions and the relationships among temperature, pressure, and volume of a substance.

8875A7EB5A0743F9B7E61E49B46089E3.description: The percent composition by mass of each element in a compound can be calculated mathematically

D9BB4F84C7854F8D9638187BFDE05C9B.description: The formula mass of a substance is the sum of the atomic masses of its atoms. The molar mass (gram-formula mass) of a substance equals one mole of that substance.

E5C1C2E9D7D445A38FA995B1B7732139.description: The empirical formula of a compound is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of the elements in a compound. It may be different from the molecular formula, which is the actual ratio of atoms in a molecule of that compound.

2E4805C9E3DA4BE4929F07369B28BF5F.description: A balanced chemical equation represents conservation of atoms. The coefficients in a balanced chemical equation can be used to determine mole ratios in the reaction.

8BF8FBFAE57F41A0A1D1DA84AE9EEADD.description: In a redox reaction the number of electrons lost is equal to the number of electrons gained.

46928F029F984B62BA5BEEBE62954E39.description: In all chemical reactions there is a conservation of mass, energy, and charge.

079DAE99A79640E393130782C7D77E07.description: Performance Indicator:  Apply the principle of conservation of mass to chemical reactions.

7C2B26B810E1488D976839CC6420697D.description: An electrolytic cell requires electrical energy to produce a chemical change. This process is known as electrolysis.

F0E3343DFF8D40A2AB2E5648BD6F97C5.description: A voltaic cell spontaneously converts chemical energy to electrical energy.

4E06DAA565EB4715BB5F23BCBC12E46E.description: An electrochemical cell can be either voltaic or electrolytic. In an electrochemical cell, oxidation occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode.

1CBF333C188F44E2A69CA77FCEF029C2.description: Oxidation numbers (states) can be assigned to atoms and ions. Changes in oxidation numbers indicate that oxidation and reduction have occurred.

E84F230FDBC44233A61AE61862D704A5.description: A half-reaction can be written to represent oxidation.

EF9727BF31354D138EB6EDBF7FF81C4B.description: Oxidation is the loss of electrons.

242C248174644485BA8C7F03B476685F.description: A half-reaction can be written to represent reduction.

AA7659BC83B7474EAB37D3DBA86C443C.description: Reduction is the gain of electrons.

A7AE2F687AF84CA48FECB148D10234CF.description: An oxidation-reduction (redox) reaction involves the transfer of electrons (e-).

B936BFF36AF4441698FE879EF75B190E.description: Types of organic reactions include addition, substitution, polymerization, esterification, fermentation, saponification, and combustion.

9DCAEA30C6A24C288195DDF3BB3D1442.description: Types of chemical reactions include synthesis, decomposition, single replacement, and double replacement.

A74557D5CAF343AFA4C5DBDD49A56766.description: A physical change results in the rearrangement of existing particles in a substance. A chemical change results in the formation of different substances with changed properties.

11620A165A50445EBCCC0824EFB18BC5.description: Performance Indicator:  Use atomic and molecular models to explain common chemical reactions.

DC770E4D032942F898C50E32BABC3F9A.description: Titration is a laboratory process in which a volume of a solution of known concentration is used to determine the concentration of another solution.

B370DE8BD2404BE2B5F5F416CDBB11D3.description: There are alternate acid-base theories. One theory states that an acid is an H+ donor and a base is an H+ acceptor.

B0B2A2086EB54008AAAEA01252C431C3.description: In the process of neutralization, an Arrhenius acid and an Arrhenius base react to form a salt and water.

EA0F71F6EB9540CD9DB62C93B670877D.description: Arrhenius bases yield OH-(aq), hydroxide ion as the only negative ion in an aqueous solution.

4C1DB5D42AFC4515801DEB40FFC1002D.description: Arrhenius acids yield H+(aq), hydrogen ion as the only positive ion in an aqueous solution. The hydrogen ion may also be written as H3O+(aq), hydronium ion.

042A9D02A3A84B2A8EF2527A5EBBD106.description: Behavior of many acids and bases can be explained by the Arrhenius theory. Arrhenius acids and bases are electrolytes.

227FBC590DB248358C9F607B5C60F151.description: On the pH scale, each decrease of one unit of pH represents a tenfold increase in hydronium ion concentration.

68EF982D6BDC402CAF1E4BC25E9C5D0A.description: The acidity or alkalinity of an aqueous solution can be measured by its pH value. The relative level of acidity or alkalinity of these solutions can be shown by using indicators.

8B854470C12F49F7BE7160EF9E87435F.description: An electrolyte is a substance which, when dissolved in water, forms a solution capable of conducting an electric current. The ability of a solution to conduct an electric current depends on the concentration of ions.

2FA6CCFBF5F0471BBB02883520A2FA37.description: The addition of a nonvolatile solute to a solvent causes the boiling point of the solvent to increase and the freezing point of the solvent to decrease. The greater the concentration of solute particles, the greater the effect.

F933C9B12FCE4C5E981E71E4A7808328.description: The concentration of a solution may be expressed in molarity (M), percent by volume, percent by mass, or parts per million (ppm).

223D7FBBBA52417C86B023C9E00F6921.description: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of a solute dissolved in a solvent. The solubility of a solute in a given amount of solvent is dependent on the temperature, the pressure, and the chemical natures of the solute and solvent.

EFA756642A7F45E0B526C0F23912440C.description: Differences in properties such as density, particle size, molecular polarity, boiling and freezing points, and solubility permit physical separation of the components of the mixture.

F15DA3E5BE564866ACA87DE4BA39EF77.description: Systems in nature tend to undergo changes toward lower energy and higher entropy.

969ABBDE09D448FAA45E964320A34253.description: Entropy is a measure of the randomness or disorder of a system. A system with greater disorder has greater entropy.

44CD414E0F964D75B16FFD8C7FCE11E3.description: The three phases of matter (solids, liquids, and gases) have different properties.

3721FF371FEE46DAB32DFB617EDAD5F7.description: The structure and arrangement of particles and their interactions determine the physical state of a substance at a given temperature and pressure.

C13A7DBF68DA43AB8C35F881E04B9CD7.description: Isomers of organic compounds have the same molecular formula, but different structures and properties.

0393B190517046A5A7F4C2ED5A53FB62.description: Organic acids, alcohols, esters, aldehydes, ketones, ethers, halides, amines, amides, and amino acids are categories of organic compounds that differ in their structures. Functional groups impart distinctive physical and chemical properties to organic compounds.

EC7E5CE900524E7A99E97726020EF432.description: Hydrocarbons are compounds that contain only carbon and hydrogen. Saturated hydrocarbons contain only single carbon-carbon bonds. Unsaturated hydrocarbons contain at least one multiple carbon-carbon bond.

137E05D78EC34BC99C5C21090C109829.description: Organic compounds contain carbon atoms, which bond to one another in chains, rings, and networks to form a variety of structures. Organic compounds can be named using the IUPAC system.

44236083AC0A41DBB13472225E186435.description: Types of chemical formulas include empirical, molecular, and structural.

9D63DE8F2EB04A9B8F5B40BB892C6020.description: Compounds can be differentiated by their physical and chemical properties.

55D466F3085D45818F205C7AA2CA21DF.description: A compound is a substance composed of two or more different elements that are chemically combined in a fixed proportion. A chemical compound can be broken down by chemical means. A chemical compound can be represented by a specific chemical formula and assigned a name based on the IUPAC system.

ED9FFE993D244CCABC8745110D4C4581.description: The succession of elements across the same period demonstrates characteristic trends: differences in atomic radius, ionic radius, electronegativity, first ionization energy, metallic/nonmetallic properties.

E7537A7B0A934F71AE1E0A0510AE7405.description: The succession of elements within the same group demonstrates characteristic trends: differences in atomic radius, ionic radius, electronegativity, first ionization energy, metallic/nonmetallic properties.

0BD326271CCB4D7988857B6C5BB74660.description: For Groups 1, 2, and 13-18 on the Periodic Table, elements within the same group have the same number of valence electrons (helium is an exception) and therefore similar chemical properties.

678A5167C4144FC2B7125E6B868EFC0B.description: The placement or location of an element on the Periodic Table gives an indication of the physical and chemical properties of that element. The elements on the Periodic Table are arranged in order of increasing atomic number.

0B845C67A2B342C9AE17EB3BF3155438.description: Elements can also be differentiated by chemical properties. Chemical properties describe how an element behaves during a chemical reaction.

546D3E87DE974024BA67753DF5806B70.description: Elements can be differentiated by physical properties. Physical properties of substances, such as density, conductivity, malleability, solubility, and hardness, differ among elements.

28F93E0075284F338AF443D86C03DE4C.description: Elements can be classified by their properties and located on the Periodic Table as metals, nonmetals, metalloids (B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te), and noble gases.

64E1502F99E3444CA5E8FC6E50D66FAD.description: Elements are substances that are composed of atoms that have the same atomic number. Elements cannot be broken down by chemical change.

A89B3B8E98BE4D80A604378D1A7F11DB.description: The proportions of components in a mixture can be varied. Each component in a mixture retains its original properties.

9034FAAFDFDC40199D256A257D059016.description: Mixtures are composed of two or more different substances that can be separated by physical means. When different substances are mixed together, a homogeneous or heterogeneous mixture is formed.

37915B7727A1486FA95AC6D879B4D467.description: A pure substance (element or compound) has a constant composition and constant properties throughout a given sample, and from sample to sample.

A472D95AF5C34173A8700C35F2EEFC32.description: Matter is classified as a pure substance or as a mixture of substances.

615C5F770100427E86C4B308F6FAB8D1.description: Spontaneous decay can involve the release of alpha particles, beta particles, positrons, and/or gamma radiation from the nucleus of an unstable isotope. These emissions differ in mass, charge, ionizing power, and penetrating power.

B57CBB6429FF4B7BA9FED035C0DE7321.description: Stability of an isotope is based on the ratio of neutrons and protons in its nucleus. Although most nuclei are stable, some are unstable and spontaneously decay, emitting radiation.

88815CE178194F258A3B727BB8FF5141.description: The average atomic mass of an element is the weighted average of the masses of its naturally occurring isotopes.

4BDF593507544F7995E41F64C3DAC3A0.description: Atoms of an element that contain the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons are called isotopes of that element.

A925D676F40B4C9F933C79F4C974CC4D.description: The outermost electrons in an atom are called the valence electrons. In general, the number of valence electrons affects the chemical properties of an element.

0BFC709693B14955B813012E64E0FF21.description: When an electron returns from a higher energy state to a lower energy state, a specific amount of energy is emitted. This emitted energy can be used to identify an element.

D84AB366C2334C188A8489C00C34BD37.description: When an electron in an atom gains a specific amount of energy, the electron is at a higher energy state (excited state).

DB373970B89D4203BA4FDCC582C67A2D.description: Each electron in an atom has its own distinct amount of energy.

2BE1FA882AC5484DBEFDFF0CA62DEB64.description: In the wave-mechanical model (electron cloud model) the electrons are in orbitals, which are defined as the regions of the most probable electron location (ground state).

4CBF7F987C63426D85F930C6EB79D666.description: The number of protons in an atom (atomic number) identifies the element. The sum of the protons and neutrons in an atom (mass number) identifies an isotope. Common notations that represent isotopes include: 14C, 14C, carbon-14, C-14. 6

62C16BE253DB4FC4A112BC96427BB862.description: The mass of each proton and each neutron is approximately equal to one atomic mass unit. An electron is much less massive than a proton or a neutron.

6B89E55043AE427FBF765D9EE4A0019D.description: Protons and electrons have equal but opposite charges. The number of protons equals the number of electrons in an atom.

24331FE3D886454FB1EB822E696DC19D.description: The proton is positively charged, and the neutron has no charge. The electron is negatively charged.

F71D6FA522C34E849939478D1438DF42.description: Subatomic particles contained in the nucleus include protons and neutrons.

A6E8AEBF83234804B8C3CC54C0F4D138.description: Each atom has a nucleus, with an overall positive charge, surrounded by negatively charged electrons.

4FBCEA5F1DF1456F9E9F299851AB59B6.description: The modern model of the atom has evolved over a long period of time through the work of many scientists.

7365DC06F3AC4A23A5D82FCC7C27D59F.description: Performance Indicator:  Explain the properties of materials in terms of the arrangement and properties of the atoms that compose them.

FAA27AB2C9BE4518A0ACE04CFF1E0C4F.description: Matter is made up of particles whose properties determine the observable characteristics of matter and its reactivity

785475A02073450286678B08273186AE.description: distinguish between nonpolar covalent bonds (two of the same nonmetals) and polar covalent bonds 5.2k

C90ED51C232245BEB2B834DC43F4BD0A.description: determine the noble gas configuration an atom will achieve by bonding 5.2b

9A94D414421F4E13A6451F0CF81CA6B4.description: explain vapor pressure, evaporation rate, and phase changes in terms of intermolecular forces 5.2m

3E5B136B14B54442ACB8CDFEB1E46F9C.description: compare the physical properties of substances based on chemical bonds and intermolecular forces, e.g., conductivity, malleability, solubility, hardness, melting point, and boiling point 5.2n

E5A55F1828DE41B6BCFBE24EAD9737E3.description:
demonstrate bonding concepts, using Lewis dot structures representing valence electrons: 5.2a, 5.2d
§ transferred (ionic bonding) 
§ shared (covalent bonding) 
§ in a stable octet Example: atom ion K. K+ .. .. - :Cl: :Cl: . ..

01DACD48B02D4677AA38BBE300C35A1D.description: Students will explain chemical bonding in terms of the behavior of electrons.

A199B1B5F7D0429FB8FB384A984E0860.description: Energy and matter interact through forces that result in changes in motion.

04722665C43D440EB5D5EC72149A7CED.description: identify specific uses of some common radioisotopes, such as I-131 in diagnosing and treating thyroid disorders, C-14 to C-12 ratio in dating once-living organisms, U-238 to Pb-206 ratio in dating geological formations, and Co-60 in treating cancer 4.4d

3EA1A520FF144D608C67B1AC444499B4.description: complete nuclear equations; predict missing particles from nuclear equations 4.4c

5169FB4858D7473C800EB634FA6BE87A.description: compare and contrast fission and fusion reactions 4.4a, 4.4f, 5.3b
