CF11D72A6A1A4F48867F7B85DCBCC710.description:
Solving interdisciplinary problems involves a variety of skills and strategies, including
effective work habits; gathering and processing information; generating and analyzing
ideas; realizing ideas; making connections among the common themes of mathematics,
science, and technology; and presenting results.
If students are asked to do a project, then the project would require students to:
• work effectively
• gather and process information
• generate and analyze ideas
• observe common themes
• realize ideas
• present results

A5F2DC5CE1564E12A9BB30E4D304A431.description:
Explain and evaluate phenomena mathematically and scientifically by formulating
a testable hypothesis, demonstrating the logical connections between the scientific
concepts guiding the hypothesis and the design of an experiment, applying and
inquiring into the mathematical ideas relating to investigation of phenomena, and
using (and if needed, designing) technological tools and procedures to assist in the
investigation and in the communication of results.
• design an experiment that requires the use of a mathematical concept to solve a
scientific problem, e.g., an experiment to compare the density of different types
of soda pop

027464DAB0E44D5AA00DABB2A11763A0.description:
Design solutions to real-world problems on a community, national, or global scale,
using a technological design process that integrates scientific investigation and rigorous
mathematical analysis of the problem and of the solution.
• design a potential solution to a regional problem, e.g., suggest a plan to adjust
the acidity of a lake in the Adirondacks

763135DBD42747D19BB190974A399FB9.description:
Analyze and quantify consumer product data, understand environmental and economic
impacts, develop a method for judging the value and efficacy of competing
products, and discuss cost-benefit and risk-benefit trade-offs made in arriving at
the optimal choice.
• compare and analyze specific consumer products, e.g., antacids, vitamin C

19B1F0570A114E7E8101551D060376FB.description:
Analyze science/technology/society problems and issues on a community,
national, or global scale and plan and carry out a remedial course of action.
• carry out a remedial course of action by communicating the plan to others, e.g.,
writing and sending “a letter to the editor”

98B7CA9426FE4A36A605BBEFF40B6C33.description:
The knowledge and skills of mathematics, science, and technology are used together to
make informed decisions and solve problems, especially those relating to issues of science/technology/society,
consumer decision making, design, and inquiry into
phenomena.

8F6309455BA04138BC2DAC0951C28E3F.description:
Identifying patterns of change is necessary for making predictions about future
behavior and conditions.
Examples include:
• use graphs to make predictions, e.g., half-life, solubility
• use graphs to identify patterns and interpret experimental data, e.g., heating
and cooling curves

DD09BC7960914CC7B0A5455C716199BA.description:
Cite specific examples of how dynamic equilibrium is achieved by equality of
change in opposing directions.
• explain how a system returns to equilibrium in response to a stress, e.g.,
LeChatelier’s principle

F0F5285894E24FD9AFB9724457FEBCD0.description:
Describe specific instances of how disturbances might affect a system’s equilibrium,
from small disturbances that do not upset the equilibrium to larger disturbances
(threshold level) that cause the system to become unstable.
• explain how a small change might not affect a system, e.g., activation energy

45629E85F4434BCE83563CB41052A312.description:
Equilibrium is a state of stability due either to a lack of change (static equilibrium) or a
balance between opposing forces (dynamic equilibrium).

94F9D56C7F244118A1F49F1DDF14073B.description:
Extend the use of powers of ten notation to understanding the exponential
function and performing operations with exponential factors.
• use powers often to represent a large range of values for a physical quantity,
e.g., pH scale

CA69582EA0234F2F8DD8F263AD1B1A2B.description:
Describe the effects of changes in scale on the functioning of physical, biological, or
designed information systems.
• show how microscale processes can resemble or differ from real-world
processes, e.g., microscale chemistry

8956FCF28DC54C7AA58721031DE20480.description:
The grouping of magnitudes of size, time, frequency, and pressures or other units of
measurement into a series of relative order provides a useful way to deal with the
immense range and the changes in scale that affect the behavior and design of systems

7818A64D8E1444F68C5C947E848C581F.description:
Compare predictions to actual observations, using test models.
• compare experimental results to a predicted value, e.g., percent error

B5464A8D075A4D0C8204D5E45B46EC94.description:
Find and use mathematical models that behave in the same manner as the
processes under investigation.
• show how mathematical models (equations) describe a process, e.g., combined
gas law

56EBEA26BF694DF698546A227F395C09.description:
Collect information about the behavior of a system and use modeling tools to
represent the operation of the system.
• show how information about a system is used to create a model, e.g., kinetic
molecular theory (KMT)

201DFE1CF171451B875C803B6509A898.description:
Revise a model to create a more complete or improved representation of the system.
• show how models are revised in response to experimental evidence, e.g., atomic
theory, Periodic Table

01361EC9542C47DBAB8CD61064156BFC.description:
Models are simplified representations of objects, structures, or systems used in analysis,
explanation, interpretation, or design

2E036B62A8384595B3BEF985600729D0.description:
Through systems thinking, people can recognize the commonalities that exist among all
systems and how parts of a system interrelate and combine to perform specific
functions.
Examples include:
• use the concept of systems and surroundings to describe heat flow in a chemical
or physical change, e.g., dissolving process

AAC74E435CBB49719D096251D69058E3.description:
Knowledge of the impacts and limitations of information systems is essential to its
effectiveness and ethical use.
Examples include:
• critically assess the value of information with or without benefit of scientific
backing and supporting data, and evaluate the effect such information could
have on public judgment or opinion, e.g., environmental issues
• discuss the use of the peer-review process in the scientific community and
explain its value in maintaining the integrity of scientific publication, e.g., “cold
fusion”

3A72A1584AB6411E89A4307C450D1A85.description:
Information technology is used to retrieve, process, and communicate information as a
tool to enhance learning.
Examples include:
• use the Internet as a source to retrieve information for classroom use, e.g.,
Periodic Table, acid rain

616C70FE4771440582A358BAF8553E23.description:
Engineering design is an iterative process involving modeling and optimization (finding
the best solution within given constraints); this process is used to develop technological
solutions to problems within given constraints.
If students are asked to do a design project, then:
• Initiate and carry out a thorough investigation of an unfamiliar situation and
identify needs and opportunities for technological invention or innovation.
• Identify, locate, and use a wide range of information resources, and document
through notes and sketches how findings relate to the problem.
• Generate creative solutions, break ideas into significant functional elements,
and explore possible refinements; predict possible outcomes, using mathematical
and functional modeling techniques; choose the optimal solution to the
problem, clearly documenting ideas against design criteria and constraints; and
explain how human understandings, economics, ergonomics, and environmental
considerations have influenced the solution.
• Develop work schedules and working plans which include optimal use and cost
of materials, processes, time, and expertise; construct a model of the solution,
incorporating developmental modifications while working to a high degree of
quality (craftsmanship). Devise a test of the solution according to the design criteria and perform the
test; record, portray, and logically evaluate performance test results through
quantitative, graphic, and verbal means. Use a variety of creative verbal and
graphic techniques effectively and persuasively to present conclusions, predict
impact and new problems, and suggest and pursue modifications.

82E9A6D28A3545F8931959CA3F31B78C.description:
Develop a written report for public scrutiny that describes the proposed explanation,
including a literature review, the research carried out, its results, and suggestions
for further research.

BAE126483F77419FACD8077A50ADC984.description:
Using results of the test and through public discussion, revise the explanation and
contemplate additional research.

CEFF016FC94D4415BE874275CFB84774.description:
Assess correspondence between the predicted result contained in the hypothesis
and the actual result, and reach a conclusion as to whether or not the explanation
on which the prediction is supported.
• evaluate experimental methodology for inherent sources of error and analyze
the possible effect on the result
• compare the experimental result to the expected result; calculate the percent
error as appropriate

75EBF30044A5440AB68D5B9FE0DC145E.description:
Apply statistical analysis techniques when appropriate to test if chance alone
explains the result

9A9FB5CC802548AF88BBC19DEF7F15BF.description:
Use various means of representing and organizing observations (e.g., diagrams,
tables, charts, graphs, equations, and matrices) and insightfully interpret the
organized data.
• organize observations in a data table, analyze the data for trends or patterns,
and interpret the trends or patterns, using scientific concepts

6F1C240B294148BC9BD9609C94AF22A5.description:
The observations made while testing proposed explanations, when analyzed using conventional
and invented methods, provide new insights into phenomena.

2BBF9F3DB2094E19998598DD79FB41CE.description:
Carry out a research plan for testing explanations, including selecting and developing
techniques, acquiring and building apparatus, and recording observations
as necessary.
• determine safety procedures to accompany a research plan

8521A527320D4762AB9CAA18545F3030.description:
Develop and present proposals including formal hypotheses to test explanations,
i.e.; they predict what should be observed under specific conditions if their explanation
is true.
• develop research proposals in the form of “if X is true and a particular test Y is
done, then prediction Z will occur”

9DA78C78563C4253937DE6F5946DD1A3.description:
Refine research ideas through library investigations, including information
retrieval and reviews of the literature, and through peer feedback obtained from
review and discussion.
• use library investigations, retrieved information, and literature reviews to
improve the experimental design of an experiment

62EDDC196D9A474A9D2CDF8D82F33804.description:
Devise ways of making observations to test proposed explanations.
• design and/or carry out experiments, using scientific methodology to test proposed
calculations

C184256A87564AC782B83F2DE1E3DDE1.description:
Beyond the use of reasoning and consensus, scientific inquiry involves the testing of proposed
explanations involving the use of conventional techniques and procedures and usually
requiring considerable ingenuity

EAC5149276494F5B8BF1A262F336A9C6.description:
Work towards reconciling competing explanations, clarifying points of agreement
and disagreement.
• evaluate the merits of various scientific theories and indicate why one theory
was accepted over another

2BA2BC98E8154F25A3D73735362E00F2.description:
Hone ideas through reasoning, library research, and discussion with others,
including experts.
• locate data from published sources to support/defend/explain patterns
observed in natural phenomena

1EF08B69C1A6455E9C7C6F4A0D3AAA6F.description:
Elaborate on basic scientific and personal explanations of natural phenomena, and
develop extended visual models and mathematical formulations to represent
thinking.
• use theories and/or models to represent and explain observations
• use theories and/or principles to make predictions about natural phenomena
• develop models to explain observations

9509F052B1EF414C80E59F07357451D5.description:
The central purpose of scientific inquiry is to develop explanations of natural phenomena
in a continuing, creative process.

02567A36E4B242CC88D0F8133138CF9C.description:
Apply algebraic and geometric concepts and skills to the solution of problems.
• state assumptions which apply to the use of a particular mathematical equation
and evaluate these assumptions to see if they have been met
• evaluate the appropriateness of an answer, based on given data

F32153A1ECB64B31B2D99C1371EBBB22.description: Critical thinking skills are used in the solution of mathematical problems.

C8AEA7A642904D4BAAADCF341A2CD15F.description:
Use deductive reasoning to construct and evaluate conjectures and arguments, recognizing
that patterns and relationships in mathematics assist them in arriving at
these conjectures and arguments.
• interpret a graph constructed from experimentally obtained data
◆ identify relationships
§ direct
§ inverse
◆ apply data showing trends to predict information

A10B43BC6BBF486CB2B91B6DBC9B7A61.description: Deductive and inductive reasoning are used to reach mathematical conclusions

19F396233CE84F94BD891C298651C87A.description:
Use algebraic and geometric representations to describe and compare data.
• organize, graph, and analyze data gathered from laboratory activities or other
sources
◆ identify independent and dependent variables
◆ create appropriate axes with labels and scale
◆ identify graph points clearly
• measure and record experimental data and use data in calculations
◆ choose appropriate measurement scales and use units in recording
◆ show mathematical work, stating formula and steps for solution
◆ estimate answers
◆ use appropriate equations and significant digits
◆ show uncertainty in measurement by the use of significant figures
◆ identify relationships within variables from data tables
◆ calculate percent error
• recognize and convert various scales of measurement
◆ temperature
§ Celsius (°C)
§ Kelvin (K)
◆ length
§ kilometers (km)
§ meters (m)
§ centimeters (cm)
§ millimeters (mm)
◆ mass
§ grams (g)
§ kilograms (kg)
◆ pressure
§ kilopascal (kPa)
§ atmosphere (atm)
• use knowledge of geometric arrangements to predict particle properties or
behavior

311E0937655D4025B52F44FCAC7BA707.description: Abstraction and symbolic representation are used to communicate mathematically.

BE0495D1550B480E8A781971FE169A72.description:
Simple machines include a lever, a pulley, a wheel and axle, and an inclined plane.
A complex machine uses a combination of interacting simple machines, e.g., a bicycle.

E95053188D944932B96BAFCC6D7814DB.description:
Machines can change the direction or amount of force, or the distance or speed of
force required to do work.

8D9A9E9740FD4872AE3606F7FAC11AE8.description:
A machine can be made more efficient by reducing friction. Some common ways of
reducing friction include lubricating or waxing surfaces.

B514D3589A894118981BBE1537394352.description: Friction is a force that opposes motion.

74FC28F403014B04A4A806D2D66BCFE3.description: Machines transfer mechanical energy from one object to another.

7371DFB2597141D880CD23E370898866.description: Electric currents and magnets can exert a force on each other.

3097F4B4DB654EB69C4C8C0DF130474C.description:
Every object exerts gravitational force on every other object. Gravitational force
depends on how much mass the objects have and on how far apart they are. Gravity is
one of the forces acting on orbiting objects and projectiles.

8117E54667BB405181DAE11A9F983029.description:
Observe, describe, and compare effects of forces (gravity, electric current, and magnetism) on the
motion of objects.

3AC1528ABF704D0D971B84B649665388.description: For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction

E82A0375B07D491BA4A54F9DEA5C7C39.description:
Force is directly related to an object’s mass and acceleration. The greater the force,
the greater the change in motion.

5BB9A29D776D4B429E3E98294EB28D81.description:
An object’s motion is the result of the combined effect of all forces acting on the
object. A moving object that is not subjected to a force will continue to move at a constant
speed in a straight line. An object at rest will remain at rest.

8EA31768D31342478E2DFFC6ADB42C4F.description: The motion of an object can be described by its position, direction of motion, and speed.

3AEEC63D0F5E48C3898ACE4740176564.description:
The motion of an object is always judged with respect to some other object or
point. The idea of absolute motion or rest is misleading.

B8D5195B633E4403AABF884A6B2B4D37.description: Describe different patterns of motion of objects.

8F69BAB535194E148962833F296EE021.description: Energy and matter interact through forces that result in changes in motion

F3225689495D4BC6A866A24787CF5A4A.description:
Energy can change from one form to another, although in the process some energy
is always converted to heat. Some systems transform energy with less loss of heat than
others.

76543F7CD56149D482202CBB02787FAF.description:
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, but only changed from one form into
another.

2389106C871A4F01BB1EAD47AAD9B21A.description: Describe situations that support the principle of conservation of energy

29786D360AE84E3BA20F5D4597264B4C.description:
Without direct contact, a magnet attracts certain materials and either attracts or
repels other magnets. The attractive force of a magnet is greatest at its poles.

A1053C4E9AFE4E1996108AE4E5A253F6.description:
Without touching them, material that has been electrically charged attracts
uncharged material, and may either attract or repel other charged material.

A8EB3475C554469DBC19F20CEE7D4EE7.description: Electrical circuits provide a means of transferring electrical energy.

1417B75C3AFB4F088EB7941535D100C0.description:
Electrical energy can be produced from a variety of energy sources and can be
transformed into almost any other form of energy.

663275362A29447FA89E53EF20AAA8AA.description:
Vibrations in materials set up wave-like disturbances that spread away from the
source. Sound waves are an example. Vibrational waves move at different speeds in
different materials. Sound cannot travel in a vacuum.

63B909E5FCC44817AFF3932425EC9FEF.description:
Light passes through some materials, sometimes refracting in the process.
Materials absorb and reflect light, and may transmit light. To see an object, light from
that object, emitted by or reflected from it, must enter the eye.

049A6A6C3BBE4191948D8152838890E1.description:
Different forms of electromagnetic energy have different wavelengths. Some examples
of electromagnetic energy are microwaves, infrared light, visible light, ultraviolet
light, X-rays, and gamma rays.

48C4B74C682E422DA1F77793F62095F3.description: Observe and describe the properties of sound, light, magnetism, and electricity

A9FDE7CF974942B386AE0EE7F9E9664D.description:
In chemical reactions, energy is transferred into or out of a system. Light, electricity,
or mechanical motion may be involved in such transfers in addition to heat.

E01B1A3AE5BB432AA6F0A6F1137EF844.description: Observe and describe energy changes as related to chemical reactions

DC284F83D0D848229C04B0FA0A043EE1.description: Temperature affects the solubility of some substances in water.

0C7011F0C2254FEF87DB7D14EB297B3D.description:
Most substances expand when heated and contract when cooled. Water is an
exception, expanding when changing to ice.

ED5AD2351D1D4CCBB074F6951CB890EB.description:
During a phase change, heat energy is absorbed or released. Energy is absorbed
when a solid changes to a liquid and when a liquid changes to a gas. Energy is released
when a gas changes to a liquid and when a liquid changes to a solid.

7AE0808479EB4E298123B83C7E8A9972.description:
Heat can be transferred through matter by the collisions of atoms and/or molecules
(conduction) or through space (radiation). In a liquid or gas, currents will facilitate
the transfer of heat (convection).

312EEF9C23EA47F6A9D2EE9924E1FC7B.description:
Heat moves in predictable ways, flowing from warmer objects to cooler ones, until
both reach the same temperature.

A3B5C03BBD4D4369BB983AD4CD1A042A.description: Observe and describe heating and cooling events.

67249352854948BA960C876F7F7E6909.description:
Energy can be considered to be either kinetic energy, which is the energy of
motion, or potential energy, which depends on relative position.

CBE5A0A545DC41FBADA91E55767E340C.description:
Different forms of energy include heat, light, electrical, mechanical, sound, nuclear,
and chemical. Energy is transformed in many ways.

A857FAA1AE864826904E2084499F5590.description:
Most activities in everyday life involve one form of energy being transformed into
another. For example, the chemical energy in gasoline is transformed into mechanical
energy in an automobile engine. Energy, in the form of heat, is almost always one of the
products of energy transformations.

0E6F69A473C848989025EB5063F30B31.description:
Fossil fuels contain stored solar energy and are considered nonrenewable resources.
They are a major source of energy in the United States. Solar energy, wind, moving water,
and biomass are some examples of renewable energy resources.

9E655A446CA84F2A9E0D20A6D0D4562D.description:
The Sun is a major source of energy for Earth. Other sources of energy include
nuclear and geothermal energy.

D3D40EDC4F814E71B5F14E72EE21A790.description: Describe the sources and identify the transformations of energy observed in everyday life.

C085F6F6C94A4863A4076138B4A610DB.description: Energy exists in many forms, and when these forms change energy is conserved.

27E0505ACE0748C3B091887FD7DF3232.description:
The periodic table is one useful model for classifying elements. The periodic table
can be used to predict properties of elements (metals, nonmetals, noble gases).

42FE04D268C5446E95073F65F9265FD9.description:
There are more than 100 elements. Elements combine in a multitude of ways to
produce compounds that account for all living and nonliving substances. Few elements
are found in their pure form

12574F7C112E471997A6D5386B2999B0.description: The atoms of any one element are different from the atoms of other elements.

16FFC58B42394E1BB72B58019C1846AB.description: Interactions among atoms and/or molecules result in chemical reactions.

D980336BC0014F2EAF00709D849EDD52.description:
Atoms may join together in well-defined molecules or may be arranged in regular
geometric patterns.

945B8B0FF02548B299C3364FA72A40FE.description:
Atoms and molecules are perpetually in motion. The greater the temperature, the
greater the motion.

6E60C7DE30BE45249538D04EE63B82C7.description:
All matter is made up of atoms. Atoms are far too small to see with a light
microscope.

4D6E524C3FBB4D438F7B5540C75201F5.description: Develop mental models to explain common chemical reactions and changes in states of matter

F398122CD98246E2881173D358E0C48B.description:
The Law of Conservation of Mass states that during an ordinary chemical reaction
matter cannot be created or destroyed. In chemical reactions, the total mass of the
reactants equals the total mass of the products.

C2448FBF37824A72987FFFF08C04F166.description:
Substances are often placed in categories if they react in similar ways. Examples
include metals, nonmetals, and noble gases.

1510629BF98A49B8B3199DB4505417BC.description:
During a chemical change, substances react in characteristic ways to form new
substances with different physical and chemical properties. Examples of chemical
changes include burning of wood, cooking of an egg, rusting of iron, and souring of
milk.

F1B66E06CBE546F6B5D7182A9DB008EA.description:
Mixtures are physical combinations of materials and can be separated by physical
means.

6A594D8DEBAC4FCD934E91FD1666F5D2.description:
During a physical change a substance keeps its chemical composition and properties.
Examples of physical changes include freezing, melting, condensation, boiling,
evaporation, tearing, and crushing.

5E164D6C9C0C42B99AF827FB469EDCC7.description: Distinguish between chemical and physical changes.

2381A278E5044A37861ADCBCF95DE55D.description: Buoyancy is determined by comparative densities.

E294D1E6C09B4878BC35F039F82149A6.description:
Density can be described as the amount of matter that is in a given amount of
space. If two objects have equal volume, but one has more mass, the one with more
mass is denser.

FB72A25215C94EEEB98AFF9D0F4D2ADF.description:
Characteristic properties can be used to identify different materials, and separate a
mixture of substances into its components. For example, iron can be removed from a
mixture by means of a magnet. An insoluble substance can be separated from a soluble
substance by such processes as filtration, settling, and evaporation.

E137C16474CB471F99D2FAFA05AF323C.description: A solid has definite shape and volume. Particles resist a change in position

2A20FBF18EFE459CA25A58DFCAC1C932.description: A liquid has definite volume, but takes the shape of a container

BBC51E9C2181464A93F6A76DA2E63EDC.description:
Gases have neither a determined shape nor a definite volume. Gases assume the
shape and volume of a closed container.

022542B0D6C348E4A6C72DC58EB12C46.description:
The motion of particles helps to explain the phases (states) of matter as well as
changes from one phase to another. The phase in which matter exists depends on the
attractive forces among its particles.

9D9A422F63C0416A92EFEE7AA8E97F03.description:
Solubility can be affected by the nature of the solute and solvent, temperature, and
pressure. The rate of solution can be affected by the size of

FFE3FAE9BA7147F6A7C50016E65BBDB7.description:
Substances have characteristic properties. Some of these properties include color,
odor, phase at room temperature, density, solubility, heat and electrical conductivity,
hardness, and boiling and freezing points.

FC5370BE725B4A88A2D17069871AB913.description: Observe and describe properties of materials, such as density, conductivity, and solubility

8CF5DF38B5ED48A080D9B56ED7D5FD3B.description: Matter is made up of particles whose properties determine the observable characteristics of matter and its reactivity

19135E3889F7491EB6A1207288592FD2.description:
Substances enter the atmosphere naturally and from human activity. Some of these
substances include dust from volcanic eruptions and greenhouse gases such as carbon
dioxide, methane, and water vapor. These substances can affect weather, climate, and
living things.

F3942045C5394EB793D548F821846691.description:
Hazardous weather conditions include thunderstorms, tornadoes, hurricanes, ice
storms, and blizzards. Humans can prepare for and respond to these conditions if given
sufficient warning.

4246D7629965476CA3E3F374EA2C4ED0.description:
High-pressure systems generally bring fair weather. Low-pressure systems usually
bring cloudy, unstable conditions. The general movement of highs and lows is from
west to east across the United States.

5567E2E1B35747E8B5E2667BB5FDE729.description:
Fronts are boundaries between air masses. Precipitation is likely to occur at these
boundaries

A8C0473E7D9A4742B2198493681B1B8D.description: The movement of air masses is determined by prevailing winds and upper air currents

FB504CD306BA42C2A4DABD27B321C2F6.description: Most local weather condition changes are caused by movement of air masses.

9E28AFA2B8E340DEA1FD01FA3DFD9BEF.description:
Air masses form when air remains nearly stationary over a large section of Earth’s
surface and takes on the conditions of temperature and humidity from that location.
Weather conditions at a location are determined primarily by temperature, humidity,
and pressure of air masses over that location.

53EF3EEBF3294D19AC6B2EF93601ACAC.description: The uneven heating of Earth’s surface is the cause of weather.

D01E862200F64DB8A1F7957F8D91DDC2.description:
Climate is the characteristic weather that prevails from season to season and year
to year.

11D75226042E47F9B6982C61DB369B0D.description:
Weather describes the conditions of the atmosphere at a given location for a short
period of time.

EE86F3F55C4E4222992F063F35DC24C2.description:
The rock cycle model shows how types of rock or rock material may be transformed
from one type of rock to another.

4F2B2017B83F47D7A6BAFE89472C59FA.description:
Rocks are classified according to their method of formation. The three classes of
rocks are sedimentary, metamorphic, and igneous. Most rocks show characteristics that
give clues to their formation conditions.

C55E5F13B5384E71B34738D468382E9F.description:
Plates may collide, move apart, or slide past one another. Most volcanic activity
and mountain building occur at the boundaries of these plates, often resulting in earthquakes.

FB08BB45AD4B4158865FDDC926846943.description:
The Theory of Plate Tectonics explains how the “solid” lithosphere consists of a
series of plates that “float” on the partially molten section of the mantle. Convection
cells within the mantle may be the driving force for the movement of the plates.

8425DE1301284F59930D4966DC57F401.description:
Continents fitting together like puzzle parts and fossil correlations provided initial
evidence that continents were once together.

F47A6C40DD22463681E26DF31356F475.description: Folded, tilted, faulted, and displaced rock layers suggest past crustal movement.

22E41C1D3F3B4E2C883D26D134DEB44E.description:
Analysis of earthquake wave data (vibrational disturbances) leads to the conclusion
that there are layers within Earth. These layers—the crust, mantle, outer core, and
inner core—have distinct properties.

7502F5206C434C46AF68F937CF854C36.description:
The interior of Earth is hot. Heat flow and movement of material within Earth
cause sections of Earth’s crust to move. This may result in earthquakes, volcanic
eruption, and the creation of mountains and ocean basins.

730A4AE258044282BD4D5D47384FF83B.description: Describe volcano and earthquake patterns, the rock cycle, and weather and climate changes

F58A5A6562E8414894BE5052CAED2F52.description:
Water circulates through the atmosphere, lithosphere, and hydrosphere in what is
known as the water cycle.

84CFF22D26BB420AA59740B33F6C4988.description:
Erosion is the transport of sediment. Gravity is the driving force behind erosion.
Gravity can act directly or through agents such as moving water, wind, and glaciers.

5E541D790C8F4A08839B3E866CC9E7A4.description:
The process of weathering breaks down rocks to form sediment. Soil consists of
sediment, organic material, water, and air.

2D11EB58DDB74E8095C35A9094550EC6.description:
The dynamic processes that wear away Earth’s surface include weathering and
erosion.

2DA25839D8564AE5947A7238318315AC.description:
Fossils are usually found in sedimentary rocks. Fossils can be used to study past
climates and environments.

59B2AAE607954DD1BA742BA81BBA3F3E.description:
Rocks are composed of minerals. Only a few rock-forming minerals make up most
of the rocks of Earth. Minerals are identified on the basis of physical properties such as
streak, hardness, and reaction to acid.

4F125C55E828410FBC51AAD4EF4258E1.description:
The majority of the lithosphere is covered by a relatively thin layer of water called
the hydrosphere

FFBB9162049A4A22B0D56A7711FCE954.description:
The rock at Earth’s surface forms a nearly continuous shell around Earth called the
lithosphere.

96087EE006354FF18E2434ECE7E1A9F8.description: As altitude increases, air pressure decreases.

CC635890F4E440519F6036C81E78B1E1.description:
Nearly all the atmosphere is confined to a thin shell surrounding Earth. The atmosphere
is a mixture of gases, including nitrogen and oxygen with small amounts of water
vapor, carbon dioxide, and other trace gases. The atmosphere is stratified into layers,
each having distinct properties. Nearly all weather occurs in the lowest layer of the
atmosphere.

191A3A77DD2042599ED909EE171A70D6.description:
Explain how the atmosphere (air), hydrosphere (water), and lithosphere (land) interact, evolve,
and change.

C7B3D14913C54015B4EA8F837FBE53A7.description:
Many of the phenomena that we observe on Earth involve interactions among components of air, water, and
land.

3253B2E3E3B34EAE89A728AF2AF84763.description: The shape of Earth, the other planets, and stars is nearly spherical.

CE44D58678194B4488193266A6D24AA8.description:
The tilt of Earth’s axis of rotation and the revolution of Earth around the Sun cause
seasons on Earth. The length of daylight varies depending on latitude and season.

86E4E189E6944A04BFF39BA0D588CC65.description:
The apparent motions of the Sun, Moon, planets, and stars across the sky can be
explained by Earth’s rotation and revolution. Earth’s rotation causes the length of one
day to be approximately 24 hours. This rotation also causes the Sun and Moon to appear
to rise along the eastern horizon and to set along the western horizon. Earth’s revolution
around the Sun defines the length of the year as 365 1/4 days.

69442ADAA42B40419B4CE5C771CE6F94.description:
Moons are seen by reflected light. Our Moon orbits Earth, while Earth orbits the
Sun. The Moon’s phases as observed from Earth are the result of seeing different portions
of the lighted area of the Moon’s surface. The phases repeat in a cyclic pattern in
about one month

E752199DEF634E928B9B7C61A24EB4F3.description:
The latitude/longitude coordinate system and our system of time are based on
celestial observations.

73C542F16B1C42FA85471BA2551B664E.description:
Most objects in the solar system have a regular and predictable motion. These
motions explain such phenomena as a day, a year, phases of the Moon, eclipses, tides,
meteor showers, and comets.

D5CF7522657945E7AA0F80493551B6D4.description:
Gravity is the force that keeps planets in orbit around the Sun and the Moon in
orbit around the Earth.

E707FD80AABA44C5AF3454B393406A3C.description:
The Sun and the planets that revolve around it are the major bodies in the solar system.
Other members include comets, moons, and asteroids. Earth’s orbit is nearly circular.

6144446533DE4E28BDF900F69C2123BF.description:
Other stars are like the Sun but are so far away that they look like points of light.
Distances between stars are vast compared to distances within our solar system.

F37A02EF1A764A6485566D33AC5A9502.description:
Earth’s Sun is an average-sized star. The Sun is more than a million times greater
in volume than Earth.

97C3743915434D9BB2C104A919D290E2.description: Explain daily, monthly, and seasonal changes on Earth.

91E5C07E68F64104A712ED8CFFEC205D.description: The Earth and celestial phenomena can be described by principles of relative motion and perspective.

397A21CE0F344AB8990F21109F5E1227.description:
Students will understand and apply scientific concepts, principles, and theories pertaining to the physical
setting and living environment and recognize the historical development of ideas in science.

document.title: Mathematics Core Curriculum

D171C280DFE601319F5F68A86D17958E.description: Construct a question that can be answered by using information from a graph

D1721730DFE601319F6068A86D17958E.description: Discuss conclusions and make predictions in terms of the words likely and unlikely

D1711F30DFE601319F5D68A86D17958E.description: Students will make predictions that are based upon data analysis.

D16F8DA0DFE601319F5868A86D17958E.description: Answer simple questions related to data displayed in pictographs (e.g., category with most, how many more in a category compared to another, how many all together in two categories)

D16FD6A0DFE601319F5968A86D17958E.description: Interpret data in terms of the words: most, least, greater than, less than, or equal to

D16E4C40DFE601319F5468A86D17958E.description: Use Venn diagrams to sort and describe data

D16E93A0DFE601319F5568A86D17958E.description: Display data in bar graphs using concrete objects with intervals of one

D16EF1D0DFE601319F5668A86D17958E.description: Display data in simple pictographs for quantities up to 20 with units of one

D1706930DFE601319F5B68A86D17958E.description: Collect and record data related to a question

D170C8D0DFE601319F5C68A86D17958E.description: Pose questions about themselves and their surroundings

D16DBCC0DFE601319F5268A86D17958E.description: Students will collect, organize, display, and analyze data.

D16D18B0DFE601319F5068A86D17958E.description: Select and use non-standard units to estimate measurements

D16C6050DFE601319F4E68A86D17958E.description: Students will develop strategies for estimating measurements.

D16A23E0DFE601319F4768A86D17958E.description: Classify months and connect to seasons and other events

D16A6F70DFE601319F4868A86D17958E.description: Know the days of the week and months of the year in sequence

D16ABB40DFE601319F4968A86D17958E.description: Tell time to the hour, using both digital and analog clocks

D16B30C0DFE601319F4A68A86D17958E.description: Recognize specific times (morning, noon, afternoon, evening)

D16B8390DFE601319F4B68A86D17958E.description: Use different combinations of coins to make money amounts up to 25 cents

D16C1840DFE601319F4D68A86D17958E.description: Know vocabulary and recognize coins (penny, nickel, dime, quarter)

D1698B10DFE601319F4568A86D17958E.description: Students will use units to give meaning to measurements.

D1689BB0DFE601319F4268A86D17958E.description: Informally explore the standard unit of measure, inch

D168E600DFE601319F4368A86D17958E.description: Use non-standard units (including finger lengths, paper clips, students' feet and paces) to measure both vertical and horizontal lengths

D1693CA0DFE601319F4468A86D17958E.description: Recognize length as an attribute that can be measured

D167FA40DFE601319F4068A86D17958E.description: Students will determine what can be measured and how, using appropriate methods and formulas.

D1674680DFE601319F3E68A86D17958E.description: Recognize geometric shapes and structures in the environment

D1669F30DFE601319F3C68A86D17958E.description: Students will apply coordinate geometry to analyze problem solving situations.

D16656E0DFE601319F3B68A86D17958E.description: Experiment with slides, flips, and turns of two-dimensional shapes

D16553F0DFE601319F3868A86D17958E.description: Students will apply transformations and symmetry to analyze problem solving situations.

D164A460DFE601319F3668A86D17958E.description: Recognize, name, describe, create, sort, and compare two-dimensional and three-dimensional shapes

D164F210DFE601319F3768A86D17958E.description: Match shapes and parts of shapes to justify congruency

D1640E20DFE601319F3468A86D17958E.description: Students will use visualization and spatial reasoning to analyze characteristics and properties of geometric shapes.

D1636890DFE601319F3268A86D17958E.description: Determine and discuss patterns in arithmetic (what comes next in a repeating pattern, using numbers or objects)

D162C170DFE601319F3068A86D17958E.description: Students will recognize, use, and represent algebraically patterns, relations, and functions.

D1620DD0DFE601319F2E68A86D17958E.description: Estimate the number in a collection to 50 and then compare by counting the actual items in the collection

D1616980DFE601319F2C68A86D17958E.description: Students will compute accurately and make reasonable estimates.

D15F7590DFE601319F2668A86D17958E.description: Understand that different parts can be added to get the same whole

D15FEDA0DFE601319F2768A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate fluency and apply addition and subtraction facts to and including 10

D1604860DFE601319F2868A86D17958E.description: Use a variety of strategies to solve addition and subtraction problems with one- and two-digit numbers without regrouping

D1609360DFE601319F2968A86D17958E.description: Create problem situations that represent a given number sentence

D160DB50DFE601319F2A68A86D17958E.description: Represent addition and subtraction word problems and their solutions as number sentences

D1612330DFE601319F2B68A86D17958E.description: Develop and use strategies to solve addition and subtraction word problems

D15ED4C0DFE601319F2468A86D17958E.description: Students will understand meanings of operations and procedures, and how they relate to one another.

D15772D0DFE601319F0D68A86D17958E.description: Use and understand verbal ordinal terms, first to twentieth

D157C200DFE601319F0E68A86D17958E.description: Use the words higher, lower, greater, and less to compare two numbers

D15819B0DFE601319F0F68A86D17958E.description: Use before, after, or between to order numbers to 100 (with or without the use of a number line)

D15865B0DFE601319F1068A86D17958E.description: Name the number before and the number after a given number, and name the number(s) between two given numbers up to 100 (with and without the use of a number line or a hundreds chart)

D158BCB0DFE601319F1168A86D17958E.description: Understand the commutative property of addition

D1590C20DFE601319F1268A86D17958E.description: Use a variety of strategies to compose and decompose one-digit numbers

D15955A0DFE601319F1368A86D17958E.description:
Develop an initial understanding of the base ten system:
  • 10 ones = 1 ten
  • 10 tens = 1 hundred

D159AE60DFE601319F1468A86D17958E.description: Compare and order whole numbers up to 100

D15A8650DFE601319F1668A86D17958E.description: Read the number words one, two, three…ten

D15B3300DFE601319F1868A86D17958E.description: Arrange objects in size order (increasing and decreasing)

D15B8560DFE601319F1968A86D17958E.description: Identify that spacing of the same number of objects does not affect the quantity (conservation)

D15BD1F0DFE601319F1A68A86D17958E.description: Draw pictures or other informal symbols to represent a spoken number up to 20

D15C6F30DFE601319F1C68A86D17958E.description: Verbally count from a number other than one by 1's

D15DE2F0DFE601319F2168A86D17958E.description: Quickly see and label with a number, collections of 1 to 10

D15E3DE0DFE601319F2268A86D17958E.description: Count out (produce) a collection of a specified size (10 to 100 items), using groups of ten

D15E8C30DFE601319F2368A86D17958E.description: Count the items in a collection and know the last counting word tells how many items are in the collection (1 to 100)

D156C9B0DFE601319F0B68A86D17958E.description: Students will understand numbers, multiple ways of representing numbers, relationships among numbers, and number systems.

D1537460DFE601319F0168A86D17958E.description: Use mathematics to show and understand mathematical phenomena (e.g., draw pictures to show a story problem, show number value using fingers on your hand)

D153CA10DFE601319F0268A86D17958E.description: Use mathematics to show and understand social phenomena (e.g., count and represent sharing cookies between friends)

D15418B0DFE601319F0368A86D17958E.description: Use mathematics to show and understand physical phenomena (e.g., estimate and represent the number of apples in a tree)

D15327D0DFE601319F0068A86D17958E.description: Students will use representations to model and interpret physical, social, and mathematical phenomena.

D1562880DFE601319F0968A86D17958E.description: Connect mathematical representations with problem solving

D155CE40DFE601319F0868A86D17958E.description: Students will select, apply, and translate among mathematical representations to solve problems.

D1550C80DFE601319F0668A86D17958E.description: Share mental images of mathematical ideas and understandings

D1556940DFE601319F0768A86D17958E.description: Use multiple representations including verbal and written language, acting out or modeling a situation, drawings, and/or symbols as representations

D1546D80DFE601319F0468A86D17958E.description: Students will create and use representations to organize, record, and communicate mathematical ideas.

D14F4A30DFE601319EF468A86D17958E.description: Recognize and apply mathematics to objects, pictures, and symbols

D14F9290DFE601319EF568A86D17958E.description: Recognize and apply mathematics to solve problems

D14FDB20DFE601319EF668A86D17958E.description: Recognize the presence of mathematics in their daily lives

D14EFF40DFE601319EF368A86D17958E.description: Students will recognize and apply mathematics in contexts outside of mathematics.

D151EEF0DFE601319EFC68A86D17958E.description: Understand how mathematical models represent quantitative relationships

D1524550DFE601319EFD68A86D17958E.description: Understand meanings of operations and how they relate to one another

D1529180DFE601319EFE68A86D17958E.description: Understand how models of situations involving objects, pictures, and symbols relate to mathematical ideas

D151A340DFE601319EFB68A86D17958E.description: Students will understand how mathematical ideas interconnect and build on one another to produce a coherent whole.

document.title: Learning Standards for Health, Physical Education, and Family and Consumer Sciences

E58ECC20DFE60131C33F68A86D17958E.description: develop job skills (e.g., communication, effective time management, problem solving, and leadership).

E58D5D80DFE60131C33B68A86D17958E.description: understand the concept of entrepreneurship as it exists in today's economy

E58E2190DFE60131C33D68A86D17958E.description: analyze abilities and interests in relation to careers, set long-term career goals, and develop a plan for progressing toward their goals

E58DAFB0DFE60131C33C68A86D17958E.description: understand the basics of an individual/family budget and plan to obtain, use, and protect money and assets

E58E82D0DFE60131C33E68A86D17958E.description: analyze a wide range of factors related to managing personal resources to balance obligations to work, family, and self

E58D1D20DFE60131C33A68A86D17958E.description: Students will understand and be able to manage personal resources of talent, time, energy, and money and make effective decisions in order to balance their obligations to work, family, and self. They will nurture and support positive relationships in their homes, workplaces, and communities. They will develop and use their abilities to contribute to society through pursuit of a career and commitment to long-range planning for their personal, professional, and academic futures. They will know and access community resources.

E58AE5F0DFE60131C33268A86D17958E.description: identify a variety of career opportunities associated with sports and fitness and understand the qualifications, educational requirements, and job responsibilities of those careers.

E58B39B0DFE60131C33368A86D17958E.description: recognize the benefits of engaging in appropriate physical activities with others, including both older and younger members of the community

E58A7A50DFE60131C33168A86D17958E.description: recognize their role as concerned and discriminating consumers of physical activities programs and understand the importance of physical activity as a resource for everyone regardless of age or ability

E58A2F90DFE60131C33068A86D17958E.description: Students will be aware of and able to access opportunities available to them within their community to engage in physical activity. They will be informed consumers and be able to evaluate facilities and programs. Students will also be aware of some career options in the field of physical fitness and sports.

E58CDCF0DFE60131C33968A86D17958E.description: demonstrate advocacy skills in promoting individual, family and community health.

E58BFAF0DFE60131C33668A86D17958E.description: use technology and the media to promote positive health messages

E58C46E0DFE60131C33768A86D17958E.description: demonstrate the ability to access community health services for self and others

E58BBC70DFE60131C33568A86D17958E.description: analyze how cultural beliefs influence health behaviors and the use of health products and services

E58C9690DFE60131C33868A86D17958E.description: demonstrate how to evaluate health information, products and services for validity and reliability

E58B7C20DFE60131C33468A86D17958E.description: Students will understand the influence of culture, media, and technology in making decisions about personal and community health issues. They will know about and use valid health information, products, and services. Students will advocate for healthy families and communities.

E589EF30DFE60131C32F68A86D17958E.description: Students will understand and be able to manage their personal and community resources.

E588E860DFE60131C32B68A86D17958E.description: apply basic rules of health and safety to a variety of home and work place situations.

E5893060DFE60131C32C68A86D17958E.description: understand essential requirements for selecting and maintaining a home

E5897210DFE60131C32D68A86D17958E.description: apply housing principles (e.g., design and safety) to meet the needs of family members of all ages and abilities

E589B0E0DFE60131C32E68A86D17958E.description: understand the stages of child development and apply this knowledge to activities designed to enrich the physical, social, mental, and emotional development of a young child

E588A060DFE60131C32A68A86D17958E.description: Students will know the basic principles of home and community safety. They can demonstrate the skills necessary to maintain their homes and workplaces in a safe and comfortable condition. They can provide a safe and nurturing environment for themselves and others.

E5867420DFE60131C32268A86D17958E.description: understand the physical, social, and emotional benefits of physical activity and can demonstrate leadership and problem solving through participation in organized games or activities.

E5862850DFE60131C32168A86D17958E.description: create a positive climate for group activities by assuming a variety of roles

document.title: New York State P-12 Common Core Learning Standards for Mathematics

328FA80DFA554B9087ABD39938562C40.description: Create and build shapes from components (e.g., sticks and clay balls).

1A366B48F75944068E2A899ED2F94AAB.description: Correctly name shapes regardless of size.

E807A580EF684434BE361FA148FC31B6.description: Identify and describe shapes (squares, circles, triangles, rectangles).

D1F9F4E608D44ED6B6EE4E5340F5D8BB.description: Duplicate and extend (eg., What comes next?) simple patterns using concrete objects.

26C1BC7B3EDF4F9188E1EE9683BC6E2C.description: Understand addition as adding to, and understand subtraction as taking from.

7A3BF3275DF94F60B0D097E813128385.description: Count to answer "how many?" questions about as many as 10 things arranged in a line, a rectangular array, or a circle, or as many as 5 things in a scattered configuration; given a number from 1–10, count out that many objects.

B9D29E82754B43B6830487B0698B2E40.description: Understand that each successive number name refers to a quantity that is one larger.

3FA1014E578B479B97619072433EFDF9.description: Understand that the last number name said tells the number of objects counted. The number of objects is the same regardless of their arrangement or the order in which they were counted.

968ED94B1D0248488F618210BD375134.description: When counting objects, say the number names in the standard order, pairing each object with one and only one number name and each number name with one and only one object.

BB968FF54DB64BE89B718076F3845916.description: Understand the relationship between numbers and quantities to 10; connect counting to cardinality.

2AE17F2EB28B45328D024575B7659101.description: Count to tell the number of objects.

5965B44CD246463EB75FBC495B85FF93.description: Represent a number of objects with a written numeral 0–5 (with 0 representing a count of no objects).

111FF6CAF6B347AAAC94077E032A7375.description: Know number names and the count sequence.

F2D9B5BCB7C64ACEA88637B1583516BD.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

F5AA67F01EFC4DF583B14BB43533BC43.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

E8435C2AF07247D7A2F6D5DBA2713056.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

820E3650651E4D3086CEE8B633115A31.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

document.title: Learning Standards for English Language Arts

DDF60180DFE60131B4CA68A86D17958E.description: read and discuss published letters, diaries, and journals to learn the conventions of social writing

DDF69BE0DFE60131B4CC68A86D17958E.description: listen attentively and recognize when it is appropriate for them to speak

DDF91640DFE60131B4D568A86D17958E.description: in writing group, critique each other's writing with reference to specific criteria and revise their writing based on the group's suggestions

DDF887E0DFE60131B4D368A86D17958E.description: use effective vocabulary and follow the rules of grammar, usage, spelling, and punctuation in persuasive writing

DDF83A70DFE60131B4D268A86D17958E.description: monitor and adjust their own oral and written presentations to meet criteria for competent performance (e.g., in writing, the criteria might include development of position, organization, appropriate vocabulary, mechanics, and neatness. In speaking, the criteria might include good content, effective delivery, diction, posture, poise, and eye contact.)

DDF7DA00DFE60131B4D168A86D17958E.description: present arguments for certain views or actions with reference to specific criteria that support the argument (e.g., an argument to purchase a particular piece of playground equipment might be based on the criteria of safety, appeal to children, durability, and low cost.)

DDF8D540DFE60131B4D468A86D17958E.description: express opinions (in such forms as oral and written reviews, letters to the editor, essays, or persuasive speeches) about events, books, issues, and experiences, supporting their opinions with some evidence

DDF79BE0DFE60131B4D068A86D17958E.description: Speaking and writing for critical analysis and evaluation requires presenting opinions and judgments on experiences, ideas, information, and issues clearly, logically, and persuasively with reference to specific criteria on which the opinion or judgment is based.

DDF9D9C0DFE60131B4D868A86D17958E.description: evaluate their own strategies for reading and listening critically (such as recognizing bias or false claims, and understanding the difference between fact and opinion) and adjust those strategies to understand the experience more fully

DDFA5E30DFE60131B4DA68A86D17958E.description: recognize that the criteria that one uses to analyze and evaluate anything depend on one's point of view and purpose for the analysis

DDF99270DFE60131B4D768A86D17958E.description: make decisions about the quality and dependability of texts and experiences based on some criteria, such as the attractiveness of the illustrations and appeal of the characters in a picture book, or the logic and believability of the claims made in an advertisement

DDFA1DD0DFE60131B4D968A86D17958E.description: read and form opinions about a variety of literary and informational texts and presentations, as well as persuasive texts such as advertisements, commercials, and letters to the editor

DDF95400DFE60131B4D668A86D17958E.description: Listening and reading to analyze and evaluate experiences, ideas, information, and issues requires using evaluative criteria from a variety of perspectives and recognizing the difference in evaluations based on different sets of criteria.

DDF75E90DFE60131B4CF68A86D17958E.description: Language for Critical Analysis and Evaluation

DDF204E0DFE60131B4BB68A86D17958E.description: perform dramatic readings or recitations of stories, poems, or plays

DDF29580DFE60131B4BD68A86D17958E.description: observe the conventions of grammar and usage, spelling, and punctuation

DDF16C60DFE60131B4B968A86D17958E.description: create their own stories, poems, and songs using the elements of the literature they have read and appropriate vocabulary

DDF24990DFE60131B4BC68A86D17958E.description: explain the meaning of literary works with some attention to meanings beyond the literal level

DDF1B520DFE60131B4BA68A86D17958E.description: present personal responses to literature that make reference to plot, characters, ideas, vocabulary, and text structure

DDF123F0DFE60131B4B868A86D17958E.description: Speaking and writing for literary response involves presenting interpretations, analyses, and reactions to the content and language of a text. DDF370D0DFE60131B4C068A86D17958E.description: choose books to read individually or with others

DDF47940DFE60131B4C468A86D17958E.description: read aloud accurately and fluently, using phonics and context clues to determine pronunciation and meaning

DDF3B320DFE60131B4C168A86D17958E.description: use inference and deduction to understand the text

DDF42F40DFE60131B4C368A86D17958E.description: recognize some features that distinguish the genres and use those features to aid comprehension

DDF2DAC0DFE60131B4BE68A86D17958E.description: Listening and reading for literary response involves comprehending, interpreting, and critiquing imaginative texts in every medium, drawing on personal experiences and knowledge to understand the text, and recognizing the social, historical and cultural features of the text.

DDF0D6B0DFE60131B4B768A86D17958E.description: Language for Literary Response and Expression

DDFC2E20DFE60131B4E068A86D17958E.description:

DDFE6C30DFE60131B4E868A86D17958E.description: accurately paraphrase what they have heard or read

DDFEEA00DFE60131B4EA68A86D17958E.description: support inferences about information and ideas with reference to text features, such as vocabulary and organizational patterns

DDFF34D0DFE60131B4EB68A86D17958E.description: make appropriate and effective use of strategies to construct meaning from print, such as prior knowledge about a subject, structural and context clues, and an understanding of letter-sound relationships to decode difficult words

DDFEAB80DFE60131B4E968A86D17958E.description:
ask specific questions to clarfy and extend meaning

DDFE29A0DFE60131B4E768A86D17958E.description:
select and use strategies they have been taught for note-taking, organizing, and categorizing information
  • use concept maps, semantic webs, or outlines to organize information they have collected

DDFDE730DFE60131B4E668A86D17958E.description: select information appropriate to the purpose of their investigation and relate ideas from one text to another

DDFF7670DFE60131B4EC68A86D17958E.description: gather and interpret information from children's reference books, magazines, textbooks, electronic bulletin boards, audio and media presentations, oral interviews, and from such forms as charts, graphs, maps, and diagrams

DDFD44C0DFE60131B4E468A86D17958E.description: Listening and reading to acquire information and understanding involves collecting data, facts, and ideas; discovering relationships, concepts, and generalizations; and using knowledge from oral, written, and electronic sources.

document.title: Learning Standards for Social Studies

D8F12B60DFE60131AB8868A86D17958E.description: participate in negotiation and compromise to resolve classroom, school, and community disagreements and problems

D8F0E150DFE60131AB8768A86D17958E.description: explain the role that civility plays in promoting effective citizenship in preserving democracy

D8F092B0DFE60131AB8668A86D17958E.description: respect the rights of others in discussions and classroom debates regardless of whether or not one agrees with their viewpoint

D8F04810DFE60131AB8568A86D17958E.description: The study of civics and citizenship requires the ability to probe ideas and assumptions, ask and answer analytical questions, take a skeptical attitude toward questionable arguments, evaluate evidence, formulate rational conclusions, and develop and refine participatory skills.

D8EFA000DFE60131AB8368A86D17958E.description: discuss the role of an informed citizen in today's changing world

D8EF4FB0DFE60131AB8268A86D17958E.description: understand that the American legal and political systems guarantee and protect the rights of citizens and assume that citizens will hold and exercise certain civic values and fulfill certain civic responsibilities

D8EF0490DFE60131AB8168A86D17958E.description: explain what citizenship means in a democratic society, how citizenship is defined in the Constitution and other laws of the land, and how the definition of citizenship has changed in the United States and New York State over time

D8EEB760DFE60131AB8068A86D17958E.description: Central to civics and citizenship is an understanding of the roles of the citizen within American constitutional democracy and the scope of a citizen's rights and responsibilities.

D8EE7240DFE60131AB7F68A86D17958E.description: understand how the United States and New York State Constitutions support majority rule but also protect the rights of the minority

D8EE1DB0DFE60131AB7E68A86D17958E.description: value the principles, ideals, and core values of the American democratic system based upon the premises of human dignity, liberty, justice, and equality

D8EDD590DFE60131AB7D68A86D17958E.description: define federalism and describe the powers granted the the national and state governments by the United States Constitution

D8ED91D0DFE60131AB7C68A86D17958E.description: compare and contrast the development and evolution of the constitutions of the United States and New York State

D8ED4830DFE60131AB7B68A86D17958E.description: understand that the New York State Constitution, along with a number of other documents, served as a model for the development of the United States Constitution

D8ECFAA0DFE60131AB7A68A86D17958E.description: understand how civic values reflected in United States and New York State Constitutions have been implemented through laws and practices

D8ECB760DFE60131AB7968A86D17958E.description: The state and federal governments established by the Constitutions of the United States and the State of New York embody basic civic values (such as justice, honesty, self-discipline, due process, equality, majority rule with respect for minority rights, and respect for self, others, and property), principles, and practices and establish a system of shared and limited government. (Adapted from The National Standards for Civics and Government, 1994)

D8EC7660DFE60131AB7868A86D17958E.description: analyze the sources of a nation's values as embodied in its constitution, statutes, and important court cases

D8EC3320DFE60131AB7768A86D17958E.description: explore the rights of citizens in other parts of the hemisphere and determine how they are similar to and different from the rights of American citizens

D8EBEE40DFE60131AB7668A86D17958E.description: consider the nature and evolution of constitutional democracies

D8EBA370DFE60131AB7568A86D17958E.description: analyze how the values of a nation affect the guarantee of human rights and make provisions for human needs

D8EB52F0DFE60131AB7468A86D17958E.description: The study of civics, citizenship, and government involves learning about political systems; the purposes of government and civic life; and the differing assumptions held by people across time and place regarding power, authority, governance, and law. (Adapted from The National Standards for Civics and Government, 1994)

D8EAFCF0DFE60131AB7368A86D17958E.description: Students will use a variety of intellectual skills to demonstrate their understanding of the necessity for establishing governments; the governmental system of the United States and other nations; the United States Constitution; the basic civic values of American constitutional democracy; and the roles, rights, and responsibilities of citizenship, including avenues of participation.

D8EA59F0DFE60131AB7168A86D17958E.description: present economic information by using media and other appropriate visuals such as tables, charts, and graphs to communicate ideas and conclusions

D8E92D30DFE60131AB6D68A86D17958E.description: identify and collect economic information from standard reference works, newspapers, periodicals, computer databases, textbooks, and other primary and secondary sources

D8E8E660DFE60131AB6C68A86D17958E.description: Economics requires the development and application of the skills needed to make informed and well-reasoned economic decisions in daily and national life.

D8E89B30DFE60131AB6B68A86D17958E.description: explain how nations throughout the world have joined with one another to promote economic development and growth

D8E83620DFE60131AB6A68A86D17958E.description: describe how traditional, command, market, and mixed economies answer the three fundamental economic questions

D8E7E0A0DFE60131AB6968A86D17958E.description: investigate how people in the United States and throughout the world answer the three fundamental economic questions and solve basic economic problems

D8E79E80DFE60131AB6868A86D17958E.description: understand how people in the United States and throughout the world are both producers and consumers of goods and services

D8E759A0DFE60131AB6768A86D17958E.description: understand how scarcity requires people and nations to make choices which involve costs and future considerations

D8E715D0DFE60131AB6668A86D17958E.description: define basic economic concepts such as scarcity, supply and demand, markets, opportunity costs, resources, productivity, economic growth, and systems

D8E6CFD0DFE60131AB6568A86D17958E.description: explain how societies and nations attempt to satisfy their basic needs and wants by utilizing scarce capital, natural, and human resources

D8E634F0DFE60131AB6368A86D17958E.description: Students will use a variety of intellectual skills to demonstrate their understanding of how the United States and other societies develop economic systems and associated institutions to allocate scarce resources, how major decision-making units function in the United States and other national economies, and how an economy solves the scarcity problem through market and nonmarket mechanisms.

D8E5B570DFE60131AB6168A86D17958E.description: interpret geographic information by synthesizing data and developing conclusions and generalizations about geographic issues and problems

D8E53460DFE60131AB5F68A86D17958E.description: use a number of research skills (e.g., computer databases, periodicals, census reports, maps, standard reference works, interviews, surveys) to locate and gather geographical information about issues and problems (Adapted from National Geography Standards, 1994)

D8E4F080DFE60131AB5E68A86D17958E.description: formulate geographic questions and define geographic issues and problems

D8E4A740DFE60131AB5D68A86D17958E.description: Geography requires the development and application of the skills of asking and answering geographic questions; analyzing theories of geography; and acquiring, organizing, and analyzing geographic information. D8DFDDE0DFE60131AB4D68A86D17958E.description: Study of the major social, political, cultural, and religious developments in world history involves learning about the important roles and contributions of individuals and groups.

D8DF50B0DFE60131AB4B68A86D17958E.description: measure time periods by years, decades, centuries, and millennia

D8DEFE40DFE60131AB4A68A86D17958E.description: develop timelines by placing important events and developments in world history in their correct chronological order

D8DEB7A0DFE60131AB4968A86D17958E.description: Establishing timeframes, exploring different periodizations, examining themes across time and within cultures, and focusing on important turning points in world history help organize the study of world cultures and civilizations.

D8DE6960DFE60131AB4868A86D17958E.description: interpret and analyze documents and artifacts related to significant developments and events in world history
