5C389A82224A441BB3E14ABB47936B8B.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

8D22461A290B495ABA40ECD41212B9BB.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

ED2721299C5F457B8E926C5D46E2F764.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

B8F7C7C730BA41C2A3C94923CCC934FE.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

document.title: New York State K-8 Social Studies Framework

44A52CBF651942E7B0D09716640DB78A.description: Students will examine how technological developments in transportation and communication have influenced trade over time.

79E0069760174328895D4A72598DAA90.description: Students will explore the basic economic concepts of supply and demand and how they influence prices and trade.

469F7E6D1FF348F4A254BBD2FCF90A87.description: Students will examine each selected world community in terms of what products and/or services it imports from other communities.

C1D32C5ED1CF42CAB972B6E31550A184.description: Students will examine each selected world community in terms of what products and/or services it exports to other communities.

AC2729CC3E4B4BB981EA4FB1F51846B8.description: World communities have needs, wants, and limited resources. To meet their needs and wants communities trade with others. Technological developments in transportation and communication have influenced trade.

266454E4DEFC4BB8B5B0D2D1B4AF4E3C.description: Students will investigate who receives the goods that are produced in each selected world community.

CC2E12A178234880830230178E17947E.description: Students will examine how the goods are produced within each selected world community.

04DADE6F281649A290FE0AD2DCCB984B.description: Students will determine what goods are produced and services are provided in each selected world community.

364B5328AF7B4CB48390DBE7100300E9.description: Communities around the world produce goods and provide services.

C6CE994D068A4771BDB2CE7C95A8E534.description: Each community develops an economic system that addresses three questions: what will be produced, how will it be produced, and who will get what is produced?

93E3E39D43AE4658B8940587EC03C59E.description: Students will examine the various ways people earn a living and how this has changed, if at all, over time in each selected world community.

8FDA9EE4358E4909B46D057244DD383E.description: Students will investigate how each selected world community meets its basic needs of food, clothing, and shelter, and compare that to their own community.

22BC1CB9E8794DA2921D993A7AF37106.description: People in communities have various ways of meeting their basic needs and earning a living.

5249B3827B60423F8A1FD9419CE5F4E3.description: Students will explore the concepts of surplus and scarcity in relation to resources for each selected world community.

8705422639D24B4CB9237130A0B909D4.description: Students will investigate available resources for each selected world community and how these resources are used to meet basic needs and wants.

CBB26429F5294779A5F250EFEB4EB6B5.description: World communities use human and natural resources in different ways.

5E8733DCDFF441478A12884A6692CD65.description: Communities meet their needs and wants in a variety of ways, forming the basis for their economy.

734DD904E19C44A5B521B0EC45BAE6C6.description: Students will investigate steps people can take to support social action and change.

BA1D1A0A74A549AD8864D002689D1095.description: When faced with prejudice and discrimination, people can take steps to support social action and change.

EBA9219049024EBAB0BC6E114F4A0B04.description: Students will examine prejudice and discrimination and how they serve as barriers to justice and equality for all people.

0E58F30270544369AD6C856C0CEC35A6.description: Across time and place, communities and cultures have struggled with prejudice and discrimination as barriers to justice and equality for all people.

BBA92A33F58E4DD2BD2554C9B1AD1E40.description: Students will examine the extent to which governments and citizens have protected human rights and treated others fairly for each world community.

789B25E8EEDC4D4A8AF7076C02C4C9A3.description: Across global communities, governments and citizens alike have a responsibility to protect human rights and to treat others fairly.

624C98DDFB3C4C339988F491D5C58FC1.description: The concept of universal human rights suggests that all people should be treated fairly and should have the opportunity to meet their basic needs.

CE81D456C2FC4DD49C0B82DFDD2A8769.description: Students will examine the role of the citizen in each selected world community and how this role is similar to or different from the role a citizen plays in the United States as well as other selected world communities.

B814BCFBC2014C85B23CDC9368036644.description: The definition of citizenship and the role of the citizen vary across different types of political systems, and citizens play a greater role in the political process in some countries than in others.

4BFC87DEC0604470833567D859402FB5.description: Students will examine how the government maintains order, keeps people safe, and makes and enforces rules and laws in each selected world community and compare and contrast it with the process in the United States as well as other selected world communities.

831822CE4C6445E0877B03BE4576EF5A.description: Different governments have different ways of maintaining order and keeping people safe. This includes making rules and laws and enforcing these rules and laws.

764276E53AD94B8F87220AAD488330B6.description: Students will examine different processes of selecting leaders, solving problems, and making decisions in nations and communities and compare and contrast them to the process used in the United States.

A239CEDFC8184C73A271F602FD4956CE.description: The process of selecting leaders, solving problems, and making decisions differs across governments in nations and communities around the world.

61C47F625D0C41019F5D57C365F3FE82.description: Students will examine what type of government is found in each selected world community and compare and contrast it with United States government as well as other selected world communities.

67A94D03671945B7A056BEA48C83C148.description: The United States government is based on democratic principles. The fundamental principles of other governments may be similar to or different from those of the United States government.

7A0480A2FFC8462CB8BB7C669869A270.description: Governments in communities and countries around the world have the authority to make and the power to enforce laws. The role of the citizen within these communities or countries varies across different types of governments.

40203D3FE31E45C2A8E4AE91B035D813.description: Students will examine people, goods, and ideas from each selected world community that have diffused into other communities and their impact on those communities.

3EF216D5C77243C597CA8A9AC594E042.description: Students will examine people, goods, and ideas that have diffused from other communities into each selected world community and the impact of the people, goods, and ideas on these communities.

9CF86E497DC94E6BB23813C79EF95C84.description: Cultural diffusion is the process by which cultures exchange and transmit ideas, beliefs, technologies, and goods over time.

1E1B19A0EA5B4295BF838FBFBC34962D.description: Communities from around the world interact with other people and communities and exchange cultural ideas and practices.

61911BE32842477B898E6F6F9572E4A3.description: Students will learn about the holidays and festivals celebrated in each selected world community and compare them to the holidays and festivals celebrated in their own community.

ECA6F9665C4A470EA2987AACFC15E2D4.description: Students will examine each selected world community in terms of its members, languages spoken, customs and traditions, and religious beliefs and practices.

CF31D6AB4F7B494297819F0E729AD8BE.description: Communities around the world can be diverse in terms of their members, languages spoken, customs and traditions, and religious beliefs and practices. People in world communities celebrate various holidays and festivals.

5F02C456DB4F408A9107B00B2D0BBD56.description: Students will compare and contrast the structure and activities of families and schools in each selected community with their own.

323150159918480381D505FE42B9E4A6.description: The structure and activities of families and schools share similarities and differences across world communities.

D923C986161E4E0EA3CF253D417407E6.description: Communities share cultural similarities and differences across the world.

67184ED8A6AF45C7B5A0E44E95F63B4B.description: Students will explore the arts, music, dance, and literature for each selected world community.

9E65B5007B904E6C89C81312B69401F1.description: Arts, music, dance, and literature develop through a community's history.

99498F62914A46EC833F9583EFA6D456.description: Students will examine symbols of each selected world community.

93AA086E536D4FD4A49AEE4CEDECB771.description: Students will examine legends, folktales, oral histories, biographies, and historical narratives to learn about the important individuals and events of each selected world community.

33BD70C45AF64BDEBDC9450ADE0CD375.description: People in world communities use legends, folktales, oral histories, biographies, and historical narratives to transmit cultural histories from one generation to the next.

A994EFD052E943B3A61E42369703E142.description: Each community or culture has a unique history, including heroic figures, traditions, and holidays.

3BC0673632D2457298671E0A2610AA78.description: Students will explore actions that are being taken to protect the environment in the selected world communities and in their own community.

4401A14B5F1147DC949559713E0FD53C.description: Students will investigate how human activities and the use of technology have altered the environment bringing about unintended consequences for each of the selected world communities and their own community.

6333A7C605ED44768780D292EDDDC583.description: Students will examine how each selected world community has adapted to and/or modified its environment to meet its needs.

EEF057C66F764769A1E1672646017CA7.description: People make adaptations and modifications to the environment. Advancements in science, technology, and industry can bring about modifications to the environment and can have unintended consequences on the environment. People have attempted to take actions to protect the environment.

20AC2FEB17EE478BB4F502ECFD4CEA5C.description: Students will investigate the lifestyle of the people who live in each selected world community and how the lifestyle has been influenced by the geographic factors.

C4B267EEF2B14BD289B22BD02B3CA08C.description: Students will examine the geographic factors of each selected world community including physical features and climate, noting how certain factors are likely to support settlement and larger populations.

827A831B87584DD8A0C4C5BD0405F306.description: Geographic factors influence where people settle and their lifestyle. Some factors are more suitable for settlement while others act as a deterrent.

C2370EAE6A6C46E4975FB999756B427A.description: Geographic factors often influence where people settle and form communities. People adapt to and modify their environment in different ways to meet their needs.

86D15CA19E31491DA433AC9C2FD15F36.description: Students will examine the location of each selected world community relative to the United States and other selected world communities. Students will locate each selected world community in relationship to principal parallels (equator, Tropic of Cancer, Tropic of Capricorn, Arctic Circle, and Antarctic Circle) and meridians (Prime Meridian) using cardinal and intermediate directions.

C89FA8178BA842CAB6BC5C185B219701.description: World communities can be located in relation to each other and to principle parallels and meridians.

A2E7E39E9EC644CEB058B6A35A3CDA78.description: Students will examine where each selected world community is located.

6471E0A0E0DD4785902E5008116B1A16.description: World communities can be located on globes and maps.

D6803A05F7724EA4A091E8AB40D4A8E3.description: The location of world communities can be described using geographic tools and vocabulary.

C7286F71D1044FADA2F6E1602A2D1DB5.description: Students will compare geographic information found in photographs and satellite images with other representations of the same area and identify differences for at least one of the selected world communities

16CC0AB03C8D401FA79FB6194E9B2BC7.description: Students will examine a variety of maps for at least two of the selected world communities looking for structural features of the map such as title, legend or key, compass orientation, author, date, grid, and scale. These should include political, physical, vegetation, and resource maps. A variety of scale should be represented (e.g., continent vs. country, country vs. city).

80112858FD6A4E7D99DF245604DF6453.description: Students will identify the differences between a globe and a map.

1D8DF57216874ADF92B27658A768B4CC.description: Globes, maps, photographs, and satellite images contain geographic information. Maps often have a title, legend or key, compass orientation, author, date, grid, and scale.

9F0A5313EB244530B8A83952D56965CA.description: Students will locate the selected world communities in relation to oceans and continents.

2F578EDA8A10436AB64FDDD13436951A.description: Students will identify the continents and oceans using globes and maps.

05FB8A39A82A4F84A70E83A0B8F063DA.description: Earth is comprised of water and large land masses that can be divided into distinct regions.

E9390A0A88D1499D8EA00574E2B5AB04.description: Geographic regions have unifying characteristics and can be studied using a variety of tools.

comments: In "Communities around the World" students learn about communities around the globe and global citizenship. Students bring with them knowledge about their community. In this course, students make comparisons across time and space, examining different communities and their cultures. Culture includes social organization, customs and traditions, language, arts and literature, religion, forms of government, and economic systems. Students are introduced to the concepts of prejudice, discrimination and human rights, as well as social action.

26ACC30A0F2C4D4096FB2844E60D7434.description: Identify rights and responsibilities within the community and compare them to those in world communities.

DED785B7684444FEA93F807C9FAB014F.description: Identify leaders of world communities and the president of the United States; identify similarities and differences in their roles.

5517BB4761DC47A882043016F636E01E.description: Identify situations in which social actions are required and suggest solutions.

F1FB4DDEFA2F4B6D9225B6CB41291074.description: Show respect in issues involving differences and conflict; participate in negotiating and compromising in the resolution of differences and conflict.

C8DF6FAC74ED49B495625557C2AEFC89.description: Identify opportunities for and the role of the individual in social and political participation in the school, community, or world community.

A4B103D3D03B4687A5EA315DB3F70E3F.description: Identify different types of political systems found in world communities.

F41ACBBA9227491D929334B63DB9115C.description: Participate in activities that focus on a classroom, school, or world community issue or problem.

D931822008754E188D30F409E59CF62E.description: Demonstrate respect for the rights of others in discussions and classroom debates regardless of whether one agrees with the other viewpoint.

C10B720E8FC644C29348BAD2F818D3C9.description: Explore the types of governments in world communities and services they provide to citizens.

F4058225240A43879A6BC6A2C18830E3.description: Examine the goods and services provided by world communities; describe what goods and services a world community trades with other world communities.

EB936D56F02545FEBC52839F7FF34B72.description: Identify the products found in world communities and the various ways people in those communities pay for products.

817BF63EA86747A185270248BFA84A65.description: Identify the variety of resources available in a particular world community used to produce goods and/or provide services.

7AAEF2BCA0D14869B7FF7FD5AD846619.description: Examine how scarcity affects the decisions about the use of resources by people and governments; examine the cost and benefits of economic decisions.

42A10FF4FC9E40F78083A3545304F988.description: Describe how human activities alter places and regions.

A3A40EF1A06D49A4A362E9EDA5D3438A.description: Recognize a process that applies to population and a resulting pattern.

7CCDF9E2E71C4C5E99647B64FA390C63.description: Describe how human activities affect the environment of a world community; describe how the environment of a specific world community affects the human activities in that community.

FCF96BFF7EE347AFBD9F84720893290C.description: Distinguish human activities and human-made features from "environments" (natural events or physical features—land, air, and water—that are not directly made by humans).

888927C5AEC74FE9884A5F8E1CB42D3A.description: Ask geographic questions about where places are located and why they are located there using geographic representations such as maps and models. Describe where places are in relation to each other and describe connections among places.

3C5F4E83B89C47C89C85E8049A8A77F7.description: Describe a historical development in a world community with specific details including time and place.

BB7B102B5579474F84FC954D48E77981.description: Recognize the relationship among geography, economics, and history in world communities.

0CAD4CE1F5B642228B65929E550D3FF1.description: Describe a historical event in a world community.

12296E1F8E3D43889F41A536402265E8.description: Identify multiple perspectives by comparing and contrasting people's point of view in differing world communities.

1D9AA64BD51E4377949F9F24AFF9FB65.description: Identify a world region by describing a characteristic that places within it have in common.

2BCE7EC118344847998C4646AE48954C.description: Recognize and identify patterns of continuity and change in world communities.

B27ADF0DAC2C4CF588E18C0E39ED6285.description: Recognize periods of time such as decades and centuries.

5570F0BF4A4C45CF9D49272D2F5D141B.description: Recognize continuity and change over periods of time.

C82A5C9495614D4D9F393B84DCD8DDCD.description: Distinguish between long-term and immediate causes and effects of an event from his/her life or current events or history.

D548CB911638426E9288302FEF77D4D5.description: Identify causes and effects using examples from his/her life or from a current event or history.

93C9425FA98E4F14BDCE1ECE8BE62EAC.description: Employ mathematical skills to measure time in years and centuries.

D8A49D97BFC54227B296E76936C86EFA.description: Explain how three or more events are related to one another.

15BAEA26FCF04E36A6B90FA55468E22F.description: Create an understanding of the past by using primary and secondary sources.

83B851127C404EF787B64D98CA36916C.description: Identify and explain creation and/or authorship, purpose, and format for evidence; where appropriate, identify point of view.

7436FB81585B494E8A1C194476BC6BA3.description: Recognize and use different forms of evidence used to make meaning in social studies (including sources such as art and photographs, artifacts, oral histories, maps, and graphs).

7DBFF01EE84E467F9612BE4D070E4F25.description: Develop questions about a world community.

document.title: Learning Standards for Mathematics, Science, and Technology - Standard 5

E705A280DFE60131C52A68A86D17958E.description: help to manage a group engaged in planning, designing, implementation, and evaluation of a project to gain understanding of the management dynamics.

E7054A50DFE60131C52968A86D17958E.description: describe new management techniques (e.g., computer-aided engineering, computer-integrated manufacturing, total quality management, just-in-time manufacturing), incorporate some of these in a technological endeavor, and explain how they have reduced the length of design to-manufacture cycles, resulted in more flexible factories, and improved quality and customer satisfaction.

E704E300DFE60131C52868A86D17958E.description: explain how technological inventions and innovations stimulate economic competitiveness and how, in order for an innovation to lead to commercial success, it must be translated into products and services with marketplace demand.

E70495B0DFE60131C52768A86D17958E.description: discuss the role technology has played in the operation of successful U.S. businesses and under what circumstances they are competitive with other countries.

E7041140DFE60131C52568A86D17958E.description: explain how statistical process control helps to assure high quality output.

E7045400DFE60131C52668A86D17958E.description: develop and use computer-based scheduling and project tracking tools, such as flow charts and graphs.

E703CD90DFE60131C52468A86D17958E.description: Project management is essential to ensuring that technological endeavors are profitable and that products and systems are of high quality and built safely, on schedule, and within budget.

E702AD10DFE60131C52068A86D17958E.description: explain how national security is dependent upon both military and nonmilitary applications of technology.

E7034650DFE60131C52268A86D17958E.description: explain how computers and automation have changed the nature of work.

E702F140DFE60131C52168A86D17958E.description: explain that although technological effects are complex and difficult to predict accurately, humans can control the development and implementation of technology.

E7026390DFE60131C51F68A86D17958E.description: Technology can have positive and negative impacts on individuals, society, and the environment and humans have the capability and responsibility to constrain or promote technological development.

E701C270DFE60131C51D68A86D17958E.description: explain how technological inventions and innovations have caused global growth and interdependence, stimulated economic competitiveness, created new jobs, and made other jobs obsolete.

E7017500DFE60131C51C68A86D17958E.description: Technology has been the driving force in the evolution of society from an agricultural to an industrial to an information base.

E700A900DFE60131C51968A86D17958E.description: explain how complex technological systems involve the confluence of numerous other systems.

E700E8F0DFE60131C51A68A86D17958E.description: model, explain, and analyze the performance of a feedback control system.

E7006A00DFE60131C51868A86D17958E.description: explain why making tradeoffs among characteristics, such as safety, function, cost, ease of operation, quality of post-purchase support, and environmental impact, is necessary when selecting systems for specific purposes.

E70029B0DFE60131C51768A86D17958E.description: Technological systems are designed to achieve specific results and produce outputs, such as products, structures, services, energy, or other systems.

E6FF9070DFE60131C51568A86D17958E.description: develop an understanding of computer programming and attain some facility in writing computer programs.

E6FF2810DFE60131C51468A86D17958E.description: use computer-aided drawing and design (CADD) software to model realistic solutions to design problems.

E6FE9E80DFE60131C51268A86D17958E.description: attach a modem to a computer system and telephone line, set up and use communications software, connect to various on-line networks, including the Internet, and access needed information using e-mail, telnet, gopher, ftp, and web searches.

E6FE61F0DFE60131C51168A86D17958E.description: select a computer system that meets personal needs.

E6FEDF20DFE60131C51368A86D17958E.description: understand basic computer architecture and describe the function of computer subsystems and peripheral devices.

E6FE2310DFE60131C51068A86D17958E.description: Computers, as tools for design, modeling, information processing, communication, and system control, have greatly increased human productivity and knowledge.

E6FD5E80DFE60131C50D68A86D17958E.description: describe and model methods (including computer-based methods) to control system processes and monitor system outputs.

E6FD1FC0DFE60131C50C68A86D17958E.description: explain tradeoffs made in selecting alternative resources in terms of safety, cost, properties, availability, ease of processing, and disposability.

E6FDA3A0DFE60131C50E68A86D17958E.description: select appropriate tools, instruments, and equipment and use them correctly to process materials, energy, and information.

E6FCDC60DFE60131C50B68A86D17958E.description: test, use, and describe the attributes of a range of material (including synthetic and composite materials), information, and energy resources.

E6FC9710DFE60131C50A68A86D17958E.description: Technological tools, materials, and other resources should be selected on the basis of safety, cost, availability, appropriateness, and environmental impact; technological processes change energy, information, and material resources into more useful forms.

E6FC0EC0DFE60131C50868A86D17958E.description: in a group setting, devise a test of the solution relative to the design criteria and perform the test; record, portray, and logically evaluate performance test results through quantitative, graphic, and verbal means; and use a variety of creative verbal and graphic techniques effectively and persuasively to present conclusions, predict impacts and new problems, and suggest and pursue modifications.

E6FBBF00DFE60131C50768A86D17958E.description: develop work schedules and plans which include optimal use and cost of materials, processes, time, and expertise; construct a model of the solution, incorporating developmental modifications while working to a high degree of quality (craftsmanship).

E6FAF9F0DFE60131C50468A86D17958E.description: generate creative solution ideas, break ideas into the significant functional elements, and explore possible refinements; predict possible outcomes using mathematical and functional modeling techniques; choose the optimal solution to the problem, clearly documenting ideas against design criteria and constraints; and explain how human values, economics, ergonomics, and environmental considerations have influenced the solution.

E6FB3FC0DFE60131C50568A86D17958E.description: identify, locate, and use a wide range of information resources including subject experts, library references, magazines, videotapes, films, electronic data bases and on-line services, and discuss and document through notes and sketches how findings relate to the problem.

E6FB7E40DFE60131C50668A86D17958E.description: initiate and carry out a thorough investigation of an unfamiliar situation and identify needs and opportunities for technological invention or innovation.

E6FAAE60DFE60131C50368A86D17958E.description: Engineering design is an iterative process involving modeling and optimization used to develop technological solutions to problems within given constraints.

E6FA1CB0DFE60131C50168A86D17958E.description: Students will apply technological knowledge and skills to design, construct, use, and evaluate products and systems to satisfy human and environmental needs.

document.title: New York State P-12 Common Core Learning Standards for English Language Arts & Literacy

DA418AC0DFE60131ADA968A86D17958E.description: Use words and phrases acquired through conversations, reading and being read to, and responding to texts, including using frequently occurring conjunctions to signal simple relationships (e.g., because).

DA412E50DFE60131ADA868A86D17958E.description: Distinguish shades of meaning among verbs differing in manner (e.g., look, peek, glance, stare, glare, scowl) and adjectives differing in intensity (e.g., large, gigantic) by defining or choosing them or by acting out the meanings.

DA40E160DFE60131ADA768A86D17958E.description: Identify real-life connections between words and their use (e.g., note places at home that are cozy).

DA4094E0DFE60131ADA668A86D17958E.description: Define words by category and by one or more key attributes (e.g., a duck is a bird that swims; a tiger is a large cat with stripes).

document.title: New York State P-12 Common Core Learning Standards for Mathematics

D5EE3CF0DFE60131A6CE68A86D17958E.description: Partition circles and rectangles into two and four equal shares, describe the shares using the words halves, fourths, and quarters, and use the phrases half of, fourth of, and quarter of. Describe the whole as two of, or four of the shares. Understand for these examples that decomposing into more equal shares creates smaller shares.

D5EDF590DFE60131A6CD68A86D17958E.description: Compose two-dimensional shapes (rectangles, squares, trapezoids, triangles, half-circles, and quarter-circles) or three-dimensional shapes (cubes, right rectangular prisms, right circular cones, and right circular cylinders) to create a composite shape, and compose new shapes from the composite shape.
comments: Students do not need to learn formal names such as "right rectangular prism."

D5EDA420DFE60131A6CC68A86D17958E.description: Distinguish between defining attributes (e.g., triangles are closed and three-sided) versus non-defining attributes (e.g., color, orientation, overall size); build and draw shapes to possess defining attributes.

D5ED59E0DFE60131A6CB68A86D17958E.description: Reason with shapes and their attributes.

D5ECCB70DFE60131A6C968A86D17958E.description: Organize, represent, and interpret data with up to three categories; ask and answer questions about the total number of data points, how many in each category, and how many more or less are in one category than in another.

D5EC08B0DFE60131A6C768A86D17958E.description: Tell and write time in hours and half-hours using analog and digital clocks. Recognize and identify coins, their names, and their value.

D5EBC1B0DFE60131A6C668A86D17958E.description: Tell and write time and money.

D5EB7CE0DFE60131A6C568A86D17958E.description: Express the length of an object as a whole number of length units, by laying multiple copies of a shorter object (the length unit) end to end; understand that the length measurement of an object is the number of same-size length units that span it with no gaps or overlaps.
comments: Limit to contexts where the object being measured is spanned by a whole number of length units with no gaps or overlaps.

D5EB3A80DFE60131A6C468A86D17958E.description: Order three objects by length; compare the lengths of two objects indirectly by using a third object.

D5EAF7D0DFE60131A6C368A86D17958E.description: Measure lengths indirectly and by iterating length units.

D5EA6BF0DFE60131A6C168A86D17958E.description: Subtract multiples of 10 in the range 10-90 from multiples of 10 in the range 10-90 (positive or zero differences), using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used.

D5EA2420DFE60131A6C068A86D17958E.description: Given a two-digit number, mentally find 10 more or 10 less than the number, without having to count; explain the reasoning used.

D5E9DDB0DFE60131A6BF68A86D17958E.description: Add within 100, including adding a two-digit number and a one-digit number, and adding a two-digit number and a multiple of 10, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used. Understand that in adding two-digit numbers, one adds tens and tens, ones and ones; and sometimes it is necessary to compose a ten.

D5E996C0DFE60131A6BE68A86D17958E.description: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to add and subtract.

D5E95100DFE60131A6BD68A86D17958E.description: Compare two two-digit numbers based on meanings of the tens and ones digits, recording the results of comparisons with the symbols >, =, and <.

D5E90C90DFE60131A6BC68A86D17958E.description: The numbers 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90 refer to one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine tens (and 0 ones).

D5E8BAA0DFE60131A6BB68A86D17958E.description: The numbers from 11 to 19 are composed of a ten and one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine ones.

D5E86960DFE60131A6BA68A86D17958E.description: 10 can be thought of as a bundle of ten ones — called a "ten."

D5E81DE0DFE60131A6B968A86D17958E.description: Understand that the two digits of a two-digit number represent amounts of tens and ones. Understand the following as special cases:

D5E79470DFE60131A6B768A86D17958E.description: Count to 120, starting at any number less than 120. In this range, read and write numerals and represent a number of objects with a written numeral.

D5E6FD30DFE60131A6B568A86D17958E.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten
comments: Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to whole numbers less than or equal to 1,000,000.

D5E628B0DFE60131A6B268A86D17958E.description: Determine the unknown whole number in an addition or subtraction equation relating three whole numbers.
comments: For example, determine the unknown number that makes the equation true in each of the equations 8 + ? = 11, 5 = - 3, 6 + 6 = .

D5E5E4C0DFE60131A6B168A86D17958E.description: Understand the meaning of the equal sign, and determine if equations involving addition and subtraction are true or false.
comments: For example, which of the following equations are true and which are false? 6 = 6, 7 = 8 - 1, 5 + 2 = 2 + 5, 4 + 1 = 5 + 2.

D5E5A0B0DFE60131A6B068A86D17958E.description: Work with addition and subtraction equations.

D5E55880DFE60131A6AF68A86D17958E.description: Add and subtract within 20, demonstrating fluency for addition and subtraction within 10. Use strategies such as counting on; making ten (e.g., 8 + 6 = 8 + 2 + 4 = 10 + 4 = 14); decomposing a number leading to a ten (e.g., 13 - 4 = 13 - 3 - 1 = 10 - 1 = 9); using the relationship between addition and subtraction (e.g., knowing that 8 + 4 = 12, one knows 12 - 8 = 4); and creating equivalent but easier or known sums (e.g., adding 6 + 7 by creating the known equivalent 6 + 6 + 1 = 12 + 1 = 13).

D5E50E70DFE60131A6AE68A86D17958E.description: Relate counting to addition and subtraction (e.g., by counting on 2 to add 2).

D5E492A0DFE60131A6AC68A86D17958E.description: Understand subtraction as an unknown-addend problem.
comments: For example, subtract 10 - 8 by finding the number that makes 10 when added to 8.

D5E45230DFE60131A6AB68A86D17958E.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to add and subtract.
comments: Students need not use formal terms for these properties.
To add 2 + 6 + 4, the second two numbers can be added to make a ten, so 2 + 6 + 4 = 2 + 10 = 12. (Associative property of addition.)
If 8 + 3 = 11 is known, then 3 + 8 = 11 is also known. (Commutative property of addition.)

D5E413B0DFE60131A6AA68A86D17958E.description: Understand and apply properties of operations and the relationship between addition and subtraction.

D5E6AEE0DFE60131A6B468A86D17958E.description: Duplicate and extend (eg., What comes next?) simple patterns using concrete objects.

D5E3D3C0DFE60131A6A968A86D17958E.description: Solve word problems that call for addition of three whole numbers whose sum is less than or equal to 20, e.g., by using objects, drawings, and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

D5E38530DFE60131A6A868A86D17958E.description: Use addition and subtraction within 20 to solve word problems involving situations of adding to, taking from, putting together, taking apart, and comparing, with unknowns in all positions, e.g., by using objects, drawings, and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

D5E33760DFE60131A6A768A86D17958E.description: Represent and solve problems involving addition and subtraction.

D5E2A090DFE60131A6A568A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

D5E25360DFE60131A6A468A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

D5E10510DFE60131A6A068A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

D5E03A00DFE60131A69E68A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

document.title: Learning Standards for Mathematics, Science, and Technology - Standards 6 & 7

D7CFAC10DFE60131A9DD68A86D17958E.description: Presenting Results: Using a variety of media to present the solution and to communicate the results.

D7D05330DFE60131A9DF68A86D17958E.description: Realizing Ideas: Constructing components or models, arriving at a solution, and evaluating the result.

D7CEEB10DFE60131A9DB68A86D17958E.description: Common Themes: Observing examples of common unifying themes, applying them to the problem, and using them to better understand the dimensions of the problem.

D7CE9F60DFE60131A9DA68A86D17958E.description: Generating and Analyzing Ideas: Developing ideas for proposed solutions, investigating ideas, collecting data, and showing relationships and patterns in the data.

D7D003D0DFE60131A9DE68A86D17958E.description: Gathering and Processing Information: Accessing information from printed media, electronic data bases, and community resources and using the information to develop a definition of the problem and to research possible solutions.

D7CF38B0DFE60131A9DC68A86D17958E.description: Working Effectively: Contributing to the work of a brainstorming group, laboratory partnership, cooperative learning group, or project team; planning procedures; identify and managing responsibilities of team members; and staying on task, whether working alone or as part of a group.

D7CE5B40DFE60131A9D968A86D17958E.description: Skills and Strategies for Interdisciplinary Problem Solving

D7CC68A0DFE60131A9D268A86D17958E.description: Solving interdisciplinary problems involves a variety of skills and strategies, including effective work habits; gathering and processing information; generating and analyzing ideas; realizing ideas; making connections among the common themes of mathematics, science, and technology; and presenting results.

D7CBE930DFE60131A9D068A86D17958E.description: observe phenomena and evaluate them scientifically and mathematically by conducting a fair test of the effect of variables and using mathematical knowledge and technological tools to collect, analyze, and present data and conclusions.

D7CB9C20DFE60131A9CF68A86D17958E.description: design solutions to problems involving a familiar and real context, investigate related science concepts to inform the solution, and use mathematics to model, quantify, measure, and compute.

D7CB5A80DFE60131A9CE68A86D17958E.description: make informed consumer decisions by applying knowledge about the attributes of particular products and making cost/benefit tradeoffs to arrive at an optimal choice.

D7CB1170DFE60131A9CD68A86D17958E.description: analyze science/technology/society problems and issues that affect their home, school, or community, and carry out a remedial course of action.

D7CAC730DFE60131A9CC68A86D17958E.description: The knowledge and skills of mathematics, science, and technology are used together to make informed decisions and solve problems, especially those relating to issues of science/technology/society, consumer decision making, design, and inquiry into phenomena.

D7CA2DF0DFE60131A9CA68A86D17958E.description: Students will apply the knowledge and thinking skills of mathematics, science, and technology to address real-life problems and make informed decisions.

D7C9A0B0DFE60131A9C868A86D17958E.description: use simple quantitative methods, such as ratios, to compare costs to benefits of a decision problem.

D7C9ED60DFE60131A9C968A86D17958E.description: determine the criteria and constraints of a simple decision making problem.

D7C96040DFE60131A9C768A86D17958E.description: In order to arrive at the best solution that meets criteria within constraints, it is often necessary to make trade-offs.

D7C89130DFE60131A9C468A86D17958E.description: analyze data by making tables and graphs and looking for patterns of change.

D7C8D810DFE60131A9C568A86D17958E.description: use simple instruments to measure such quantities as distance, size, and weight and look for patterns in the data.

D7C84F20DFE60131A9C368A86D17958E.description: Identifying patterns of change is necessary for making predictions about future behavior and conditions.

D7C75130DFE60131A9C068A86D17958E.description: distinguish between reasons for stability—from lack of changes to changes that counterbalance one another to changes within cycles.

D7C54460DFE60131A9B868A86D17958E.description: analyze, construct, and operate models in order to discover attributes of the real thing.
