DACB9530DFE60131AEA668A86D17958E.description: Write narratives to develop real or imagined experiences or events using effective technique, descriptive details, and clear event sequences.

DACB45A0DFE60131AEA568A86D17958E.description: Provide a concluding statement or section.

DACAE5C0DFE60131AEA468A86D17958E.description: Use linking words and phrases (e.g., also, another, and, more, but) to connect ideas within categories of information.

DACA7350DFE60131AEA368A86D17958E.description: Develop the topic with facts, definitions, and details.

DACA1300DFE60131AEA268A86D17958E.description: Introduce a topic and group related information together; include illustrations when useful to aiding comprehension.

DAC9C790DFE60131AEA168A86D17958E.description: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas and information clearly.

DAC97AC0DFE60131AEA068A86D17958E.description: Provide a concluding statement or section.

DAC92020DFE60131AE9F68A86D17958E.description: Use linking words and phrases (e.g., because, therefore, since, for example) to connect opinion and reasons.

DAC86BB0DFE60131AE9E68A86D17958E.description: Provide reasons that support the opinion.

DAC77A20DFE60131AE9D68A86D17958E.description: Introduce the topic or text they are writing about, state an opinion, and create an organizational structure that lists reasons.

DAC70970DFE60131AE9C68A86D17958E.description: Write opinion pieces on topics or texts, supporting a point of view with reasons.

DAC5BD00DFE60131AE9968A86D17958E.description: Develop personal, cultural, textual, and thematic connections within and across genres as they respond to texts through written, digital, and oral presentations, employing a variety of media and genres.

DAC4CDB0DFE60131AE9768A86D17958E.description: Write routinely over extended time frames (time for research, reflection, and revision) and shorter time frames (a single sitting or a day or two) for a range of tasks, purposes, and audiences.

DAC428A0DFE60131AE9568A86D17958E.description: Draw evidence from literary or informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and research.

DAC3D570DFE60131AE9468A86D17958E.description: Gather relevant information from multiple print and digital sources, assess the credibility and accuracy of each source, and integrate the information while avoiding plagiarism.

DAC377E0DFE60131AE9368A86D17958E.description: Conduct short as well as more sustained research projects based on focused questions, demonstrating understanding of the subject under investigation.

DAC31970DFE60131AE9268A86D17958E.description: Research to Build and Present Knowledge

DAC2B490DFE60131AE9168A86D17958E.description: Use technology, including the Internet, to produce and publish writing and to interact and collaborate with others.

DAC25FD0DFE60131AE9068A86D17958E.description: Develop and strengthen writing as needed by planning, revising, editing, rewriting, or trying a new approach.

DAC1F710DFE60131AE8F68A86D17958E.description: Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development, organization, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.

DAC14690DFE60131AE8D68A86D17958E.description: Write narratives to develop real or imagined experiences or events using effective technique, well-chosen details, and well-structured event sequences.

DAC0FB40DFE60131AE8C68A86D17958E.description: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine and convey complex ideas and information clearly and accurately through the effective selection, organization, and analysis of content.

DAC0B0D0DFE60131AE8B68A86D17958E.description: Write arguments to support claims in an analysis of substantive topics or texts, using valid reasoning and relevant and sufficient evidence.

DABFBCD0DFE60131AE8868A86D17958E.description: Use context to confirm or self-correct word recognition and understanding, rereading as necessary.

DABF73A0DFE60131AE8768A86D17958E.description: Read on-level prose and poetry orally with accuracy, appropriate rate, and expression on successive readings

DABF2910DFE60131AE8668A86D17958E.description: Read on-level text with purpose and understanding.

DABEDD80DFE60131AE8568A86D17958E.description: Read with sufficient accuracy and fluency to support comprehension.

DABBD540DFE60131AE7C68A86D17958E.description: By the end of the year, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, at the high end of the grades 2—3 text complexity band independently and proficiently.

DABB8AF0DFE60131AE7B68A86D17958E.description: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity

DABB36E0DFE60131AE7A68A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast the most important points and key details presented in two texts on the same topic.

DABAD810DFE60131AE7968A86D17958E.description: Describe the logical connection between particular sentences and paragraphs in a text (e.g., comparison, cause/effect, first/second/third in a sequence).

DABA6CF0DFE60131AE7868A86D17958E.description: Use information gained from illustrations (e.g., maps, photographs) and the words in a text to demonstrate understanding of the text (e.g., where, when, why, and how key events occur).

DAB9DAE0DFE60131AE7668A86D17958E.description: Distinguish their own point of view from that of the author of a text.

DAB98E70DFE60131AE7568A86D17958E.description: Use text features and search tools (e.g., key words, sidebars, hyperlinks) to locate information relevant to a given topic efficiently.

DAB93DC0DFE60131AE7468A86D17958E.description: Determine the meaning of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases in a text relevant to a grade 3 topic or subject area.

DAB87AA0DFE60131AE7268A86D17958E.description: Describe the relationship between a series of historical events, scientific ideas or concepts, or steps in technical procedures in a text, using language that pertains to time, sequence, and cause/effect.

DAB82D70DFE60131AE7168A86D17958E.description: Determine the main idea of a text; recount the key details and explain how they support the main idea.

DAB7E470DFE60131AE7068A86D17958E.description: Ask and answer questions to demonstrate understanding of a text, referring explicitly to the text as the basis for the answers.

DAB6FB50DFE60131AE6D68A86D17958E.description: Self-select text based upon personal preferences.

DAB69460DFE60131AE6C68A86D17958E.description: Recognize and make connections in narratives, poetry, and drama to other texts, ideas, cultural perspectives, personal events, and situations.

DAB5FF70DFE60131AE6A68A86D17958E.description: By the end of the year, read and comprehend literature, including stories, dramas, and poetry, at the high end of the grades 2—3 text complexity band independently and proficiently.

DAB5B650DFE60131AE6968A86D17958E.description: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity

DAB52070DFE60131AE6768A86D17958E.description: With prompting and support, students will make cultural connections to text and self.

DAB4C910DFE60131AE6668A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast the themes, settings, and plots of stories written by the same author about the same or similar characters (e.g., in books from a series).

DAB47A30DFE60131AE6568A86D17958E.description: Explain how specific aspects of a text's illustrations contribute to what is conveyed by the words in a story (e.g., create mood, emphasize aspects of a character or setting).

DAB3C940DFE60131AE6368A86D17958E.description: Distinguish their own point of view from that of the narrator or those of the characters.

DAB35AB0DFE60131AE6268A86D17958E.description: Refer to parts of stories, dramas, and poems when writing or speaking about a text, using terms such as chapter, scene, and stanza; describe how each successive part builds on earlier sections.

DAB2FDC0DFE60131AE6168A86D17958E.description: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, distinguishing literal from nonliteral language.

DAB26910DFE60131AE5F68A86D17958E.description: Describe characters in a story (e.g., their traits, motivations, or feelings) and explain how their actions contribute to the sequence of events.

DAB21D40DFE60131AE5E68A86D17958E.description: Recount stories, including fables, folktales, and myths from diverse cultures; determine the central message, lesson, or moral and explain how it is conveyed through key details in the text.

DAB1D000DFE60131AE5D68A86D17958E.description: Ask and answer questions to demonstrate understanding of a text, referring explicitly to the text as the basis for the answers.

DAB0B210DFE60131AE5A68A86D17958E.description: Respond to literature by employing knowledge of literary language, textual features, and forms to read and comprehend, reflect upon, and interpret literary texts from a variety of genres and a wide spectrum of American and world cultures.

DAB02420DFE60131AE5868A86D17958E.description: Read and comprehend complex literary and informational texts independently and proficiently.

DAAFDAE0DFE60131AE5768A86D17958E.description: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity

DAAF8FC0DFE60131AE5668A86D17958E.description: Analyze how two or more texts address similar themes or topics in order to build knowledge or to compare the approaches the authors take.

DAAF3580DFE60131AE5568A86D17958E.description: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, including the validity of the reasoning as well as the relevance and sufficiency of the evidence.

DAAEE960DFE60131AE5468A86D17958E.description: Integrate and evaluate content presented in diverse media and formats, including visually and quantitatively, as well as in words.
comments: Please see "Research to Build and Present Knowledge" in Writing and "Comprehension and Collaboration" in Speaking and Listening for additional standards relevant to gathering, assessing, and applying information from print and digital sources.

DAAE4DA0DFE60131AE5268A86D17958E.description: Assess how point of view or purpose shapes the content and style of a text.

DAAE0100DFE60131AE5168A86D17958E.description: Analyze the structure of texts, including how specific sentences, paragraphs, and larger portions of the text (e.g., a section, chapter, scene, or stanza) relate to each other and the whole.

DAADB1E0DFE60131AE5068A86D17958E.description: Interpret words and phrases as they are used in a text, including determining technical, connotative, and figurative meanings, and analyze how specific word choices shape meaning or tone.

DAAD1230DFE60131AE4E68A86D17958E.description: Analyze how and why individuals, events, and ideas develop and interact over the course of a text.

DAACC400DFE60131AE4D68A86D17958E.description: Determine central ideas or themes of a text and analyze their development; summarize the key supporting details and ideas.

DAAC75C0DFE60131AE4C68A86D17958E.description: Read closely to determine what the text says explicitly and to make logical inferences from it; cite specific textual evidence when writing or speaking to support conclusions drawn from the text.

document.title: New York State P-12 Common Core Learning Standards for English Language Arts & Literacy

DA90C8C0DFE60131AE4868A86D17958E.description: Use words and phrases acquired through conversations, reading and being read to, and responding to texts, including using adjectives and adverbs to describe (e.g., When other kids are happy that makes me happy).

DA907EC0DFE60131AE4768A86D17958E.description: Distinguish shades of meaning among closely related verbs (e.g., toss, throw, hurl) and closely related adjectives (e.g., thin, slender, skinny, scrawny).

DA903100DFE60131AE4668A86D17958E.description: Identify real-life connections between words and their use (e.g., describe foods that are spicy or juicy).

DA8FD590DFE60131AE4568A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate understanding of word relationships and nuances in word meanings.

DA8F8E60DFE60131AE4468A86D17958E.description: Use glossaries and beginning dictionaries, both print and digital, to determine or clarify the meaning of words and phrases.

DA8F4680DFE60131AE4368A86D17958E.description: Use knowledge of the meaning of individual words to predict the meaning of compound words (e.g., birdhouse, lighthouse, housefly; bookshelf, notebook, bookmark).

DA8EFCE0DFE60131AE4268A86D17958E.description: Use a known root word as a clue to the meaning of an unknown word with the same root (e.g., addition, additional).

DA8EB320DFE60131AE4168A86D17958E.description: Determine the meaning of the new word formed when a known prefix is added to a known word (e.g., happy/unhappy, tell/retell).

DA8E6200DFE60131AE4068A86D17958E.description: Use sentence-level context as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.

DA8E0BB0DFE60131AE3F68A86D17958E.description: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases based on grade 2 reading and content, choosing flexibly from an array of strategies.

DA8D56D0DFE60131AE3D68A86D17958E.description: Compare formal and informal uses of English.

DA8CF600DFE60131AE3C68A86D17958E.description: Use knowledge of language and its conventions when writing, speaking, reading, or listening.

DA8C4EE0DFE60131AE3A68A86D17958E.description: Consult reference materials, including beginning dictionaries, as needed to check and correct spellings.

DA8C0660DFE60131AE3968A86D17958E.description: Generalize learned spelling patterns when writing words (e.g., cage → badge; boy → boil).

DA8BBBB0DFE60131AE3868A86D17958E.description: Use an apostrophe to form contractions and frequently occurring possessives.

DA8B66C0DFE60131AE3768A86D17958E.description: Use commas in greetings and closings of letters.

DA8B0380DFE60131AE3668A86D17958E.description: Capitalize holidays, product names, and geographic names.

DA8AA260DFE60131AE3568A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.

DA8A3B40DFE60131AE3468A86D17958E.description: Produce, expand, and rearrange complete simple and compound sentences (e.g., The boy watched the movie; The little boy watched the movie; The action movie was watched by the little boy).

DA89EF90DFE60131AE3368A86D17958E.description: Use adjectives and adverbs, and choose between them depending on what is to be modified.

DA89A520DFE60131AE3268A86D17958E.description: Form and use the past tense of frequently occurring irregular verbs (e.g., sat, hid, told).

DA88FD20DFE60131AE3068A86D17958E.description: Form and use frequently occurring irregular plural nouns (e.g., feet, children, teeth, mice, fish).

DA8854F0DFE60131AE2E68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage when writing or speaking.

DA874670DFE60131AE2B68A86D17958E.description: Acquire and use accurately a range of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases sufficient for reading, writing, speaking, and listening at the college and career readiness level; demonstrate independence in gathering vocabulary knowledge when encountering an unknown term important to comprehension or expression.

DA86FF40DFE60131AE2A68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.

DA86B5B0DFE60131AE2968A86D17958E.description: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases by using context clues, analyzing meaningful word parts, and consulting general and specialized reference materials, as appropriate.

DA861E70DFE60131AE2768A86D17958E.description: Apply knowledge of language to understand how language functions in different contexts, to make effective choices for meaning or style, and to comprehend more fully when reading or listening.

DA856010DFE60131AE2568A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.

DA851430DFE60131AE2468A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage when writing or speaking.

DA847F50DFE60131AE2268A86D17958E.description: College and Career Readiness Anchor Standards for Language

DA843230DFE60131AE2168A86D17958E.description: Produce complete sentences when appropriate to task and situation in order to provide requested detail or clarification.

DA83E360DFE60131AE2068A86D17958E.description: Create audio recordings of stories or poems; add drawings or other visual displays to stories or recounts of experiences when appropriate to clarify ideas, thoughts, and feelings.

DA838A50DFE60131AE1F68A86D17958E.description: Tell a story or recount an experience with appropriate facts and relevant, descriptive details, speaking audibly in coherent sentences.

DA82E320DFE60131AE1D68A86D17958E.description: Ask and answer questions about what a speaker says in order to clarify comprehension, gather additional information, or deepen understanding of a topic or issue.

DA829610DFE60131AE1C68A86D17958E.description: Recount or describe key ideas or details from a text read aloud or information presented orally or through other media.

DA8246C0DFE60131AE1B68A86D17958E.description: Seek to understand and communicate with individuals from different cultural backgrounds.

DA81F600DFE60131AE1A68A86D17958E.description: Ask for clarification and further explanation as needed about the topics and texts under discussion.

DA81A4A0DFE60131AE1968A86D17958E.description: Build on others' talk in conversations by linking their comments to the remarks of others.

DA815BF0DFE60131AE1868A86D17958E.description: Follow agreed-upon rules for discussions (e.g., gaining the floor in respectful ways, listening to others with care, speaking one at a time about the topics and texts under discussion).

DA8111D0DFE60131AE1768A86D17958E.description: Participate in collaborative conversations with diverse partners about grade 2 topics and texts with peers and adults in small and larger groups.

DA801940DFE60131AE1468A86D17958E.description: Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and communicative tasks, demonstrating command of formal English when indicated or appropriate.

DA7FA5C0DFE60131AE1368A86D17958E.description: Make strategic use of digital media and visual displays of data to express information and enhance understanding of presentations.

DA7F5F00DFE60131AE1268A86D17958E.description: Present information, findings, and supporting evidence such that listeners can follow the line of reasoning and the organization, development, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.

DA7ECDE0DFE60131AE1068A86D17958E.description: Evaluate a speaker's point of view, reasoning, and use of evidence and rhetoric.

DA7E7E10DFE60131AE0F68A86D17958E.description: Integrate and evaluate information presented in diverse media and formats, including visually, quantitatively, and orally.

DA7E2C50DFE60131AE0E68A86D17958E.description: Prepare for and participate effectively in a range of conversations and collaborations with diverse partners, building on others' ideas and expressing their own clearly and persuasively.

DA7D7960DFE60131AE0C68A86D17958E.description: College and Career Readiness Anchor Standards for Speaking and Listening

DA7D3140DFE60131AE0B68A86D17958E.description: Create and present a poem, narrative, play, art work, or personal response to a particular author or theme studied in class, with support as needed.

DA7BA690DFE60131AE0668A86D17958E.description: Recall information from experiences or gather information from provided sources to answer a question.

DA7B4EF0DFE60131AE0568A86D17958E.description: Participate in shared research and writing projects (e.g., read a number of books on a single topic to produce a report; record science observations).

DA7AEFE0DFE60131AE0468A86D17958E.description: Research to Build and Present Knowledge

DA7A2A70DFE60131AE0268A86D17958E.description: With guidance and support from adults, use a variety of digital tools to produce and publish writing, including in collaboration with peers.

DA79C800DFE60131AE0168A86D17958E.description: With guidance and support from adults and peers, focus on a topic and strengthen writing as needed by revising and editing.

DA792C30DFE60131ADFF68A86D17958E.description: Write narratives in which they recount a well-elaborated event or short sequence of events, include details to describe actions, thoughts, and feelings, use temporal words to signal event order, and provide a sense of closure.

DA78D450DFE60131ADFE68A86D17958E.description: Write informative/explanatory texts in which they introduce a topic, use facts and definitions to develop points, and provide a concluding statement or section.

DA788C80DFE60131ADFD68A86D17958E.description: Write opinion pieces in which they introduce the topic or book they are writing about, state an opinion, supply reasons that support the opinion, use linking words (e.g., because, and, also) to connect opinion and reasons, and provide a concluding statement or section.

DA77B210DFE60131ADFA68A86D17958E.description: Develop personal, cultural, textual, and thematic connections within and across genres as they respond to texts through written, digital, and oral presentations, employing a variety of media and genres.

DA770200DFE60131ADF868A86D17958E.description: Write routinely over extended time frames (time for research, reflection, and revision) and shorter time frames (a single sitting or a day or two) for a range of tasks, purposes, and audiences.

DA7652D0DFE60131ADF668A86D17958E.description: Draw evidence from literary or informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and research.

DA75F0B0DFE60131ADF568A86D17958E.description: Gather relevant information from multiple print and digital sources, assess the credibility and accuracy of each source, and integrate the information while avoiding plagiarism.

DA759890DFE60131ADF468A86D17958E.description: Conduct short as well as more sustained research projects based on focused questions, demonstrating understanding of the subject under investigation.

DA754570DFE60131ADF368A86D17958E.description: Research to Build and Present Knowledge

DA74F990DFE60131ADF268A86D17958E.description: Use technology, including the Internet, to produce and publish writing and to interact and collaborate with others.

DA749ED0DFE60131ADF168A86D17958E.description: Develop and strengthen writing as needed by planning, revising, editing, rewriting, or trying a new approach.

DA7438A0DFE60131ADF068A86D17958E.description: Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development, organization, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.

DA738590DFE60131ADEE68A86D17958E.description: Write narratives to develop real or imagined experiences or events using effective technique, well-chosen details, and well-structured event sequences.

DA733760DFE60131ADED68A86D17958E.description: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine and convey complex ideas and information clearly and accurately through the effective selection, organization, and analysis of content.

DA72ED00DFE60131ADEC68A86D17958E.description: Write arguments to support claims in an analysis of substantive topics or texts, using valid reasoning and relevant and sufficient evidence.

DA720870DFE60131ADE968A86D17958E.description: Use context to confirm or self-correct word recognition and understanding, rereading as necessary.

DA719DF0DFE60131ADE868A86D17958E.description: Read on-level text orally with accuracy, appropriate rate, and expression on successive readings.

DA7148B0DFE60131ADE768A86D17958E.description: Read on-level text with purpose and understanding.

DA70EEA0DFE60131ADE668A86D17958E.description: Read with sufficient accuracy and fluency to support comprehension.

DA7060A0DFE60131ADE468A86D17958E.description: Recognize and read grade-appropriate irregularly spelled words.

DA701740DFE60131ADE368A86D17958E.description: Identify words with inconsistent but common spelling-sound correspondences.

DA6FC690DFE60131ADE268A86D17958E.description: Decode words with common prefixes and suffixes.

DA6F7D00DFE60131ADE168A86D17958E.description: Decode regularly spelled two-syllable words with long vowels.

DA6F3300DFE60131ADE068A86D17958E.description: Know spelling-sound correspondences for additional common vowel teams.

DA6ED8D0DFE60131ADDF68A86D17958E.description: Distinguish long and short vowels when reading regularly spelled one-syllable words.

DA6E7880DFE60131ADDE68A86D17958E.description: Know and apply grade-level phonics and word analysis skills in decoding words.

DA6D89E0DFE60131ADDB68A86D17958E.description: By the end of year, read and comprehend informational texts, including history/social studies, science, and technical texts, in the grades 2—3 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.

DA6D42B0DFE60131ADDA68A86D17958E.description: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity

DA6CFB20DFE60131ADD968A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast the most important points presented by two texts on the same topic.

DA6CA8E0DFE60131ADD868A86D17958E.description: Describe how reasons support specific points the author makes in a text.

DA6C51F0DFE60131ADD768A86D17958E.description: Explain how specific images (e.g., a diagram showing how a machine works) contribute to and clarify a text.

DA6B9E00DFE60131ADD568A86D17958E.description: Identify the main purpose of a text, including what the author wants to answer, explain, or describe.

DA6B5390DFE60131ADD468A86D17958E.description: Know and use various text features (e.g., captions, bold print, subheadings, glossaries, indexes, electronic menus, icons) to locate key facts or information in a text efficiently.

DA6B0880DFE60131ADD368A86D17958E.description: Determine the meaning of words and phrases in a text relevant to a grade 2 topic or subject area.

DA6A6C40DFE60131ADD168A86D17958E.description: Describe the connection between a series of historical events, scientific ideas or concepts, or steps in technical procedures in a text.

DA6A20F0DFE60131ADD068A86D17958E.description: Identify the main topic of a multiparagraph text as well as the focus of specific paragraphs within the text.

DA69D570DFE60131ADCF68A86D17958E.description: Ask and answer such questions as who, what, where, when, why, and how to demonstrate understanding of key details in a text.

DA68CD30DFE60131ADCC68A86D17958E.description: Make connections between self, text, and the world around them (text, media, social interaction).

DA6820F0DFE60131ADCA68A86D17958E.description: By the end of the year, read and comprehend literature, including stories and poetry, in the grades 2—3 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.

DA673A20DFE60131ADC768A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast two or more versions of the same story (e.g., Cinderella stories) by different authors or from different cultures.

DA66D170DFE60131ADC668A86D17958E.description: Use information gained from the illustrations and words in a print or digital text to demonstrate understanding of its characters, setting, or plot.

DA6634A0DFE60131ADC468A86D17958E.description: Acknowledge differences in the points of view of characters, including by speaking in a different voice for each character when reading dialogue aloud.

DA65E7E0DFE60131ADC368A86D17958E.description: Describe the overall structure of a story, including describing how the beginning introduces the story and the ending concludes the action.

DA659800DFE60131ADC268A86D17958E.description: Describe how words and phrases (e.g., regular beats, alliteration, rhymes, repeated lines) supply rhythm and meaning in a story, poem, or song.

DA64E700DFE60131ADC068A86D17958E.description: Describe how characters in a story respond to major events and challenges.

DA615F90DFE60131ADB568A86D17958E.description: Integrate and evaluate content presented in diverse media and formats, including visually and quantitatively, as well as in words.

document.title: New York State P-12 Common Core Learning Standards for Mathematics

D7B32BD0DFE60131A9AE68A86D17958E.description: (+) Analyze decisions and strategies using probability concepts (e.g., product testing, medical testing, pulling a hockey goalie at the end of a game).

D7B2D970DFE60131A9AD68A86D17958E.description: (+) Use probabilities to make fair decisions (e.g., drawing by lots, using a random number generator).

D7B287C0DFE60131A9AC68A86D17958E.description: Evaluate and compare strategies on the basis of expected values.
comments: For example, compare a high-deductible versus a low-deductible automobile insurance policy using various, but reasonable, chances of having a minor or a major accident.

D7B23550DFE60131A9AB68A86D17958E.description: Find the expected payoff for a game of chance.
comments: For example, find the expected winnings from a state lottery ticket or a game at a fast-food restaurant.

D7B1D080DFE60131A9AA68A86D17958E.description: (+) Weigh the possible outcomes of a decision by assigning probabilities to payoff values and finding expected values.

D7B17770DFE60131A9A968A86D17958E.description: Use probability to evaluate outcomes of decisions

D7B11830DFE60131A9A868A86D17958E.description: (+) Develop a probability distribution for a random variable defined for a sample space in which probabilities are assigned empirically; find the expected value.
comments: For example, find a current data distribution on the number of TV sets per household in the United States, and calculate the expected number of sets per household. How many TV sets would you expect to find in 100 randomly selected households?

For example, find the theoretical probability distribution for the number of correct answers obtained by guessing on all five questions of a multiple-choice test where each question has four choices, and find the expected grade under various grading schemes.
D7B0B7A0DFE60131A9A768A86D17958E.description: (+) Develop a probability distribution for a random variable defined for a sample space in which theoretical probabilities can be calculated; find the expected value.

D7B065E0DFE60131A9A668A86D17958E.description: (+) Calculate the expected value of a random variable; interpret it as the mean of the probability distribution.

D7B01390DFE60131A9A568A86D17958E.description: (+) Define a random variable for a quantity of interest by assigning a numerical value to each event in a sample space; graph the corresponding probability distribution using the same graphical displays as for data distributions.

D7AFBF20DFE60131A9A468A86D17958E.description: Calculate expected values and use them to solve problems

D7AF07A0DFE60131A9A268A86D17958E.description: (+) Use permutations and combinations to compute probabilities of compound events and solve problems.

D7AEA9D0DFE60131A9A168A86D17958E.description: (+) Apply the general Multiplication Rule in a uniform probability model, P(A and B) = P(A)P(B|A) = P(B)P(A|B), and interpret the answer in terms of the model.

D7AE4B20DFE60131A9A068A86D17958E.description: Apply the Addition Rule, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B), and interpret the answer in terms of the model.

comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.
48A1FD821C9B41DB8B1F6CD7ED8EDC47.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.

comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.
C368B2ADB43D4276B620A373EF3DEF0D.description: Look for and make use of structure.

comments: Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

F337069BAD814894A4E896B2384986EE.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

EE94DE6604C44F06ABBE124EA5D74417.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

document.title: New York State K-8 Social Studies Framework

3A4648B17B694A7F8E1A7650F4F809DA.description: Students will explore how communities share resources and services with other communities.

14DB16847D034C12961AD10A0F7E2F64.description: At times, neighboring communities share resources and workers to support multiple communities.

A19C766F34ED4C35BB7298CCA3F38CDA.description: Students will explain the services provided by community workers.

971F8DEC67234FE093BEBA091C95E4C3.description: Students will identify different types of jobs performed in their community.

009151F5CE284A5B8B4072703530F17D.description: Members of a community specialize in different types of jobs that provide goods and/or services to the community. Community workers such as teachers, firefighters, sanitation workers, and police provide services.

5690D16D71514F0B8C1000DF937603BC.description: Students will distinguish between goods and services and identify goods produced in their community.

02915410B812496190656777041338FD.description: Goods are the products a person or group of people makes. Services are actions performed by a person or group of people with a certain skill.

C54E6BE8B2B841739B811EE659319926.description: A community requires the interdependence of many people performing a variety of jobs and services to provide basic needs and wants.

BBE6701B69FA4C8AB53117544E676040.description: Students will explore the purpose of taxes and how they are collected in their community.

7309DBC3C8E04338B09498FD792BF8DA.description: Taxes are collected to provide communities with goods and services.

265C94A29F7E4F1FBA46D5DE4EF0526F.description: Students will examine how consumers react to changes in the prices of goods.

211848223ABA4ED0B380A3B4DA425EF4.description: Scarcity, the price of goods and services, and choice all influence economic decisions made by individuals and communities.

D204A9242DFA44B0A69CDA002F2A3FFA.description: Students will explore economic decision making and the use of money.

2B1229C275CE4C219AA22DA79FD89EDF.description: People make decisions to buy, sell, and use money based on their needs, wants, and the availability of resources.

65C21B208B0F43A6AA15AC9B695A70C3.description: Students will examine how available resources differ in communities (e.g., home-grown food available in rural farm areas vs. shopping in supermarkets).

D3DBEDB4B2F142349A58127E776D4CA4.description: Students will investigate what resources are available in their community and what resources are obtained from neighboring communities.

335F3DFD867240AD8889B5BAFB2DAE95.description: The availability of resources to meet basic needs varies across urban, suburban, and rural communities.

288BA991BDEF420EB31525330054ED54.description: Communities face different challenges in meeting their needs and wants.

2B0D62DC999F48D3AB63F7CD1B64F3A3.description: Students will distinguish between cause and effect and will examine changes in their community in terms of cause and effect (e.g., automobiles and the growth of suburbs, growing population in suburban areas, and reduction of farms).

0E78542397204B67A8A45798A3C099A7.description: Cause-and-effect relationships help us understand the changes in communities.

9195AF6F516F41BFA2A1FD5E10B55283.description: Cause-and-effect relationships help us recount events and understand historical development.

EC1E12C3FED740C5A9295DA97935E7D6.description: Students will develop a time line for their community including important events, such as when the school was built.

356D02F957B14FD69ED450A1E8F0B102.description: Students will examine continuities and changes over time in their community using evidence such as maps, population charts, photographs, newspapers, biographies, artifacts, and other historical materials.

2EA44AF2434E4B988AF1BF6240048383.description: Continuities and changes over time in communities can be examined by interpreting evidence such as maps, population charts, photographs, newspapers, biographies, artifacts, and other historical materials.

182697A0400B40A4A4CE89617695512A.description: Continuities and changes over time in communities can be described using historical thinking, vocabulary, and tools such as time lines.

C007A5AE40E14B49AE67F4D55B65F713.description: Identifying continuities and changes over time can help understand historical developments.

E8B13CB1AF664B3DB7EE87B3D2E25A6B.description: Students will use maps and legends to identify major physical features such as mountains, rivers, lakes, and oceans of the local community, New York, and the nation.

71082C18943843AAB86E4662770A3AD6.description: Students will locate the equator, northern and southern hemispheres, and poles on a globe.

3C0B99BFAF3741EC98CAF1014504CE7E.description: Students will use a compass rose to identify cardinal (North, South, East, West) and intermediate (Northeast, Southeast, Southwest, Northwest) directions on maps and in their community.

9E70A2A398A44B558F85E12D4B19942D.description: The location and place of physical features and man-made structures can be described using symbols and specific geography vocabulary.

4AEBE7A2780544FF9127C5EA639B133F.description: Students will describe the means people create for moving people, goods, and ideas in their communities.

021A797A31FE487C95597A72BDC73C7C.description: Students will explore how humans have positively and negatively impacted the environment of their community though such features as roads, highways, buildings, bridges, shopping malls, railroads, and parks.

718353EE21EB490489B250E79F81A0D8.description: Humans modify the environment of their communities through housing, transportation systems, schools, marketplaces, and recreation areas.

1637C3D3B36741E1BD4BC30E6D1ECCE5.description: Students will compare how different communities in their state or nation have developed and explain how physical features of the community affect the people living there.

402E5B5FFD964E499759B928791FF4F7.description: The location of physical features and natural resources often affects where people settle and may affect how those people sustain themselves.

870F6093E7D747A18815D81DDB32BF13.description: Students will create maps including maps that represent their classroom, school, or community, and maps that illustrate places in stories.

DDBF6AC785B849849DABCE094F2CB970.description: Students will examine how land within a community is used and classify land use as "residential" (used for housing), "industrial" (used to make things), "commercial" (used to provide services), and "recreational" (where people play or do sports).

E5EA939AA6CA4A39925356398260992E.description: Students will locate their communities on maps and/or globes.

4466B8A3ED924C0684AFA5F70D60DE88.description: Urban, suburban, and rural communities can be located on maps, and the geographic characteristics of these communities can be described using symbols, map legends, and geographic vocabulary.

1A3DE2FFA7FF42B2B4367EB90C337210.description: Geography and natural resources shape where and how urban, suburban, and rural communities develop and how they sustain themselves.

F8F805557C934166B87D3DF97BAA75EF.description: Students will identify how adults can provide service to the school and the community at large.

98412CBBC12647D7A1756CA15EA2C1A1.description: Students will explore opportunities to provide service to their school community and the community at large (e.g., beautifying school grounds, writing thank-you notes to helpers).

2077730F573B4D2396FF3921942BFC19.description: Citizens provide service to their community in a variety of ways.

BFA56C34558E49179CCEA4BBF8A94149.description: Students will identify who makes and enforces the rules and laws in their community. They will also explore how leaders make and enforce these rules and laws.

79954B218C5F4D789EF1DD88174C5F3C.description: Communities have leaders who are responsible for making laws and enforcing laws.

A1C540AC53E84DDBBA6DAE80827AC472.description: Students will explain the importance of making fair laws and rules, the benefits of following them, and the consequences of violating them.

2716A9A908AC4127ABA72A5394EEEB55.description: Communities have the responsibility to make and enforce fair laws and rules that provide for the common good.

ED945F67AAB7452290A7587042A12540.description: Communities have rules and laws that affect how they function. Citizens contribute to a community's government through leadership and service.

1F1D664A83CC4D48A6F7C956C2698E8F.description: Students will examine the symbols of the country including the eagle, American flag, the Statue of Liberty, the White House, and Mount Rushmore.

9E6A7A120A4A44938C0A87761DC2984C.description: Symbols of American democracy serve to unite community members.

06E8B89EF64D4E039BA499CB77BA6181.description: Students will participate in voting within the classroom and in school as appropriate.

FDA91BD440ED4071A03536032A993CBC.description: Students will learn about the process of voting and what opportunities adults in the community have for participation.

7274CE4BE3A24F14B4B8A4984E18BCB8.description: The process of holding elections and voting is an example of democracy in action in schools, communities, New York State, and the nation.

AF6153E876884B9CA00C184927749093.description: Students will examine the ways in which the government in their community provides order and keeps people safe and how citizens can demonstrate respect for authority.

5FE72EF4934F4F9795923A243C8D2269.description: Government is established to maintain order and keep people safe. Citizens demonstrate respect for authority by obeying rules and laws.

87028EFEF6F740A2A27C3F08A470B601.description: Students will explore democratic principles such as dignity for all, equality, fairness, and respect for authority and rules, and how those principles are applied to their community.

594D6C3E68E14C889C20E5DDDDC4CFB7.description: The United States is founded on the democratic principles of equality, fairness, and respect for authority and rules.

DF01E0F52F8B4DD59C53F1EE3A7B469E.description: The United States is founded on the principles of democracy, and these principles are reflected in all types of communities.

35CF76BB41F849D5B085D4F2AA4C4103.description: Students will explore how different ideas, talents, perspectives, and culture are shared across their community.

04CC13AB4F004DD8BA0C02F18BE7AF8D.description: A community is strengthened by the diversity of its members with ideas, talents, perspectives, and cultures that can be shared across the community.

4A0D3C6683794478A850297EADE4A6D5.description: Students will identify community events that help promote a common community identity.

4013D3759048438EA90AD30A22E07A1E.description: Students will explore the cultural diversity of their local community by identifying activities that have been introduced by different culture groups.

5FFDA2DD31D04A088AF98D383B122515.description: Students will examine the ethnic and/or cultural groups represented in their classroom.

540F9F76F809490880B0EB757674D378.description: People living in urban, suburban, and rural communities embrace traditions and celebrate holidays that reflect both diverse cultures and a common community identity.

FAFDAD8363C6452CA3D267E9851166F8.description: People share similarities and differences with others in their own community and with other communities.

7284E5ECB95F4E5EB735A3A88BA8F157.description: Students will identify activities that are available in each community type and discuss how those activities affect the people living in that community.

4FCC8457DA34465E91011A5138F13B48.description: Activities available for people living in urban, suburban, and rural communities are different. The type of community a person grows up in will affect a person's development and identity.

7897CE4D033840E2A09FE3D2CA1F9F54.description: By discussing different types of housing (apartment, single-family house, etc.) and the proximity of houses to each other, students will understand the term "population density" and how it applies to different communities.

6FFF01792B4C4885A02EA158BBE4E6C9.description: Suburban communities are on the outskirts of cities, where human population is less dense, and buildings and homes are spaced farther apart.

C375BDAF86214E4389B98300474B5706.description: An urban community, or city, is characterized by dense population and land primarily occupied by buildings and structures used for residential and business purposes.

D7A97A0D842B489B80301A60C90A867B.description: A community is a population of various individuals in a common location. It can be characterized as urban, suburban, or rural. Population density and use of the land are some characteristics that define and distinguish types of communities.

FD0E09FEBAE94626A9CD53126F15411F.description: My Community and Other United States Communities
comments: "My Community and Other Communities" is organized into five units of study—Individual Development and Cultural Identity; Civic Ideals and Practices; Geography, Humans, and the Environment; Time, Continuity, and Change; and Economic Systems. These units represent five of the unifying themes of social studies and may be presented in any order.

B408BEACB78A45B487D327B604109F7A.description: Describe the goods and services that people in the local community produce and those that are produced in other communities.

45E8D9AA595C4B748A3110BD0D353778.description: Describe the role of banks, saving, and borrowing in the economy.

5EF2CC4EEBC2404BA0C9740D493C7D12.description: Describe the resources used to produce goods and provide services in the local community.

B867375E267E4A74AA6D23EC62CA7277.description: Explain how scarcity necessitates decision making; identify the benefits and costs of decisions.

2D4A69CD11CE4BEDAA3F434384407D1E.description: Describe how human activities alter places in a community.

2790A488860040E380F864DF34CBCD33.description: Recognize a process that applies to population and a resulting pattern.

2213A5A4A60A4BF48C80638277E8A667.description: Describe how his/her actions affect the environment of the community; describe how the environment of the community affects human activities.

E14C1B0ED5E94E24B673BA65781DFCE2.description: Distinguish human activities and human-made features from "environments" (natural events or physical features—land, air, and water—that are not directly made by humans).

57376AF67CD14A8EAFC2E6F3C3A81B03.description: Ask geographic questions about where places are located and why they are located there using geographic representations such as maps and models. Describe where places are in relation to each other and describe connections among places.

407BF62F861A4260BCC24FDF6C306A23.description: Describe a historical development in his/her community with specific details including time and place.

9514EABDD86C4C20A8B3BD25DBF47160.description: Describe an event in his/her community.

FA35EB35394445779AB026B90777BD67.description: Identify similarities and differences between his/her community and other communities.

F3303EDDF1754607B6B9F7FD28817A25.description: Identify similarities and differences between communities.

47A16098C72B4A7689ECCFCCF2AFE2DE.description: Recognize and identify patterns of continuity and change in his/her community.

29D018834F7D458187A3BF5DC4EB9344.description: Identify events of the past, present, and future in his/her community.

E113219F8E3648BC9196EF4879F5D2A9.description: Identify change over time in his/her community.

31718CAE39344BB79A4C1158E911E213.description: Identify causes and effects using examples from his/her family life or from the community.

6B3FC23AB4BA4C3B82C040FD490CF6B4.description: Understand the concept of time measurements including minutes, hours, days, weeks, months, years.

C81AABE1261641E9922D6D924DA8AAAB.description: Recognize different forms of evidence used to make meaning in social studies (including sources such as art and photographs, artifacts, oral histories, maps, and graphs).

document.title: New York State P-12 Common Core Learning Standards for Mathematics

D613C080DFE60131A70468A86D17958E.description: Partition circles and rectangles into two, three, or four equal shares, describe the shares using the words halves, thirds, half of, a third of, etc., and describe the whole as two halves, three thirds, four fourths. Recognize that equal shares of identical wholes need not have the same shape.

D6137D70DFE60131A70368A86D17958E.description: Partition a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares and count to find the total number of them.

D6133460DFE60131A70268A86D17958E.description: Recognize and draw shapes having specified attributes, such as a given number of angles or a given number of equal faces. Identify triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons, hexagons, and cubes.
comments: Sizes are compared directly or visually, not compared by measuring.

D612E2B0DFE60131A70168A86D17958E.description: Reason with shapes and their attributes.

D60EFD70DFE60131A6F368A86D17958E.description: Draw a picture graph and a bar graph (with single-unit scale) to represent a data set with up to four categories. Solve simple put-together, take-apart, and compare problems using information presented in a bar graph.

D60F3B00DFE60131A6F468A86D17958E.description: Generate measurement data by measuring lengths of several objects to the nearest whole unit, or by making repeated measurements of the same object. Show the measurements by making a line plot, where the horizontal scale is marked off in whole-number units.

D6126760DFE60131A6FF68A86D17958E.description: Solve word problems involving dollar bills, quarters, dimes, nickels, and pennies, using $ and ¢ symbols appropriately.
comments: Example: If you have 2 dimes and 3 pennies, how many cents do you have?

D61229A0DFE60131A6FE68A86D17958E.description: Tell and write time from analog and digital clocks to the nearest five minutes, using a.m. and p.m.

D611A730DFE60131A6FC68A86D17958E.description: Represent whole numbers as lengths from 0 on a number line diagram with equally spaced points corresponding to the numbers 0, 1, 2, …, and represent whole-number sums and differences within 100 on a number line diagram.

D6115890DFE60131A6FB68A86D17958E.description: Use addition and subtraction within 100 to solve word problems involving lengths that are given in the same units, e.g., by using drawings (such as drawings of rulers) and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

D61107D0DFE60131A6FA68A86D17958E.description: Relate addition and subtraction to length.

D610BE20DFE60131A6F968A86D17958E.description: Measure to determine how much longer one object is than another, expressing the length difference in terms of a standard length unit.

D6107830DFE60131A6F868A86D17958E.description: Estimate lengths using units of inches, feet, centimeters, and meters.

D6102480DFE60131A6F768A86D17958E.description: Measure the length of an object twice, using length units of different lengths for the two measurements; describe how the two measurements relate to the size of the unit chosen.

D60FD3E0DFE60131A6F668A86D17958E.description: Measure the length of an object by selecting and using appropriate tools such as rulers, yardsticks, meter sticks, and measuring tapes.

D60F8C90DFE60131A6F568A86D17958E.description: Measure and estimate lengths in standard units.

D60E3DB0DFE60131A6F068A86D17958E.description: Explain why addition and subtraction strategies work, using place value and the properties of operations.
comments: Explanations may be supported by drawings or objects.

D60DFCC0DFE60131A6EF68A86D17958E.description: Mentally add 10 or 100 to a given number 100—900, and mentally subtract 10 or 100 from a given number 100—900.

D60DB7E0DFE60131A6EE68A86D17958E.description: Add and subtract within 1000, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method. Understand that in adding or subtracting three-digit numbers, one adds or subtracts hundreds and hundreds, tens and tens, ones and ones; and sometimes it is necessary to compose or decompose tens or hundreds.

D60D6480DFE60131A6ED68A86D17958E.description: Add up to four two-digit numbers using strategies based on place value and properties of operations.

D60D12E0DFE60131A6EC68A86D17958E.description: Fluently add and subtract within 100 using strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction.

D60CD490DFE60131A6EB68A86D17958E.description: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to add and subtract.

D60C8E80DFE60131A6EA68A86D17958E.description: Compare two three-digit numbers based on meanings of the hundreds, tens, and ones digits, using >, =, and < symbols to record the results of comparisons.

D60C4230DFE60131A6E968A86D17958E.description: Read and write numbers to 1000 using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form.

D60B9140DFE60131A6E768A86D17958E.description: The numbers 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 700, 800, 900 refer to one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine hundreds (and 0 tens and 0 ones).

D60B51A0DFE60131A6E668A86D17958E.description: 100 can be thought of as a bundle of ten tens — called a "hundred."

D60B0F60DFE60131A6E568A86D17958E.description: Understand that the three digits of a three-digit number represent amounts of hundreds, tens, and ones; e.g., 706 equals 7 hundreds, 0 tens, and 6 ones. Understand the following as special cases:

D60A7D10DFE60131A6E368A86D17958E.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten
comments: Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to whole numbers less than or equal to 1,000,000.

D609AC10DFE60131A6E068A86D17958E.description: Use addition to find the total number of objects arranged in rectangular arrays with up to 5 rows and up to 5 columns; write an equation to express the total as a sum of equal addends.

D6096F50DFE60131A6DF68A86D17958E.description: Determine whether a group of objects (up to 20) has an odd or even number of members, e.g., by pairing objects or counting them by 2s; write an equation to express an even number as a sum of two equal addends.

D60932E0DFE60131A6DE68A86D17958E.description: Work with equal groups of objects to gain foundations for multiplication.

D608F4E0DFE60131A6DD68A86D17958E.description: Fluently add and subtract within 20 using mental strategies. By end of Grade 2, know from memory all sums of two one-digit numbers.
comments: See standard 1.OA.6 for a list of mental strategies.

D60A2560DFE60131A6E268A86D17958E.description: Duplicate and extend (eg., What comes next?) simple patterns using concrete objects.

D6087660DFE60131A6DB68A86D17958E.description: Use addition and subtraction within 100 to solve one- and two-step word problems involving situations of adding to, taking from, putting together, taking apart, and comparing, with unknowns in all positions, e.g., by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

D6082DF0DFE60131A6DA68A86D17958E.description: Represent and solve problems involving addition and subtraction.

D607A390DFE60131A6D868A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

D6075700DFE60131A6D768A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

D60615A0DFE60131A6D368A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

D6055A00DFE60131A6D168A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.
