When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

37F346C909204783B682F4671E33C7EA.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

6DE14B82F83E48F8BE4D3645ADA0926C.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

document.title: New York State K-8 Social Studies Framework

A492FC701EBA4B6C8B14516C6B28F961.description: Students will explain how events of the Civil War led to the establishment of federal supremacy.

1AF7F5C8669D4910A653B6B72E36E8EF.description: Students will examine the aftermath of the war in terms of destruction, impact on population, and economic capacity by comparing impacts of the war on New York State and Georgia.

C2526C272DBD448F8E772F1B7127D7B5.description: Students will examine the roles of women, civilians, and free African Americans during the Civil War.

3705D6849F3D4813A3295C1B2AA4D35F.description: The Civil War impacted human lives, physical infrastructure, economic capacity, and governance of the United States.

C77430C5160C45418E30F260819B850E.description: Students will examine the topography and geographic conditions at Gettysburg and Antietam, and analyze the military strategies employed by the North and the South at Gettysburg or Antietam.

00D7F52413074B238E36B919A1F58E3B.description: Students will examine the enlistment of freed slaves and how it helped to change the course of the Civil War.

EEA124BF618343EBA6572F3CF91640E1.description: Students will examine how the use of various technologies affected the conduct and outcome of the Civil War.

AC6DF03D5B644A7F8AFEA971A9077296.description: Students will examine the goals and content of Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation.

A64D3A6595CC449DB9E88E23ABF9D699.description: Students will compare the advantages and disadvantages of the North and the South at the outset of the Civil War.

1CA673C3929145E4A9561851CCAF8CFA.description: The course and outcome of the Civil War were influenced by strategic leaders from both the North and South, decisive battles, and military strategy and technology that utilized the region's geography.

639014516CFC46A3A892B91DFD472BEC.description: Students will examine the role of New York State in the Civil War, including its contributions to the war effort and the controversy over the draft.

97D6EDEAB349410F964666B8B53B2661.description: Students will identify which states seceded to form the Confederate States of America and will explore the reasons presented for secession. Students will also identify the states that remained in the Union.

5292B3E193674A5AAE32E42D33C55B30.description: Students will examine both long- and short-term causes of the Civil War.

1AAEC0F9AC18423588CB46A4FFE77DC6.description: Perspectives on the causes of the Civil War varied based on geographic region, but the election of a Republican president was one of the immediate causes for the secession of the Southern states.

FF00DF217BA145B88CAC4D6561D91EAA.description: Students will examine growing sectional tensions including the decision in Dred Scott v. Sanford (1857) and the founding of the Republican Party.

88E4D9C21D6C4A9E93643DA3D089AA1A.description: Students will examine attempts at resolving conflicts over whether new territories would permit slavery, including the Missouri Compromise, the Compromise of 1850, and the Kansas-Nebraska Act.

506A229E0B28444C8E20978794FC22BC.description: As the nation expanded geographically, the question of slavery in new territories and states led to increased sectional tensions. Attempts at compromise ended in failure.

81F2EAE3158F4BD482E3C40EE8FF8A24.description: Students will examine regional economic differences as they relate to industrialization.

0D138E3C58F940FD852430697ED49088.description: Early United States industrialization affected different parts of the country in different ways. Regional economic differences and values, as well as different conceptions of the Constitution, laid the basis for tensions between States rights advocates and supporters of a strong federal government.

6EE29ACBC98F423DB4BD320070E63509.description: A Nation Divided: Westward expansion, the industrialization of the North, and the increase of slavery in the South contributed to the growth of sectionalism. Constitutional conflicts between advocates of States rights and supporters of federal power increased tensions in the nation; attempts to compromise ultimately failed to keep the nation together, leading to the Civil War.

AEE345627F9E4D59AE7D7C99B15B5AEB.description: Students will trace the Anti-Rent movement in New York State.

5EAA325D4D314876A28AB32B3DFFC404.description: The Anti-Rent movement in New York State was an attempt by tenant farmers to the protest the landownership system.

741EB65D62DB4E909B5ED51DD1AF6161.description: Students will explain the significance of the Seneca Falls Convention and the Declaration of Sentiments.

3518545B42964D3FB8A3789DCB9084E4.description: Students will examine efforts of women to acquire more rights, including Sojourner Truth, Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Matilda Joslyn Gage, and Susan B. Anthony.

4FA57554054D4D5490B3E0E30E6B41B1.description: Women joined the movements for abolition and temperance and organized to advocate for women's property rights, fair wages, education, and political equality.

BA6279ABA2C642FF847A6DC01C476D25.description: Students will examine the seizure of the ship, La Amistad, carrying enslaved Africans, off the coast of Long Island and the resulting Supreme Court decision in United States v. The Amistad (1841).

CB2B0C04CFF642DE91DB5BD06DBDBA0A.description: Students will investigate New York State and its role in the abolition movement, including the locations of Underground Railroad stations.

492F50335CA143EBA6E0A8BCE82B0AFA.description: Students will examine the impact of Uncle Tom's Cabin on the public perception of slavery.

5014AFD85B9A45D98298DD1205014AD0.description: Students will explore efforts of William Lloyd Garrison, Frederick Douglass, and Harriet Tubman to abolish slavery.

F0143AFA2F6D4E87A20C20FCD16B44E8.description: Students will examine ways in which enslaved Africans organized and resisted their conditions.

DCD23B2EA5534EA39BBF3D823E190295.description: Enslaved African Americans resisted slavery in various ways in the 19th century. The abolitionist movement also worked to raise awareness and generate resistance to the institution of slavery.

52F31772706B4A7B9DDB6B30F6F23B72.description: Students will investigate examples of early 19th-century reform movements such as education, prisons, temperance, and mental health care, examining the circumstances that led to the need for reform.

529B43263687492796A8A02BF71070E6.description: The Second Great Awakening, which had a strong showing in New York, inspired reform movements.

14AAD1DC25554C8691D305885A325608.description: Reform Movements: Social, political, and economic inequalities sparked various reform movements and resistance efforts. Influenced by the Second Great Awakening, New York played a key role in major reform efforts.

007458DBC7F6467D974A4D2C25F820DD.description: Students will examine the policies of New York State toward Native Americans at this time.

368EA2AAC60A44E3A13BD57FEE07BDFA.description: Students will examine the ways in which westward movement had an impact on the lives of women and African Americans.

6C88E0EECD01472A80CBFBF36EE801DC.description: Students will examine examples of Native American resistance to the western encroachment including the Seminole Wars and Cherokee judicial efforts.

0EB51B2BE43F4697A9AA0789FA596DD6.description: Students will examine the conditions faced on the Trail of Tears by the Cherokee and the impact the removal had on their people and culture.

01F8234713754247BF77E0EAB5B4F19C.description: Students will examine the growth of suffrage for white men under Andrew Jackson.

B678F3C6C41A436E8C78DD5739E38FA5.description: Students will examine the Erie Canal as a gateway to westward expansion that resulted in economic growth for New York State, economic opportunities for Irish immigrants working on its construction, and its use by religious groups such as the Mormons to move westward.

06C9582B9C444D8E8423506E419C84B3.description: Westward expansion provided opportunities for some groups while harming others.

7B56FF545FF442C09BD7BE8D1C7EB514.description: Students will compare and evaluate the ways by which Florida, Texas, and territories from the Mexican Cession were acquired by the United States.

7AD12F19742A4772845F5A410D2C3D9F.description: Some Native Americans who aligned with the British during the American Revolution lost land and were forced to move.

C635421B69584EEC960A93034371460E.description: Some Native Americans who aligned with the British during the American Revolution lost land and were forced to move.

A608009AF4D54EE49BD154C3E35B7719.description: Westward Expansion: Driven by political and economic motives, the United States expanded its physical boundaries to the Pacific Ocean between 1800 and 1860. This settlement displaced Native Americans as the frontier was pushed westward.

0E803CC9A8894F5E80ADB5282BABDDEC.description: Students will examine the Monroe Doctrine and its impact on foreign policy.

D16533676CD24A1BBF471D213A57A520.description: Students will examine events of the early nation including Hamilton's economic plan, the Louisiana Purchase, the Supreme Court decision in Marbury v. Madison, and the War of 1812 in terms of testing the strength of the Constitution.

D53DCBAF5A694481B5973B18CB5991B9.description: Foreign and domestic disputes tested the strength of the Constitution, particularly the separation of powers, the system of checks and balances, and the issue of States rights. The United States sought to implement isolationism while protecting the Western Hemisphere from European interference.

B7F93A56534B4B578E1ECF7DAFE72588.description: Students will examine the changes to the New York State Constitution and how they were made during the 19th century.

8A18DF2D1CBA44DFAACE0EEE65B3D5B4.description: Students will examine the evolution of the unwritten constitution such as Washington's creation of the presidential cabinet and the development of political parties.

12133E3194FE4DED85E939D133B77638.description: Students will examine the process for amending the constitution.

38DA2EAE9D184F8BBEAFDB155D17ADE3.description: While the Constitution provides a formal process for change through amendments, the Constitution can respond to change in other ways. The New York State Constitution changed over time with changes in the early 19th century making it more democratic.

165255F2390D46F1808BAD3975C7C4D9.description: Students will identify the individual rights of citizens that are protected by the Bill of Rights.

8ED668E38A0C4D77AB32A913BB32E42E.description: Students will examine how checks and balances work by tracing how a bill becomes a law

65FD7F1402E444E291AF302FF01A8378.description: Students will compare and contrast the powers granted to Congress, the president, and the Supreme Court by the Constitution.

B34EBF23DBA74960953442C73D1C3DCC.description: The Constitution established three branches of government as well as a system of checks and balances that guides the relationship between the branches. Individual rights of citizens are addressed in the Bill of Rights.

2B8DF0A9727B4B1DBD282CA51C536D35.description: Students will identify powers granted to the federal government and examine the language used to grant powers to the states.

576A3C47FD8441F1B09AEF48B1E51442.description: The Constitution outlined a federalist system of government that shares powers among the federal, state, and local governments.

189DFF6070D544BCB7767EDBB9144201.description: The Constitution in Practice: The United States Constitution serves as the foundation of the United States government and outlines the rights of citizens. The Constitution is considered a living document that can respond to political and social changes. The New York Constitution also has been changed over time.

648D1029C21F4C0AB94C7901D81D0DAE.description: the counting of the enslaved African American community for purposes of congressional representation and taxation (the Three-Fifths Compromise)

36348BEBD7AD4D30B63FFDC2A60747F2.description:
Students will examine how key issues were resolved during the Constitutional Convention including:
  • state representation in Congress (Great Compromise or bicameral legislature)
  • the balance of power between the federal and state governments (establishment of the system of federalism)
  • the prevention of parts of government becoming too powerful (the establishment of the three branches)
  • the counting of the enslaved African American community for purposes of congressional representation and taxation (the Three-Fifths Compromise)

635451F181F94503B9A7FB4CFB90EC26.description: Students will examine from multiple perspectives arguments regarding the balance of power between the federal and state governments, the power of government, and the rights of individuals.

F8584B83AB424FA78FF9FEF41C7A65E4.description: Advocates for and against a strong central government were divided on issues of States rights, role/limits of federal power, and guarantees of individual freedoms. Compromises were needed between the states in order to ratify the Constitution.

85CCC9CAD0E040A5B7B3F15DDE3E13E0.description: Students will examine the New York State Constitution, its main ideas and provisions, and its influence on the formation of the United States Constitution.

483FB4A2F161436AB8FF1A48067B8575.description: Students will investigate the successes and failures of the Articles of Confederation, determine why many felt a new plan of government was needed, and explain how the United States Constitution attempted to address the weaknesses of the Articles.

494FF673C0FF4F70AFE8EEC1A497FE67.description: The lack of a strong central government under the Articles of Confederation presented numerous challenges. A convention was held to revise the Articles, the result of which was the Constitution. The Constitution established a democratic republic with a stronger central government.

E9CEF2C8C53646D883E7DA845D503966.description: Throughout the American Revolution, the colonies struggled to address their differing social, political, and economic interests and to establish unity. The Articles of Confederation created a form of government that loosely united the states, but allowed states to maintain a large degree of sovereignty.

0F6FBD045E1E44278516AA6A34B8590F.description: Historical Development of the Constitution: The newly independent states faced political and economic struggles under the Articles of Confederation. These challenges resulted in a Constitutional Convention, a debate over ratification, and the eventual adoption of the Bill of Rights.

B63EB54124EF4AB69C3A9FA6E3330A51.description: Students will examine the terms of the Treaty of Paris, determine what boundary was set for the United States, and illustrate this on a map.

E2F10588652345C8A598A27BA5929AD6.description: Students will examine the strategic importance of the New York colony. Students will examine the American victory at the Battle of Saratoga in terms of its effects on American and British morale and on European views on American prospects for victory in the Revolution.

4AA3FB8E64C04573A10AA77D5B4A1CDB.description: Students will explore the different military strategies used by the Americans and their allies, including various Native American groups, during the American Revolution.

7A7F9E6C2D7A4C2DBE057164F3F9A77E.description: The outcome of the American Revolution was influenced by military strategies, geographic considerations, the involvement of the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) and other Native American groups in the war, and aid from other nations. The Treaty of Paris (1789) established the terms of peace.

F31479C07CAD4BA8B8AD8431706D90B0.description: Students will examine the Declaration of Independence and the arguments for independence stated within it.

7D3C13D57C4D47E180C992238A9FF66C.description: Students will examine the influence Enlightenment ideas such as natural rights and social contract and ideas expressed in Thomas Paine's Common Sense had on colonial leaders in their debates on independence.

686495AEE3FA4146B6331247B048D226.description: Influenced by Enlightenment ideas and their rights as Englishmen, American colonial leaders outlined their grievances against British policies and actions in the Declaration of Independence.

0FA5DD1D14F943E3B71113972D80975B.description: Students will examine the events at Lexington and Concord as the triggering events for the Revolutionary War.

6957605436E8405FB2DA35C66C249FE0.description: Students will compare the proportions of loyalists and patriots in different regions of New York State.

54F4B8B953C4448C84740F0770E80900.description: Students will compare British and colonial patriot portrayals of the Boston Massacre using historical evidence.

7BC0F18868824C2CB2743A83C78F19D2.description: Students will examine actions taken by the British including the Proclamation of 1763, the Quartering Act, the Stamp Act, the Tea Act, and the Coercive Acts, and colonial responses to those actions.

A005418BF2BB49799EE8CAF25DCE5BD5.description: Students will investigate the Albany Congress and the Albany Plan of Union as a plan for colonial unification.

50BA6E6F09884F018522CA6DF3B97A82.description: Stemming from the French and Indian War, the British government enacted and attempted to enforce new political and economic policies in the colonies. These policies triggered varied colonial responses, including protests and dissent.

135A2871957E4ACAB5AF286D9ABFC8B1.description: Students will identify the issues stemming from the Zenger Trial that affected the development of individual rights in colonial America.

4052E1994215484C81EB9E9BAF29ADAA.description: Students will examine the changing economic relationship between the colonies and Great Britain, including mercantilism and the practice of salutary neglect.

1CE7FF0D78374BD6B3C56034A586428E.description: Students will locate battles fought between France and Great Britain during the 17th and 18th centuries, and how this led to the importance of British troops in the area of New York.

5DA41D7C803C41188226084D098CDFDC.description: Conflicts between France and Great Britain in the 17th and 18th centuries in North America altered the relationship between the colonies and Great Britain.

035ACC0766214391B6C44F7CE64A2018.description: American Independence: Growing tensions over political power and economic issues sparked a movement for independence from Great Britain. New York played a critical role in the course and outcome of the American Revolution.

FD9CA9AC5D114524ADC48225C3748998.description: Within the context of New York history, students will distinguish between indentured servitude and slavery.

ED505E93CB464CD18E99BBBD6D3C0D1F.description: Students will investigate different methods enslaved Africans used to survive and resist their conditions, including slave revolts in New York.

754EF807B7964236B349ADF089444B39.description: Students will explain why and where slavery grew over time in the United States and students will examine the living conditions of slaves, including those in New York State.

A13BC16D0A894C279064FBBB47E11187.description: Students will describe the conditions of the Middle Passage.

E1D7E62466614D329D8A154C57A302F0.description: Over the course of the 17th and 18th centuries, slavery grew in the colonies. Enslaved Africans utilized a variety of strategies to both survive and resist their conditions.

4AD2CAED2A7C497A9A1EF318861C556A.description: Student will examine Dutch contributions to American society including acceptance of a diverse population, a degree of religious toleration and right to petition. Students will examine Dutch relations with Native Americans.

98F9500041CE407D88A88ED6007E1193.description: Students will examine the changing status and role of African Americans under the Dutch and English colonial systems.

2527E0E36AE746A6B143AB0E8F664DEF.description: Students will compare and contrast the early Dutch settlements with French settlements and with those in the subsequent British colony of New York in terms of political, economic, and social characteristics, including an examination of the patroon system.

F22D3743E21B4645977D708FDC408115.description: In New York, the Dutch established settlements along the Hudson River and the French established settlements in the Champlain Valley. Dutch contributions to American society were long-lasting.

150AC02C92424C709868056D85A48074.description: Students will examine the economic, social and political characteristics of each colonial region.

6DBAD3EFDBE540788A839D993E93CBD6.description: Students will investigate the reasons for colonization and the role of geography in the development of each colonial region.

76AF9947EAB04A938A29D695BA47D57D.description: European nations established colonies in North America for economic, religious, and political reasons. Differences in climate, physical features, access to water, and sources of labor contributed to the development of different economies in the New England, Middle, and Southern Colonies.

96220A54490E4B8CA5713B01EC39E881.description: Students will examine the major reasons Native American societies declined in population and lost land to the Europeans.

9510C042B3EE408BA9A350E9F3329D95.description: Students will investigate other Native American societies found in their locality and their interactions with European groups.

103E0DD75FA543F2B4B5EC4702690774.description: Students will compare and contrast British interactions with southern New England Algonquians, Dutch interactions and French interactions with Algonquians and Iroquoians, and Spanish interactions with Muscogee.

0CB83910F16441D192EC99A9ECC1A25B.description: Different European groups had varied interactions and relationships with the Native American societies they encountered. Native American societies suffered from losses of life due to disease and conflict and loss of land due to the encroachment of European settlers and differing conceptions of property and land ownership.

556C7FDC85BC496AA3705CC6B0009977.description: Students will examine the voyage of Columbus, leading to the Columbian Exchange and the voyages of other explorers such as Champlain, Hudson, and Verrazano.

07E49AF156404278ADC0A50382BFF78A.description: Students will explain the significance of the technological developments and scientific understandings that improved European exploration such as the caravel, magnetic compass, astrolabe, and Mercator projection.

26A227A4C2F84CB2A7FC3FC01BC54E3D.description: Social, economic, and scientific improvements helped European nations launch an Age of Exploration.

D9F6FD4E601B428795B75D5C4C5C15BB.description: Colonial Developments: European exploration of the New World resulted in various interactions with Native Americans and in colonization. The American colonies were established for a variety of reasons and developed differently based on economic, social, and geographic factors. Colonial America had a variety of social structures under which not all people were treated equally.

E9439FB2F5E14FDDBA4D83928E2B6BCD.description: Students will examine the various Native American culture groups located within what became New York State, and the influence geographic factors had on their development.

FFB0E4AE07454DF899FD499D0D8D192A.description: Students will compare and contrast different Native American culture groups with a focus on the influence geographic factors had on their development.

7747E803E2F34D90A1365FFBCC52A398.description: Students will examine theories of human settlement of the Americas.

8D85B58AAAC14AF5BE8BE0FA0961E454.description: Geography and climate influenced the migration and cultural development of Native Americans. Native Americans in North America settled into different regions and developed distinct cultures.

991B27C528EA4B8482EDDEBF2A2425CB.description: Native Americans: The physical environment and natural resources of North America influenced the development of the first human settlements and the culture of Native Americans. Native American societies varied across North America.
comments: For this document, the term "Native Americans" is used with the understanding it could say "American Indians."

B010A73A17FD44D39C9A092AD8B44521.description: History of the United States and New York – I
comments: In Grades 7 and 8, students will examine the United States and New York State through a historical lens. The two-year sequence is arranged chronologically beginning with the settlement of North America by Native Americans and ending with an examination of the United States in the 21st century. Although the courses emphasize the skill of chronological reasoning and causation, the courses also integrate the skills and content from geography, politics, economy, and culture into the study of history.
For this document, the term "Native Americans" is used with the understanding it could say "American Indians."

88A5378E3EDE43528DDD199F22A14B90.description: Identify how social and political responsibilities developed in American society.

678C6E2D44974FF6A0525CC5EC4CFF2D.description: Identify how people in power have acted to extend the concept of freedom, the practice of social justice, and the protection of human rights in United States history.

D3011CD394F447C6ADFA00D2965E892D.description: Identify situations in which social actions are required and determine an appropriate course of action.

DE2709713CF640A798E4563ADF8B73D4.description: Participate in negotiating and compromising in the resolution of differences and conflict; introduce and examine the role of conflict resolution.

454F4962B7254CA0A9C8B5F761CC73BB.description: Identify, describe, and compare the role of the individual in social and political participation in, and as an agent of, historical change at various times and in various locations in colonial North America and in the early history of the United States.

977BD032452B43B582DB677437784F4F.description: Identify and explain different types of political systems and ideologies used at various times in colonial history and the early history of the United States and explain the role of individuals and key groups in those political and social systems.

2F1D09CDFE24412286A2501F2D11CFBB.description: Participate in activities that focus on a classroom, school, community, state, or national issue or problem.

23AFE32173D74F11B99DD702198CC881.description: Demonstrate respect for the rights of others in discussions and classroom; respectfully disagree with other viewpoints. Use techniques and strategies to be an active and engaged member of class discussions of fellow classmates' views and statements with teacher support.

A956E76054804704B9F26DCB6C2C75DC.description: Explain how government policies affected the economies in colonial and early United States history.

B74CC72CDEB2454FBD6208F85E7BEE8F.description: Examine data on the state of employment, unemployment, inflation, total production, income, and economic growth in the economy.

FB58328F25674731B4D8664C775A5915.description: Examine the role of institutions such as joint stock companies, banks, and the government in the development of the United States economy before the Civil War.

B57C0C1F932F438EA57A854C35AA5B9A.description: Describe the role that competition has in the determination of prices and wages; identify other factors that help to determine prices.

B87733D48B8A4F1D8FC750CE1D156F48.description: Identify examples of buyers and sellers in product, labor, and financial markets.

9B9E13A2376348D18AFC3A22918AB0B2.description: Explain how economic decisions affect the well-being of individuals, businesses, and society; evaluate alternative approaches or solutions to economic issues in terms of benefits and costs for different groups of people.

F6F0D49C66384A53B4E9E3D11FC4F2FF.description: Describe the spatial organization of place considering the historical, social, political, and economic implication of that organization. Describe how boundaries and definition of location are historically constructed.

2846279B528141C2BEFFA23F33167D23.description: Characterize and analyze changing interconnections among places and regions.

DA29210168BF48B8B31845F7F21A1BB6.description: Recognize and analyze how characteristics (cultural, economic, and physical-environmental) of regions affect the history of the United States.

62B3535C7C0B472FAB2BA44A24CB589E.description: Identify and analyze how environments affect human activities and how human activities affect physical environments in the United States.

E8322852AB474F7898E1D7513640A1D8.description: Distinguish human activities and human-made features from "environments" (natural events or physical features—land, air, and water—that are not directly made by humans) and describe the relationship between human activities and the environment.

AFEB92172B0D4402BFA1597E3DDE72EF.description: Use location terms and geographic representations such as maps, photographs, satellite images, and models to describe where places in early United States history were in relation to each other, to describe connections among places, and to evaluate effectively the benefits of particular places for purposeful activities.

5507F1CA08714607BBD3612A2C3BDC18.description: Understand the role that periodization and region play in developing the comparison of colonial settlements in North America. Identify general characteristics that can be employed to conduct comparative analysis of case studies in the early history of the United States.

A2D127DAF7E44A83B46133A69B6022CD.description: Connect historical developments to specific circumstances of time and place and to broader regional, national, or global processes.

3DB26B4928404C1BAF77FBD30F5D022D.description: Identify how the relationship among geography, economics, and history helps to define a context for events in the study of the United States.

DCC4C83F5EEC4BBB977286C8C5B0FC98.description: Describe, compare, and evaluate multiple historical developments within the United States in various chronological and geographical contexts.

C0069A1E0AAE4C1EADA4B2618CC676E8.description: Identify and categorize multiple perspectives on a given historical experience.

737683006C094A0BAED9D6A443710FE9.description: Identify a region of colonial North America or the early United States by describing multiple characteristics common to places within it, and then identify other similar regions (inside or outside the continental United States) with similar characteristics.

71379792D4B5452FB3675B5533041F70.description: Identify models of historical periodization that historians use to categorize events.

2EF0D1BEE24147E4A4D39021431A3628.description: Identify patterns of continuity and change as they relate to larger historical process and themes.

D281D9F5501340A89A750AF45779C1AA.description: Recognize that changing the periodization affects the historical narrative.

8D0FF26B934C490BA60462A9BF8C843A.description: Recognize, analyze, and evaluate dynamics of historical continuity and change over periods of time.

AC6608A11D914F31B6AC1A4F710156CD.description: Distinguish between long-term and immediate causes and effects of an event from current events or history.

E1D54139E9FC458E811BAEAAF653BC1A.description: Identify and analyze the relationship between multiple causes and effects.

85F62B3C7718449B9965F798974221B8.description: Identify causes and effects using examples from current events, grade-level content, and historical events.

995D9C370D034E36A66101A1EFB4FD6F.description: Employ mathematical skills to measure time by years, decades, centuries, and millennia; to calculate time from the fixed points of the calendar system (B.C.E. and C.E.); and to interpret the data presented in time lines.

6BBC230D240C4FC49CC1BF47C7EC1845.description: Identify how events are related chronologically to one another in time and explain the ways in which earlier ideas and events may influence subsequent ideas and events.

55D8EEF2E2E749FCA550F406AAB51ADE.description: Recognize an argument and identify supporting evidence related to a specific social studies topic. Examine arguments related to a specific social studies topic from multiple perspectives. Recognize that the perspective of the argument's author shapes the selection of evidence used to support it.

0B759244F120468385F8AE6259DD9D34.description: Make inferences and draw general conclusions from evidence.

A8DB4FF547C748D49F29C6E9842CABB1.description: Describe and analyze arguments of others with supports.

7F661F61BB8042959B2B06E4256FF59D.description: Analyze evidence in terms of historical context, content, authorship, point of view, purpose, and format; identify bias; explain the role of bias and audience in presenting arguments or evidence.

B3646CDA62E7480688DEB177B87C4923.description: Identify, select, and evaluate evidence about events from diverse sources (including written documents, works of art, photographs, charts and graphs, artifacts, oral traditions, and other primary and secondary sources).

559C9F5B4C4044B5B06B3E38CEEA508E.description: Define and frame questions about the United States that can be answered by gathering, using, and interpreting evidence.

document.title: New York State K-8 Social Studies Framework

805ACC9EF8F6431AA7B505C697F39307.description: Students will examine how various technologies affected trade and exchanges. Some examples are types of ships including junks and caravels, improvements to ships such as sails and rudders, navigation tools such as the compass and astrolabe, and gunpowder.

D5908CE42B7342D6AE4202E21BB9C230.description: Complex societies and civilizations adapted and designed technologies for transportation that allowed them to cross challenging landscapes and move people and goods efficiently.

0F7C21D67E61498CB066ED94927B28AE.description: Students will examine the spread of the Black Death (Bubonic Plague) as a result of interregional exchange and its impact on various regions within Afro-Eurasia using a variety of sources such as maps, poetry, and other primary source documents.

8AF664E7E8664F5F8C225B514C71F323.description: Students will examine the methods used by the Mongols to enable them to rule over a diverse population noting how Mongol rule expanded trade.

FC78A6736ABD4D94A8611DD204FC49D6.description: Students will map the extent of the Mongol Empire at the height of its power.

D64C1329C8244F3684FB4EFDAF21C719.description: The Mongol conquests in Eurasia fostered connections between the East and the West and the Mongols served as important agents of change and cultural diffusion.

4C6E359A641E48A6A19D3C4178A3EF3B.description: Students will study interregional travelers such as Marco Polo, Ibn Battuta, Mansa Musa, and Zheng He and examine why they traveled, the places visited, what was learned, and what was exchanged as a result of their travel.

7560977A2BEA4308BF975F10B105AA0C.description: Students will examine how the location of resources helped determine the location of trade routes and the economic impact of the exchange of resources.

84E64D66748E4F3891C106B41FFB5456.description: Students will create maps that illustrate items exchanged and ideas spread along the Silk Roads, across the Indian Ocean, and on the Trans-Saharan trade routes.

AC113F85317C4C93A7FEE0E6C307DEB8.description: The Silk Roads, the Indian Ocean, and the Trans-Saharan routes formed the major Afro-Eurasian trade networks connecting the East and the West. Ideas, people, technologies, products, and diseases moved along these routes.

5DABA5434EC1498EB6C9D45778FAC6F5.description: Interactions Across the Eastern Hemisphere (ca. 600 C.E. – ca. 1450): Trade networks promoted the exchange and diffusion of language, belief systems, tools, intellectual ideas, inventions, and diseases.

E9D0FD12669E4036B2D866DD27EC0AC7.description: Students will examine the conflict of the Crusades from three different perspectives: feudal Europe, Byzantine, and Islamic.

59255990E87945459C89036F4F1ECDAE.description: Students will examine the three distinct cultural regions of the Mediterranean world in terms of their location, the extent of each region at the height of its power, and the political, economic, and social interactions between these regions.

7F170642BEE44A5CBAE391C2ECF67BE5.description: Competition and rivalry over religious, economic, and political control over the holy lands led to conflict such as the Crusades.

C3D79825B6FA4B418CCAC7BD206539C4.description: Students will examine the Umayyad and Abbasid caliphates, noting how the introduction of Islam changed the societies and cultures each conquered, blending with those societies and cultures and creating dynamic new Islamic societies and cultures.

E3A5145693054503893847879CDCC4A4.description: Islam spread within the Mediterranean region from southwest Asia to northern Africa and the Iberian Peninsula.

A862D37EFD474A8C9C2E20703021C028.description: Students will examine how the Byzantine Empire preserved elements of the Roman Empire by blending Roman traditions with Greek culture and developed a Christian faith, known as Orthodox Christianity, which united Church and state authority in the person of the emperor.

B9F64FB6D6C84C0DAC0C3FA015DA1A0F.description: The Byzantine Empire preserved elements of the Roman Empire, controlled lands within the Mediterranean basin, and began to develop Orthodox Christianity.

21859F3C69CD40FD9801CA47305EBA3C.description: Students will examine reasons for the fall of the Roman Empire and the development of feudalism in Western Europe, including efforts to restore the empire, the decentralization of political authority, and the role of the Christian Church in providing some measure of central authority.

365A23A5BFF9422D9FA90FE6EFA3F4F0.description: Overexpansion, corruption, invasions, civil wars, and discord led to the fall of Rome. Feudalism developed in Western Europe in reaction to a need for order and to meet basic needs.

4CD0EA96252A491CBD6EAECB24A777C6.description: Mediterranean World: Feudal Western Europe, The Byzantine Empire, and the Islamic Caliphates (ca. 600 C.E. – ca. 1450): The Mediterranean world was reshaped with the fall of the Roman Empire. Three distinct cultural regions developed: feudal Western Europe, the Byzantine Empire, and the Islamic caliphates. These regions interacted with each other and clashed over control of holy lands.

E83A2AA836F549D0B5CFA7C2E49B4B48.description: Students will examine how cultural achievements of these civilizations have influenced contemporary societies.

3556C06238AE48ABB6850A93FE60A69E.description: Students will examine evidence related to the Qin, Han, and Greco-Roman (Athens and Roman Empire) civilizations and determine if these civilizations have experienced a golden age.

0E5B682F18DC449DBDA1C9E4C66369E9.description: A period of peace, prosperity, and cultural achievements may be indicative of a golden age.

C2513E01130E46EEAB4DFD89BEE73880.description: Students will examine the similarities and differences in the political systems of Chinese (Qin, Han) and Greco-Roman (Athens, Sparta, Roman Republic, Roman Empire) classical civilizations.

EB2E43E139D64A09973553AAC538F694.description: Political structures were developed to establish order, to create and enforce laws, and to enable decision making.

7DD7C9D665704BA58D670D53EF8A75FE.description: Students will compare and contrast the similarities and differences of the Chinese (Qin, Han) and Greco-Roman classical civilizations by examining religion, job specialization, cities, government, language/record keeping system, technology, and social hierarchy.

803D8F47DDC541FF8F30DAC7B7EE3B7D.description: Students will locate the classical civilizations on a map and identify geographic factors that influenced the extent of their boundaries, locate their cities on a map, and identify their political structures

0B9D271C296C41CD9826C10635F2616A.description: Geographic factors influence the development of classical civilizations and their political structures.

B8ED300807514CDD894F835E3443B0AA.description: Comparative Classical Civilizations in the Eastern Hemisphere (ca. 600 B.C.E. – ca. 500 C.E.): As complex societies and civilizations change over time, their political and economic structures evolve. A golden age may be indicated when there is an extended period of time that is peaceful, prosperous, and demonstrates great cultural achievements.

A71ED83DEF8840A3882DBAC7EF446903.description: Students will explore the influence of various belief systems on contemporary cultures and events.

8BA8FCCA30E3469DB96C761ED187290D.description: Students will be able to identify similarities and differences across belief systems including their effect on social order and gender roles.

3601651B3ABC4753BF0906F070BADAE2.description: Belief systems and religions often are used to unify groups of people and may affect social order and gender roles.

720BDD90566C435999F4A11955069D5B.description: Students will study the belief systems of Judaism, Christianity, Islam, Buddhism, Hinduism, and Confucianism by looking at where the belief system originated, when it originated, founder(s) if any, and the major tenets, practices, and sacred writings or holy texts for each. (Note: Although not within this historic period, students may also study Sikhism and other major belief systems at this point.)

18CF89345CE248F889D6B9E0298FEE2C.description: Belief systems and religions are based on a set of mutually held values.

FE87DA3E2BAD406EA46EAC2F5897D60B.description: Civilizations and complex societies developed belief systems and religions that have similar as well as different characteristics.

42C79C7E285443F582A874160AF61ED3.description: Comparative World Religions (ca. 2000 B.C.E – ca. 630 C.E): Major religions and belief systems developed in the Eastern Hemisphere. There were important similarities and differences between these belief systems.

E28D7EAEA9F44A3586121C1A2C3D4E35.description: Students will examine the unique achievements of each of the selected complex societies and civilizations that served as lasting contributions.

7F0CD1A6281C4571BDD253FB17FFC4B4.description: Students will compare and contrast the gender roles, access to wealth and power, and division of labor within the political and social structures of the selected river valley societies and civilizations.

7D92D265FADB43B4AA827EF4A86E78DD.description: Political and social hierarchies influenced the access that groups and individuals had to power, wealth, and jobs and influenced their roles within a society.

695567E8E4064CD8817DED7AFDD909D2.description: Students will explore how the selected complex societies and civilizations adapted to and modified their environment to meet their basic needs of food, clothing, and shelter.

0103109095EF4200998F992B308BA471.description: Mesopotamia, Yellow River valley, Indus River valley, and Nile River valley complex societies and civilizations adapted to and modified their environment to meet the needs of their population.

51F1A668C4014AD28DD40C46F8DE3C0F.description: Students will explore at least two river valley societies and civilizations: one in the Middle East (Mesopotamia or Nile river valley), one in South Asia (Indus river valley), or one in East Asia (Yellow river valley) by examining archaeological and historical evidence to compare and contrast characteristics of these complex societies and civilizations.

425E7F8E9025428EB1EF0ABC422D11E9.description: Complex societies and civilizations share the common characteristics of religion, job specialization, cities, government, language/record keeping system, technology, and social hierarchy. People in Mesopotamia, Yellow River valley, Indus River valley, and Nile River valley developed complex societies and civilizations.

52A8B22745EA4CCEA7FEDCCAC6E08906.description: Humans living together in settlements develop shared customs, beliefs, ideas, and languages that give identity to the group.

A439C2457C714402911FF7B092C5EA1E.description: Early River Valley Civilizations in the Eastern Hemisphere (ca. 3500 B.C.E. – ca. 500 B.C.E.): Complex societies and civilizations developed in the Eastern Hemisphere. Although these complex societies and civilizations have certain defining characteristics in common, each is also known for unique cultural achievements and contributions. Early human communities in the Eastern Hemisphere adapted to and modified the physical environment.

2BC6A43775864553A4A0DC3D707D7368.description: Students will determine if the Neolithic Revolution is a turning point in world history using various forms of evidence.

C2EB2CB518F04931B5EB98AC18256DE4.description: Historians use archaeological and other types of evidence to investigate patterns in history and identify turning points. A turning point can be an event, era, and/or development in history that has brought about significant social, cultural, ecological, political, or economic change.

F96AC4D0C99845D3960DA3B46263EBC5.description: Students will compare the use of tools and animals, types of dwellings, art, and social organizations of early peoples and distinguish between the Paleolithic Age and Neolithic Age.

5ED40307F10B4A038C33FCC6753B0E3C.description: Students will be introduced to pastoral nomadic peoples as a culture type that existed throughout history.

C99F3F0C68654B42A071FAA5070B96F9.description: Students will explore the early human migration patterns and settlements through the use of multiple maps and the examination of various forms of archaeological evidence.

371A57A2410F4FBE9DCB48A131702A4F.description: The Neolithic Revolution was marked by technological advances in agriculture and domestication of animals that allowed people to form semi-sedentary and sedentary settlements.

10DE13AED76241268609A7C2038807F6.description: Early peoples in the Eastern Hemisphere are often studied by analyzing artifacts and archaeological features. Archaeologists engage in digs and study artifacts and features in a particular location to gather evidence about a group of people and how they lived at a particular time.

01BE6C8416214363A8B489028C07D4AB.description: Human populations that settled along rivers, in rainforests, along coastlines, in deserts, and in mountains made use of the resources and the environment around them in developing distinct ways of life.

1A8BFE23D86D4C0F856B35646A45F7F2.description: The First Humans Through the Neolithic Revolution in the Eastern Hemisphere: The first humans modified their physical environment as well as adapted to their environment.

D05197B178174CD79A25C7D93E52F2C6.description: Students will examine current political and environmental issues in a region or country of the Eastern Hemisphere being studied.

514A4E598B494D449A2D5356157D6C1D.description: Issues and problems experienced in the regions of the Eastern Hemisphere have roots in the past.

D582EB67385B47FD8E9CDC9A194CF881.description: To understand scale, students will work with maps at a variety of scales so they can compare patterns in population density and land use, economic activity, and political connections across the present-day Eastern Hemisphere, within a region of the Eastern Hemisphere, and in a specific country. In doing so, students will examine maps of the hemisphere, three regions within the present-day Eastern Hemisphere, and one specific country within each region.

5A598B20C5B0494598605D7F23B6ECA5.description: Students will use physical, climate, and vegetation maps in combination with population density, land use, and resource distribution maps in order to discern patterns in human settlement, economic activity, and the relationship to scarcity of resources in the present-day Eastern Hemisphere.

84AE775866CF4103B0D6219F39C6C6B0.description: The physical environment influences human population distribution, land use, economic activities, and political connections.

F3FF846BE06042968163638AD1D87FCA.description:
The Eastern Hemisphere can be divided into regions. Regions are areas that share common identifiable characteristics, such as physical, political, economic, or cultural features. Regions within the Eastern Hemisphere include:
  • Middle East (North Africa and Southwest Asia)
  • Sub-Saharan Africa
  • Europe (West, North, South, Central, and Southeast)
  • Russia and the Independent States (Russia, Caucasia, Central Asia, the region of Belarus, Moldova, and Ukraine)
  • East Asia (People's Republic of China, North Korea, South Korea, Japan, and Taiwan)
  • Southeast Asia (Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, Thailand, Myanmar [Burma], Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Brunei, Philippines)
  • South Asia (Afghanistan, Pakistan, India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan)
  • Oceania (Australia, New Zealand, the Pacific)

1074C7511A204A0CA91C7D1EE44B2055.description: Maps can be used to represent varied climate zones, landforms, bodies of water, and resources of the Eastern Hemisphere.

B8650C40B43F46C8A08935B82C69A15B.description: Present-Day Eastern Hemisphere Geography: The diverse geography of the Eastern Hemisphere has influenced human culture and settlement patterns in distinct ways. Human communities in the Eastern Hemisphere have adapted to or modified the physical environment.

comments: Grade 6 Social Studies is based on the geography and history of the Eastern Hemisphere, including the development of cultures, civilizations, and empires; interaction between societies; and the comparison of trends in government and economics. It also incorporates some elements of other social sciences.

1ED32B9EC2074DEAAFDC5C969577680B.description: Develop an understanding of an interdependent global community by developing awareness and/or engaging in the political process as it relates to a global context.

91FFF60473F940A99A09C4686EC9DDB9.description: Identify rights and responsibilities of citizens within societies in the Eastern Hemisphere.

8917A87C2E3947CAA5363ECA3CC09654.description: Describe the roles of people in power in the Eastern Hemisphere both historically and currently. Identify ways that current figures can influence people's rights and freedom.

25C72EE808A9412AB15F26E2F7B4563C.description: Identify situations with a global focus in which social actions are required and suggest solutions.

EAAED65F929B424EABF887DA8B5DC88F.description: Participate in negotiating and compromising in the resolution of differences and conflict; introduce and examine the role of conflict resolution.

412E64080E304ABEAB45E5F29E460BA6.description: Identify and describe opportunities for and the role of the individual in social and political participation at various times and in various locations in the Eastern Hemisphere.

66127C42E8624C9584EBE3CC7E2747C9.description: Identify and explore different types of political systems and ideologies used at various times and in various locations in the Eastern Hemisphere and identify the role of individuals and key groups in those political and social systems.

7E24111057734A6AACC4681787AA7230.description: Participate in activities that focus on a localized issue or problem in a country in the Eastern Hemisphere.

5299032BC8DF4C58BDFBF278776A66C1.description: Demonstrate respect for the rights of others in discussion and classroom debates regardless of whether one agrees with the other viewpoint. Consider alternate views in discussion.

8042CBE2639649E88E195B09B29951D7.description: Describe government decisions that impact economies in case studies from the Eastern Hemisphere.

97E7E2B5B2D34AD78C8F12794830164A.description: Provide examples of unemployment, inflation, total production, income, and economic growth in economies in the Eastern Hemisphere.

2973352D62AB43EFAA57E98DDC693B1F.description: Examine the role of job specialization and trade historically and during contemporary times in the Eastern Hemisphere.

500DA9534F7C4CC0AA4021442838CF55.description: Compare market economies to other economic systems in the Eastern Hemisphere.

34D3F1D5B3714D60A8A0D512E7854A69.description: Examine the role that various types of resources (human capital, physical capital, and natural resources) have in providing goods and services.

4856727A06734A6782707693F7B233CB.description: Explain how scarcity necessitates decision making; employ examples from the Eastern Hemisphere to illustrate the role of scarcity historically and in current events; compare through historical examples the costs and benefits of economic decisions.

CA5216E8B8584BE1AE1152BA32354351.description: Describe the spatial organization of place considering the historical, social, political, and economic implication of that organization. Recognize that boundaries and definitions of location are historically constructed.

AEE6E54B1FD04C6EA0F9EE72403CF69D.description: Describe how human activities alter places and regions in the Eastern Hemisphere.

30495BE1529E4FEB963BABC3D1274B9E.description: Recognize and explain how characteristics (cultural, economic, and physical-environmental) of regions affect the history of societies in the Eastern Hemisphere.

604EA81B361444F48FE1A527C9F9EB5D.description: Identify and describe how environments affect human activities and how human activities affect physical environments through the study of cases in the Eastern Hemisphere.

ADA698B72AAF433D91A1C8F026F68947.description: Distinguish human activities and human-made features from "environments" (natural events or physical features—land, air, and water—that are not directly made by humans) in the Eastern Hemisphere; identify the relationship between human activities and the environment.

9A0053B40B5245BF99CC254FC75D8EAA.description: Use location terms and geographic representations such as maps, photographs, satellite images, and models to describe where places in the Eastern Hemisphere are in relation to each other, to describe connections among places, and to evaluate the benefits of particular places for purposeful activities.

6D54A0A0B2A54E0F8D3ED174A90E5E77.description: Understand the role that periodization and region play in developing the comparison of historical civilizations. Identify general characteristics that can be employed to conduct comparative analysis of case studies in the Eastern Hemisphere in the same historical period with teacher support.

E6B850592DA14625853A5ED4A856E916.description: Describe historical developments in the history of the Eastern Hemisphere with specific references to circumstances of time and place and to connections to broader regional or global processes.

B5BC07462D154131B55E131EDEF24F04.description: Identify how the relationship among geography, economics, and history helps to define a context for events in the study of the Eastern Hemisphere.

8B091D694B1B438EBDF7BF189B24D841.description: Describe and compare multiple events in the history of the Eastern Hemisphere in societies in similar chronological contexts and in various geographical contexts.

8CC02B4965AF47A6BE023F1866948975.description: Categorize and evaluate divergent perspectives on an individual historical event.

EAA42B1A197648589546C60B74B836D1.description: Identify a region in the Eastern Hemisphere by describing a characteristic that places within it have in common, and then compare it to other regions.

D2F15266C3EA4AF0B5817ED1F4A374CA.description: Understand that historians use periodization to categorize events. Describe general models of periodization in history.

2A47E1937A8F4B80B0DE9E2B560C1E00.description: Identify the relationships of patterns of continuity and change to larger historical processes and themes.

FDBEAAB64B0F4EDD8C823246E8A948C5.description: Compare histories in different places in the Eastern Hemisphere utilizing time lines. Identify ways that changing periodization affects the historical narrative.

ACC0F8E5DF104C00812355E0432D7A04.description: Recognize and analyze the dynamics of historical continuity and change over periods of time. Identify the role of turning points as an important dynamic in historical change.

81E14465FF144E07B8CB03959EBED8DE.description: Distinguish between long-term and immediate causes and effects of an event from current events or history.

D0AF5566FEED4E4A8A5AA03990BDBBF0.description: Identify and classify the relationship between multiple causes and multiple effects.

1ECA3D74903848CA81443DD1A18BEBCD.description: Identify causes and effects from current events, grade-level content, and historical events.

1108BED937824E5CBC962B055FEDFBD4.description: Employ mathematical skills to measure time by years, decades, centuries, and millennia; to calculate time from the fixed points of the calendar system (B.C.E. and C.E.); and to interpret the data presented in time lines with teacher support.

232C2C3E50BC4130B3C12691CD413190.description: Identify ways that events are related chronologically to one another in time.

666CC8328DB4497CB5B44D034F3BAD8F.description: Recognize arguments on specific social studies topics and identify evidence to support the arguments. Examine arguments related to a specific social studies topic from multiple perspectives.

4FE744A48C24475F939E4AF9E4B6815B.description: Identify implicit ideas and draw inferences with support.

C80918C3869347E9A0A85A3EFAD9A29D.description: Identify evidence and explain content, authorship, point of view, purpose, and format; identify bias; explain the role of bias and potential audience.

A8D25108026A4FDF97BB9384DC239D13.description: Identify, effectively select, and analyze different forms of evidence used to make meaning in social studies (including primary and secondary sources such as art and photographs, artifacts, oral histories, maps, and graphs).

04F7BCAAD7944E6F8F12648D3362343D.description: Develop and frame questions about topics related to historical events occurring in the Eastern Hemisphere that can be answered by gathering, using, and interpreting evidence.

document.title: Learning Standards for Mathematics, Science, and Technology - Standards 6 & 7

D80A0CF0DFE60131AA4068A86D17958E.description: Presenting Results: Using a variety of media to present the solution and to communicate the results.

D80B8CB0DFE60131AA4568A86D17958E.description: Realizing Ideas: Constructing components or models, arriving at a solution, and evaluating the result.

D80AB300DFE60131AA4268A86D17958E.description: Common Themes: Observing examples of common unifying themes, applying them to the problem, and using them to better understand the dimensions of the problem.

D80A6310DFE60131AA4168A86D17958E.description: Generating and Analyzing Ideas: Developing ideas for proposed solutions, investigating ideas, collecting data, and showing relationships and patterns in the data.

D80B4AC0DFE60131AA4468A86D17958E.description: Gathering and Processing Information: Accessing information from printed media, electronic data bases, and community resources and using the information to develop a definition of the problem and to research possible solutions.

D80B0530DFE60131AA4368A86D17958E.description: Working Effectively: Contributing to the work of a brainstorming group, laboratory partnership, cooperative learning group, or project team; planning procedures; identify and managing responsibilities of team members; and staying on task, whether working alone or as part of a group.

D809C120DFE60131AA3F68A86D17958E.description: Skills and Strategies for Interdisciplinary Problem Solving

D807CB80DFE60131AA3868A86D17958E.description: Solving interdisciplinary problems involves a variety of skills and strategies, including effective work habits; gathering and processing information; generating and analyzing ideas; realizing ideas; making connections among the common themes of mathematics, science, and technology; and presenting results.

D806BEB0DFE60131AA3468A86D17958E.description: explain and evaluate phenomena mathematically and scientifically by formulating a testable hypothesis, demonstrating the logical connections between the scientific concepts guiding the hypothesis and the design of an experiment, applying and inquiring into the mathematical ideas relating to investigation of phenomena, and using (and if needed, designing) technological tools and procedures to assist in the investigation and in the communication of results.

D8067180DFE60131AA3368A86D17958E.description: design solutions to real-world problems on a community, national, or global scale using a technological design process that integrates scientific investigation and rigorous mathematical analysis of the problem and of the solution.

D8070690DFE60131AA3568A86D17958E.description: analyze and quantify consumer product data, understand environmental and economic impacts, develop a method for judging the value and efficacy of competing products, and discuss cost/benefit and risk/benefit tradeoffs made in arriving at the optimal choice.

D80748B0DFE60131AA3668A86D17958E.description: analyze science/technology/society problems and issues on a community, national, or global scale and plan and carry out a remedial course of action.

D8062ED0DFE60131AA3268A86D17958E.description: The knowledge and skills of mathematics, science, and technology are used together to make informed decisions and solve problems, especially those relating to issues of science/technology/society, consumer decision making, design, and inquiry into phenomena.

D8059380DFE60131AA3068A86D17958E.description: Students will apply the knowledge and thinking skills of mathematics, science, and technology to address real-life problems and make informed decisions.

D8054380DFE60131AA2F68A86D17958E.description: analyze subjective decision making problems to explain the trade-offs that can be made to arrive at the best solution.

D804EF80DFE60131AA2E68A86D17958E.description: use optimization techniques, such as linear programming, to determine optimum solutions to problems that can be solved using quantitative methods.

D8049DE0DFE60131AA2D68A86D17958E.description: In order to arrive at the best solution that meets criteria within constraints, it is often necessary to make trade-offs.

D803F9B0DFE60131AA2B68A86D17958E.description: search for multiple trends when analyzing data for patterns, and identify data that do not fit the trends.

D8039DF0DFE60131AA2A68A86D17958E.description: use sophisticated mathematical models, such as graphs and equations of various algebraic or trigonometric functions.

D8035270DFE60131AA2968A86D17958E.description: Identifying patterns of change is necessary for making predictions about future behavior and conditions.

D8026B10DFE60131AA2668A86D17958E.description: cite specific examples of how dynamic equilibrium is achieved by equality of change in opposing directions.

D802BA70DFE60131AA2768A86D17958E.description: describe specific instances of how disturbances might affect a system's equilibrium, from small disturbances that do not upset the equilibrium to larger disturbances (threshold level) that cause the system to become unstable.

D80215C0DFE60131AA2568A86D17958E.description: Equilibrium is a state of stability due either to a lack of changes (static equilibrium) or a balance between opposing forces (dynamic equilibrium).

D80198B0DFE60131AA2368A86D17958E.description: extend their use of powers of ten notation to understanding the exponential function and performing operations with exponential factors.

D8015760DFE60131AA2268A86D17958E.description: describe the effects of changes in scale on the functioning of physical, biological, or designed systems.

D8010C00DFE60131AA2168A86D17958E.description: The grouping of magnitudes of size, time, frequency, and pressures or other units of measurement into a series of relative order provides a useful way to deal with the immense range and the changes in scale that affect the behavior and design of systems.

D8008CD0DFE60131AA1F68A86D17958E.description: compare predictions to actual observations using test models.

D8004EC0DFE60131AA1E68A86D17958E.description: find and use mathematical models that behave in the same manner as the processes under investigation.

D8000E80DFE60131AA1D68A86D17958E.description: collect information about the behavior of a system and use modeling tools to represent the operation of the system.

D7FFCDD0DFE60131AA1C68A86D17958E.description: revise a model to create a more complete or improved representation of the system.

D7FF8760DFE60131AA1B68A86D17958E.description: Models are simplified representations of objects, structures, or systems used in analysis, explanation, interpretation, or design.

D7FEFDC0DFE60131AA1968A86D17958E.description: define boundary conditions when doing systems analysis to determine what influences a system and how it behaves.

D7FEBD90DFE60131AA1868A86D17958E.description: use an input-process-output-feedback diagram to model and compare the behavior of natural and engineered systems.

D7FE7DD0DFE60131AA1768A86D17958E.description: explain how positive feedback and negative feedback have opposite effects on system outputs.

D7FE3DD0DFE60131AA1668A86D17958E.description: Through systems thinking, people can recognize the commonalities that exist among all systems and how parts of a system interrelate and combine to perform specific functions.

D7FDA2A0DFE60131AA1468A86D17958E.description: Students will understand the relationships and common themes that connect mathematics, science, and technology and apply the themes to these and other areas of learning.

document.title: Learning Standards for Social Studies

D9545A70DFE60131ABED68A86D17958E.description: explain how democratic principles have been used in resolving an issue or problem

D95416F0DFE60131ABEC68A86D17958E.description: prepare a plan of action that defines an issue or problem, suggests alternative solutions or courses of action, evaluates the consequences for each alternative solution or course of action, prioritizes the solutions based on established criteria, and proposes an action plan to address the issue or to resolve the problem

D953D1B0DFE60131ABEB68A86D17958E.description: participate in school/classroom/community activities that focus on an issue or problem

D9538EE0DFE60131ABEA68A86D17958E.description: consider the need to respect the rights of others, to respect others' points of view (Adapted from The National Standards for Civics and Government, 1996)

D9534B10DFE60131ABE968A86D17958E.description: take, defend, and evaluate positions about attitudes that facilitate thoughtful and effective participation in public affairs

D9530560DFE60131ABE868A86D17958E.description: evaluate, take, and defend positions on what the fundamental values and principles of American political life are and their importance to the maintenance of constitutional democracy (Adapted from The National Standards for Civics and Government, 1994)

D952B8F0DFE60131ABE768A86D17958E.description: participate as informed citizens in the political justice system and processes of the United States, including voting

D9526380DFE60131ABE668A86D17958E.description: The study of civics and citizenship requires the ability to probe ideas and assumptions, ask and answer analytical questions, take a skeptical attitude toward questionable arguments, evaluate evidence, formulate rational conclusions, and develop and refine participatory skills.

D95219B0DFE60131ABE568A86D17958E.description: explore how citizens influence public policy in a representative democracy

D951C530DFE60131ABE468A86D17958E.description: describe how citizenship is defined by the Constitution and important laws

D9517D80DFE60131ABE368A86D17958E.description: analyze issues at the local, state, and national levels and prescribe responses that promote the public interest or general welfare, such as planning and carrying out a voter registration campaign

D9513440DFE60131ABE268A86D17958E.description: understand how citizenship includes the exercise of certain personal responsibilities, including voting, considering the rights and interests of others, behaving in a civil manner, and accepting responsibility for the consequences of one's actions (Adapted from The National Standards for Civics and Government, 1994)

D950E170DFE60131ABE168A86D17958E.description: Central to civics and citizenship is an understanding of the roles of the citizen within American constitutional democracy and the scope of a citizen's rights and responsibilities.

D9508080DFE60131ABE068A86D17958E.description: understand the dynamic relationship between federalism and state's rights

D9503020DFE60131ABDF68A86D17958E.description: compare and contrast the Constitutions of the United States and New York State

D94FEBE0DFE60131ABDE68A86D17958E.description: identify, respect, and model those core civic values inherent in our founding documents that have been forces for unity in American society

D94FA460DFE60131ABDD68A86D17958E.description: analyze the disparities between civic values expressed in the United States Constitution and the United Nation Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the realities as evidenced in the political, social, and economic life in the United States and throughout the world

D94F5500DFE60131ABDC68A86D17958E.description: trace the evolution of American values, beliefs, and institutions

D94EFEC0DFE60131ABDB68A86D17958E.description: The state and federal governments established by the Constitutions of the United States and the State of New York embody basic civic values (such as justice, honesty, self-discipline, due process, equality, majority rule with respect for minority rights, and respect for self, others, and property), principles, and practices and establish a system of shared and limited government. (Adapted from The National Standards for Civics and Government, 1994)

D94EA0B0DFE60131ABDA68A86D17958E.description: identify and analyze advantages and disadvantages of various governmental systems

D94E5D10DFE60131ABD968A86D17958E.description: compare various political systems with that of the United States in terms of ideology, structure, function, institutions, decision-making processes, citizenship roles, and political culture

D94E1240DFE60131ABD868A86D17958E.description: consider the nature and evolution of constitutional democracies throughout the world

D94DC950DFE60131ABD768A86D17958E.description: analyze how the values of a nation and international organizations affect the guarantee of human rights and make provisions for human needs

D94D81E0DFE60131ABD668A86D17958E.description: The study of civics, citizenship, and government involves learning about political systems; the purposes of government and civic life; and the differing assumptions held by people across time and place regarding power, authority, governance, and law. (Adapted from The National Standards for Civics and Government, 1994)

D94D3300DFE60131ABD568A86D17958E.description: Students will use a variety of intellectual skills to demonstrate their understanding of the necessity for establishing governments; the governmental system of the United States and other nations; the United States Constitution; the basic civic values of American constitutional democracy; and the roles, rights, and responsibilities of citizenship, including avenues of participation.

D94C9380DFE60131ABD368A86D17958E.description: present economic information and conclusions in different formats, including graphic representations, computer models, research reports, and oral presentations

D94C4A70DFE60131ABD268A86D17958E.description: apply a problem-solving model to identify economic problems or issues, generate hypotheses, test hypotheses, investigate and analyze selected data, consider alternative solutions or positions, and make decisions about the best solution or position

D94BFB90DFE60131ABD168A86D17958E.description: use economic information by identifying similarities and differences in trends; inferring relationships between various elements of an economy: organizing and arranging information in charts, tables, and graphs; extrapolating and making conclusions about economic questions, issues, and problems

D94BAAE0DFE60131ABD068A86D17958E.description: identify, locate, and evaluate economic information from standard reference works, newspapers, periodicals, computer databases, monographs, textbooks, government publications, and other primary and secondary sources

D94B51A0DFE60131ABCF68A86D17958E.description: Economics requires the development and application of the skills needed to make informed and well-reasoned economic decisions in daily and national life.

D94AFE90DFE60131ABCE68A86D17958E.description: understand the roles in the economic system of consumers, producers, workers, investors, and voters

D94ABC00DFE60131ABCD68A86D17958E.description: explain how economic decision making has become global as a result of an interdependent world economy

D94A7620DFE60131ABCC68A86D17958E.description: compare and contrast the United States economic system with other national economic systems, focusing on the three fundamental economic questions

D94A30F0DFE60131ABCB68A86D17958E.description: describe the ideals, principles, structure, practices, accomplishments, and problems related to the United States economic system

D949EA40DFE60131ABCA68A86D17958E.description: understand the nature of scarcity and how nations of the world make choices which involve economic and social costs and benefits

D9499160DFE60131ABC968A86D17958E.description: define and apply basic economic concepts such as scarcity, supply/demand, opportunity costs, production, resources, money and banking, economic growth, markets, costs, competition, and world economic systems

D94920A0DFE60131ABC868A86D17958E.description: analyze the effectiveness of varying ways societies, nations, and regions of the world attempt to satisfy their basic needs and wants by utilizing scarce resources

D948CC00DFE60131ABC768A86D17958E.description: The study of economics requires an understanding of major economic concepts and systems, the principles of economic decision making, and the interdependence of economies and economic systems throughout the world.
