371AFE83E95B4E2EA0E9057097807E0A.description: Students will investigate and analyze the historical context of the Holocaust, Nuremberg Trials, and Tokyo Trials and their impact on the UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

70BC1366AE6348BE9CDB7C4C862892B1.description: Following World War II, the United Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) was written. This provides a set of principles to guide efforts to protect threatened groups.

86C1F095FB044925BD47D5BDC65021D6.description: Human Rights Violations: Since the Holocaust, human rights violations have generated worldwide attention and concern. The United Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights has provided a set of principles to guide efforts to protect threatened groups and has served as a lens by which historical occurrences of oppression can be evaluated.

D9D6DD48F1684220B4F804DD6CDCC358.description: Students will examine threats to global security such as international trade in weapons (e.g., chemical, biological, and nuclear), nuclear proliferation, cyber war, and terrorism including a discussion of the events of September 11, 2001.

94717BA6BEA34403824EBED51E813D05.description: Students will investigate one organization and one international action that sought to provide solutions to environmental issues including the Kyoto Protocol.

7BAF8932D9EB44EFA505A745769E9CF1.description: Students will examine the role of the United Nations (UN), North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), the European Union, nongovernmental organizations (NGOs), and efforts to build coalitions to promote international cooperation to address conflicts and issues. They will also examine the extent to which these efforts were successful.

35F9DE8F98F949979022878126B3FED7.description: Globalization has created new possibilities for international cooperation and for international conflict.

B4F386AC75174752AF823B755A8BB0CD.description: Students will examine strains on the environment such as threats to wildlife and degradation of the physical environment (i.e., desertification, deforestation and pollution) due to population growth, industrialization, and urbanization.

D5220BC5E1AA437DB0E192CC040449A6.description: Students will explore efforts to increase and intensify food production through industrial agriculture (e.g., Green Revolutions, use of fertilizers and pesticides, irrigation, and genetic modifications).

D15EFAE11076421287E62B5E23C5089C.description: Students will examine how the world's population is growing exponentially for numerous reasons and how it is not evenly distributed.

C09E011DA6E94D0FA36D96B259062500.description: Population pressures, industrialization and urbanization have increased demands for limited natural resources and food resources, often straining the environment.

61C6CFD852B749469AF7C2264D9E3241.description:
Students will compare and contrast arguments supporting and criticizing globalization by examining concerns including:
  • free market export-oriented economies vs. localized sustainable activities
  • development of a mixed economy in China and its role in the global economy
  • multinational corporations and cartels (e.g., Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries)
  • roles of World Trade Organization, World Bank, International Monetary Fund and microfinance institutions
  • economic growth and economic downturns (e.g., recession, depression) on a national and a global scale
  • economic development and inequality (e.g., access to water, food, education, health care, energy)
  • migration and labor
  • ethnic diversity vs. homogenization (e.g., shopping malls, fast food franchises, language, popular culture)

65A6F9298D4A484CB8624F4853ED9933.description: Globalization is contentious, supported by some and criticized by others.

0AD99325B4C24C9082190A5B9FEA9EFD.description: Students will investigate the causes and effects of, and responses to, one infectious disease (e.g., malaria, HIV/AIDS).

8EAEF2C4E7374C02833FDDA285A41AED.description: Students will explore how information is accessed, exchanged, and controlled and how business is conducted in light of changing technology.

5141CE35AB8C47A6A95BFA826A098943.description: Technological changes in communication and transportation systems allow for instantaneous interconnections and new networks of exchange between people and places that have lessened the impact of time and distance.

A549A5E9542B488EB9ABD1C7D2A4D861.description: Globalization and a Changing Global Environment (1990–PRESENT): Technological changes have resulted in a more interconnected world affecting economic and political relations in some cases leading to conflict and in others to efforts to cooperate. Globalization and population pressures have led to strains on the environment.

877901387042410EB3019741857B13DB.description: Students will explore how changes in technology such as communication and transportation have affected interactions between people and those in authority (e.g., efforts to affect change in government policy, engage people in the political process including use of social media, control access to information, and use terrorism as a tactic).

EB03F2AF81E24A82BD84BE0836D55651.description: Students will investigate, compare, and contrast tensions between modernization and traditional culture in Turkey under the rule of Kemal Atatürk and in Iran under the Pahlavis and the Ayatollahs.

508350F4165D43A6B7AEAB19A95492C3.description: Tensions between agents of modernization and traditional cultures have resulted in ongoing debates within affected societies regarding social norms, gender roles, and the role of authorities and institutions.

7AF9E367F4814460B0DFEA11980568FA.description: Students will investigate the extent to which urbanization and industrialization have modified the roles of social institutions such as family, religion, education, and government by examining one case study in each of these regions: Africa (e.g., Zimbabwe, Kenya, Nigeria, Sierra Leone), Latin America (e.g., Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Mexico), and Asia (e.g., China, India, Indonesia, South Korea).

267239093EFF4F349D33D217659ECFAA.description: Cultures and countries experience and view modernization differently. For some, it is a change from a traditional rural, agrarian condition to a secular, urban, industrial condition. Some see modernization as a potential threat and others as an opportunity to be met.

EB6357858BAA44D4AAF29BE2F4D5367E.description: Tensions Between Traditional Cultures and Modernization: Tensions exist between traditional cultures and agents of modernization. Reactions for and against modernization depend on perspective and context.

55D40E61893C4D22BA24075D593DCB73.description: Students will investigate political, economic, and social policies under Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping and compare and contrast these policies.

7ED53931DC0D428084AA2060315F8E4A.description: Students will trace the Chinese Civil War including the role of warlords, nationalists, communists, and the world wars that resulted in the division of China into a communist-run People's Republic of China and a nationalist-run Taiwan.

227EA5558DF645A39BED2D20EF9A7DEF.description: Nationalism in China influenced the removal of the imperial regime, led to numerous conflicts, and resulted in the formation of the communist People's Republic of China.

265B1B106D764D55A15A6C1441B84334.description: Students will examine the creation of the State of Israel and the Arab-Israeli conflict.

A1CA7EC0341E4561A2DCE9060CDB5F1F.description: Students will investigate Zionism, the mandates created at the end of World War I, and Arab nationalism.

4F59478C12F0411FB1FCD8D404789BBB.description: Nationalism in the Middle East was often influenced by factors such as religious beliefs and secularism.

30F4B0DDD5384043A372B24E8B03821E.description: Students will explore at least two of these three African independence movements: Ghana, Algeria, Kenya.

ED898EA634A34F06A5FCA1D2734C991D.description: African independence movements gained strength as European states struggled economically after World War II. European efforts to limit African nationalist movements were often unsuccessful.

DAD860350A51446EA8EEFF1F8D186B8A.description: Students will compare and contrast the ideologies and methodologies of Gandhi and Ho Chi Minh as nationalist leaders.

B28926084A394296B49B097BE3D1265E.description: Students will explore Gandhi's nonviolent nationalist movement and nationalist efforts led by the Muslim League aimed at the masses that resulted in a British-partitioned subcontinent.

F466FF76109649279762FACFCC9C0BF5.description: Independence movements in India and Indochina developed in response to European control.

A0148354DCC943B79F6A3C5E197D110B.description: Decolonization and Nationalism (1900–2000): Nationalist and decolonization movements employed a variety of methods, including nonviolent resistance and armed struggle. Tensions and conflicts often continued after independence as new challenges arose.

6E19D0DC25C945839ADBD842CC31884E.description: Students will examine the impact of those reforms within the Soviet Union, on the Soviet communist bloc, and in the world.

91FDE658068A4C638363E31BDBD66A7B.description: Students will investigate the political reforms of glasnost and economic reforms of perestroika.

76C97FC867ED42DAA8DF078D393B1580.description: The end of the Cold War and the collapse of the communist bloc in Europe had a global impact.

A6E1F806DCFC4051B618E2E4173B94C4.description: Students will explore the era of détente from both American and Soviet perspectives.

037AA4D4D1BC47E5A3AB65A404BE90D2.description: Students will examine the reasons countries such as Egypt and India chose nonalignment.

17ECCC64E03343E6BF586E4850A77531.description: Students will examine the new military alliances, nuclear proliferation, and the rise of the military-industrial complex.

D33E3F32E8E349F8BB94CF352E63AEB2.description: Students will investigate the efforts to expand and contain communism in Cuba, Vietnam, and Afghanistan from multiple perspectives.

D25D16AE98C44DE3A1B033D92DBF4AFE.description: The Cold War was a period of confrontations and attempts at peaceful coexistence.

C38C5756D59D4827A4BD12C408A5CAAF.description: Students will compare and contrast how peace was conceived at Yalta and Potsdam with what happened in Europe in the four years after World War II (i.e., Soviet occupation of Eastern Europe, Truman Doctrine, Berlin blockade, NATO).

8E28C0203CBF429B96F27BDF8BA045E0.description: The Cold War originated from tensions near the end of World War II as plans for peace were made and implemented. The Cold War was characterized by competition for power and ideological differences between the United States and the Soviet Union.

A87E3DAEE84749CA97FB895044AAC190.description: Unresolved Global Conflict (1945–1991: THE COLD WAR): The second half of the 20th century was shaped by the Cold War, a legacy of World War II. The United States and the Soviet Union emerged as global superpowers engaged in ideological, political, economic, and military competition.

F7DEC36E755941FCAA69AA27A8D23F3F.description: Students will examine the atrocities against the Armenians, the Ukrainian Holodomor, and the Holocaust.

C69020FD6A1D47BEAD7E184482F5FF42.description: Human atrocities and mass murders occurred in this time period.

774022E2A46A4616BCC902D4CF4C33DA.description: Students will investigate the causes of the Great Depression and its influence on the rise of totalitarian dictators and determine the common characteristics of these dictators.

40D64EB36E5645F0BEC71869B04525F6.description: Students will examine the role of nationalism and militarism in Japan.

251AE33747DF4131922310854B7CE6D0.description: Students will examine the role of nationalism and the development of the National Socialist state under Hitler in Germany.

B83D18780CE341FBB71D7B94C3F386C1.description: Students will examine the Russian Revolution and the development of Soviet ideology and nationalism under Lenin and Stalin.

855B5BA9CBC44959883EDA1FE7F4842C.description: Nationalism and ideology played a significant role in shaping the period between the world wars.

87E524A2E0F1409CBFE4C54A2FC3FCC2.description: Students will examine international efforts to work together to build stability and peace including Wilson's Fourteen Points, the Treaty of Versailles, the League of Nations, and the United Nations.

149A203A50CF4C47A96F52D70DFAC1D4.description: The devastation of the world wars and use of total war led people to explore ways to prevent future world wars.

648D24C9FB5440C6A21B9280F63CF1E7.description: Students will compare and contrast the technologies utilized in both World War I and World War II noting the human and environmental devastation.

806E0A192A614CA3809DC3C83E50F5B9.description: Technological developments increased the extent of damage and casualties in both World War I and World War II.

D03D99DAAA14432B9B750B6E959029F5.description: Students will compare and contrast long- and short-term causes and effects for World War I and World War II.

9E44942AD8BF4D9CBA23BAC5879421CF.description: International competition fueled by nationalism, imperialism, and militarism along with shifts in the balance of power and alliances led to world wars.

D980A30935984D33B44F8BF8C9965F1D.description: Unresolved Global Conflict (1914–1945): World War I and World War II led to geopolitical changes, human and environmental devastation, and attempts to bring stability and peace.

A24E9B9C93EB4EFFBFCF7662A05338C3.description: Students will compare and contrast maps of Africa from ca. 1800 and ca. 1914 noting the changes and continuities of ethnic groups and regions, African states, and European claims.

A95AC265E4D6459FB26E026E04D16FC4.description: International conflicts developed as imperial powers competed for control. Claims over land often resulted in borders being shifted on political maps often with little regard for traditional cultures and commerce (e.g., Berlin Conference).

3FEBC319B909483FB5BBF24C9FEBDFEF.description: Students will investigate how Japan reacted to the threat of Western imperialism in Asia.

7CAB29B5A96A48FBA60DFE3C55FFAF2C.description: Students will investigate one example of resistance in Africa (Zulu, Ethiopia, or Southern Egypt/Sudan) and one in China (Taiping Rebellion or Boxer Rebellion and the role of Empress Dowager CiXi).

7999CA0B057543EC887E0C5A813B30F3.description: Those who faced being colonized engaged in varying forms of resistance and adaptation to colonial rule with varying degrees of success.

3DCE4FF4262D490CA038A3DB2C6E9C7E.description: Students will trace how imperial powers politically and economically controlled territories and people including direct and indirect rule in Africa (South Africa, Congo, and one other territory), India, Indochina, and spheres of influence in China.

9DD5B5371A974797AEED106FB05E1E9C.description: Students will explore imperialism from a variety of perspectives such as missionaries, indigenous people, women, merchants/business people, and government officials.

DFFC0C015B1248219BD4DF6F192E9808.description: European industrialized states and Japan sought to play a dominant role in the world and to control natural resources for political, economic, and cultural reasons.

13FA6D2A465A4C5DB0679BAEF88851B3.description: Imperialism: Western European interactions with Africa and Asia shifted from limited regional contacts along the coast to greater influence and connections throughout these regions. Competing industrialized states sought to control and transport raw materials and create new markets across the world.

4C44FF326CBD46C8B2963CD3334B7831.description: Students will examine the Irish potato famine within the context of the British agricultural revolution and Industrial Revolution.

9891F582D3B64A31AD5DB93A8FFA18FA.description: Students will investigate suffrage, education, and labor reforms as well as ideologies such as Marxism intended to transform society.

717973F9AA524E12ADD98C8CA5E0A339.description: Social and political reform as well as new ideologies developed in response to industrial growth.

5ED6CAB5670F4601890EBA4ACCA96071.description: Students will investigate the social, political, and economic impacts of industrialization in Victorian England and Meiji Japan and compare and contrast them.

BD85403BCC2E4108A958D9CE6AD9E8D6.description: Shifts in population from rural to urban areas led to social changes in class structure, family structure, and the daily lives of people.

C7FFD499F8FB49E09B774A54AAC8D87E.description: Students will examine changes and innovations in energy, technology, communication, and transportation that enabled industrialization.

3A8DA850A86147F4A2ADC7F60D6CFE76.description: Students will examine the economic theory presented in The Wealth of Nations.

713BFE2498B5438786E337DD048A1804.description: Students will analyze the factors and conditions needed to industrialize and to expand industrial production as well as shifts in economic practices.

6B24DEBB478D4E5E881396FC9487D914.description: Factors including new economic theories and practices, new sources of energy, and technological innovations influenced the development of new communication and transportation systems and new methods of production. These developments had numerous effects.

A48B90E0E0604388A36CB7BBFA7215DB.description: Students will examine the agricultural revolution in Great Britain.

C1D5BB1F5E864E3BB8B14B9778207D37.description: Agricultural innovations and technologies enabled people to alter their environment allowing them to increase and support farming on a large scale.

442B3B100BF441539C27BFBD3019EFB6.description: Causes and Effects of the Industrial Revolution: Innovations in agriculture, production, and transportation led to the Industrial Revolution, which originated in Western Europe and spread over time to Japan and other regions. This led to major population shifts and transformed economic and social systems.

F41699D6AC7E45AE8DE1A67ABC3E56E6.description: Students will investigate the role of cultural identity and nationalism in the unification of Italy and Germany and in the dissolution of the Ottoman and Austrian Empires.

85F9C80D9B134DD2920E5C71C907D13D.description: Cultural identity and nationalism inspired political movements that attempted to unify people into new nation-states and posed challenges to multinational states.

FE319CDE202249B3AB99946E03F4EBC3.description: Students will examine the evidence related to the impact of the French Revolution on resistance and revolutionary movements, noting the roles of Toussaint L'Ouverture and Simon Bolivar.

A73D7989484B45EE827AE101BAFACDCF.description: Students will examine evidence related to the preconditions of the French Revolution and the course of the revolution, noting the roles of Olympe de Gouges, Maximilien Robespierre and Napoleon Bonaparte.

566A9813E6854FBE8E6F1A9D7D9F8757.description: Individuals and groups drew upon principles of the Enlightenment to spread rebellions and call for revolutions in France and the Americas.

74D02E8ED23F4C67AB3F3BA42FF557D9.description: Students will examine enlightened despots including Catherine the Great.

66834317C5004C37B42397646DFEC96B.description: Students will explore the influence of Enlightenment ideals on issues of gender and abolition by examining the ideas of individuals such as Mary Wollstonecraft and William Wilberforce.

7555463B07654C3B83221E8ADEF2F43E.description: Individuals used Enlightenment ideals to challenge traditional beliefs and secure people's rights in reform movements such as women's rights and abolition; some leaders may be considered enlightened despots.

4612AA906E5B4226ADC169FDB27DA650.description: Students will examine at least three Enlightenment thinkers including John Locke, Baron de Montesquieu, and Jean-Jacques Rousseau and key ideas from their written works.

7E4A6F2A8906482C85B12B7988B6B254.description: Enlightenment thinkers developed political philosophies based on natural laws which included the concepts of social contract, consent of the governed, and the rights of citizens.

8376EF5C098E4B42BD60DA795DD13AFB.description: Enlightenment, Revolution, and Nationalism: The Enlightenment called into question traditional beliefs and inspired widespread political, economic, and social change. This intellectual movement was used to challenge political authorities in Europe and colonial rule in the Americas. These ideals inspired political and social movements.

2B6138B858D848518333F8EF0C47F56B.description: Students will compare the size of these states, empires, and kingdoms relative to the power they wielded in their regions and in the world.

4326BDD516DB4A438685B0D05CEFDDE2.description: Students will create a world map showing the extent of European maritime empires, the Russian Empire, the Ottoman Empire, Mughal Empire, China under the Qing Dynasty, Japan under the Tokugawa Shogunate, Ashanti, Benin, and Dahomey ca. 1750.

D5C989F824CB4561B411F142FAFD42E7.description: Students will compare and contrast the Tokugawa and Mughal response to outsiders with attention to the impact of those decisions.

79DB153B408C4319B874099CB60C64A8.description: Perceptions of outsiders and interactions with them varied across Eurasia.

7932199B129A45A9B483F7EB30BC9030.description: Students will compare and contrast the Tokugawa Shogunate in Japan with France under the rule of the Bourbon Dynasty, looking at the role of Edo and Paris/Versailles, attempts to control the daimyo and nobles, and the development of bureaucracies.

ACC8AD07C56742149C75BF8B6886F5CE.description: Students will examine efforts to unify, stabilize, and centralize Japan under the rule of the Tokugawa Shogunate.

E63486DBEF1D4931964C7F8F39FE798E.description: Students will compare and contrast the Mughal Empire and the Ottoman Empire in 1750 in terms of religious and ethnic tolerance, political organization, and commercial activity.

8967CB6A591C452E9E68CE0C9E27D8DA.description: Powerful Eurasian states and empires faced and responded to challenges ca. 1750.

10611C465A4B484D8EBD1ADCB1D33DF8.description: The World in 1750: The world in 1750 was marked by powerful Eurasian states and empires, coastal African kingdoms, and growing European maritime empires. The interaction of these states, empires, and kingdoms disrupted regional trade networks and influenced the development of new global trade networks.

comments: Grade 10 provides a snapshot of the world circa 1750. The course continues chronologically up to the present. Several concepts are woven throughout the course including industrialization, nationalism, imperialism, conflict, technology, and the interconnectedness of the world. The last three Key Ideas focus on global issues applying a more thematic approach.

5A059A20530F44C58DF48255F9E946CE.description: Fulfill social and political responsibilities associated with citizenship in a democratic society and interdependent global community by developing awareness and/or engaging in the political process.

4A44A0EE52094D8DB03817D2119C7E36.description: Work to influence those in positions of power to strive for extensions of freedom, social justice, and human rights.

1E0CE54DEAD54D26A8FF6C8329EEF82F.description: Identify situations in which social actions are required and determine an appropriate course of action.

088E12891BB34D32B227E2F3B94CC8C0.description: Participate in persuading, debating, negotiating, and compromising in the resolution of conflicts and differences.

3E4E9426904E43088FEB72317C4B7795.description: Identify, describe, and contrast the role of the individual in opportunities for social and political participation in different societies.

A8E5E86F79F548C08EF11C6F0F8424FE.description: Explain differing philosophies of social and political participation and the role of the individual leading to group-driven philosophies.

F9C198DAD8D142C696D278693A64D4DF.description: Participate in activities that focus on a classroom, school, community, state, or national issue or problem.

75DA613607C3400BA4BCE1991928323E.description: Demonstrate respect for the rights of others in discussions and classroom; respectfully disagree with other viewpoints and provide evidence for a counter-argument.

D4A3F31EE6B14E30919F62977A94BEFF.description: Analyze government economic policies and the impact on the national and global economy.

F9BEA44F790B4AB59B084659F789689E.description: Use economic indicators to analyze the current and future state of the economy.

20B8BEE2BADA472DAD492576E346C674.description: Describe concepts of property rights and rule of law as they apply to a market economy.

6BBEB0ED35C249E6B827F147DD239AF7.description: Evaluate the extent to which competition among sellers and among buyers exists in specific markets.

E9F9AD8159A444FFA59CF1F28B317DFB.description: Analyze the ways in which incentives influence what is produced and distributed in a market system.

8599B31B1FC2410390B4CBBFD9ED0059.description: Use marginal benefits and marginal costs to construct an argument for or against an approach or solution to an economic issue.

6562BA0C7CDA43EDAE6B1C1778370B69.description: Characterize and analyze changing interconnections among places and regions.

893A63C4C5114197A560E16F586183BA.description: Recognize and analyze how place and region influence the social, cultural, and economic characteristics of civilizations.

82DC01E1E7C3429BB551A3DAB299AD6F.description: Recognize and interpret (at different scales) the relationships among patterns and processes.

E24E992BFBA34FD6889CE534808A1181.description: Identify, analyze, and evaluate the relationship between the environment and human activities, how the physical environment is modified by human activities, and how human activities are also influenced by Earth's physical features and processes.

13D9F3578C6F438FA8EE1440484D043A.description: Identify, describe, and evaluate the relationships between people, places, regions, and environments by using geographic tools to place them in a spatial context.

999F658001974194A7D307F62C4AE7B9.description: Ask geographic questions about where places are located, why their location is important, and how their locations are related to the location of other places and people.

5B4AE595252142AAB6CD45FF7C831B37.description: Connect historical developments to specific circumstances of time and place and to broader regional, national, or global processes and draw connections to the present (where appropriate).

5C9493F9897C413791C1CC959F744277.description: Recognize the relationship between geography, economics, and history as a context for events and movements and as a matrix of time and place.

CFF614F544CB4DCA8B668067CC89A036.description: Describe, compare, and evaluate multiple historical developments (within societies; across and between societies; in various chronological and geographical contexts).

D757EB077D0743B08912085B501C1033.description: Identify and compare similarities and differences among historical developments over time and in different geographical and cultural contexts.

1F7ACE5DBBB042B793E726A1527AB8A2.description: Identify, compare, and evaluate multiple perspectives on a given historical experience.

16DFC32B78764DFCBF5C0F94637C1F65.description: Identify similarities and differences among geographic regions across historical time periods, and relate differences in geography to different historical events and outcomes.

F014B44260C444D0879BE0A64C62C752.description: Describe, analyze, evaluate, and construct models of historical periodization that historians use to categorize events.

B59747DAC3584B30948C0D8E097AE064.description: Relate patterns of continuity and change to larger historical processes and themes.

8186A4C19E0A4872802815DCF0F02C62.description: Recognize that choice of specific periodizations favors or advantages one narrative, region, or group over another narrative, region, or group.

A335E2630CE44726887F371FCEB3401E.description: Recognize, analyze, and evaluate dynamics of historical continuity and change over periods of time and investigate factors that caused those changes over time.

2635B286179F4B4E99B0545F34EF907F.description: Distinguish between long-term and immediate causes and multiple effects (time, continuity, and change).

27F1CBD7DE1F48E194C831BA32BE191F.description: Identify, analyze, and evaluate the relationship between multiple causes and effects

C31CA0D2317A4B97A51C11BD3DEE02B4.description: Identify causes and effects using examples from different time periods and courses of study across several grade levels.

6ECE4231BE3D411795E2E1D52594CAD5.description: Articulate how events are related chronologically to one another in time and explain the ways in which earlier ideas and events may influence subsequent ideas and events.

BC42C153AB7A4BD5A243DCD2DE79EFF8.description: Create meaningful and persuasive understandings of the past by fusing disparate and relevant evidence from primary and secondary sources and drawing connections to the present.

154789E4B6C643CF8E96DBAC3BD684D0.description: Deconstruct and construct plausible and persuasive arguments using evidence.

2525DE376EA5461D9285043896E1DD35.description: Make inferences and draw conclusions from evidence.

F37923D047ED410FAFD1D0255C6694B8.description: Describe, analyze, and evaluate arguments of others.

A3DFE67DFBE14DF485118BD37FDEDDC9.description: Analyze evidence in terms of content, authorship, point of view, bias, purpose, format, and audience.

2AD8EBF973BC44548C4C9316C945A899.description: Identify, describe, and evaluate evidence about events from diverse sources (including written documents, works of art, photographs, charts and graphs, artifacts, oral traditions, and other primary and secondary sources).

7048CB80E7C348F892C776DB17FA9165.description: Define and frame questions about events and the world in which we live, form hypotheses as potential answers to these questions, use evidence to answer these questions, and consider and analyze counter-hypotheses.

document.title: NYS Intermediate Level Science Core Curriculum

14D9C3F750E44DFDBB1F7F6FB109EF48.description: Since the Industrial Revolution, human activities have resulted in major pollution of air, water, and soil. Pollution has cumulative ecological effects such as acid rain, global warming, or ozone depletion. The survival of living things on our planet depends on the conservation and protection of Earth’s resources.

6B311A4A74E54F079AF950FA81691F91.description: Overpopulation by any species impacts the environment due to the increased use of resources. Human activities can bring about environmental degradation through resource acquisition, urban growth, land-use decisions, waste disposal, etc.

E3398C786BAD4F78B22D6B2330FE2D15.description: The environment may be altered through the activities of organisms. Alterations are sometimes abrupt. Some species may replace others over time, resulting in longterm gradual changes (ecological succession).

EF56EF89852848408A2B0E20F1EBB559.description:
In ecosystems, balance is the result of interactions between community members
and their environment.

DAED86D1BC724F58B73D05E77D4B3741.description: Describe the effects of environmental changes on humans and other populations

0EBDBE1ADF544F18A513D619CD914215.description: The environment may contain dangerous levels of substances (pollutants) that are harmful to organisms. Therefore, the good health of environments and individuals requires the monitoring of soil, air, and water, and taking steps to keep them safe.

0AE95EF8E1214A45853D200A150F8F1B.description: Some microorganisms are essential to the survival of other living things.

084C5004D173443A8C75152B2BA7DAC1.description: In all environments, organisms interact with one another in many ways. Relationships among organisms may be competitive, harmful, or beneficial. Some species have adapted to be dependent upon each other with the result that neither could survive without the other.

8332A27F801F451DABDCE154C16E5B7E.description: Given adequate resources and no disease or predators, populations (including humans) increase. Lack of resources, habitat destruction, and other factors such as predation and climate limit the growth of certain populations in the ecosystem.

F6E62F3BC9DD4AB4B8E0D1B8EC8EE85E.description:
A population consists of all individuals of a species that are found together at a
given place and time. Populations living in one place form a community. The community
and the physical factors with which it interacts compose an ecosystem.

C744994B19E14BC9B84011E739C9DD31.description:
Describe how living things, including humans, depend upon the living and nonliving environment
for their survival.

B6130AB95D4D4B40B213F6027EA7E265.description: Human decisions and activities have had a profound impact on the physical and living environment.

B26D4D5A83914ADDAF9CBA8A3500BA9B.description: Green plants are the producers of food which is used directly or indirectly by consumers.

7EC75D4D4E5B4C81BCE6A8190B7EDFDD.description: The major source of atmospheric oxygen is photosynthesis. Carbon dioxide is removed from the atmosphere and oxygen is released during photosynthesis.

F6B1EFDBD06240A8B5D95F7FBFFBD8B3.description:
Photosynthesis is carried on by green plants and other organisms containing
chlorophyll. In this process, the Sun’s energy is converted into and stored as chemical
energy in the form of a sugar. The quantity of sugar molecules increases in green plants
during photosynthesis in the presence of sunlight.

271819E30563424B8F7FD0D770ACA8D1.description:
Provide evidence that green plants make food and explain the significance of this process to
other organisms.

C865A73C493743A9BA3DDD5C395564AE.description: Matter is transferred from one organism to another and between organisms and their physical environment. Water, nitrogen, carbon dioxide, and oxygen are examples of substances cycled between the living and nonliving environment.

F305F47A3C2A4D4AA4882ACA88AD7B38.description: Food webs identify feeding relationships among producers, consumers, and decomposers in an ecosystem.

8F80B61302F6496188F3324578F52CF4.description:
Energy flows through ecosystems in one direction, usually from the Sun, through
producers to consumers and then to decomposers. This process may be visualized with
food chains or energy pyramids.

31832D5AB227490A92B857FCDDCCF177.description: Describe the flow of energy and matter through food chains and food webs.

6EACA3E985C642F3890C7A70B1819C4A.description: Plants and animals depend on each other and their physical environment.

4ED4ED0F8262403AA53810BB7781D953.description: Contraction of infectious disease, and personal behaviors such as use of toxic substances and some dietary habits, may interfere with one’s dynamic equilibrium. During pregnancy these conditions may also affect the development of the child. Some effects of these conditions are immediate; others may not appear for many years.

C8B25F182F6D42818A42B261410E353D.description: In order to maintain a balanced state, all organisms have a minimum daily intake of each type of nutrient based on species, size, age, sex, activity, etc. An imbalance in any of the nutrients might result in weight gain, weight loss, or a diseased state.

BA832E5E0E9848A0BC7A5B5F6EBEA5B9.description: Energy in foods is measured in Calories. The total caloric value of each type of food varies. The number of Calories a person requires varies from person to person.

41105E1E11DC4CD3A8608672BD6F68F4.description: Metabolism is the sum of all chemical reactions in an organism. Metabolism can be influenced by hormones, exercise, diet, and aging.

7F49B085189B451A9A1799F49DBC64CA.description:
Foods contain a variety of substances, which include carbohydrates, fats, vitamins,
proteins, minerals, and water. Each substance is vital to the survival of the organism.

4E79F9CD84834D56BE96F21089A1A187.description:
Food provides molecules that serve as fuel and building material for all organisms.
All living things, including plants, must release energy from their food, using it to carry
on their life processes.

6E4584BD133546848795B7D913ED5601.description:
Describe the importance of major nutrients, vitamins, and minerals in maintaining health and
promoting growth, and explain the need for a constant input of energy for living organisms.

5B80C006E9584EC7B794C1945A8CECB4.description:
The survival of an organism depends on its ability to sense and respond to its
external environment.

D70DE92F1DF84C648C3C88C79EBBF038.description:
Regulation of an organism’s internal environment involves sensing the internal
environment and changing physiological activities to keep conditions within the range
required for survival. Regulation includes a variety of nervous and hormonal feedback
systems.

85DFCD2DD4044A3D9BC0AC2BC27E21F7.description:
Herbivores obtain energy from plants. Carnivores obtain energy from animals.
Omnivores obtain energy from both plants and animals. Decomposers, such as bacteria
and fungi, obtain energy by consuming wastes and/or dead organisms.

3B2272B57D0248F58D7D4EB61FA4ABFC.description:
The methods for obtaining nutrients vary among organisms. Producers, such as
green plants, use light energy to make their food. Consumers, such as animals, take in
energy-rich foods.

E019AE2C185F4F73A9E736B51B92FD11.description:
All organisms require energy to survive. The amount of energy needed and the
method for obtaining this energy vary among cells. Some cells use oxygen to release the
energy stored in food.

05B35156B13E44C28DF4640BAA9FB34A.description:
An organism’s overall body plan and its environment determine the way that the
organism carries out the life processes.

020D942BFDA046698ECC916223D6107F.description:
Animals and plants have a great variety of body plans and internal structures that
contribute to their ability to maintain a balanced condition

A0F597DCDA8E459FA1FE559CC99B4CCE.description:
Compare the way a variety of living specimens carry out basic life functions and maintain
dynamic equilibrium.

F4A0B3B46D4049FD87DAB0435800E5F1.description: Organisms maintain a dynamic equilibrium that sustains life.

91A78DBA18D5405A8873F063B24BC536.description: Cancers are a result of abnormal cell division.

9B364660BA2A42A4B861F3B440534A59.description:
Another type of cell division accounts for the production of egg and sperm cells in
sexually reproducing organisms. The eggs and sperm resulting from this type of cell
division contain one-half of the hereditary information.

3F635FDCB3C2456B935570E8D6EDEC22.description:
In one type of cell division, chromosomes are duplicated and then separated into
two identical and complete sets to be passed to each of the two resulting cells. In this
type of cell division, the hereditary information is identical in all the cells that result.

1F72778A932A4EEFB2D0D437F73AE0C1.description:
In multicellular organisms, cell division is responsible for growth, maintenance,
and repair. In some one-celled organisms, cell division is a method of asexual
reproduction.

15C43A9748B24B5294D5DA2ED98D270F.description: Observe and describe cell division at the microscopic level and its macroscopic effects

43E69A5551AE47E6B6D48E0F0055502E.description: As an individual organism ages, various body structures and functions change.

BD9F5778582C46D5A32AF22F04F75D96.description:
Patterns of development vary among plants. In seed-bearing plants, seeds contain
stored food for early development. Their later development into adulthood is characterized
by varying patterns of growth from species to species.

2E39E2F5D59A4EEAB5C342300E00937C.description:
Patterns of development vary among animals. In some species the young resemble
the adult, while in others they do not. Some insects and amphibians undergo metamorphosis
as they mature.

B7A2753B3074485397F85E33F07023C5.description:
Various body structures and functions change as an organism goes through its life
cycle.

E93EB9D7353A4F2DBF80C68402FF0E85.description:
In humans, the fertilized egg grows into tissue which develops into organs and
organ systems before birth.

E0795CC0D61A4D5C9BC2027D4A246558.description:
Multicellular organisms exhibit complex changes in development, which begin
after fertilization. The fertilized egg undergoes numerous cellular divisions that will
result in a multicellular organism, with each cell having identical genetic information

EFFC849E96344387B411098020089DB4.description:
Observe and describe developmental patterns in selected plants and animals (e.g., insects, frogs,
humans, seed-bearing plants).

F1098067051F49C2BDFF390A59AF633D.description:
In sexual reproduction, sperm and egg each carry one-half of the genetic information
for the new individual. Therefore, the fertilized egg contains genetic information
from each parent.

8EC84EC391974D9F823E76C9AE9265D4.description:
The male sex cell is the sperm. The female sex cell is the egg. The fertilization of an
egg by a sperm results in a fertilized egg.

6490121C8EEC4CFBAD9D98C410B62EC5.description: Explain the role of sperm and egg cells in sexual reproduction.

EC67020466FE4B93A928EA0ED1BFA1FD.description: Fertilization and/or development in organisms may be internal or external.

706F89092E3E4B21AB1C82EA4A5537B4.description:
Methods of sexual reproduction depend upon the species. All methods involve the
merging of sex cells to begin the development of a new individual. In many species,
including plants and humans, eggs and sperm are produced.

2D9E54D4A0AB4770AA02589CE4A27858.description:
There are many methods of asexual reproduction, including division of a cell into
two cells, or separation of part of an animal or plant from the parent, resulting in the
growth of another individual.

8275BA40B2FA4E24AE62C7B3F34FD342.description:
Some organisms reproduce asexually. Other organisms reproduce sexually. Some
organisms can reproduce both sexually and asexually.

EC132ED2BBBB43EE9140CCB9B983100E.description:
Observe and describe the variations in reproductive patterns of organisms, including asexual
and sexual reproduction.

ECDBB77302ED4363899DC0F69F0371F2.description: The continuity of life is sustained through reproduction and development.

52EAC25931824BBD9A906E1CBE27A15F.description:
Although the time needed for change in a species is usually great, some species of
insects and bacteria have undergone significant change in just a few years.

1505E695F2C94E9D84B60C546B20C1D6.description:
Many thousands of layers of sedimentary rock provide evidence for the long history
of Earth and for the long history of changing lifeforms whose remains are found in
the rocks. Recently deposited rock layers are more likely to contain fossils resembling
existing species.

B76A92E08F744061B75A24B47A3ECCF1.description:
Extinction of a species occurs when the environment changes and the adaptive
characteristics of a species are insufficient to permit its survival. Extinction of species is
common. Fossils are evidence that a great variety of species existed in the past.

62C6E47674094B91870C7C796A70E5AC.description:
In all environments, organisms with similar needs may compete with one another
for resources

B5C01455B97C4A30892C76A41DE72DF5.description:
Describe factors responsible for competition within species and the significance of that
competition.

789919BD2EC4458787946E9EFD49C729.description: Human activities such as selective breeding and advances in genetic engineering may affect the variations of species.

E06A7BE6B0C34129A370BE6C23A4AE2C.description: Changes in environmental conditions can affect the survival of individual organisms with a particular trait. Small differences between parents and offspring can accumulate in successive generations so that descendants are very different from their ancestors. Individual organisms with certain traits are more likely to survive and have offspring than individuals without those traits.

5EBA0AA7B41B40628035F8469FE137E8.description:
The processes of sexual reproduction and mutation have given rise to a variety of
traits within a species.

16A62290DF054DFCB77364160D866D30.description:
Describe sources of variation in organisms and their structures and relate the variations to
survival.

2A5CAA69C15F48C6958E97B9574E2A08.description: Individual organisms and species change over time.

19CB5F08EF0B450C9FA677FF33C81416.description: The probability of traits being expressed can be determined using models of genetic inheritance. Some models of prediction are pedigree charts and Punnett squares.

89CD294F3AE54047BD7B85196F56AFC6.description: Some genes are dominant and some are recessive. Some traits are inherited by mechanisms other than dominance and recessiveness.

59C81427610D4C8E8B2D14B981C58BDE.description: In all organisms, genetic traits are passed on from generation to generation.

E3642186F6E3415EB2085E69039B2CFA.description: Describe simple mechanisms related to the inheritance of some physical traits in offspring.

8E46C7E0A4234A1BB9486BB93947BA5D.description: In sexual reproduction typically half of the genes come from each parent. Sexually produced offspring are not identical to either parent.

7C16A168ECE34F35ACB3318EE31B0A62.description: In asexual reproduction, all the genes come from a single parent. Asexually produced offspring are genetically identical to the parent.

303D986D2A1F4874B8235E8D30995E8E.description: Each human cell contains a copy of all the genes needed to produce a human being.

688686F0A70247B68B80D10016A422BF.description: Each gene carries a single unit of information. A single inherited trait of an individual can be determined by one pair or by many pairs of genes. A human cell contains thousands of different genes.

ED480A10C85A49C4AF91AE4E5884CE0F.description:
Hereditary information is contained in genes. Genes are composed of DNA that
makes up the chromosomes of cells.

6AC017AA1BD14098B541B372ADF71430.description:
Describe sexual and asexual mechanisms for passing genetic materials from generation to
generation.

3FFC101C86A8402F8895EB7000EA2C97.description:
Organisms inherit genetic information in a variety of ways that result in continuity of structure and function
between parents and offspring.

A03C84939AAC49E2A2497B6A8E6A7D80.description:
Disease breaks down the structures or functions of an organism. Some diseases are
the result of failures of the system. Other diseases are the result of damage by infection
from other organisms (germ theory). Specialized cells protect the body from infectious
disease. The chemicals they produce identify and destroy microbes that enter the body.

02C1077D023A4AA0A5058A3ACFBF6F53.description:
The male and female reproductive systems are responsible for producing sex cells
necessary for the production of offspring.

67F576BB1D464F2D9FB20C48E2DA6135.description:
The nervous and endocrine systems interact to control and coordinate the body’s
responses to changes in the environment, and to regulate growth, development, and
reproduction. Hormones are chemicals produced by the endocrine system; hormones
regulate many body functions.

7DA7CEEE6A024F8BBB6B37DF8131A9DE.description:
Locomotion, necessary to escape danger, obtain food and shelter, and reproduce, is
accomplished by the interaction of the skeletal and muscular systems, and coordinated
by the nervous system.

920F65751FA140798A1CE74C760949C3.description:
The circulatory system moves substances to and from cells, where they are needed
or produced, responding to changing demands.

80AF763B1A8D476F8B737C204A6DEB45.description:
The excretory system functions in the disposal of dissolved waste molecules, the
elimination of liquid and gaseous wastes, and the removal of excess heat energy.

CEB4D99E17DD425E95ABC9095D731359.description:
During respiration, cells use oxygen to release the energy stored in food. The respiratory
system supplies oxygen and removes carbon dioxide (gas exchange).

FDDF8551D3BC4925BFDBD2FE6CAD79A0.description:
The digestive system consists of organs that are responsible for the mechanical and
chemical breakdown of food. The breakdown process results in molecules that can be
absorbed and transported to cells.

5A2B7D02EDDE40538DB3228DC29DB079.description:
Tissues, organs, and organ systems help to provide all cells with nutrients, oxygen,
and waste removal.

EDB35AD4756843DABA3DDB7887CA0900.description:
Each system is composed of organs and tissues which perform specific functions
and interact with each other, e.g., digestion, gas exchange, excretion, circulation, locomotion,
control, coordination, reproduction, and protection from disease.

C72F62C2DE0E4608948BD55290A73F9E.description: Explain the functioning of the major human organ systems and their interactions

65E7F257B82642C3BB2713D70D2873F9.description: Living things are classified by shared characteristics on the cellular and organism level. In classifying organisms, biologists consider details of internal and external structures. Biological classification systems are arranged from general (kingdom) to specific (species).

449C7906F5BD4FF881D356B40D910498.description: Multicellular animals often have similar organs and specialized systems for carrying out major life activities.

494C69112B914C1B806ADFB32CBFEB3D.description: Many plants have roots, stems, leaves, and reproductive structures. These organized groups of tissues are responsible for a plant’s life activities.

3ED884CA50C24C588FC968BDAFE47DC9.description:
Cells are organized for more effective functioning in multicellular organisms.
Levels of organization for structure and function of a multicellular organism include
cells, tissues, organs, and organ systems.

A31E00C63A1C457D8C1BD0276826D6C1.description: Some organisms are single cells; others, including humans, are multicellular.

9643C99812194CAABFC91A29B99461E6.description:
Most cells have cell membranes, genetic material, and cytoplasm. Some cells have
a cell wall and/or chloroplasts. Many cells have a nucleus.

1557A46CBF8343E389BD8D4C289D5DC8.description:
The way in which cells function is similar in all living things. Cells grow and
divide, producing more cells. Cells take in nutrients, which they use to provide energy
for the work that cells do and to make the materials that a cell or an organism needs

C79AE54D105B4D5C89EF4048E3DD65F9.description:
Living things are composed of cells. Cells provide structure and carry on major
functions to sustain life. Cells are usually microscopic in size.

5EC98FD1C0BB4D14AD076B5EF1C3412C.description: Compare and contrast the parts of plants, animals, and one-celled organisms

B98AD06EF5A047E484E4E1138BF9CF48.description: Living things are both similar to and different from each other and from nonliving things.

F98AC904E980464DAAF338BAD703697D.description: Students will understand and apply scientific concepts, principles, and theories pertaining to the physical setting and living environment and recognize the historical development of ideas in science.

document.title: New York State P-12 Science Learning Standards

D114022144874AB5ACF7C52770BE0A5B.description:
Evaluate the evidence supporting claims that changes in environmental conditions may result in: (1) increases in
the number of individuals of some species, (2) the emergence of new species over time, and (3) the extinction of
other species.

C347F1426C314EBA84B96438C22B254B.description: Construct an explanation based on evidence for how natural selection leads to adaptation of populations.

65210730622F44DD952811852674E659.description:
Apply concepts of statistics and probability to support explanations that organisms with an advantageous
heritable trait tend to increase in proportion to organisms lacking this trait.

4631CBA5E63349DAAAE82DD39E0DC176.description:
Construct an explanation based on evidence that the process of evolution primarily results from four factors: (1)
the potential for a species to increase in number, (2) the heritable genetic variation of individuals in a species due
to mutation and sexual reproduction, (3) competition for limited resources, and (4) the proliferation of those
organisms that are better able to survive and reproduce in the environment.

48EC3419213A49E586041DE284CEFFB9.description:
Communicate scientific information that common ancestry and biological evolution are supported by multiple lines
of empirical evidence

59F7DE487D0E4DD7AF08B5230B83A00A.description: Use models to illustrate how human reproduction and development maintains continuity of life.

77E0248A19A043528C4F5B6E8BC66942.description:
Apply concepts of statistics and probability to explain the variation and distribution of expressed traits in a
population.

ED4D667A582247FB91D33059BB0D7F91.description:
Make and defend a claim based on evidence that inheritable genetic variations may result from: (1) new genetic
combinations through meiosis, (2) viable errors occurring during replication, (3) mutations caused by
environmental factors and/or (4) genetic engineering

1DBA2CA5B3744C6A9B03090BF4961C47.description:
Ask questions to clarify relationships about the role of DNA and chromosomes in coding the instructions for
characteristic traits passed from parents to offspring

D42DB27BF9A446C5BC2071B9EFEE8C96.description: Use a model to illustrate cellular division (mitosis) and differentiation.

E787E159A1BE41B5A4A7EC8968C81A1F.description: Evaluate the evidence for the role of group behavior on individual and species’ chances to survive and reproduce

883C9FCD1EA747F9A64219A8D3AB543A.description:
Design, evaluate, and refine a solution for reducing the impacts of human activities on the environment and
biodiversity.*

A26DA7E21648492FBDF508274992BE61.description:
Evaluate the claims, evidence, and reasoning that the complex interactions in ecosystems maintain relatively
consistent numbers and types of organisms in stable conditions, but changing conditions may result in a new
ecosystem.

DAA5A0792BB7426582CFF9C9BD45D276.description:
Use mathematical representations to support and revise explanations based on evidence about factors affecting
biodiversity and populations in ecosystems of different scales.

9E17F06E8EF144248168AF61029A4191.description:
Use mathematical and/or computational representations to support explanations of biotic and abiotic factors
that affect carrying capacity of ecosystems at different scales.

2A6FAC88FFF2495EACB8A36518D55DDC.description:
Use a model to illustrate that aerobic cellular respiration is a chemical process whereby the bonds of food
molecules and oxygen molecules are broken and the bonds in new compounds are formed resulting in a net
transfer of energy.

98F6EAF5CBF14B64BF6FCC7E8A194775.description: Use a model to illustrate how photosynthesis transforms light energy into stored chemical energy.

3C706B64BE614AE08243A1AA2B47114F.description: Plan and conduct an investigation to provide evidence that feedback mechanisms maintain homeostasis

3F611BD2CB824140988A1E2015AF9B04.description:
Develop and use a model to illustrate the hierarchical organization of interacting systems that provide specific
functions within multicellular organisms.

E7BA1989297D47CAADA3EDFD3A784ACA.description:
Construct an explanation based on evidence for how the structure of DNA determines the structure of proteins
which carry out the essential functions of life through systems of specialized cells.

document.title: Elementary Science, Intermediate Science, Living Environment, Earth Science, Chemistry, and Physics Core Curriculum

A0B7071CD2C7471BA38F02B753E3C20C.description: Solving interdisciplinary problems involves a variety of skills and strategies, including effective work habits; gathering and processing information; generating and analyzing ideas; realizing ideas; making connections among the common themes of mathematics, science, and technology; and presenting results.

D4B95CAFFCC24CADA5A0D31516872184.description: observe phenomena and evaluate them scientifically and mathematically by conducting a fair test of the effect of variables and using mathematical knowledge and technological tools to collect, analyze, and present data and conclusions

F6C7E8D6CCEC4C6CB6659FE361ABE5BB.description: design solutions to problems involving a familiar and real context, investigate related science concepts to inform the solution, and use mathematics to model, quantify, measure, and compute

FE504F5802B64635AA8BC36564272199.description: make informed consumer decisions by applying knowledge about the attributes of particular products and making cost/benefit tradeoffs to arrive at an optimal choice

181E16F372FC451B9E62D80DC02702B4.description: analyze science/technology/society problems and issues that affect their home, school, or community, and carry out a remedial course of action

CD95CF3487DC4D959682C1DA907E9A22.description: The knowledge and skills of mathematics, science, and technology are used together to make informed decisions and solve problems, especially those relating to issues of science/technology/society, consumer decision making, design, and inquiry into phenomena.

7D35DD42696A44489E4703BE4F536ED1.description: Students will apply the knowledge and thinking skills of mathematics, science, and technology to address real-life problems and make informed decisions.

D6877FAA15894F14959CA464EDBA8121.description: explain the criteria used in selecting a solution orally and in writing

5E6FADBE368C44C3997A236F2BF5BB61.description: choose the best alternative of a set of solutions under given constraints

44C4FA5C8933478B890CA908B30255FE.description: In order to arrive at the best solution that meets criteria within constraints, it is often necessary to make trade-offs.

D8604C979AE747AA885B7F0490024391.description: analyze data by making tables and graphs and looking for patterns of change

7823ECEBC0F24640BD6BA1E25493B7CA.description: use simple instruments to measure such quantities as distance, size, and weight and look for patterns in the data

86232DD5739E4EEB9664F248C64BDD9B.description: Identifying patterns of change is necessary for making predictions about future behavior and conditions

AD2AF92D23B741AEADF29DC7C2945696.description: recognize that things can change in different ways such as size, weight, color, and movement. Some small changes can be detected by taking measurements.

56A7ABA154074E7DA0B7DA7A01FC7F8A.description: observe that things change in some ways and stay the same in some ways

DF0587EBCF934ECD9FC07C6DAC4CEF3C.description: Equilibrium is a state of stability due either to a lack of changes (static equilibrium) or a balance between opposing forces (dynamic equilibrium).

45FED83ADAAD49D1862D86648652937D.description: recognize that almost anything has limits on how big or small it can be

50B32771498F46999D43458647D460AF.description: observe that things in nature and things that people make have very different sizes, weights, and ages

8532A9AA03074C3F93B54BBDAB4AE59D.description: The grouping of magnitudes of size, time, frequency, and pressures or other units of measurement into a series of relative order provides a useful way to deal with the immense range and the changes in scale that affect the behavior and design of systems

79D57BBB6C47443E987E06BA9CE16AE5.description: use different types of models, such as graphs, sketches, diagrams, and maps, to represent various aspects of the real world

B01C28FD85C64B9595170B17AD0C3106.description: discover that a model of something is different from the real thing but can be used to study the real thing

92AC25E5FFF84FCAB12405E63526A36F.description: analyze, construct, and operate models in order to discover attributes of the real thing

264CDE130510424A9DED3A3750B3FAF7.description: Models are simplified representations of objects, structures, or systems used in analysis, explanation, interpretation, or design.

9EB8E593525645CEA23DF43B8FAF4B9A.description: identify common things that can be considered to be systems (e.g., a plant population, a subway system, human beings)

48572D352FB74614ADEF4CC6720B247F.description: observe and describe interactions among components of simple systems

6FE8984AD4664C1D99A823BDF8515FF2.description: Through systems thinking, people can recognize the commonalities that exist among all systems and how parts of a system interrelate and combine to perform specific functions.

E9BDAD1279054F58A0803136CA2D8B11.description: Students will understand the relationships and common themes that connect mathematics, science, and technology and apply the themes to these and other areas of learning.

79ACFC3CA25644DEA0EF644E14627CEA.description: Humans, as individuals or communities, change environments in ways that can be either helpful or harmful for themselves and other organisms.

0A649F717654404F8AF16BE1C53FDA89.description: Over time humans have changed their environment by cultivating crops and raising animals, creating shelter, using energy, manufacturing goods, developing means of transportation, changing populations, and carrying out other activities.

C81D97DD0E2448EF922D1D4EBC56B7CA.description: Humans depend on their natural and constructed environments.

AED5D3022B5342DFB46FB6FBABFD80AC.description: Identify ways in which humans have changed their environment and the effects of those changes

DDB723FCB9EA4103B032EC837A70FB2B.description: Human decisions and activities have had a profound impact on the physical and living environment.

3E24139F101A4F728EFE45B33C6D6107.description: Heat energy from the Sun powers the water cycle (see Physical Science Key Idea 2).

7AFE5F12EB734991908F693F499AF943.description: The Sun's energy is transferred on Earth from plants to animals through the food chain.

26353CBCAD4A4855970BB32C6FB54F6E.description: Plants manufacture food by utilizing air, water, and energy from the Sun.

D98AF7F29F314C7B81BD383B630ACE5B.description: Describe the relationship of the sun as an energy source for living and nonliving cycles

1661ED4BAB1A4026890935C1837F12FA.description: When the environment changes, some plants and animals survive and reproduce, and others die or move to new locations.

F1F8FAE4D0724CA38F86AA95432AB3ED.description: An organism's pattern of behavior is related to the nature of that organism's environment, including the kinds and numbers of other organisms present, the availability of food and other resources, and the physical characteristics of the environment.

CECBE17BE1FD4017B234AC47FBE356A2.description: Decomposers are living things that play a vital role in recycling nutrients.

A5525F45FC414B42A7D2B4B715EA97AF.description: Animals that eat plants for food may in turn become food for other animals. This sequence is called a food chain.

EC570D196DFF4B1AA2A69FD410EAA8ED.description: All animals depend on plants. Some animals (predators) eat other animals (prey).

E7E2E7DE6AAD4372B4C2B942E42ED6EF.description: Green plants are producers because they provide the basic food supply for themselves and animals.

F4AF1460BB5740F6A076F76455FAD7E8.description: Describe how plants and animals, including humans, depend upon each other and the nonliving environment

EB977AD8B02A4378AF068FE5258ECD37.description: Plants and animals depend on each other and their physical environment.

78B1C081BA3A42698E006C1F1E088B9B.description: Good health habits include hand washing and personal cleanliness; avoiding harmful substances (including alcohol, tobacco, illicit drugs); eating a balanced diet; engaging in regular exercise.

8E04393BE68E4E8ABC2F5F40B303C1F5.description: Humans need a variety of healthy foods, exercise, and rest in order to grow and maintain good health.

4929CB5577CF47C1ABE8A54E25861856.description: Describe the factors that help promote good health and growth in humans

DD31029448394D10B6178C47CAB24344.description: The health, growth, and development of organisms are affected by environmental conditions such as the availability of food, air, water, space, shelter, heat, and sunlight.

FEEDE3F7E4BF425D94CD7CA448CB2C25.description: Some animal behaviors are influenced by environmental conditions. These behaviors may include: nest building, hibernating, hunting, migrating, and communicating.

477795B393564E65A811585FB8CB86D5.description: Particular animal characteristics are influenced by changing environmental conditions including: fat storage in winter, coat thickness in winter, camouflage, shedding of fur.

E2E1E4334B524A62AB5B1BECB9AA5704.description: Some animals, including humans, move from place to place to meet their needs.

8895E5637EB24EFBB38CDA0BD558CC15.description: Senses can provide essential information (regarding danger, food, mates, etc.) to animals about their environment.

76C3693F29FB43BDB6C04594BB1A0455.description: Animals respond to change in their environment, (e.g., perspiration, heart rate, breathing rate, eye blinking, shivering, and salivating).

113A4366472447EF9CEC66DD55BACA2D.description: Plants respond to changes in their environment. For example, the leaves of some green plants change position as the direction of light changes; the parts of some plants undergo seasonal changes that enable the plant to grow; seeds germinate, and leaves form and grow.

47D0C6558CC9444BAC70BE0557406DC7.description: Describe some survival behaviors of common living specimens

AF321B1A772D4C05AB126A347856C22A.description: An organism's external physical features can enable it to carry out life functions in its particular environment.

1A8B3D016AEF4F35AE7480A05D9EEECE.description: All living things grow, take in nutrients, breathe, reproduce, and eliminate waste.

1CC83A6BC48746838BB3ADAEB6DC944C.description: Describe basic life functions of common living specimens (guppy, mealworm, gerbil)

1D5E2863DDC94A69BBBBCADB616815B7.description: Organisms maintain a dynamic equilibrium that sustains life.

02D9971C7A774F5A9B94C83A967E0959.description: Food supplies the energy and materials necessary for growth and repair.

F2C43296A2AD4487A743CD1740E97A80.description: Growth is the process by which plants and animals increase in size.

23BA67F1DEE44EDEA03CDB6238A761E8.description: Describe evidence of growth, repair, and maintenance, such as nails, hair, and bone, and the healing of cuts and bruises

D35E395B1D024A85AC82BD99A70D6C60.description: The length of time from an animal's birth to its death is called its life span. Life spans of different animals vary.

F54F985656B841B9AECE3CBF718E7E1B.description: Each kind of animal goes through its own stages of growth and development during its life span.

396081B707784A9D861DD25426C48277.description: Each generation of animals goes through changes in form from young to adult. This completed sequence of changes in form is called a life cycle. Some insects change from egg to larva to pupa to adult.

696E8C92E456488DBB372EC9AB6D38CC.description: Life cycles of some plants include changes from seed to mature plant.

807BA81063B44589B1F55F17B5C1A1D6.description: The length of time from beginning of development to death of the plant is called its life span.

5689438586464616A41226D93FC20D7C.description: Each kind of plant goes through its own stages of growth and development that may include seed, young plant, and mature plant.

4D409846BE4D4236B0D7700AD2ABE938.description: Plants and animals have life cycles. These may include beginning of a life, development into an adult, reproduction as an adult, and eventually death.

E9240498260247ED909A14634774D74C.description: Describe the major stages in the life cycles of selected plants and animals

4A16E7E3FA384F4FA83BB51626966833.description: The continuity of life is sustained through reproduction and development.

341538C0B00548679EE08B1FCDA9573F.description: All individuals have variations, and because of these variations, individuals of a species may have an advantage in surviving and reproducing.

03AFB6A9F06B4EFA8CFAF2DF21A10433.description: Individuals within a species may compete with each other for food, mates, space, water, and shelter in their environment.

CF745566D7454CB9BAADB13E7BDD0F93.description: Observe that differences within a species may give individuals an advantage in surviving and reproducing

FFCFB0E9415944CFA056E4748CD6CF2D.description:
In order to survive in their environment, plants and animals must be adapted to that environment.
  • seeds disperse by a plant's own mechanism and/or in a variety of ways that can include wind, water, and animals
  • leaf, flower, stem, and root adaptations may include variations in size, shape, thickness, color, smell, and texture
  • animal adaptations include coloration for warning or attraction, camouflage, defense mechanisms, movement, hibernation, and migration

124D29BD3DDE4C6A97FB101FC3359ED9.description:
Each plant has different structures that serve different functions in growth, survival, and reproduction.
  • roots help support the plant and take in water and nutrients
  • leaves help plants utilize sunlight to make food for the plant
  • stems, stalks, trunks, and other similar structures provide support for the plant
  • some plants have flowers
  • flowers are reproductive structures of plants that produce fruit which contains seeds
  • seeds contain stored food that aids in germination and the growth of young plants

5CFC272F08154CFAB45D3AAEB81ED977.description:
Each animal has different structures that serve different functions in growth, survival, and reproduction.
  • wings, legs, or fins enable some animals to seek shelter and escape predators
  • the mouth, including teeth, jaws, and tongue, enables some animals to eat and drink
  • eyes, nose, ears, tongue, and skin of some animals enable the animals to sense their surroundings
  • claws, shells, spines, feathers, fur, scales, and color of body covering enable some animals to protect themselves from predators and other environmental conditions, or enable them to obtain food
  • some animals have parts that are used to produce sounds and smells to help the animal meet its needs
  • the characteristics of some animals change as seasonal conditions change (e.g., fur grows and is shed to help regulate body heat; body fat is a form of stored energy and it changes as the seasons change)

8ACBB5ED0C224DB69B8BB514FF12BCF0.description: Describe how the structures of plants and animals complement the environment of the plant or animal

2D88F0F7ABB24A8198E1DC1D18A970F9.description: Individual organisms and species change over time.

8FCDFAC2F76C48AAA8CCA1B835EFFCD1.description: Plants and animals can transfer specific traits to their offspring when they reproduce.

BAED4A2F9BE5499493086CAF5B55EEA3.description: Plants and animals closely resemble their parents and other individuals in their species.

DB14699B667E4806A4C42520E42A55E9.description: Recognize that for humans and other living things there is genetic continuity between generations

Pollution has cumulative ecological effects such as acid rain, global warming, or ozone depletion. The survival of living things on our planet depends on the conservation and protection of Earth's resources.

1FAF4814AB8C439BB632D72092C4934C.description: Overpopulation by any species impacts the environment due to the increased use of resources. Human activities can bring about environmental degradation through resource acquisition, urban growth, land-use decisions, waste disposal, etc.

FA0EA087F5194E7396154EA114CD7E7A.description: The environment may be altered through the activities of organisms. Alterations are sometimes abrupt. Some species may replace others over time, resulting in longterm gradual changes (ecological succession).

9F4753955D9B43F2B48FAF64D2D7CFB2.description: In ecosystems, balance is the result of interactions between community members and their environment.

A03CDE7915154ACCBE9950FFBE72E04C.description: Describe the effects of environmental changes on humans and other populations

7105179AD1CB4B68947F9FCBC6CB5FC6.description: The environment may contain dangerous levels of substances (pollutants) that are harmful to organisms. Therefore, the good health of environments and individuals requires the monitoring of soil, air, and water, and taking steps to keep them safe.

071765E836994A8B96A4EA1464FA7EF9.description: Some microorganisms are essential to the survival of other living things.

7460E25C92494F6699E1071F2C065FDE.description: In all environments, organisms interact with one another in many ways. Relationships among organisms may be competitive, harmful, or beneficial. Some species have adapted to be dependent upon each other with the result that neither could survive without the other.

4F36B76F861F4757B5C01AF515CB8340.description: Given adequate resources and no disease or predators, populations (including humans) increase. Lack of resources, habitat destruction, and other factors such as predation and climate limit the growth of certain populations in the ecosystem.

812BF2B6F8B74A269F111EF2E5D76FEF.description: A population consists of all individuals of a species that are found together at a given place and time. Populations living in one place form a community. The community and the physical factors with which it interacts compose an ecosystem.

D899068B093E4A57B9A99CA7CEE7BEE9.description: Describe how living things, including humans, depend upon the living and nonliving environment for their survival

105D0C6CA0E145288B3F76FBD004E310.description: Human decisions and activities have had a profound impact on the physical and living environment.

A6AD28195A994B30B8EEC2EF24FDC9AB.description: Green plants are the producers of food which is used directly or indirectly by consumers.

D5F24E6590474DAC8E51B11D594B5625.description: The major source of atmospheric oxygen is photosynthesis. Carbon dioxide is removed from the atmosphere and oxygen is released during photosynthesis.

F46D1987E688406EA919B40BC29336CA.description: Photosynthesis is carried on by green plants and other organisms containing chlorophyll. In this process, the Sun's energy is converted into and stored as chemical energy in the form of a sugar. The quantity of sugar molecules increases in green plants during photosynthesis in the presence of sunlight.

6306358F6B6B4C09B21B3DA729493A54.description: Provide evidence that green plants make food and explain the significance of this process to other organisms

B75E4F1099C84414B8DC22A9F39DFED5.description: Matter is transferred from one organism to another and between organisms and their physical environment. Water, nitrogen, carbon dioxide, and oxygen are examples of substances cycled between the living and nonliving environment.

906A2279F1FB4295A09EF730B6A1457F.description: Food webs identify feeding relationships among producers, consumers, and decomposers in an ecosystem.

823BE301CF1B4C7D9CAF76D814E91F7F.description: Energy flows through ecosystems in one direction, usually from the Sun, through producers to consumers and then to decomposers. This process may be visualized with food chains or energy pyramids.

2E0715AABCFE427889B013CDF44CF957.description: Describe the flow of energy and matter through food chains and food webs

C1315E931DAD468AB13BDFF3F85B862E.description: Plants and animals depend on each other and their physical environment.

8912788696CA43BD9C3ACCF8DFF67A42.description: Contraction of infectious disease, and personal behaviors such as use of toxic substances and some dietary habits, may interfere with one's dynamic equilibrium. During pregnancy these conditions may also affect the development of the child. Some effects of these conditions are immediate; others may not appear for many years.

16B9B1EA1D3F462E885E7F3EB48DD266.description: In order to maintain a balanced state, all organisms have a minimum daily intake of each type of nutrient based on species, size, age, sex, activity, etc. An imbalance in any of the nutrients might result in weight gain, weight loss, or a diseased state.

3D3FA01B6D1041578BD99355C788BBDB.description: Energy in foods is measured in Calories. The total caloric value of each type of food varies. The number of Calories a person requires varies from person to person.

6BC79CF833EF46B291EA965C284B22DD.description: Metabolism is the sum of all chemical reactions in an organism. Metabolism can be influenced by hormones, exercise, diet, and aging.

B7124C1AEC694B94A1724DFDF05C2E39.description: Foods contain a variety of substances, which include carbohydrates, fats, vitamins, proteins, minerals, and water. Each substance is vital to the survival of the organism.

EEF475855875498AB79E7BA06C6A26C6.description: Food provides molecules that serve as fuel and building material for all organisms. All living things, including plants, must release energy from their food, using it to carry on their life processes.

9E69429A4C4848DBB95FC2BC9A9576CB.description: Describe the importance of major nutrients, vitamins, and minerals in maintaining health and promoting growth and explain the need for a constant input of energy for living organisms

D4B04EA74C9745B39453C8EE0DFC83CC.description: The survival of an organism depends on its ability to sense and respond to its external environment.

0972AF800A3A42EFB435851A05FDC933.description: Regulation of an organism's internal environment involves sensing the internal environment and changing physiological activities to keep conditions within the range required for survival. Regulation includes a variety of nervous and hormonal feedback systems.

F9B9239700ED4F72BBD1AFF632924E93.description: Herbivores obtain energy from plants. Carnivores obtain energy from animals. Omnivores obtain energy from both plants and animals. Decomposers, such as bacteria and fungi, obtain energy by consuming wastes and/or dead organisms.

439BD9223EC14958940B2DC0B81A19FD.description: The methods for obtaining nutrients vary among organisms. Producers, such as green plants, use light energy to make their food. Consumers, such as animals, take in energy-rich foods.

4FAF41E3745E4836B3774BB7392A1680.description: All organisms require energy to survive. The amount of energy needed and the method for obtaining this energy vary among cells. Some cells use oxygen to release the energy stored in food.

483D0EE6CF3247F3A0F23136730ABA12.description: An organism's overall body plan and its environment determine the way that the organism carries out the life processes.

E4507FC49D534DC99F085EA53B9431B7.description: Animals and plants have a great variety of body plans and internal structures that contribute to their ability to maintain a balanced condition.

969CD2AAE422407CAB4570CBDC98FFE5.description: Compare the way a variety of living specimens carry out basic life functions and maintain dynamic equilibrium

75B40EE217774BD5A228FA1312B8405F.description: Organisms maintain a dynamic equilibrium that sustains life.

8FBC1DC958C649D6B500A72752489E63.description: Cancers are a result of abnormal cell division.

6E7AFB88EE8A4B96AFE4C1BB38C16F4C.description: Another type of cell division accounts for the production of egg and sperm cells in sexually reproducing organisms. The eggs and sperm resulting from this type of cell division contain one-half of the hereditary information.

6022BFEA1EE14E0FBA169DD139066DD2.description: In one type of cell division, chromosomes are duplicated and then separated into two identical and complete sets to be passed to each of the two resulting cells. In this type of cell division, the hereditary information is identical in all the cells that result.

3FE408784D814BA3A4CD277B50DF2180.description: In multicellular organisms, cell division is responsible for growth, maintenance, and repair. In some one-celled organisms, cell division is a method of asexual reproduction.
