54E9AD798D054E53ACAC76A6A80DEF20.description: Physical properties of substances can be explained in terms of chemical bonds and intermolecular forces. These properties include conductivity, malleability, solubility, hardness, melting point, and boiling point.

97453C118B6B4A5385ECB1BD607E91E8.description: Intermolecular forces created by the unequal distribution of charge result in varying degrees of attraction between molecules. Hydrogen bonding is an example of a strong intermolecular force.

9CA3A4203F11438793C5B8F3424C4388.description: Molecular polarity can be determined by the shape of the molecule and distribution of charge. Symmetrical (nonpolar) molecules include CO<sub>2</sub>, CH<sub>4</sub>, and diatomic elements. Asymmetrical (polar) molecules include HCl, NH<sub>3</sub>, and H<sub>2</sub>O.

3924A922323B4234AB7FBAF3F823DB88.description: The electronegativity difference between two bonded atoms is used to assess the degree of polarity in the bond.

F8ADC5615E42480AAEA8145B95564FD6.description: Electronegativity indicates how strongly an atom of an element attracts electrons in a chemical bond. Electronegativity values are assigned according to arbitrary scales.

D12CFB611DBA496E8515CDBB3C3A8CCB.description: When a bond is broken, energy is absorbed. When a bond is formed, energy is released.

104AEBC9913F4EE6A32AFB8AF3D87E40.description: Metals tend to react with nonmetals to form ionic compounds. Nonmetals tend to react with other nonmetals to form molecular (covalent) compounds. Ionic compounds containing polyatomic ions have both ionic and covalent bonding.

7D5E55657CB848E6A26236870350D2B5.description: Two major categories of compounds are ionic and molecular (covalent) compounds.

140AF936229B487D952C1CB4E5577ADC.description: Some elements exist in two or more forms in the same phase. These forms differ in their molecular or crystal structure, and hence in their properties.

15DA59A42B8340D0AA2BF183D9198268.description: In a multiple covalent bond, more than one pair of electrons are shared between two atoms. Unsaturated organic compounds contain at least one double or triple bond.

D1C9809739F84D76AE64F311A47E6060.description: Electron-dot diagrams (Lewis structures) can represent the valence electron arrangement in elements, compounds, and ions.

A81F7109B96C49DAA7F3646D0A71896E.description: When an atom gains one or more electrons, it becomes a negative ion and its radius increases. When an atom loses one or more electrons, it becomes a positive ion and its radius decreases.

28726B7D2FE949B289E948DEDCE3A67B.description: Atoms attain a stable valence electron configuration by bonding with other atoms. Noble gases have stable valence configurations and tend not to bond.

9C1CE89E29CB4DA5A3C47ACF67B06D41.description:
Chemical bonds are formed when valence electrons are:
  • transferred from one atom to another (ionic)
  • shared between atoms (covalent)
  • mobile within a metal (metallic)

7731E21699354152BA365CF08A8A2DF0.description: Explain chemical bonding in terms of the motion of electrons

ED629E6304B8489A98F1CEEEB8C1D58E.description: Energy and matter interact through forces that result in changes in motion.

D503602CF96B4498A0AF27CD744E11BE.description: There are benefits and risks associated with fission and fusion reactions.

E6FD396C070D426787919392A6D8E175.description: There are inherent risks associated with radioactivity and the use of radioactive isotopes. Risks can include biological exposure, long-term storage and disposal, and nuclear accidents.

C775857D858441D080A8CC18F6F38898.description: Radioactive isotopes have many beneficial uses. Radioactive isotopes are used in medicine and industrial chemistry for radioactive dating, tracing chemical and biological processes, industrial measurement, nuclear power, and detection and treatment of diseases.

E0F0FCE65F1E4709809DACED2B1F058E.description: Nuclear reactions can be represented by equations that include symbols which represent atomic nuclei (with mass number and atomic number), subatomic particles (with mass number and charge), and/or emissions such as gamma radiation.

D72A479588AB4F299F758768944E19FD.description: Nuclear reactions include natural and artificial transmutation, fission, and fusion.

8F0EB1DCDA134021A2C86D81E6237CE9.description: Each radioactive isotope has a specific mode and rate of decay (half-life).

DE399BE24A1C4D9DBEB3AB16745C700C.description: Explain the benefits and risks of radioactivity.

C532D1285AD245AF8DD56C1C9426F2E0.description: The concepts of kinetic and potential energy can be used to explain physical processes that include: fusion (melting), solidification (freezing), vaporization (boiling, evaporation), condensation, sublimation, and deposition.

A0A6C9C5E44548F6B84AE43E85942E6F.description: Temperature is a measurement of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a sample of material. Temperature is not a form of energy.

58B553787BE54C0B8D192EEABA3FB86C.description: Heat is a transfer of energy (usually thermal energy) from a body of higher temperature to a body of lower temperature. Thermal energy is the energy associated with the random motion of atoms and molecules.

7E4EDED056E34207AED92BFD2380A08D.description: Explain heat in terms of kinetic molecular theory

F832098F1E824BB18E263A22E1FACF42.description: Energy released or absorbed during a chemical reaction (heat of reaction) is equal to the difference between the potential energy of the products and potential energy of the reactants.

B83AB2DEDE6A493287D39897FD8BB350.description: Energy released or absorbed during a chemical reaction can be represented by a potential energy diagram.

98F600D5424D424EAE7E9943AEE7BF57.description: Chemical and physical changes can be exothermic or endothermic.

E18CCC616D244DB98B37B653962F9E00.description: Energy can exist in different forms, such as chemical, electrical, electromagnetic, thermal, mechanical, nuclear.

4530D10664784ED1BCFB330E86518779.description: Observe and describe transmission of various forms of energy

302AE672B5534171A8B24711B490649D.description: Energy exists in many forms, and when these forms change energy is conserved.

4C30ACD4AE1742BD8D12AEA7C13F331E.description: LeChatelier's principle can be used to predict the effect of stress (change in pressure, volume, concentration, and temperature) on a system at equilibrium.

E792DBE49E074B509B2D4B6630BFF0FD.description: At equilibrium the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction. The measurable quantities of reactants and products remain constant at equilibrium.

E216F45A95E04B14B7EDAAEEC3C6DCC1.description: Some chemical and physical changes can reach equilibrium.

B95616FE43F44DA5A26548E64E8F3A78.description: A catalyst provides an alternate reaction pathway, which has a lower activation energy than an uncatalyzed reaction.

459267CF5D3148F4BDDF9310A3E6C378.description: The rate of a chemical reaction depends on several factors: temperature, concentration, nature of the reactants, surface area, and the presence of a catalyst.

BB110DD765CF43ECAB9C34BCDBE4BA3B.description: Equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain an equal number of particles.

A73A641CA49C4A1194CCA73538EAA0F8.description: Collision theory states that a reaction is most likely to occur if reactant particles collide with the proper energy and orientation.

D704B70D0790466783AC359A2625FD6C.description: Kinetic molecular theory describes the relationships of pressure, volume, temperature, velocity, and frequency and force of collisions among gas molecules.

72D79F8DBB404849B95A4C45F409E4E9.description:
Kinetic molecular theory (KMT) for an ideal gas states that all gas particles:
  • are in random, constant, straight-line motion.
  • are separated by great distances relative to their size; the volume of the gas particles is considered negligible.
  • have no attractive forces between them.
  • have collisions that may result in a transfer of energy between gas particles, but the total energy of the system remains constant.

06341D181FF64F81A0D7495C552E675C.description: The concept of an ideal gas is a model to explain the behavior of gases. A real gas is most like an ideal gas when the real gas is at low pressure and high temperature.

0ECF254C66804FC5BCB725A6036196B9.description: Use kinetic molecular theory to explain rates of reactions and the relationships among temperature, pressure, and volume of a substance

6F7837F092CF46AB87045D0280F1CADB.description: The percent composition by mass of each element in a compound can be calculated mathematically.

543ABBCC5F024A519739539EA75CA1D9.description: The formula mass of a substance is the sum of the atomic masses of its atoms. The molar mass (gram-formula mass) of a substance equals one mole of that substance.

03C7FBEAACC849EDA4D8910095BDE228.description: The empirical formula of a compound is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of the elements in a compound. It may be different from the molecular formula, which is the actual ratio of atoms in a molecule of that compound.

CCB295ACF680404F8A3C70FAA996BDFC.description: A balanced chemical equation represents conservation of atoms. The coefficients in a balanced chemical equation can be used to determine mole ratios in the reaction.

4F4CB386F7DB49A9BDBA167A1F09AC53.description: In a redox reaction the number of electrons lost is equal to the number of electrons gained.

BCB16AB7A29A402EB8C8C1E189FDD3E8.description: In all chemical reactions there is a conservation of mass, energy, and charge.

C020E2E14DB44ABA9CE5036C531745F6.description: Apply the principle of conservation of mass to chemical reactions

45905D8EF52F4BCBB50B1CAFA9EEB553.description: An electrolytic cell requires electrical energy to produce a chemical change. This process is known as electrolysis.

DF05AD7EB87C410D9122467DA524D340.description: A voltaic cell spontaneously converts chemical energy to electrical energy.

664BA235E6674DE5892109158248D6F3.description: An electrochemical cell can be either voltaic or electrolytic. In an electrochemical cell, oxidation occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode.

1E0A7DDDA28E4786B4D5BD40EFA08184.description: Oxidation numbers (states) can be assigned to atoms and ions. Changes in oxidation numbers indicate that oxidation and reduction have occurred.

793F9C3092084CA1A2B32EC8C90C5010.description: A half-reaction can be written to represent oxidation.

AC2FC68E84324E679F50E7341F8734E7.description: Oxidation is the loss of electrons.

D55A3BB6AA2E48BF85F0F30C5D403C14.description: A half-reaction can be written to represent reduction.

3C1BF1840DA64E6691A479B2A794037A.description: Reduction is the gain of electrons.

D18283C7D59A429EAD9DB76A051E8D13.description: An oxidation-reduction (redox) reaction involves the transfer of electrons (e-).

AEC5684968A44CF5A04DA0944F7B4848.description: Types of organic reactions include addition, substitution, polymerization, esterification, fermentation, saponification, and combustion.

8FF8A43FDA4D4432B7C906F607DC9C6C.description: Types of chemical reactions include synthesis, decomposition, single replacement, and double replacement.

F4D372BA7CC54B8BB4178927FDC2CD4E.description: Aphysical change results in the rearrangement of existing particles in a substance. A chemical change results in the formation of different substances with changed properties.

3FACC277F68F4CAA91D0C7257AA03546.description: Use atomic and molecular models to explain common chemical reactions

DD0FDBF8C722492CA4F5B0E2B814DB2C.description: Titration is a laboratory process in which a volume of a solution of known concentration is used to determine the concentration of another solution.

D871A9506D524645A3E3E3FA8F380D1C.description: There are alternate acid-base theories. One theory states that an acid is an H+ donor and a base is an H+ acceptor.

17DE212D37474F57B17E1F33528289D7.description: In the process of neutralization, an Arrhenius acid and an Arrhenius base react to form a salt and water.

B77287AA07894E29BA75155803B379A1.description: Arrhenius bases yield OH-(aq), hydroxide ion as the only negative ion in an aqueous solution.

CCD518F30A8C42E79CB327AA7B4190E9.description: Arrhenius acids yield H+(aq), hydrogen ion as the only positive ion in an aqueous solution. The hydrogen ion may also be written as H3O+(aq), hydronium ion.

3CD08A804B844BAD9C02B33D92086D8C.description: Behavior of many acids and bases can be explained by the Arrhenius theory. Arrhenius acids and bases are electrolytes.

5517CEB6185F4E4FA6CB7E471B8B1E53.description: On the pH scale, each decrease of one unit of pH represents a tenfold increase in hydronium ion concentration.

A694F495AAE44D939814EF1FFCE32609.description: The acidity or alkalinity of an aqueous solution can be measured by its pH value. The relative level of acidity or alkalinity of these solutions can be shown by using indicators.

615C4EEBBFDC4DC8A569522A334E2A00.description: An electrolyte is a substance which, when dissolved in water, forms a solution capable of conducting an electric current. The ability of a solution to conduct an electric current depends on the concentration of ions.

F589973BC3C24A26B6459EC728E56CF9.description: The addition of a nonvolatile solute to a solvent causes the boiling point of the solvent to increase and the freezing point of the solvent to decrease. The greater the concentration of solute particles, the greater the effect.

53F0807D3D064A129799C638A17069FA.description: The concentration of a solution may be expressed in molarity (M), percent by volume, percent by mass, or parts per million (ppm).

5EA5D312EA234EB095B6BCDDEE2D6142.description: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of a solute dissolved in a solvent. The solubility of a solute in a given amount of solvent is dependent on the temperature, the pressure, and the chemical natures of the solute and solvent.

61BCD9B645794B41AFC87130880A112C.description: Differences in properties such as density, particle size, molecular polarity, boiling and freezing points, and solubility permit physical separation of the components of the mixture.

443019A6986249C697C37483614A85D6.description: Systems in nature tend to undergo changes toward lower energy and higher entropy.

C96C97AC3D2644B6AD4ABFF48B817883.description: Entropy is a measure of the randomness or disorder of a system. A system with greater disorder has greater entropy.

875F55F0B9834994A57EB098FB6B7211.description: The three phases of matter (solids, liquids, and gases) have different properties.

C132AEF763704CF3B266E318402B7B55.description: The structure and arrangement of particles and their interactions determine the physical state of a substance at a given temperature and pressure.

6C3E7A5F438449AB8F2E0474E0B7B3FE.description: Isomers of organic compounds have the same molecular formula, but different structures and properties.

C5417292C7C345CFBFDE620EC5A03525.description: Organic acids, alcohols, esters, aldehydes, ketones, ethers, halides, amines, amides, and amino acids are categories of organic compounds that differ in their structures. Functional groups impart distinctive physical and chemical properties to organic compounds.

51F8C7D328774547BF27DED7885193C2.description: Hydrocarbons are compounds that contain only carbon and hydrogen. Saturated hydrocarbons contain only single carbon-carbon bonds. Unsaturated hydrocarbons contain at least one multiple carbon-carbon bond.

3E4FCFF0FD1F4DEF9AE0AD1820D5C1A1.description: Organic compounds contain carbon atoms, which bond to one another in chains, rings, and networks to form a variety of structures. Organic compounds can be named using the IUPAC system.

F17A30EAF5A94905BB1FA9D908581BAF.description: Types of chemical formulas include empirical, molecular, and structural.

3066999400144D87B339458A7EE0DB32.description: Compounds can be differentiated by their physical and chemical properties.

19BA3705692D4B7C9D74408C11D17A70.description: A compound is a substance composed of two or more different elements that are chemically combined in a fixed proportion. A chemical compound can be broken down by chemical means. A chemical compound can be represented by a specific chemical formula and assigned a name based on the IUPAC system.

AE55279B846C4C1C95E96053249A8E65.description: The succession of elements across the same period demonstrates characteristic trends: differences in atomic radius, ionic radius, electronegativity, first ionization energy, metallic/nonmetallic properties.

A618DA06DFA048DC80B8B1A1D5D2AFC3.description: The succession of elements within the same group demonstrates characteristic trends: differences in atomic radius, ionic radius, electronegativity, first ionization energy, metallic/nonmetallic properties.

0C477E63F9924C6FA178C58D277A39DF.description: For Groups 1, 2, and 13-18 on the Periodic Table, elements within the same group have the same number of valence electrons (helium is an exception) and therefore similar chemical properties.

DD3B826593E7459684144ACE47D6D06D.description: The placement or location of an element on the Periodic Table gives an indication of the physical and chemical properties of that element. The elements on the Periodic Table are arranged in order of increasing atomic number.

C3C8F4D988584927BD5C1783AD97FDA4.description: Elements can also be differentiated by chemical properties. Chemical properties describe how an element behaves during a chemical reaction.

D387D9A35413487097504BC570EE95AC.description: Elements can be differentiated by physical properties. Physical properties of substances, such as density, conductivity, malleability, solubility, and hardness, differ among elements.

2A107CB6C2AB4AECADC90A052795637B.description: Elements can be classified by their properties and located on the Periodic Table as metals, nonmetals, metalloids (B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te), and noble gases.

EE6089B214E54B6C9EFB7522C352D3AA.description: Elements are substances that are composed of atoms that have the same atomic number. Elements cannot be broken down by chemical change.

8FF9506972044BD09BE55AC1B0C76222.description: The proportions of components in a mixture can be varied. Each component in a mixture retains its original properties.

E3887C67E1054B68BC0AA31C495C1607.description: Mixtures are composed of two or more different substances that can be separated by physical means. When different substances are mixed together, a homogeneous or heterogeneous mixture is formed.

C50CD629A4764AEAB3A6B56E34AF9D1F.description: A pure substance (element or compound) has a constant composition and constant properties throughout a given sample, and from sample to sample.

72EC0042F5E0407491739E8B0FBE3909.description: Matter is classified as a pure substance or as a mixture of substances.

5EBA8286F695405F9B67C42046924334.description: Spontaneous decay can involve the release of alpha particles, beta particles, positrons, and/or gamma radiation from the nucleus of an unstable isotope. These emissions differ in mass, charge, ionizing power, and penetrating power.

FC348BAD26B048638CDE4431ADC4CC83.description: Stability of an isotope is based on the ratio of neutrons and protons in its nucleus. Although most nuclei are stable, some are unstable and spontaneously decay, emitting radiation.

3714DF1E00B24177899BC45C9072A47B.description: The average atomic mass of an element is the weighted average of the masses of its naturally occurring isotopes.

2AD354BE7B924E6EA36BE3C56D8AAECB.description: Atoms of an element that contain the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons are called isotopes of that element.

A3934C4307F548BC8ABC142ED48216F6.description: The outermost electrons in an atom are called the valence electrons. In general, the number of valence electrons affects the chemical properties of an element.

C6DD747DFC01465F85B338005E9E5048.description: When an electron returns from a higher energy state to a lower energy state, a specific amount of energy is emitted. This emitted energy can be used to identify an element.

13A7E01B4BE44FAF9570B61A3902E308.description: When an electron in an atom gains a specific amount of energy, the electron is at a higher energy state (excited state).

D96F34234F0245859F5F23CBA64D94C5.description: Each electron in an atom has its own distinct amount of energy.

7B5F0B09E90F4CC5B2BDAA2C66282C1C.description: In the wave-mechanical model (electron cloud model) the electrons are in orbitals, which are defined as the regions of the most probable electron location (ground state).

256E978B1E474D728439C784BA5C05FB.description: The number of protons in an atom (atomic number) identifies the element. The sum of the protons and neutrons in an atom (mass number) identifies an isotope. Common notations that represent isotopes include: 14C, 14C, carbon-14, C-14.

E086FA45A6B24CF49565D23D9E1B445D.description: The mass of each proton and each neutron is approximately equal to one atomic mass unit. An electron is much less massive than a proton or a neutron.

DD04B3FEE4F449388E0A49380184EBB8.description: Protons and electrons have equal but opposite charges. The number of protons equals the number of electrons in an atom.

FC770D2D8D27465D98BA462CE43E86D3.description: The proton is positively charged, and the neutron has no charge. The electron is negatively charged.

1E7ABEB3A8BC494789C5FAFF8510F699.description: Subatomic particles contained in the nucleus include protons and neutrons.

8891040AB7A14FD1AB23072FDE47F6A8.description: Each atom has a nucleus, with an overall positive charge, surrounded by negatively charged electrons.

35C22BAB53954EF0B13B13DA5D12855C.description: The modern model of the atom has evolved over a long period of time through the work of many scientists.

0ACD59B9EA6A472B8AB8CCB02FE3D456.description: Explain the properties of materials in terms of the arrangement and properties of the atoms that compose them

225F4D36F194409086428F8B9C0C4313.description: Matter is made up of particles whose properties determine the observable characteristics of matter and its reactivity.

40F0A6CDBA9046B0830D41945B376771.description: Students will understand and apply scientific concepts, principles, and theories pertaining to the physical setting and living environment and recognize the historical development of ideas in science.

CF0ABD5A80764DBC9956ECE1F25CDCF5.description: discuss the use of the peer-review process in the scientific community and explain its value in maintaining the integrity of scientific publication, e.g., "cold fusion"

56A36FA5D58E4331BA80D481F111BC5E.description: critically assess the value of information with or without benefit of scientific backing and supporting data, and evaluate the effect such information could have on public judgment or opinion, e.g., environmental issues

B774B270A24645D496EE7C87A18E0EB0.description: Knowledge of the impacts and limitations of information systems is essential to its effectiveness and ethical use.

46C1B3B30E0D4B72B70189538817253D.description: use the Internet as a source to retrieve information for classroom use, e.g., Periodic Table, acid rain

1BD38800F09D49C58551A3E0AB035D1E.description: Information technology is used to retrieve, process, and communicate information as a tool to enhance learning.

15AF0A8334024FB3B284E5C9F427701F.description: Students will access, generate, process, and transfer information using appropriate technologies.

81A72EB00FF84E61B4FF791B2A62D588.description: devise a test of the solution according to the design criteria and perform the test; record, portray, and logically evaluate performance test results through quantitative, graphic, and verbal means. Use a variety of creative verbal and graphic techniques effectively and persuasively to present conclusions, predict impacts and new problems, and suggest and pursue modifications

24433EF204894BE58767FA9DE82F531C.description: develop work schedules and working plans which include optimal use and cost of materials, processes, time, and expertise; construct a model of the solution, incorporating developmental modifications while working to a high degree of quality (craftsmanship)

3AC041B55195483BA1B41965CE4295F0.description: generate creative solutions, break ideas into significant functional elements, and explore possible refinements; predict possible outcomes using mathematical and functional modeling techniques; choose the optimal solution to the problem, clearly documenting ideas against design criteria and constraints; and explain how human understands, economics, ergonomics, and environmental considerations have influenced the solution.

6D04499402834489B1C309730682483C.description: identify, locate, and use a wide range of information resources, and document through notes and sketches how findings relate to the problem

C991DAD7FC7E462DBF71C37764718F60.description: initiate and carry out a thorough investigation of an unfamiliar situation and identify needs and opportunities for technological invention or innovation

DC9708BE01D444628106E67DBAF0880D.description: Engineering design is an iterative process involving modeling and optimization (finding the best solution within given constraints); this process is used to develop technological solutions to problems within given constraints.

F4CB3423A7D64B22995CF8F4B95C3075.description: Develop a written report for public scrutiny that describes the proposed explanation, including a literature review, the research carried out, its results, and suggestions for further research.

6FAABB1B90224A149F4251259E4422F8.description: Based on the results of the test and through public discussion, revise the explanation and contemplate additional research.
comments: Note: Public discussion may include lab partners, lab groups, classes, etc.

B861EFD643DD402D820F0C64E434D29C.description: compare the experimental result to the expected result; calculate the percent error as appropriate

BE72ED68B8714A019F4E1949015D5024.description: evaluate experimental methodology for inherent sources of error and analyze the possible effect on the result

319F60FF3C98414CAB1AA8DDAECF4F01.description: Assess correspondence between the predicted result contained in the hypothesis and the actual result and reach a conclusion as to whether or not the explanation on which the prediction was based is supported

6F1D43555EE94638AF29F10E86A85413.description: Apply statistical analysis techniques when appropriate to test if chance alone explains the result.

888C74D8717343A0B1F26A5A5BE48378.description: organize observations in a data table, analyze the data for trends or patterns, and interpret the trends or patterns, using scientific concepts

74F8FE539B63487989B5953FA3116D4B.description: Use various means of representing and organizing observations (e.g., diagrams, tables, charts, graphs, equations, and matrices) and insightfully interpret the organized data.

D81005CA6E8046D1981E6288FCC2F66A.description: The observations made while testing proposed explanations, when analyzed using conventional and invented methods, provide new insights into phenomena.

9FB258E79A2344E2A52DD6285D3739C2.description: determine safety procedures to accompany a research plan

5A0EB43563A043D3A58A01104FA21652.description: Carry out their research plan for testing explanations, including selecting and developing techniques, acquiring and building apparatus, and recording observations as necessary

DFA582F428D64160AC207763A6D758B1.description: develop research proposals in the form of "if X is true and a particular test Y is done, then prediction Z will occur"

8256703322A946F1A1734B5305306C69.description: Develop and present proposals including formal hypotheses to test their explanations, i.e., they predict what should be observed under specified conditions if the explanation is true

C2BE6462928D45BDB4DFCBFF08AA89B9.description: use library investigations, retrieved information, and literature reviews to improve the experimental design of an experiment

88A466562AE648EEB394C8E698989E9A.description: Refine their research ideas through library investigations, including electronic information retrieval and reviews of the literature, and through peer feedback obtained from review and discussion

C2B61807AB4B404DB9CB1E34337989B6.description: design and/or carry out experiments, using scientific methodology to test proposed calculations

87E5ADEFBF0C4ADFB72C6CDFC5C48840.description: Devise ways of making observations to test proposed explanations

9A7FC232DD5C4DBAB92DDF37CDAC6349.description: Beyond the use of reasoning and consensus, scientific inquiry involves the testing of proposed explanations involving the use of conventional techniques and procedures and usually requiring considerable ingenuity.

73121352BCC14012A84754A7223B6966.description: evaluate the merits of various scientific theories and indicate why one theory was accepted over another

8AC4328C4B9B4F1B93DF43EB732DEA16.description: Work toward reconciling competing explanations; clarifying points of agreement and disagreement

BB39EDE4FA7F4673B1CECDA7E222F8D6.description: locate data from published sources to support/defend/explain patterns observed in natural phenomena

7EA93AB3FE2F4FF08451DA4932DAFC37.description: Hone ideas through reasoning, library research, and discussion with others, including experts

597D0E4B6ABC408B9D1FF7407FF2B492.description: use theories and/or principles to make predictions about natural phenomena

90B9D56261F1431F8699067D807CBCD6.description: use theories and/or models to represent and explain observations

4A1322B4D90243B7B64300D7893FBE81.description: Elaborate on basic scientific and personal explanations of natural phenomena, and develop extended visual models and mathematical formulations to represent their thinking

8BD85667220641B8A6A57E1585D3BCA1.description: The central purpose of scientific inquiry is to develop explanations of natural phenomena in a continuing, creative process.

967E0286070948F183F36C709554D816.description: evaluate the appropriateness of an answer, based on given data

37EE41E8F2B543AD8B0E0001DC0D098D.description: state assumptions which apply to the use of a particular mathematical equation and evaluate these assumptions to see if they have been met

691B020798DF43B198C6D5D2D505BD1D.description: Apply algebraic and geometric concepts and skills to the solution of problems

41C34B9505474AD0A63D9CE9A499FD18.description: Critical thinking skills are used in the solution of mathematical problems.

8ABCD6B243B84144A830E4986DBAD623.description: apply data showing trends to predict information

80EC14AE401046C2BE25E0D85F2D0794.description: interpret a graph constructed from experimentally obtained data

1749FC1AB05D42378E2C999C45CD5511.description: Use deductive reasoning to construct and evaluate conjectures and arguments, recognizing that patterns and relationships in mathematics assist them in arriving at these conjectures and arguments

24B9E0C4CA3842F29E9F76E1B5C94254.description: Deductive and inductive reasoning are used to reach mathematical conclusions.

7530D88B8369405B99C49B1744B59D36.description: use knowledge of geometric arrangements to predict particle properties or behavior

65594685B93C41E68E8087C118088F99.description: recognize and convert various scales of measurement

9122487EFCAD41C19BDFF63BFF10D8C7.description: identify relationships within variables from data tables

5272925AD8CF45EF9C251B79FC19BDD8.description: show uncertainty in measurement by the use of significant figures

7CEB4EBD012F4222B7EABA2AA4A6A92B.description: use appropriate equations and significant digits

5273EDD0551F4181ADB6EC53DFE205DC.description: show mathematical work, stating formula and steps for solution

B44CBAD13A1949B3BF9811DE9207B6F7.description: choose appropriate measurement scales and use units in recording

7EFE632D38E04C629F8154743AD5B3DA.description: measure and record experimental data and use data in calculations

91648156560442AE95C0BB8CB51DA213.description: create appropriate axes with labels and scale

62890A2917F74FBFAF9AD5A4D1923182.description: organize, graph, and analyze data gathered from laboratory activities or other sources

5D090631B4844129838EA0B2415F2B69.description: Industrialization brings an increased demand for and use of energy and other resources including fossil and nuclear fuels. This usage can have positive and negative effects on humans and ecosystems.

23F1B99951904895BFEF0116B90057EF.description: When humans alter ecosystems either by adding or removing specific organisms, serious consequences may result. For example, planting large expanses of one crop reduces the biodiversity of the area.

A3FE0E1071DB43F49EF7002215A2547D.description: Human activities that degrade ecosystems result in a loss of diversity of the living and nonliving environment. For example, the influence of humans on other organisms occurs through land use and pollution. Land use decreases the space and resources available to other species, and pollution changes the chemical composition of air, soil, and water.

4DD11640E40F4B97BE9D1AB56A75E5C2.description: Explain the impact of technological development and growth in the human population on the living and nonliving environment.

BE1EABC4F3BF4712B14D1F00249D4152.description: Human beings are part of the Earth's ecosystems. Human activities can, deliberately or inadvertently, alter the equilibrium in ecosystems. Humans modify ecosystems as a result of population growth, consumption, and technology. Human destruction of habitats through direct harvesting, pollution, atmospheric changes, and other factors is threatening current global stability, and if not addressed, ecosystems may be irreversibly affected.

029E4B7ED27C49E19C176C776FC3C0CE.description: Natural ecosystems provide an array of basic processes that affect humans. Those processes include but are not limited to: maintenance of the quality of the atmosphere, generation of soils, control of the water cycle, removal of wastes, energy flow, and recycling of nutrients. Humans are changing many of these basic processes and the changes may be detrimental.

AB07A17661884005BDA102843733D072.description: The Earth has finite resources; increasing human consumption of resources places stress on the natural processes that renew some resources and deplete those resources that cannot be renewed.

E84CA6CB628C4AE5BC19B3A7FC03D3E1.description: Describe the range of interrelationships of humans with the living and nonliving environment.

C83D4A0F042D403484BC6FC091040265.description: Human decisions and activities have had a profound impact on the physical and living environment.

E7C2385C41414D09AA651F8701BD39CD.description: A stable ecosystem can be altered, either rapidly or slowly, through the activities of organisms (including humans), or through climatic changes or natural disasters. The altered ecosystem can usually recover through gradual changes back to a point of longterm stability.

8AEB265823664AD3A3D27A0A7FECE0BF.description: Through ecological succession, all ecosystems progress through a sequence of changes during which one ecological community modifies the environment, making it more suitable for another community. These long-term gradual changes result in the community reaching a point of stability that can last for hundreds or thousands of years.

E164CF0AD9AA4A34ADA4E0811A66F8AD.description: The interrelationships and interdependencies of organisms affect the development of stable ecosystems.

C992766644FF4BD8A99C5C228DDCC37E.description: Explain how the living and nonliving environments change over time and respond to disturbances.

D41491C9C4EB4AF29D8C2802875CACF3.description: Biodiversity also ensures the availability of a rich variety of genetic material that may lead to future agricultural or medical discoveries with significant value to humankind. As diversity is lost, potential sources of these materials may be lost with it.

F886920900AE4F369ABCEDEA29010598.description: As a result of evolutionary processes, there is a diversity of organisms and roles in ecosystems. This diversity of species increases the chance that at least some will survive in the face of large environmental changes. Biodiversity increases the stability of the ecosystem.

0E1FB04E41B94C4FBE1D9AD82B52A5C7.description: Explain the importance of preserving diversity of species and habitats.

232E5E7EB5BC47B68BCA10FCF6899D49.description: Relationships between organisms may be negative, neutral, or positive. Some organisms may interact with one another in several ways. They may be in a producer/consumer, predator/prey, or parasite/host relationship; or one organism may cause disease in, scavenge, or decompose another.

F4AD9CDD14474778A17846C69DD64BCA.description: Living organisms have the capacity to produce populations of unlimited size, but environments and resources are finite. This has profound effects on the interactions among organisms.

802E6965DDD142F59E8139C7D079D678.description: In any particular environment, the growth and survival of organisms depend on the physical conditions including light intensity, temperature range, mineral availability, soil/rock type, and relative acidity (pH).

F5BCD604A1A94531BC072F39CC38B864.description: The number of organisms any habitat can support (carrying capacity) is limited by the available energy, water, oxygen, and minerals, and by the ability of ecosystems to recycle the residue of dead organisms through the activities of bacteria and fungi.

63607BA85FF24E23A4918A70292004D1.description: The chemical elements, such as carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, and oxygen, that make up the molecules of living things pass through food webs and are combined and recombined in different ways. At each link in a food web, some energy is stored in newly made structures but much is dissipated into the environment as heat.

745732562F98405E8FCCA41D8ABC285C.description: The atoms and molecules on the Earth cycle among the living and nonliving components of the biosphere. For example, carbon dioxide and water molecules used in photosynthesis to form energy-rich organic compounds are returned to the environment when the energy in these compounds is eventually released by cells. Continual input of energy from sunlight keeps the process going. This concept may be illustrated with an energy pyramid.

ABCC20D730F4483D84B5CE10BACF9BBE.description: Energy flows through ecosystems in one direction, typically from the Sun, through photosynthetic organisms including green plants and algae, to herbivores to carnivores and decomposers.

5AED94EC7187414E891948578145A16F.description: Explain factors that limit growth of individuals and populations.

3B2D650B677546A191F49A1472118EEB.description: Plants and animals depend on each other and their physical environment.

CD61C9AE1DFF436A83683322C2108088.description: Feedback mechanisms have evolved that maintain homeostasis. Examples include the changes in heart rate or respiratory rate in response to increased activity in muscle cells, the maintenance of blood sugar levels by insulin from the pancreas, and the changes in openings in the leaves of plants by guard cells to regulate water loss and gas exchange.

035A899A950746249701E6D22578F147.description: Dynamic equilibrium results from detection of and response to stimuli. Organisms detect and respond to change in a variety of ways both at the cellular level and at the organismal level.

2EF60ADF345F4E7DBF4DB1A4876CBF5D.description: Relate processes at the system level to the cellular level in order to explain dynamic equilibrium in multicelled organisms.

3AD710E775A64CAB80FA3CC53ABDA17C.description: Biological research generates knowledge used to design ways of diagnosing, preventing, treating, controlling, or curing diseases of plants and animals.

4F972BA2B95A46D89E72040665C735D6.description: Gene mutations in a cell can result in uncontrolled cell division, called cancer. Exposure of cells to certain chemicals and radiation increases mutations and thus increases the chance of cancer.

371F5B1E5D024E0490974C442379A188.description: Disease may also be caused by inheritance, toxic substances, poor nutrition, organ malfunction, and some personal behavior. Some effects show up right away; others may not show up for many years.

7B90FC8311F3442F8BED16C68B4CC9DE.description: Some allergic reactions are caused by the body's immune responses to usually harmless environmental substances. Sometimes the immune system may attack some of the body's own cells or transplanted organs.

0B6EC1330FC04312BAAD7D38A754A890.description: Some viral diseases, such as AIDS, damage the immune system, leaving the body unable to deal with multiple infectious agents and cancerous cells.

3027FDCBDD2F426E93A775F25C65BE43.description: Vaccinations use weakened microbes (or parts of them) to stimulate the immune system to react. This reaction prepares the body to fight subsequent invasions by the same microbes.

AE82300BA84845FA84AB0458BD5E4B17.description: Some white blood cells engulf invaders. Others produce antibodies that attack them or mark them for killing. Some specialized white blood cells will remain, able to fight off subsequent invaders of the same kind.

0E4851EC05DC41A09EF5917A80D9BC29.description: The immune system protects against antigens associated with pathogenic organisms or foreign substances and some cancer cells.

A661E4C7291046D88D83F6CC55465B06.description: Viruses, bacteria, fungi, and other parasites may infect plants and animals and interfere with normal life functions.

0B958DC1C6F64421ABEBABF0B89E0077.description: Homeostasis in an organism is constantly threatened. Failure to respond effectively can result in disease or death.

877FB915101E423AA3D1C041C31718D6.description: Explain disease as a failure of homeostasis.

C9AFE34668B94FDABE683B6544A1EB96.description: Enzymes and other molecules, such as hormones, receptor molecules, and antibodies, have specific shapes that influence both how they function and how they interact with other molecules.

BC9736F11E3E45ADADCBB414DF1EA36D.description: Biochemical processes, both breakdown and synthesis, are made possible by a large set of biological catalysts called enzymes. Enzymes can affect the rates of chemical change. The rate at which enzymes work can be influenced by internal environmental factors such as pH and temperature.

967E4A1C06214C7884CCEF51AD261B23.description: The energy from ATP is used by the organism to obtain, transform, and transport materials, and to eliminate wastes.

244EEA3CF41E49DF9F0D8D67D8578CD0.description: In all organisms, the energy stored in organic molecules may be released during cellular respiration. This energy is temporarily stored in ATP molecules. In many organisms, the process of cellular respiration is concluded in mitochondria, in which ATP is produced more efficiently, oxygen is used, and carbon dioxide and water are released as wastes.

2C76E2E8501544D99A11904D25A8A4E2.description: In all organisms, organic compounds can be used to assemble other molecules such as proteins, DNA, starch, and fats. The chemical energy stored in bonds can be used as a source of energy for life processes.

A8E937972E924A90BBD681BE59A621EA.description: Plant cells and some one-celled organisms contain chloroplasts, the site of photosynthesis. The process of photosynthesis uses solar energy to combine the inorganic molecules carbon dioxide and water into energy-rich organic compounds (e.g., glucose) and release oxygen to the environment.

EF026DA0E96E4B709ED71888F3EDA83C.description: The energy for life comes primarily from the Sun. Photosynthesis provides a vital connection between the Sun and the energy needs of living systems.

4A9BD4F5E8B5405F8D3E48D79718C856.description: Explain the basic biochemical processes in living organisms and their importance in maintaining dynamic equilibrium.

7143CE5236794764A07F70F6DE967F2C.description: Organisms maintain a dynamic equilibrium that sustains life.

EDAE886085734D868A07B5E4664B39EB.description: In humans, the embryonic development of essential organs occurs in early stages of pregnancy. The embryo may encounter risks from faults in its genes and from its mother's exposure to environmental factors such as inadequate diet, use of alcohol/drugs/tobacco, other toxins, or infections throughout her pregnancy.

F4DBA966AF2E4FC385BC0D3379FF1FB5.description: The structures and functions of the human male reproductive system, as in other mammals, are designed to produce gametes in testes and make possible the delivery of these gametes for fertilization.

3F1AD6490A10466AAA6C31839A6C3DAA.description: The structures and functions of the human female reproductive system, as in almost all other mammals, are designed to produce gametes in ovaries, allow for internal fertilization, support the internal development of the embryo and fetus in the uterus, and provide essential materials through the placenta, and nutrition through milk for the newborn.

43BA772D0B3642CB95EAD64BA4E43BF2.description: Human reproduction and development are influenced by factors such as gene expression, hormones, and the environment. The reproductive cycle in both males and females is regulated by hormones such as testosterone, estrogen, and progesterone.

AE33F404E99A466CB4522228D91CA35D.description: The zygote may divide by mitosis and differentiate to form the specialized cells, tissues, and organs of multicellular organisms.

46727AE509EC4F9B9A6522B2D946802E.description: The processes of meiosis and fertilization are key to sexual reproduction in a wide variety of organisms. The process of meiosis results in the production of eggs and sperm which each contain half of the genetic information. During fertilization, gametes unite to form a zygote, which contains the complete genetic information for the offspring.

6CDAE879927A4DFBB7C2CE14C213D0EB.description: Some organisms reproduce asexually with all the genetic information coming from one parent. Other organisms reproduce sexually with half the genetic information typically contributed by each parent. Cloning is the production of identical genetic copies.

3EA8A896F77341D2B49EEFC7A93B05D5.description: Reproduction and development are necessary for the continuation of any species.

C0361797281F44709A186BEA706C745B.description: Explain how organisms, including humans, reproduce their own kind.

ADA9D178FB584A25AB1AE514A097A904.description: The continuity of life is sustained through reproduction and development.

E556CC57778D44C8AB97D1A1A9A57D50.description: Extinction of a species occurs when the environment changes and the adaptive characteristics of a species are insufficient to allow its survival. Fossils indicate that many organisms that lived long ago are extinct. Extinction of species is common; most of the species that have lived on Earth no longer exist.

02EEA1FAC8D04C5BA39EAD3034209BAF.description: Evolution does not necessitate long-term progress in some set direction. Evolutionary changes appear to be like the growth of a bush: Some branches survive from the beginning with little or no change, many die out altogether, and others branch repeatedly, sometimes giving rise to more complex organisms.

6FC6CE7EE48B41759C2E3E3DFEBEEAC4.description: Billions of years ago, life on Earth is thought by many scientists to have begun as simple, single-celled organisms. About a billion years ago, increasingly complex multicellular organisms began to evolve.

105AF018B59340ED8C7C8B48D5B567AD.description: Behaviors have evolved through natural selection. The broad patterns of behavior exhibited by organisms are those that have resulted in greater reproductive success.

5177BA8EFEE646258DA1C90BB502332B.description: The variation of organisms within a species increases the likelihood that at least some members of the species will survive under changed environmental conditions.

D9DF1E192DD04239B6A2BA3FC79C1A8C.description: Some characteristics give individuals an advantage over others in surviving and reproducing, and the advantaged offspring, in turn, are more likely than others to survive and reproduce. The proportion of individuals that have advantageous characteristics will increase.

9F13A6693E8C4D2B9E748BB50CD1726E.description: Species evolve over time. Evolution is the consequence of the interactions of (1) the potential for a species to increase its numbers, (2) the genetic variability of offspring due to mutation and recombination of genes, (3) a finite supply of the resources required for life, and (4) the ensuing selection by the environment of those offspring better able to survive and leave offspring.

D60FD693E2934663B4FF6BFFA80A09BE.description: Natural selection and its evolutionary consequences provide a scientific explanation for the fossil record of ancient life-forms, as well as for the molecular and structural similarities observed among the diverse species of living organisms.

E544126F923645FA83FDDF9E5A978FB9.description: Mutations occur as random chance events. Gene mutations can also be caused by such agents as radiation and chemicals. When they occur in sex cells, the mutations can be passed on to offspring; if they occur in other cells, they can be passed on to other body cells only.

83DEE7FE3BE74C7CB0319FDFC89491B3.description: Mutation and the sorting and recombining of genes during meiosis and fertilization result in a great variety of possible gene combinations.

3128800290E94DD7818ECA53D378E6F8.description: New inheritable characteristics can result from new combinations of existing genes or from mutations of genes in reproductive cells.

9943CE97B38A4583B41E5BC9F2D56B4D.description: The basic theory of biological evolution states that the Earth's present-day species developed from earlier, distinctly different species.

F7037C90CA3A4F86BD5E9C830D0D8686.description: Explain the mechanisms and patterns of evolution.

C6BA0AAD9C174360A5684E23390D4F1E.description: Individual organisms and species change over time.

68ED20181F4F465CA93D75CD7A253FDB.description: Knowledge of genetics is making possible new fields of health care; for example, finding genes which may have mutations that can cause disease will aid in the development of preventive measures to fight disease. Substances, such as hormones and enzymes, from genetically engineered organisms may reduce the cost and side effects of replacing missing body chemicals.

A5A44C8B336248D1A8E087DDED3410C7.description: Inserting, deleting, or substituting DNA segments can alter genes. An altered gene may be passed on to every cell that develops from it.

821BAD5B3EE24FD6B0BC226C2BCD06E6.description: Different enzymes can be used to cut, copy, and move segments of DNA. Characteristics produced by the segments of DNA may be expressed when these segments are inserted into new organisms, such as bacteria.

E3CD36379EF545A9B6511B623D41AE9E.description: In recent years new varieties of farm plants and animals have been engineered by manipulating their genetic instructions to produce new characteristics.

B1866AE377CD4BDCBC4E6AFD9FEF3B15.description: For thousands of years new varieties of cultivated plants and domestic animals have resulted from selective breeding for particular traits.

430593DD36DA4ABFA55D9C8E3B757398.description: Explain how the technology of genetic engineering allows humans to alter genetic makeup of organisms.

3CAE537508334D688F68B9D1D69655C5.description: The many body cells in an individual can be very different from one another, even though they are all descended from a single cell and thus have essentially identical genetic instructions. This is because different parts of these instructions are used in different types of cells, and are influenced by the cell's environment and past history.

1ADCD3663E2B4C0F9158972772A45905.description: Offspring resemble their parents because they inherit similar genes that code for the production of proteins that form similar structures and perform similar functions.

60F8B34ABB16417894B276BC22A01BE5.description: The work of the cell is carried out by the many different types of molecules it assembles, mostly proteins. Protein molecules are long, usually folded chains made from 20 different kinds of amino acids in a specific sequence. This sequence influences the shape of the protein. The shape of the protein, in turn, determines its function.

3137F1381301480D80913F1CFC490D33.description: Genes are segments of DNA molecules. Any alteration of the DNA sequence is a mutation. Usually, an altered gene will be passed on to every cell that develops from it.

DA53705A43B7447DB64269B49DD4F42E.description: Cells store and use coded information. The genetic information stored in DNA is used to direct the synthesis of the thousands of proteins that each cell requires.

17A9E1C646B8483593A32986C72096FB.description: In all organisms, the coded instructions for specifying the characteristics of the organism are carried in DNA, a large molecule formed from subunits arranged in a sequence with bases of four kinds (represented by A, G, C, and T). The chemical and structural properties of DNA are the basis for how the genetic information that underlies heredity is both encoded in genes (as a string of molecular "bases") and replicated by means of a template.

270E31B55AD7485FBFC245F18AFCFCB2.description: In sexually reproducing organisms, the new individual receives half of the genetic information from its mother (via the egg) and half fromits father (via the sperm). Sexually produced offspringoften resemble, but are not identical to, either of their parents.

AFA02F14662946588CC0B0386C364174.description: In asexually reproducing organisms, all the genes come from a single parent. Asexually produced offspring are normally genetically identical to the parent.

6EF1A2B4011E42A19AAC67344EE2DC37.description: Hereditary information is contained in genes, located in the chromosomes of each cell. An inherited trait of an individual can be determined by one or by many genes, and a single gene can influence more than one trait. A human cell contains many thousands of different genes in its nucleus.

59BC4DF8DDFF42E49038701C38652294.description: Every organism requires a set of coded instructions for specifying its traits. For offspring to resemble their parents, there must be a reliable way to transfer information from one generation to the next. Heredity is the passage of these instructions from one generation to another.

315E1DF8BCCD4C778B5C21534534E9A0.description: Genes are inherited, but their expression can be modified by interactions with the environment.

02F95CCE8B5F4045A16ADDB5F0B4E7C3.description: Explain how the structure and replication of genetic material result in offspring that resemble their parents.

730C472F4BA04CBABEC7E7C4F1D3AB9F.description: Organisms inherit genetic information in a variety of ways that result in continuity of structure and function between parents and offspring.

60142A224186406AA9EABB428AE2BCE2.description: The structures present in some single-celled organisms act in a manner similar to the tissues and systems found in multicellular organisms, thus enabling them to perform all of the life processes needed to maintain homeostasis.

FD6DEC90B4894C448017230684E0C286.description: Explain how a one-celled organism is able to function despite lacking the levels of organization present in more complex organisms.

574CB186BF5A4C7891128A8D24E90767.description: Receptor molecules play an important role in the interactions between cells. Two primary agents of cellular communication are hormones and chemicals produced by nerve cells. If nerve or hormone signals are blocked, cellular communication is disrupted and the organism's stability is affected.

FB7749BFCA3A446194D64346FA8193E1.description: Inside the cell a variety of specialized structures, formed from many different molecules, carry out the transport of materials (cytoplasm), extraction of energy from nutrients (mitochondria), protein building (ribosomes), waste disposal (cell membrane), storage (vacuole), and information storage (nucleus).

7E8818FDA5544DDA9170D02B9B5952BD.description: Many organic and inorganic substances dissolved in cells allow necessary chemical reactions to take place in order to maintain life. Large organic food molecules such as proteins and starches must initially be broken down (digested to amino acids and simple sugars respectively), in order to enter cells. Once nutrients enter a cell, the cell will use them as building blocks in the synthesis of compounds necessary for life.

0ACAD06F49C3449B9E79F766D5869EAB.description: Each cell is covered by a membrane that performs a number of important functions for the cell. These include: separation from its outside environment, controlling which molecules enter and leave the cell, and recognition of chemical signals. The processes of diffusion and active transport are important in the movement of materials in and out of cells.

D72F7D79DDFC4C15966F01F5C985C62D.description: Cells have particular structures that perform specific jobs. These structures perform the actual work of the cell. Just as systems are coordinated and work together, cell parts must also be coordinated and work together.

86D5D29D214D469CAFCD2802F2B42B24.description: The organs and systems of the body help to provide all the cells with their basic needs. The cells of the body are of different kinds and are grouped in ways that enhance how they function together.

4B4E3277F1DD4C1EAA1486179873B963.description: If there is a disruption in any human system, there may be a corresponding imbalance in homeostasis.

5B0E25A95101447895DC017B5A76ED24.description: The components of the human body, from organ systems to cell organelles, interact to maintain a balanced internal environment. To successfully accomplish this, organisms possess a diversity of control mechanisms that detect deviations and make corrective actions.

47DA6DB1AA36437E8057FD541F27F71D.description: Humans are complex organisms. They require multiple systems for digestion, respiration, reproduction, circulation, excretion, movement, coordination, and immunity. The systems interact to perform the life functions.

AB5FB7202AF9479CBDD7DEC64D034139.description: Important levels of organization for structure and function include organelles, cells, tissues, organs, organ systems, and whole organisms.

1AD45BD1D18544F396286259D3F45E38.description: Describe and explain the structures and functions of the human body at different organizational levels (e.g., systems, tissues, cells, organelles).

5F29A9AAB7914E729C906EB4C0668E0B.description: Every population is linked, directly or indirectly, with many others in an ecosystem. Disruptions in the numbers and types of species and environmental changes can upset ecosystem stability.

E4AFA00FBCA0494C945CE0A6FBDD0C32.description: Ecosystems, like many other complex systems, tend to show cyclic changes around a state of approximate equilibrium.

983CB36090A24E5D81E1E93BF381E308.description: The interdependence of organisms in an established ecosystem often results in approximate stability over hundreds and thousands of years. For example, as one population increases, it is held in check by one or more environmental factors or another species.

DDF5388469404827BC0C9D115389070D.description: In all environments, organisms compete for vital resources. The linked and changing interactions of populations and the environment compose the total ecosystem.

BFDDE0CC94D3442F94B958180541BEDD.description: An ecosystem is shaped by the nonliving environment as well as its interacting species. The world contains a wide diversity of physical conditions, which creates a variety of environments.

E3CE776309E247DE9B2E8C0841020E3D.description: Populations can be categorized by the function they serve. Food webs identify the relationships among producers, consumers, and decomposers carrying out either autotropic or heterotropic nutrition.

045865FE42384D9A89DBF74605D98750.description: Explain how diversity of populations within ecosystems relates to the stability of ecosy

8E900E75DC2540E2BBB34C4C495F733E.description: Living things are both similar to and different from each other and from nonliving things.

140B732CD13149A1AF246F122AD2038B.description: Students will understand and apply scientific concepts, principles, and theories pertaining to the physical setting and living environment and recognize the historical development of ideas in science.

DBCDF147F0ED4C1088CB2F568C127306.description: Scientists use peer review to evaluate the results of scientific investigations and the explanations proposed by other scientists. They analyze the experimental procedures, examine the evidence, identify faulty reasoning, point out statements that go beyond the evidence, and suggest alternative explanations for the same observations.

A8EE4F93C748497B9694E3D29DBD8629.description: One assumption of science is that other individuals could arrive at the same explanation if they had access to similar evidence. Scientists make the results of their investigations public; they should describe the investigations in ways that enable others to repeat the investigations.

77CC2C1B18DD4D2DB8CB387BFB6E10AD.description: Develop a written report for public scrutiny that describes the proposed explanation, including a literature review, the research carried out, its result, and suggestions for further research.

1309C30B8A24408788DFBE17551B3ABA.description: Claims should be questioned if fact and opinion are intermingled, if adequate evidence is not cited, or if the conclusions do not follow logically from the evidence given.

CAF0072C917B4878A86DFEAD4C14F887.description: Claims should be questioned if the data are based on samples that are very small, biased, or inadequately controlled or if the conclusions are based on the faulty, incomplete, or misleading use of numbers.

0A04C70F25E14D53A369D440050F1FF4.description: Hypotheses are valuable, even if they turn out not to be true, because they may lead to further investigation.

BE055B3705C44A619C363A2FCCB10CFA.description: Based on the results of the test and through public discussion, revise the explanation and contemplate additional research.

775AF20207324CE1BFDCF7F4C6BF4E47.description: Assess correspondence between the predicted result contained in the hypothesis and actual result, and reach a conclusion as to whether the explanation on which the prediction was based is supported.

90A34F905CFB493B9F77D1D76048D413.description: Apply statistical analysis techniques when appropriate to test if chance alone explains the results.

E51B16C129594623A4EB24F23FF714AB.description: Interpretation of data leads to development of additional hypotheses, the formulation of generalizations, or explanations of natural phenomena.

3BA1FB4792874D26A84B4EA9A097B21D.description: Use various methods of representing and organizing observations (e.g., diagrams, tables, charts, graphs, equations, matrices) and insightfully interpret the organized data.

2D4E381F5BD746B39728FBF882F0FB74.description: The observations made while testing proposed explanations, when analyzed using conventional and invented methods, provide new insights into natural phenomena.

F1D7E836F3374C398340D42100395089.description: Carry out a research plan for testing explanations, including selecting and developing techniques, acquiring and building apparatus, and recording observations as necessary.

6CE0F81707C842758AC5FC2910B48A83.description: Development of a research plan for testing a hypothesis requires planning to avoid bias (e.g., repeated trials, large sample size, and objective data-collection techniques).

02BDCBB9AD0E4FACA5259190C78594FA.description: Hypotheses are widely used in science for determining what data to collect and as a guide for interpreting the data.

242F43C03D9C44CFBBA67B198F5422B9.description: Hypotheses are predictions based upon both research and observation.

E67E378614EB4B9F87E5AC29E21A560A.description: Develop and present proposals including formal hypotheses to test explanations; i.e., predict what should be observed under specific conditions if the explanation is true.

7920A40C073B40F1B6DA5851DE713B84.description: Development of a research plan involves researching background information and understanding the major concepts in the area being investigated. Recommendations for methodologies, use of technologies, proper equipment, and safety precautions should also be included.

13182F1A9D664BFE8D133634BFF59D7A.description: Refine research ideas through library investigations, including electronic information retrieval and reviews of the literature, and through peer feedback obtained from review and discussion.

895857792F1945ECB9DFE95E7E21A3A4.description: Devise ways of making observations to test proposed explanations.

03AEE605B5624956983D79648D6BEE03.description: Beyond the use of reasoning and consensus, scientific inquiry involves the testing of proposed explanations involving the use of conventional techniques and procedures and usually requiring considerable ingenuity.

9338223056184F36842C628B9563995E.description: Well-accepted theories are ones that are supported by different kinds of scientific investigations often involving the contributions of individuals from different disciplines.

document.title: New York State Next Generation Mathematics Learning Standards (K-8)

3ED329F26F274093800222CA443FC226.description: Develop a probability model (which may not be uniform) by observing frequencies in data generated from a chance process

15D7C4D40A664B39A8223A6DE8F627D1.description: Develop a uniform probability model by assigning equal probability to all outcomes, and use the model to determine probabilities of simple events.

83C4BA633E7E43E4B23C464A73834FC8.description: Develop a probability model and use it to find probabilities of simple events. Compare probabilities from a model to observed frequencies; if the agreement is not good, explain possible sources of the discrepancy.

0F68B0E2A8A24980935556F729579E54.description: Approximate the probability of a simple event by collecting data on the chance process that produces it and observing its long-run relative frequency, and predict the approximate relative frequency given the probability.

0A8859146A39472687CF8A84CF2B9C5E.description: Understand that the probability of a chance event is a number between 0 and 1 inclusive, that expresses the likelihood of the event occurring. Larger numbers indicate greater likelihood. A probability near 0 indicates an unlikely event, a probability around ½ indicates an event that is neither unlikely nor likely, and a probability near 1 indicates a likely event.

827AE749543F436F887B07F4F704BFFE.description: Investigate chance processes and develop, use, and evaluate probability models.

6ADBA109CB5F432D9EBBF4440D8C1773.description: Relate the range and the choice of measures of center to the shape of the data distribution and the context in which the data were gathered.

B220F78B7C65408F8735A24EEA5BC8E2.description: Calculate range and measures of center, as well as describe any overall pattern and any striking deviations from the overall pattern with reference to the context in which the data were gathered.

038660ED58D24924B74583119687B3C7.description: Describe the nature of the attribute under investigation, including how it was measured and its units of measurement.

DB21ABEFDFFA4890BA141DF2173E1831.description: Summarize quantitative data sets in relation to their context.

8BCDC4F989A5420CB9DC05A568ECAB8A.description: Display quantitative data in plots on a number line, including dot plots, and histograms.

46BDE6AB3C0E4F1CBC7883E4C23146CF.description: Recognize that a measure of center for a quantitative data set summarizes all of its values with a single number while a measure of variation describes how its values vary with a single number.

EAAE6E62D84A40DE9841392A4FFE7733.description: Understand that a set of quantitative data collected to answer a statistical question has a distribution which can be described by its center, spread, and overall shape.

E3C6C12CAB6D4D8699A243FB2EB2F5D7.description: Understand that the method and sample size used to collect data for a particular question is intended to reduce the difference between a population and a sample taken from the population so valid inferences can be drawn about the population. Generate multiple samples (or simulated samples) of the same size to recognize the variation in estimates or predictions.

2FD2325C5F6E4E85B1AC13767C14286E.description: Understand that statistics can be used to gain information about a population by examining a sample of the population; generalizations about a population from a sample are valid only if the sample is representative of that population.

B4A3CE11FF1C440299BA53C759FDCFEC.description: Recognize that a statistical question is one that anticipates variability in the data related to the question and accounts for it in the answers.

115FDEBF94064871AE83480C26C4096E.description: Use variables to represent two quantities in a real-world problem that change in relationship to one another. Given a verbal context and an equation, identify the dependent variable, in terms of the other quantity, thought of as the independent variable. Analyze the relationship between the dependent and independent variables using graphs and tables, and relate these to the equation.

979807B0278B4BC8ACD1A516B8540E4A.description: Represent and analyze quantitative relationships between dependent and independent variables.

D00E106A58BD4714820FB37CD04F3849.description: Write an inequality of the form x > c, x ≥ c, x ≤ c, or x < c to represent a constraint or condition in a real-world or mathematical problem. Recognize that inequalities of these forms have infinitely many solutions; represent solutions of such inequalities on a number line.

C2FDE938FF8A44758F4183CA99B5DE79.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems by writing and solving equations of the form x + p = q; x – p = q; px = q; and x/p = q for cases in which p, q, and x are all non-negative rational numbers.

C791298BADFB4745BB3A4D4736D79DB7.description: Use variables to represent numbers and write expressions when solving a real-world or mathematical problem. Understand that a variable can represent an unknown number, or, depending on the purpose at hand, any number in a specified set.

12F6AD32C1EC47BA9EAA6C77DC1F4DE3.description: Understand solving an equation or inequality as a process of answering a question: which values from a specified set, if any, make the equation or inequality true? Use substitution to determine whether a given number in a specified set makes an equation or inequality true.

83D07978D7A74563A491F522E2CDCF09.description: Reason about and solve one-variable equations and inequalities.

668FEC1B01BD47F994B4EEA769C51558.description: Identify when two expressions are equivalent.

CD71E94B7EB7479F963F3EDED9C4AF7D.description: Apply the properties of operations to generate equivalent expressions.

1509FA00E6A540E9A4501721409596FE.description: Evaluate expressions given specific values for their variables. Include expressions that arise from formulas in real-world problems. Perform arithmetic operations, including those involving whole-number exponents, in the conventional order (Order of Operations).

18A57F72357744189E55771830A33129.description: Identify parts of an expression using mathematical terms (term, coefficient, sum, difference, product, factor, and quotient); view one or more parts of an expression as a single entity.

C0C82B1C7AC044A19F37283A3287C2D3.description: Write expressions that record operations with numbers and with letters standing for numbers.

294267FA0CC34742B4F3DDF82824603C.description: Write, read, and evaluate expressions in which letters stand for numbers.

20635C1947324C48A8A9D17DC2B11237.description: Write and evaluate numerical expressions involving whole-number exponents.

CE304ECD375444E49376DDC203D82C69.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of arithmetic to algebraic expressions.

A1F60FC6A83F441E9875223ACADF978D.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems by graphing points on a coordinate plane. Include use of coordinates and absolute value to find distances between points with the same first coordinate or the same second coordinate.

2F284F4AF9C7469E80A1DA36182EC4B5.description: Distinguish comparisons of absolute value from statements about order.

88876F2367354DECB07FC3E603433D2B.description: Understand the absolute value of a rational number as its distance from 0 on the number line. Interpret absolute value as magnitude for a positive or negative quantity in a real-world situation.

B8FCB89BCEAE490CB836FE39413FF769.description: Write, interpret, and explain statements of order for rational numbers in real-world contexts.

621E6EF3A4A34EA0B9DB6EF49DFACAF2.description: Interpret statements of inequality as statements about the relative position of two numbers on a number line.

B3B4046432BD47F399D68C59A7DD7716.description: Understand ordering and absolute value of rational numbers.

04EF77B24D4740BBAF72B4093F68001F.description: Find and position integers and other rational numbers on a horizontal or vertical number line. Find and position pairs of integers and other rational numbers on a coordinate plane.

EA6D71D7C29E472AAC92FF9B80AE3C4E.description: Understand signs of numbers in ordered pairs as indicating locations in quadrants of the coordinate plane. Recognize that when two ordered pairs differ only by signs, the locations of the points are related by reflections across one or both axes.

C5754B8F1F1A492A95E6881CB06802AC.description: Recognize opposite signs of numbers as indicating locations on opposite sides of 0 on the number line. Recognize that the opposite of the opposite of a number is the number itself, and that 0 is its own opposite.

4C7982A840A94D598B6EEC670C0CA393.description: Understand a rational number as a point on the number line. Use number lines and coordinate axes to represent points on a number line and in the coordinate plane with negative number coordinates.

D4F7AE4660A04893AE163E1093814768.description: Understand that positive and negative numbers are used together to describe quantities having opposite directions or values. A18B2CB7CBB7424B9132E120C896ED1C.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of numbers to the system of rational numbers.

3F9AD9FB8C284F7E95019D9B23D65076.description: Find the greatest common factor of two whole numbers less than or equal to 100. Use the distributive property to express a sum of two whole numbers 1–100 with a common factor as a multiple of a sum of two whole numbers with no common factor other than 1. Find the least common multiple of two whole numbers less than or equal to 12.

0F4948EBD99F40458A99488F70A842C3.description: Fluently add, subtract, multiply, and divide multi-digit decimals using a standard algorithm for each operation.

6B2DEFBF9431404A96EF24725B3C4CC1.description: Fluently divide multi-digit numbers using a standard algorithm.

8989279A20FE4FA995D3B0AA3E9E5C45.description: Compute fluently with multi-digit numbers and find common factors and multiples.

FBBB1E2DECBA4A3C9B4F0ED41779A19C.description: Interpret and compute quotients of fractions, and solve word problems involving division of fractions by fractions.

280631D6D9AC45B38146ED7CD4FF9154.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication and division to divide fractions by fractions.

31B41149EC974CEF9E52A0E8E5D3CB2F.description: Use ratio reasoning to convert measurement units; manipulate and transform units appropriately when multiplying or dividing quantities.

24E5B5E6D3884A5F9C4240C5ADA49FF7.description: Find a percent of a quantity as a rate per 100. Solve problems that involve finding the whole given a part and the percent, and finding a part of a whole given the percent.

B481DA6990C04268A820ED8165A5DAE6.description: Make tables of equivalent ratios relating quantities with whole-number measurements, find missing values in the tables, and plot the pairs of values on the coordinate plane. Use tables to compare ratios.

BFF8B852A34E45C5ACF837BBF69C3CB2.description: Use ratio and rate reasoning to solve real-world and mathematical problems.

7EDB816A1C16494698C94D38D0101E2D.description: Understand the concept of a unit rate a/b associated with a ratio a:b with b ≠ 0 (b not equal to zero), and use rate language in the context of a ratio relationship.

4909F3DDC68E4D0B85D4E52833F73D49.description: Understand the concept of a ratio and use ratio language to describe a ratio relationship between two quantities.

97BF10FFF1D2452FAEEE00D8EAED5E18.description: Understand ratio concepts and use ratio reasoning to solve problems.

F7EF2A186C5944C4B18A3D112CA8D006.description: Use area and volume models to explain perfect squares and perfect cubes.

6EC8A02007484537BFA2CD56A6C2F29F.description: Represent three-dimensional figures using nets made up of rectangles and triangles, and use the nets to find the surface area of these figures. Apply these techniques in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems.

DA5EBEED4FE945B69DBB134B44515843.description: Draw polygons in the coordinate plane given coordinates for the vertices. Use coordinates to find the length of a side joining points with the same first coordinate or the same second coordinate. Apply these techniques in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems.

A63808AF858547A9B152A312C06F3F4D.description: Find volumes of right rectangular prisms with fractional edge lengths in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems.

DC049AB05E9F4E5080BFF1B512FEE6C4.description: Find area of triangles, trapezoids, and other polygons by composing into rectangles or decomposing into triangles and quadrilaterals. Apply these techniques in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems.

2AB95AC318B942BAA5E59BD2380A5BBF.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving area, surface area, and volume.

39EAE8F4D4374A1B94DCE50B3BFEA465.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.

BD1AB6753E1948608AF5C2BF99740DBE.description: Look for and make use of structure.

E408E6DE54144A7C86FAA16B153FC9F0.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

4BCA36D912F24164BA66E176AC363EAC.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.

D73144EB2AD943A18DA90A51BA46643A.description: Interpret division of a whole number by a unit fraction, and compute such quotients.

8C6E0F58D013491D9AA9CAC5FD984715.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of division to divide unit fractions by whole numbers and whole numbers by unit fractions.

0EDC31599E024D3E83A2FAEFAAD646FC.description: Solve real world problems involving multiplication of fractions and mixed numbers.

321DD2FC8C31481585C00A849F6397E1.description: Explain why multiplying a given number by a fraction greater than 1 results in a product greater than the given number (recognizing multiplication by whole numbers greater than 1 as a familiar case). 92EDBC6985FF4053A558F554702A6796.description: Compare the size of a product to the size of one factor on the basis of the size of the other factor, without performing the indicated multiplication.

086066E6974F47D2AA0B4A2D6BD4AA2C.description: Interpret the product a/b × q as a parts of a partition of q into b equal parts; equivalently, as the result of a sequence of operations a × q ÷ b.
