57FFD29596A44B49888CA837EF21BE9A.description: Integrate qualitative scientific and technical information in written text with that contained in media and visual displays to clarify claims and findings.

C84829E5793443D2BB52D867781A1883.description: Gather, read and synthesize information from multiple appropriate sources and assess the credibility, accuracy and possible bias of each publication and methods used, and describe how they are supported or not supported by evidence.

A9705901BD6C4D80A7DDB146F0492F69.description: Construct and present oral and written arguments supported by empirical evidence and scientific reasoning to support or refute an explanation or a model for a phenomenon or a solution to a problem.

5AD6606255A2417498C1593B7B1987B7.description: Apply scientific ideas or principles to design, construct, and test a design of an object, tool, process or system.

0BFC94920F214ED0A7463D1A4CA143CE.description: Undertake a design project, engaging in the design cycle, to construct and/or implement a solution that meets specific design criteria and constraints.

3F6DA84847074DE19618A3106B344F28.description: Use mathematical representations to describe and/or support scientific conclusions and design solutions.

0A63E6CE8CE043E0A9842FB24BB2AF71.description: Construct and interpret graphical displays of data to identify linear and nonlinear relationships.

181CAFE3A854488A83609FDA0A3F8286.description: Analyze and interpret data to determine similarities and differences in findings.

511E29CFBD4E4C2998EFE3280BB3519D.description: Conduct an investigation and evaluate the experimental design to produce data to serve as the basis for evidence that can meet the goals of the investigation.

68A06C6CA8EE4BB1A51505BE030400F3.description: Collect data to produce data to serve as the basis for evidence to answer scientific questions or test design solutions under a range of conditions.

D1019F363CE241BD879BD0F90CD59503.description: Plan an investigation individually and collaboratively, and in the design:  identify independent and dependent variables and controls, what tools are needed to to the gathering, how measurements will be recorded, and how many data are needed to support a claim.

9CFA479DBFD54967AA1B32BDDB5B77A7.description: Develop a model to describe unobservable mechanisms.

FD1B3A1770274F48B4D62C77E0CF3597.description: Develop a model to predict and/or describe phenomena.

FA043AF2EBFD44FA807D4DA26F043F53.description: Ask questions that can be investigated within the scope of the classroom, outdoor environment, and museums and other public facilities with available resources and, when appropriate, frame a hypothesis based on observations and scientific principles.

document.title: New York State P-12 Science Learning Standards

AB82A1559C274C0890A45DAC09FD1360.description: The iterative process of testing the most promising solutions and modifying what is proposed on the basis of the test results leads to greater refinement and ultimately to an optimal solution.

49E57F0D2D6B4E0996FBB23C18D55473.description: Although one design may not perform the best across all tests, identifying the characteristics of the design that performed the best in each test can provide useful information for the redesign process - that is, some of the characteristics may be incorporated into the new design.

581DE76A8D4041E8AFD3B4ED4418C470.description: A solution needs to be tested, and then modified on the basis of the test results, in order to improve it.  There are systematic processes for evaluating solutions with respect to how well they meet criteria and constraints of a problem.

EE2AD53932104B50A274943CCFEC8F5A.description: The more precisely a design task's criteria and constraints can be defined, the more likely it is that the designed solution will be successful.  Specification of constraints includes consideration of scientific principles and other relevant knowledge that is likely to limit possible solutions.

F49331C0109841959E25AE388A1AAB0C.description: Defining and Delimiting an Engineering Problem

6C649EE356A84F2B8629B06252D92E21.description: Digitized signals (sent as wave pulses) are a more reliable way to encode and transmit information.

B8BF598AC364471C83B678728C2A5D4C.description: However, because light can travel through space, it cannot be a mechanical wave, like sound or water waves.

54DCF597AC7C4B7AB6FA698C6600DBB4.description: A wave model of light is useful for explaining brightness, color and the frequency-dependent bending of light at a surface between media.

212EE41F39374FA9B108B49AC7D8792B.description: The path that light travels can be traced as straight lines, except when it hits a surface between different transparent materials (e.g. air and water, air and glass) obliquely where the light path bends.

9BF194A8C95B4A7E99BC7391A7255509.description: When light shines on an object, it is reflected, absorbed or transmitted through the object, depending on the object's material and the frequency (color) of the light.

8E5A3C7999DE422086A350979DFFD153.description: A sound wave needs a medium through which it is transmitted.

74F7603DB82640638906BB6744100699.description: A simple wave has a repeating pattern with a specific wavelength, frequency and amplitude.

D4DC2021AA1B47AF8B9928FECCDB9888.description: When two objects interact, each one exerts a force on the other that can cause energy to be transferred to or from the object.

040B6AD4CF674F74AC858F44A0B394BC.description: An electric circuit is a closed path in which an electric current can exist.

33827A871EB644F1B83362CF1D62FA2A.description: Energy is spontaneously transferred out of hotter regions or objects and into colder ones.

AA0F5E4C4AC34A259AB41180B429EE41.description: The amount of energy transfer needed to change the temperature of a matter sample by a given amount depends on the nature of the matter, the mass of the sample and the environment.

04F8F711AD0641C38DF8EBB6A4810002.description: When the motion energy of an object changes, there is inevitably some other change in energy at the same time.

2459DB04054640B1A57BFC858B7454F0.description: Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer

5CEDC83EE8B149AABF1196DDEED63BE0.description: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles of matter.  The relationship between the temperature and the total energy of a system depends on the types, phases (states) and amounts of matter present.

C4211B418ED4430B97E48A3188CA8DBA.description: A system of objects may also contain stored (potential) energy, depending on their relative positions.

02F711D1DF5840D48B59BC23E6E6E0BA.description: Motion energy is properly called kinetic energy; it is proportional to the mass of the moving object and grows with the square of its speed.

7BDE0B501DF54102A4489C71D7801354.description: Temperature is not a form of energy.  Temperature is a measurement of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a sample of matter.

8AE2E2DF28E64495BB04B9E574B12596.description: The term "heat" is used in everyday language refers both to thermal energy (the motion of particles within a substance) and the transfer of that thermal energy from one object to another.  In science, heat is used only for this second meaning; if refers to the energy transferred due to the temperature difference between two objects.

71DB6899B1DB4BE8B5BD16B6E0E24E2A.description: Forces that act at a distance (electric, magnetic and gravitational) can be explained by fields that extend through space and can be mapped by their effect on a test object (a charged object, or a ball, respectively).

638E691FDB2F43439840D5D72BC570C9.description: Gravitational forces are always attractive.  There is a gravitational force between any two masses, but it is very small except when one or both of the objects has a large mass - e.g Earth and the sun.

0FEA32104B844050BF0F87940CE1BD15.description: Electric and magnet (electromagnetic) forces can be attractive or repulsive, and their sizes depend on the magnitudes of the charges, currents, or magnetic strengths involved and on the distances between the interacting objects.

1AE610390F7E42B8AFB0760F9A23F324.description: All positions of objects and the directions of forces and motions must be described in an arbitrarily chosen reference frame and arbitrarily chosen units of size.  In order to share information with other people, these choices must also be shared.

AEC296EA32A84866B369C7A6B2BAD1E7.description: The motion of an object is determined by the sum of the forces acting on it; if the total force on the object is not zero, its motion will change.  The greater the mass of the object, the greater the force needed to achieve the same change in motion.  For any given object, a larger force causes a larger change in motion.

7CA816DBE64E4E71B9FF8BF49A73853A.description: For any pair of interacting objects, the force exerted by the first object on the second object is equal in strength to the force that the second object exerts on the first, but in the opposite direction (Newton's third law).

6B23D89FE2544116A66F6286645AF487.description: Some chemical reactions release energy, others absorb energy.

AF0FE59E06D741B7B1113787F618501F.description: The total number of each type of atom is conserved, and thus the mass does not change.

49A02D550A3E430199B882630FD136F0.description: Substances react chemically in characteristic ways.  In a chemical process, the atoms that make up the original substances are regrouped into different particles, and these new substances have different properties from those of the reactants.

B41CB1E5F5FA4BE7BD330B9B15D10E1A.description: Each substance has characteristic physical and chemical properties (for any bulk quantity under given conditions) that can be used to identify it.

F8DFC65F0EE54E9C863B96A4968614A0.description: Mixtures are physical combinations of one or more samples of matter and can be separated by physical means.

3B0B94094AA74011ABB608E4EB56DEA4.description: The changes of state that occur with variations in temperature and/or pressure can be described and predicted using these models of matter.

851DF8A3DCF74361893ACEF431581CCE.description: Solids may be formed from molecules, or they may be extended structures with repeating subunits (e.g., crystals).

644A10F0CADB4903BA6E679F00A9BACD.description: In a solid, the particles are closely spaced and vibrate in position but do not change their relative locations.  In a liquid, the particles are closely spaced but are able to change their relative locations.  In a gas, the particles are widely spaced except when they happen to collide and constantly change their relative locations.

3ED3D3434BAE43DBB1574CEF3F346C2F.description: Each substance has characteristic physical and chemical properties (for any bulk quantity under given conditions) that can be used to identify it.

6AF350084DD643409EA1F98008C5B71C.description: Substances are made of one type of atom or combinations of different types of atoms.  Individual atoms are particles and can combine to form larger particles that range in size from two to thousands of atoms.

document.title: New York State P-12 Science Learning Standards

2A2BF821BD48400C84544AFB3344E79B.description: Explanations of stability and change in natural or designed systems can be constructed by examining the changes over time and forces at different scales.

3B28CA05107C44038A6E9C6ECA8D9F5E.description: Structures can be designed to serve particular functions.

C489EF3FEEF04E8B9FA1EFDC57894414.description: Structures can be designed to serve particular functions by taking into account properties of different materials, and how materials can be shaped and used.

F98F514CF3774C2A86F6C36DCD383525.description: Energy may take different forms (e.g. energy in fields, thermal energy, energy of motion).

4B907D2B91CB4C769BFF449BF2EB4C94.description: The transfer of energy can be tracked as energy flows through a designed or natural system.

FAAF9430DBF94BBDB62DDFBF054C47F5.description: Matter is conserved because atoms are conserved in physical and chemical processes.

E98A2652943C4B4BA9BA54B2AECE3B68.description: Models can be used to represent systems and their interactions - such as inputs, processes and outputs - and energy and matter flows within systems.

0E193BDFBC014AD795A750FAA7DFE9AA.description: Proportional relationships (e.g. speed as the ratio of distance traveled to time taken) among different types of quantities provide information about the magnitude of properties and processes.

2BCB8463C4F94D86BAC35FA9B1561867.description: Time, space and energy phenomena can be observed at various scales using models to study systems that are too large or too small.

CB6DB466DAE9418B86FF8F0B25A54C6D.description: Cause and effect relationships may be used to predict phenomena in natural or designed systems.

981643FD60944F1B895FBC37C7EE244F.description: Graphs, charts and images can be used to identify patterns in data.

0BBCAE7B0F3F4267BBD57193CC77A8C4.description: Macroscopic patterns are related tot he nature of microscopic and atomic-level structure.

5511C9DDD121467290F049D1731ACF1B.description: Recognizes assumptions and limitations of the experiment

40BCF3B2ABD6430CA4DE0C3B03A5BF5D.description: Formulates an appropriate conclusion or generalization from the results of an experiment

F60DED0D704D449E853DF56F61910959.description: Organizes data through the use of data tables and graphs

AD6D927F155B4FCB89D915E27CAA2EDD.description: Collects, organizes, and analyzes data, using a computer and/or other laboratory equipment

9C6FA8FF979E4403A9B06F3FE9BB09EB.description: Identifies the control group and/or controlled variables

EF10E7E186AD45C9BBEE8F06374A3252.description: Differentiates between independent and dependent variables

2AB33355E7844522A6A04079F4739CFD.description: Designs and carries out a controlled, scientific experiment based on biological processes

7452EEA69B114DCCB9239A85E7F25260.description: Uses chromatography and/or electrophoresis to separate molecules

CECEF5E8AED944AB969224F29B3083E7.description: Follows directions to correctly use and interpret chemical indicators

5B97E15D2EE044498E8CA59E41AC6174.description: Dissects plant and/or animal specimens to expose and identify internal structures

DDDA31ECE1E14BEF8A62D7528C4AA5C8.description: Designs and uses dichotomous keys to identify specimens

0CE834CD42A6430E8D274AC0489EBEDB.description:
Uses a compound microscope/stereoscope effectively to see specimens clearly, using different magnifications
• Identifies and compares parts of a variety of cells
• Compares relative sizes of cells and organelles
• Prepares wet-mount slides and uses appropriate staining techniques

C3F90B5AB4814CAA973387B64A467B48.description:

• Uses graduated cylinders to measure volume
• Uses metric ruler to measure length

• Uses triple-beam or electronic balance to measure mass

60AEE5BE46D843A08D1F7F572221B040.description: Follows safety rules in the laboratory

9B7ACEC998E24A49A3D5F020FCE2B692.description: The decisions of one generation both provide and limit the range of possibilities open to the next generation.

429088E0327D4B9A884972D1DF9BC0C5.description: Societies must decide on proposals which involve the introduction of new technologies. Individuals need to make decisions which will assess risks, costs, benefits, and trade-offs.

11EDFE5B1E3F42F19D45DA67A52C1EAA.description:
Performance Indicator 7.3: Explain how individual choices and societal actions can contribute to improving the
environment.

BB03F938F3F84542A63A952EEA1CD66F.description: Industrialization brings an increased demand for and use of energy and other resources including fossil and nuclear fuels. This usage can have positive and negative effects on humans and ecosystems.

C904EC52BCA940B991DE7675D3BBA2C2.description: When humans alter ecosystems either by adding or removing specific organisms, serious consequences may result. For example, planting large expanses of one crop reduces the biodiversity of the area.

809747C9B00C4082BFA0422D2C5A6AA6.description: Human activities that degrade ecosystems result in a loss of diversity of the living and nonliving environment. For example, the influence of humans on other organisms occurs through land use and pollution. Land use decreases the space and resources available to other species, and pollution changes the chemical composition of air, soil, and water.

32120BF9F7804E61BCC001DD53B181F1.description:
Performance Indicator 7.2: Explain the impact of technological development and growth in the human population on
the living and nonliving environment.

92BBCE935C004F31812D68F92BCBB6D8.description: Human beings are part of the Earth’s ecosystems. Human activities can, deliberately or inadvertently, alter the equilibrium in ecosystems. Humans modify ecosystems as a result of population growth, consumption, and technology. Human destruction of habitats through direct harvesting, pollution, atmospheric changes, and other factors is threatening current global stability, and if not addressed, ecosystems may be irreversibly affected.

79D09B560F8C44D9A622C4441359996B.description: Natural ecosystems provide an array of basic processes that affect humans. Those processes include but are not limited to: maintenance of the quality of the atmosphere, generation of soils, control of the water cycle, removal of wastes, energy flow, and recycling of nutrients. Humans are changing many of these basic processes and the changes may be detrimental.

21242ED6D60D41C78A91E2D3AD978A26.description: The Earth has finite resources; increasing human consumption of resources places stress on the natural processes that renew some resources and deplete those resources that cannot be renewed.

EE8930837E1D4768B826FD8777571FEB.description:
Performance Indicator 7.1: Describe the range of interrelationships of humans with the living and nonliving
environment.

F185F78074CC47DBBDE94F1E5E9E394F.description: Key Idea 7: Human decisions and activities have had a profound impact on the physical and living environment.

75B2BFA3CD584415909CDD9F3E491F22.description: A stable ecosystem can be altered, either rapidly or slowly, through the activities of organisms (including humans), or through climatic changes or natural disasters. The altered ecosystem can usually recover through gradual changes back to a point of longterm stability.

F5C2670265844660AB4079170A2BB75F.description: Through ecological succession, all ecosystems progress through a sequence of changes during which one ecological community modifies the environment, making it more suitable for another community. These long-term gradual changes result in the community reaching a point of stability that can last for hundreds or thousands of years.

05FC030A2CBA431E9C2A37F6004CEE00.description: The interrelationships and interdependencies of organisms affect the development of stable ecosystems.

BC828F1F58A54F7082610400A73059A5.description: Performance Indicator 6.3: Explain how the living and nonliving environments change over time and respond to disturbances.

D503CD08A9FF43A79DA1FB9827AC5A7B.description: Biodiversity also ensures the availability of a rich variety of genetic material that may lead to future agricultural or medical discoveries with significant value to humankind. As diversity is lost, potential sources of these materials may be lost with it.

AC2CDCEBED194CA09243C20C282A0D7A.description: As a result of evolutionary processes, there is a diversity of organisms and roles in ecosystems. This diversity of species increases the chance that at least some will survive in the face of large environmental changes. Biodiversity increases the stability of the ecosystem.

031478BFCB3744E4B5455AE50A3468BA.description: Performance Indicator 6.2: Explain the importance of preserving diversity of species and habitats.

D17D8B31E42A48A396FFAD399000EF50.description: Relationships between organisms may be negative, neutral, or positive. Some organisms may interact with one another in several ways. They may be in a producer/consumer, predator/prey, or parasite/host relationship; or one organism may cause disease in, scavenge, or decompose another.

BFAB26111162445294EA4BE7604452BD.description: Living organisms have the capacity to produce populations of unlimited size, but environments and resources are finite. This has profound effects on the interactions among organisms.

21E419FF9CC94ABDB287A261A0F577C8.description: In any particular environment, the growth and survival of organisms depend on the physical conditions including light intensity, temperature range, mineral availability, soil/rock type, and relative acidity (pH).

75FC44D059524DA3B19B19C0B24BDC29.description: The number of organisms any habitat can support (carrying capacity) is limited by the available energy, water, oxygen, and minerals, and by the ability of ecosystems to recycle the residue of dead organisms through the activities of bacteria and fungi.

A8FF4A4EC6784BCEAF32B8301653C6F6.description: The chemical elements, such as carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, and oxygen, that make up the molecules of living things pass through food webs and are combined and recombined in different ways. At each link in a food web, some energy is stored in newly made structures but much is dissipated into the environment as heat.

888FA18EC31841448B587C4367B044A4.description: The atoms and molecules on the Earth cycle among the living and nonliving components of the biosphere. For example, carbon dioxide and water molecules used in photosynthesis to form energy-rich organic compounds are returned to the environment when the energy in these compounds is eventually released by cells. Continual input of energy from sunlight keeps the process going. This concept may be illustrated with an energy pyramid.

C72D0B1F48B84EEB8FD38664D6495C9C.description: Energy flows through ecosystems in one direction, typically from the Sun, through photosynthetic organisms including green plants and algae, to herbivores to carnivores and decomposers.

EE3971C4F4AE4DB3975EF5FCB6BE8FB6.description: Performance Indicator 6.1: Explain factors that limit growth of individuals and populations.

322FFE69BD3F4B6D91CCB58D3730C63A.description: Key Idea 6: Plants and animals depend on each other and their physical environment.

1B787A549ED24868A0C5C878E5056A01.description: Feedback mechanisms have evolved that maintain homeostasis. Examples include the changes in heart rate or respiratory rate in response to increased activity in muscle cells, the maintenance of blood sugar levels by insulin from the pancreas, and the changes in openings in the leaves of plants by guard cells to regulate water loss and gas exchange.

622E9C76138B45B499D8EA8A27C1DD2A.description: Dynamic equilibrium results from detection of and response to stimuli. Organisms detect and respond to change in a variety of ways both at the cellular level and at the organismal level.

4BB891031F7847D1AB458C5F9A980178.description: Performance Indicator 5.3: Relate processes at the system level to the cellular level in order to explain dynamic equilibrium in multicelled organisms.

E22A36CC53664DC8BA559329BCA25644.description: Biological research generates knowledge used to design ways of diagnosing, preventing, treating, controlling, or curing diseases of plants and animals.

C79C825E26E44DEB8A0944701C11F47D.description: Gene mutations in a cell can result in uncontrolled cell division, called cancer. Exposure of cells to certain chemicals and radiation increases mutations and thus increases the chance of cancer.

88D6531C182E46298C473C282D6E45DB.description: Disease may also be caused by inheritance, toxic substances, poor nutrition, organ malfunction, and some personal behavior. Some effects show up right away; others may not show up for many years.

B6103CA4FAA944F3BE235B3F6E263B98.description: Some allergic reactions are caused by the body’s immune responses to usually harmless environmental substances. Sometimes the immune system may attack some of the body’s own cells or transplanted organs.

EC1780435BA04373A7852FBCE63B8D2A.description: Some viral diseases, such as AIDS, damage the immune system, leaving the body unable to deal with multiple infectious agents and cancerous cells.

92FFF3B3CC8142328571974732A25301.description: Vaccinations use weakened microbes (or parts of them) to stimulate the immune system to react. This reaction prepares the body to fight subsequent invasions by the same microbes.

66DB325EC9FA453EA84615640047CA31.description: Some white blood cells engulf invaders. Others produce antibodies that attack them or mark them for killing. Some specialized white blood cells will remain, able to fight off subsequent invaders of the same kind.

8FB1E008EBD94CF2804CDE6D3B458980.description: The immune system protects against antigens associated with pathogenic organisms or foreign substances and some cancer cells.

45C57CEE312C4A0599B85E527ECEA5D2.description: Viruses, bacteria, fungi, and other parasites may infect plants and animals and interfere with normal life functions.

3AB1F5CA5BDC4DF8B8802A630152ECA0.description: Homeostasis in an organism is constantly threatened. Failure to respond effectively can result in disease or death.

0EBE2C2CCD4147E19320D340CEAE3593.description: Performance Indicator 5.2: Explain disease as a failure of homeostasis.

55AA1E46AA3144E7AD65447F79A15B3C.description: Enzymes and other molecules, such as hormones, receptor molecules, and antibodies, have specific shapes that influence both how they function and how they interact with other molecules.

5602C4B2599642829E8148A80A2DF19A.description: Biochemical processes, both breakdown and synthesis, are made possible by a large set of biological catalysts called enzymes. Enzymes can affect the rates of chemical change. The rate at which enzymes work can be influenced by internal environmental factors such as pH and temperature.

3953A0C7607C4AFA9B3162E985557C9C.description: The energy from ATP is used by the organism to obtain, transform, and transport materials, and to eliminate wastes.

6F0FD99A14E74E859A6FB3A606C37980.description: In all organisms, the energy stored in organic molecules may be released during cellular respiration. This energy is temporarily stored in ATP molecules. In many organisms, the process of cellular respiration is concluded in mitochondria, in which ATP is produced more efficiently, oxygen is used, and carbon dioxide and water are released as wastes.

51675313D6814F8F961D46450CB57FD2.description: In all organisms, organic compounds can be used to assemble other molecules such as proteins, DNA, starch, and fats. The chemical energy stored in bonds can be used as a source of energy for life processes.

715050FC89E942DBAEFD78DBE2E6FB50.description: Plant cells and some one-celled organisms contain chloroplasts, the site of photosynthesis. The process of photosynthesis uses solar energy to combine the inorganic molecules carbon dioxide and water into energy-rich organic compounds (e.g., glucose) and release oxygen to the environment.

3DC873DB4E2840C7BF2DA11AC5D93EF4.description: The energy for life comes primarily from the Sun. Photosynthesis provides a vital connection between the Sun and the energy needs of living systems.

8EB917D3CB924D81BF3676061C3DE477.description: Performance Indicator 5.1: Explain the basic biochemical processes in living organisms and their importance in maintaining dynamic equilibrium.

55AFFCE0E60A4D54B9DCEF67EE4FE691.description: Key Idea 5: Organisms maintain a dynamic equilibrium that sustains life.

582DB922D4884D569FB538D2740D66FD.description: In humans, the embryonic development of essential organs occurs in early stages of pregnancy. The embryo may encounter risks from faults in its genes and from its mother’s exposure to environmental factors such as inadequate diet, use of alcohol/drugs/tobacco, other toxins, or infections throughout her pregnancy.

B2BCE33F273B4168AA284FFE972FD736.description: The structures and functions of the human male reproductive system, as in other mammals, are designed to produce gametes in testes and make possible the delivery of these gametes for fertilization.

98B6FF98BFD8499797D911B183571CE6.description: The structures and functions of the human female reproductive system, as in almost all other mammals, are designed to produce gametes in ovaries, allow for internal fertilization, support the internal development of the embryo and fetus in the uterus, and provide essential materials through the placenta, and nutrition through milk for the newborn.

97E39B2FFA47476D9CD879B81003AB47.description: Human reproduction and development are influenced by factors such as gene expression, hormones, and the environment. The reproductive cycle in both males and females is regulated by hormones such as testosterone, estrogen, and progesterone.

C7B5B7977B814E8198659D92EDE03038.description: The zygote may divide by mitosis and differentiate to form the specialized cells, tissues, and organs of multicellular organisms.

7F9BDE96D8A146AB8F03421DCEDD75AD.description: The processes of meiosis and fertilization are key to sexual reproduction in a wide variety of organisms. The process of meiosis results in the production of eggs and sperm which each contain half of the genetic information. During fertilization, gametes unite to form a zygote, which contains the complete genetic information for the offspring.

F3EF43A1F97B4F758D7797596BB3C845.description: Some organisms reproduce asexually with all the genetic information coming from one parent. Other organisms reproduce sexually with half the genetic information typically contributed by each parent. Cloning is the production of identical genetic copies.

20FB3B90A79547688425B4412E0DDDFC.description: Reproduction and development are necessary for the continuation of any species.

0A87F0D4949E4A75B8A1B8F85E469595.description: Performance Indicator 4.1: Explain how organisms, including humans, reproduce their own kind.

8D2F9C5473464570A8AED5F5E0B5AEB4.description: Key Idea 4: The continuity of life is sustained through reproduction and development.

6CDF9181FF4A492CA81F25A7E2CB0B79.description: Extinction of a species occurs when the environment changes and the adaptive characteristics of a species are insufficient to allow its survival. Fossils indicate that many organisms that lived long ago are extinct. Extinction of species is common; most of the species that have lived on Earth no longer exist.

85D4BDF74352488699D545F3B16FF7A9.description: Evolution does not necessitate long-term progress in some set direction. Evolutionary changes appear to be like the growth of a bush: Some branches survive from the beginning with little or no change, many die out altogether, and others branch repeatedly, sometimes giving rise to more complex organisms.

B3DDEEBD2CBC4B738E775F5C7C71587A.description: Billions of years ago, life on Earth is thought by many scientists to have begun as simple, single-celled organisms. About a billion years ago, increasingly complex multicellular organisms began to evolve.

1C1DFDA3B47B4A2C8177B56C37FC8BE0.description: Behaviors have evolved through natural selection. The broad patterns of behavior exhibited by organisms are those that have resulted in greater reproductive success.

A48B045D1B0E49C286ED510F3C700951.description: The variation of organisms within a species increases the likelihood that at least some members of the species will survive under changed environmental conditions.

1F29C815E7AB4897A55D367B40B9FCC2.description: Some characteristics give individuals an advantage over others in surviving and reproducing, and the advantaged offspring, in turn, are more likely than others to survive and reproduce. The proportion of individuals that have advantageous characteristics will increase.

F0481314F1884E55BBDDE6BBFFA19C9F.description: Species evolve over time. Evolution is the consequence of the interactions of (1) the potential for a species to increase its numbers, (2) the genetic variability of offspring due to mutation and recombination of genes, (3) a finite supply of the resources required for life, and (4) the ensuing selection by the environment of those offspring better able to survive and leave offspring.

7A140440BEA14CAE9E0A724C2A2A06D4.description: Natural selection and its evolutionary consequences provide a scientific explanation for the fossil record of ancient life-forms, as well as for the molecular and structural similarities observed among the diverse species of living organisms.

4264F9C722144F46AC8B5D6AE90D8642.description: Mutations occur as random chance events. Gene mutations can also be caused by such agents as radiation and chemicals. When they occur in sex cells, the mutations can be passed on to offspring; if they occur in other cells, they can be passed on to other body cells only.

DA727EAC69C149358ACADA83B9800542.description: Mutation and the sorting and recombining of genes during meiosis and fertilization result in a great variety of possible gene combinations.

0947A70CC85744A59B0904EDDA402CB5.description: New inheritable characteristics can result from new combinations of existing genes or from mutations of genes in reproductive cells.

ECC03522A26F4AE79B402E2163608A64.description: The basic theory of biological evolution states that the Earth’s present-day species developed from earlier, distinctly different species.

8FC9CF728BF94FDCAFB4647995233E85.description: Performance Indicator 3.1: Explain the mechanisms and patterns of evolution.

DA8322F4DDF54822B35FAC7D68CC0F09.description: Key Idea 3: Individual organisms and species change over time.

F7A150390FAC4F70B741B946465DBD38.description: Knowledge of genetics is making possible new fields of health care; for example, finding genes which may have mutations that can cause disease will aid in the development of preventive measures to fight disease. Substances, such as hormones and enzymes, from genetically engineered organisms may reduce the cost and side effects of replacing missing body chemicals.

F4749DD8748C41CE8D8CF4C6F10FCCC8.description: Inserting, deleting, or substituting DNA segments can alter genes. An altered gene may be passed on to every cell that develops from it.

5B493B0AC6734D5AAECD7EDFCC33BDDB.description: Different enzymes can be used to cut, copy, and move segments of DNA. Characteristics produced by the segments of DNA may be expressed when these segments are inserted into new organisms, such as bacteria.

C2B733A856154FC7BAB6427E9297E1E0.description: In recent years new varieties of farm plants and animals have been engineered by manipulating their genetic instructions to produce new characteristics.

423C91B067C5425C9D463F73A841BDB4.description: For thousands of years new varieties of cultivated plants and domestic animals have resulted from selective breeding for particular traits.

9F30B738348344078C98D68B357A116C.description:
Performance Indicator 2.2: Explain how the technology of genetic engineering allows humans to alter genetic makeup of
organisms.

0C41B9D21E4847D9A8A95607393FBAC0.description: The many body cells in an individual can be very different from one another, even though they are all descended from a single cell and thus have essentially identical genetic instructions. This is because different parts of these instructions are used in different types of cells, and are influenced by the cell’s environment and past history.

68CCB67FF07945178569ADB2E1B672C2.description: Offspring resemble their parents because they inherit similar genes that code for the production of proteins that form similar structures and perform similar functions.

1DB126C8632F48918C52D4E8D996E74F.description: The work of the cell is carried out by the many different types of molecules it assembles, mostly proteins. Protein molecules are long, usually folded chains made from 20 different kinds of amino acids in a specific sequence. This sequence influences the shape of the protein. The shape of the protein, in turn, determines its function.

FCF5AFBBB38E4AC2BF7A3027A262F6AC.description: Genes are segments of DNA molecules. Any alteration of the DNA sequence is a mutation. Usually, an altered gene will be passed on to every cell that develops from it.

E06F5335CC8D42DCA4CF9C231989EE04.description: Cells store and use coded information. The genetic information stored in DNA is used to direct the synthesis of the thousands of proteins that each cell requires.

3100500A7D994913AD3C2408DF3F9CC4.description: In all organisms, the coded instructions for specifying the characteristics of the organism are carried in DNA, a large molecule formed from subunits arranged in a sequence with bases of four kinds (represented by A, G, C, and T). The chemical and structural properties of DNA are the basis for how the genetic information that underlies heredity is both encoded in genes (as a string of molecular “bases”) and replicated by means of a template.

1F71395E2A134D9B909DC814384A7C37.description: In sexually reproducing organisms, the new individual receives half of the genetic information from its mother (via the egg) and half fromits father (via the sperm). Sexually produced offspringoften resemble, but are not identical to, either of their parents.

3CAF54CFA72942AF86ABAB7358DDED84.description: In asexually reproducing organisms, all the genes come from a single parent. Asexually produced offspring are normally genetically identical to the parent.

47D55297B9844BE58ACDE16F89FD5FFF.description: Hereditary information is contained in genes, located in the chromosomes of each cell. An inherited trait of an individual can be determined by one or by many genes, and a single gene can influence more than one trait. A human cell contains many thousands of different genes in its nucleus.

501B43C75FAF4DCCB256AD2DF253A648.description: Every organism requires a set of coded instructions for specifying its traits. For offspring to resemble their parents, there must be a reliable way to transfer information from one generation to the next. Heredity is the passage of these instructions from one generation to another.

6FA85E9F1B4C4D34A4046D3D7504150B.description: Genes are inherited, but their expression can be modified by interactions with the environment.

4B2DCA0825CC413895E2659C4665CA9F.description: Performance Indicator 2.1: Explain how the structure and replication of genetic material result in offspring that resemble their parents.

4A7806A4D15F4E52B36767CA04A4DE61.description:
Key Idea 2: Organisms inherit genetic information in a variety of ways that result in continuity of structure and function
between parents and offspring.

D69D6A62BDC94F8C9E7DD8EE4F704572.description:
The structures present in some single-celled organisms act in a manner similar to
the tissues and systems found in multicellular organisms, thus enabling them to
perform all of the life processes needed to maintain homeostasis.

5DCC5CC0ED2B4E0893921E8A10531E45.description:
Performance Indicator 1.3: Explain how a one-celled organism is able to function despite lacking the levels of
organization present in more complex organisms.

81C9614C76414E18A554EA6A15DFD09C.description: Receptor molecules play an important role in the interactions between cells. Two primary agents of cellular communication are hormones and chemicals produced by nerve cells. If nerve or hormone signals are blocked, cellular communication is disrupted and the organism’s stability is affected.

4F2D53D76A334623BCA7ECFFFA6C4C48.description: Inside the cell a variety of specialized structures, formed from many different molecules, carry out the transport of materials (cytoplasm), extraction of energy from nutrients (mitochondria), protein building (ribosomes), waste disposal (cell membrane), storage (vacuole), and information storage (nucleus).

F85836F4AF6F4388A82167868867DB2A.description: Many organic and inorganic substances dissolved in cells allow necessary chemical reactions to take place in order to maintain life. Large organic food molecules such as proteins and starches must initially be broken down (digested to amino acids and simple sugars respectively), in order to enter cells. Once nutrients enter a cell, the cell will use them as building blocks in the synthesis of compounds necessary for life.

35EB2A9110ED43C5AC02E1807DC53BB8.description: Each cell is covered by a membrane that performs a number of important functions for the cell. These include: separation from its outside environment, controlling which molecules enter and leave the cell, and recognition of chemical signals. The processes of diffusion and active transport are important in the movement of materials in and out of cells.

B794031F0814437EABBFD715548DF593.description: Cells have particular structures that perform specific jobs. These structures perform the actual work of the cell. Just as systems are coordinated and work together, cell parts must also be coordinated and work together.

81B859EDFDDE4ACBA32C3243B4AE75DE.description: The organs and systems of the body help to provide all the cells with their basic needs. The cells of the body are of different kinds and are grouped in ways that enhance how they function together.

6F8951E1C91F41849DF169B75C118DBE.description: If there is a disruption in any human system, there may be a corresponding imbalance in homeostasis.

BD90B1E79065402F8D8ECD69070D54ED.description: The components of the human body, from organ systems to cell organelles, interact to maintain a balanced internal environment. To successfully accomplish this, organisms possess a diversity of control mechanisms that detect deviations and make corrective actions.

3D88FB309F694483811964AA97330060.description: Humans are complex organisms. They require multiple systems for digestion, respiration, reproduction, circulation, excretion, movement, coordination, and immunity. The systems interact to perform the life functions.

11E307334A38471ABD4326C622B40C43.description:
Important levels of organization for structure and function include organelles,
cells, tissues, organs, organ systems, and whole organisms.

64C4A5B5EB8C420F8DCCB8B345161B1D.description: Performance Indicator 1.2: Describe and explain the structures and functions of the human body at different organizational levels (e.g., systems, tissues, cells, organelles).

54E8D10E7BA04220AAA5D441F9D01D4A.description:
Every population is linked, directly or indirectly, with many others in an ecosystem. Disruptions in the numbers and types of species and environmental changes can
upset ecosystem stability.

F41B0CC7313944EBBDCA10B639756515.description:
Ecosystems, like many other complex systems, tend to show cyclic changes around
a state of approximate equilibrium.

4020E9C3C34548D39C72FEE87C79D5F8.description:
The interdependence of organisms in an established ecosystem often results in
approximate stability over hundreds and thousands of years. For example, as one population increases, it is held in check by one or more environmental factors or another species.

F8FDB4799970473AA8C92653A386CBB5.description: In all environments, organisms compete for vital resources. The linked and changing interactions of populations and the environment compose the total ecosystem.

5FCC0084D6BF44D9B2CFCDD8BC970742.description: An ecosystem is shaped by the nonliving environment as well as its interacting species. The world contains a wide diversity of physical conditions, which creates a variety of environments.

DFCE8FDCF31147BAA1F38E1EC3F9D9D0.description: Populations can be categorized by the function they serve. Food webs identify the relationships among producers, consumers, and decomposers carrying out either autotropic or heterotropic nutrition.

49F81AB468EB46838E0EEA9B87FC9E5E.description: Performance Indicator 1.1: Explain how diversity of populations within ecosystems relates to the stability of ecosystems.

06E125D265F64E31899C242798FAD33E.description: Key Idea 1: Living things are both similar to and different from each other and from nonliving things.

D74659D0D8144DD28AD5FD4676B759EB.description:
Standard 4 - Students will understand and apply scientific concepts, principles, and theories pertaining to the physical
setting and living environment and recognize the historical development of ideas in science.

58CDA04EDA9D46908E2230C53EC0F90D.description: Scientists use peer review to evaluate the results of scientific investigations and the explanations proposed by other scientists. They analyze the experimental procedures, examine the evidence, identify faulty reasoning, point out statements that go beyond the evidence, and suggest alternative explanations for the same observations.

FA797D6B5CEF4E31A6C35F79EC44E3EA.description: One assumption of science is that other individuals could arrive at the same explanation if they had access to similar evidence. Scientists make the results of their investigations public; they should describe the investigations in ways that enable others to repeat the investigations.

E55B45AE20804D39BFA26CC116247EAA.description: Performance Indicator 3.5: Develop a written report for public scrutiny that describes the proposed explanation, including a literature review, the research carried out, its result, and suggestions for further research.

D48575D5AB694F78848899F87446FADC.description: Claims should be questioned if fact and opinion are intermingled, if adequate evidence is not cited, or if the conclusions do not follow logically from the evidence given.

804F8689FEDE4F6AA6EFA0C809C9FAE0.description: Claims should be questioned if the data are based on samples that are very small, biased, or inadequately controlled or if the conclusions are based on the faulty, incomplete, or misleading use of numbers.

B5D8D2657AA542CD8F6B608FCE68AF1B.description:
Hypotheses are valuable, even if they turn out not to be true, because they may
lead to further investigation.

1D51171CEA3B464B880DB75B760B1FB2.description:
Performance Indicator 3.4: Based on the results of the test and through public discussion, revise the explanation and
contemplate additional research.

DABEF15DC5DF44C7B2ECE5296A571CFA.description:
Performance Indicator 3.3: Assess correspondence between the predicted result contained in the hypothesis and actual
result, and reach a conclusion as to whether the explanation on which the prediction was based is supported.

DE91CCD3635348AE8A710CA7967CFA36.description:
Performance Indicator 3.2: Apply statistical analysis techniques when appropriate to test if chance alone explains the
results.

307CF480593D4923825A2D5DA2F57370.description: Interpretation of data leads to development of additional hypotheses, the formulation of generalizations, or explanations of natural phenomena.

085CD15E0D0E4A9AB742F8C1AEA0BA49.description:
Performance Indicator 3.1: Use various methods of representing and organizing observations (e.g., diagrams, tables,
charts, graphs, equations, matrices) and insightfully interpret the organized data.

A6BF1C46923641568016A4317453C926.description:
Key Idea 3: The observations made while testing proposed explanations, when analyzed using conventional and invented
methods, provide new insights into natural phenomena.

B1C8C1E06B1549ACB79450315517B08E.description: Performance Indicator 2.4: Carry out a research plan for testing explanations, including selecting and developing techniques, acquiring and building apparatus, and recording observations as necessary.

8E13D8CDA9C245A2A7CCDAC4B33A755D.description:
Development of a research plan for testing a hypothesis requires planning to avoid
bias (e.g., repeated trials, large sample size, and objective data-collection techniques).

252228F51784475CA9319CFF492147FA.description:
Hypotheses are widely used in science for determining what data to collect and as
a guide for interpreting the data.

1BE4F70D929F405A8E6B04E0A5638169.description: Hypotheses are predictions based upon both research and observation.

86FB472B63B5476C9611404EFE8E1A5F.description:
Performance Indicator 2.3: Develop and present proposals including formal hypotheses to test explanations; i.e., predict
what should be observed under specific conditions if the explanation is true.

607E7960E29E4748AC94FAD7520120B0.description: Development of a research plan involves researching background information and understanding the major concepts in the area being investigated. Recommendations for methodologies, use of technologies, proper equipment, and safety precautions should also be included.

BE9BDE98C2AF4EC8A0C229EB3BA6FCA5.description:
Performance Indicator 2.2: Refine research ideas through library investigations, including electronic information
retrieval and reviews of the literature, and through peer feedback obtained from review and discussion.

DD08B2B018584333B80BDEF3017AF0DD.description: Performance Indicator 2.1: Devise ways of making observations to test proposed explanations.

F4315E5FEB3D459CAAE55BC4E1C375E2.description:
Key Idea 2: Beyond the use of reasoning and consensus, scientific inquiry involves the testing of proposed explanations
involving the use of conventional techniques and procedures and usually requiring considerable ingenuity.

B0AB1D6589CF45259939DFA1BD1077F6.description:
Well-accepted theories are ones that are supported by different kinds of scientific
investigations often involving the contributions of individuals from different disciplines.

225B4C600C3D4054AF21C40B2608D239.description: Performance Indicator 1.4: Coordinate explanations at different levels of scale, points of focus, and degrees of complexity and specificity, and recognize the need for such alternative representations of the natural world.

701EA3CD82F741D69A8FA94EB5EF432D.description:
All scientific explanations are tentative and subject to change or improvement.
Each new bit of evidence can create more questions than it answers. This leads to
increasingly better understanding of how things work in the living world.

10B9450DE8BC4169A10CF99879990FA7.description:
Scientific explanations are accepted when they are consistent with experimental
and observational evidence and when they lead to accurate predictions.

F2069F5D58054D97B62C305932FAABEE.description:
Performance Indicator 1.3: Work toward reconciling competing explanations; clarify points of agreement and
disagreement

8F916C75535649A7B23034BB259713BB.description:
Inquiry involves making judgments about the reliability of the source and
relevance of information.

C762F2F25CD643FD993FE09717B5D00E.description:
Inquiry involves asking questions and locating, interpreting, and processing
information from a variety of sources.

AC58733599874041B99017DB434B0272.description:
Performanc Indicator 1.2: Hone ideas through reasoning, library research, and discussion with others, including
experts.

B3DDD1B546274DF1A8447CD296A055BA.description:
Science provides knowledge, but values are also essential to making effective and
ethical decisions about the application of scientific knowledge.

508EB9BC1EC242B486C87B26E57985AC.description: Learning about the historical development of scientific concepts or about individuals who have contributed to scientific knowledge provides a better understanding of scientific inquiry and the relationship between science and society.

A8B650CD77834BDC814FCAF82FB339AD.description:
Scientific explanations are built by combining evidence that can be observed with
what people already know about the world.

D22F03536E0842D88AC0FC5E0E9C1416.description:
Performance Indicator 1.1: Elaborate on basic scientific and personal explanations of natural phenomena, and develop
extended visual models and mathematical formulations to represent one’s thinking.

730A0FC59CE447029028E2E8E5D1C6AD.description:
Key Idea 1: The central purpose of scientific inquiry is to develop explanations of natural phenomena in a continuing and
creative process.

BC71F617102F46F0912B6D818AA52E68.description:
Standard 1 - Students will use mathematical analysis, scientific inquiry, and engineering design, as appropriate, to pose
questions, seek answers, and develop solutions.

document.title: NY Physical Setting/Physics

045C476224964BDEA9BD119B7E346C33.description: The fundamental source of all energy in the universe is the conversion of mass into energy.*

3487DAD3B7134741AD9ABA25D4A8BBBC.description: The total of the fundamental interactions is responsible for the appearance and behavior of the objects in the universe.

CBD462AF7DE24C12AFDEA9D16084A6E5.description: Behaviors and characteristics of matter, from the microscopic to the cosmic levels, are manifestations of its atomic structure. The macroscopic characteristics of matter, such as electrical and optical properties, are the result of microscopic interactions.

04046764426E4D5AA9384E61A07CCD58.description: The Standard Model of Particle Physics has evolved from previous attempts to explain the nature of the atom and states that: • atomic particles are composed of subnuclear particles • the nucleus is a comglomeration of quarks which manifest themselves as protons and neutrons • each elementary particle has a corresponding antiparticle

5021860F55D24B1B88605FA3DFDE1C1F.description: Among other things, mass-energy and charge are conserved at all levels (from subnuclear to cosmic).

3E992F34BC144C0FAAF31FB949B2AC26.description: On the atomic level, energy and matter exhibit the characteristics of both waves and particles.

4954B9D00079463A9D8E5D2F660B7DB5.description: The energy of a photon is proportional to its frequency.*

103138E6C18649E5B5E0413E45FDE199.description: On the atomic level, energy is emitted or absorbed in discrete packets called photons.*

A79A1A612BFB4F5AA613302E6A08162F.description: Charge is quantized on two levels. On the atomic level, charge is restricted to multiples of the elementary charge (charge on the electron or proton). On the subnuclear level, charge appears as fractional values of the elementary charge (quarks).

E5310EC207814D118198D6723CD4BBEB.description: States of matter and energy are restricted to discrete values (quantized).

6F90E83B97934F1A9197C8A708DC2C16.description:
Performance Indicator 5.3: Students can compare energy relationships within an atom’s nucleus to those outside the
nucleus.

A37A473F15944C499B7C5530D00D2EC3.description: The inverse square law applies to electrical* and gravitational* fields produced by point sources.

4206B13A87774096AD131B6E490F76D2.description: Gravitational forces are only attractive, whereas electrical and magnetic forces can be attractive or repulsive.

5BC4CE7195D0499DA5B15EC7D1E3E2F3.description: Field strength* and direction are determined using a suitable test particle.

5CC4A39A6A8A402584A5EF8FDAD13CC7.description: Momentum is conserved in a closed system.*

30CAFD76977342E1B845EB0E40883998.description: According to Newton’s Third Law, forces occur in action/reaction pairs. When one object exerts a force on a second, the second exerts a force on the first that is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction

E028CBF9F57D4B789E8F3C58147F16FC.description: The impulse* imparted to an object causes a change in its momentum*.

936226FF4CDF4198A1029E46D71CCF53.description: Kinetic friction* is a force that opposes motion.

F0FD2DE2FF93437A89CAA0E5878CBF02.description: Centripetal force* is the net force which produces centripetal acceleration.* In uniform circular motion, the centripetal force is perpendicular to the tangential velocity.

90155EA45BF24EE9B9BDD02C95B44FE7.description: The elongation or compression of a spring depends upon the nature of the spring (its spring constant) and the magnitude of the applied force.*

37D7FB087F5945E285913F70ED14D5D6.description: Weight is the gravitational force with which a planet attracts a mass*. The mass of an object is independent of the gravitational field in which it is located.

1F145EF6157E44FCA371FE76E781B91C.description: According to Newton’s Second Law, an unbalanced force causes a mass to accelerate*.

2891F92ABACA48BEAB46F262FCE8F24E.description: When the net force on a system is zero, the system is in equilibrium.

AE364D9CDA04498B8ABFACE0DACA770B.description: According to Newton’s First Law, the inertia of an object is directly proportional to its mass. An object remains at rest or moves with constant velocity, unless acted upon by an unbalanced force.

E0008BF5B60D400BBCF27BA5F8EF556C.description: The horizontal displacement of a projectile is dependent upon the horizontal component of its motion and its time of flight.

5DFC77561DA84A1CAB03B7DC7DA4A0FA.description: A projectile’s time of flight is dependent upon the vertical component of its motion.

ABEDFD400055496D889F803214E03F9B.description: The path of a projectile is the result of the simultaneous effect of the horizontal and vertical components of its motion; these components act independently.

08DB4C52A90D431E88FBC9AAC3D2DF77.description: An object in free fall accelerates due to the force of gravity.* Friction and other forces cause the actual motion of a falling object to deviate from its theoretical motion.

3DC281275F5B418C9F2C8EE6B030D3C4.description: An object in linear motion may travel with a constant velocity* or with acceleration*.

DB2BA4CD4E4042988E64DBABAEB77FD3.description: The resultant of two or more vectors, acting at any angle, is determined by vector addition.

A4329E4F599647C990FB77995A928A13.description: A vector may be resolved into perpendicular components.*

A4ED7CCFF5FD45FD8B084E40273E6F58.description: Measured quantities can be classified as either vector or scalar.

A68905CB3B384816B32E00E4C9431B7E.description:
Performance Indicator 5.1: Students can explain and predict different patterns of motion of objects (e.g., linear and uniform
circular motion, velocity and acceleration, momentum and inertia).

BB3F3ABFAFB848BE98CC7F46156AA0B8.description: When a wave source and an observer are in relative motion, the observed frequency of the waves traveling between them is shifted (Doppler effect).

C9F6E105D6594E98A5A76F2162709F00.description: When waves of a similar nature meet, the resulting interference may be explained using the principle of superposition. Standing waves are a special case of interference.

FE763412F78542BF93386AF2AF21AE0B.description: Diffraction occurs when waves pass by obstacles or through openings. The wavelength of the incident wave and the size of the obstacle or opening affect how the wave spreads out.

85D3A431964E4289AE67C25424DC7BD5.description: All frequencies of electromagnetic radiation travel at the same speed in a vacuum.*

4FA386C2F0224B4CB1468A847F47AD1E.description: The absolute index of refraction is inversely proportional to the speed of a wave.*

87719444C6104C60B427854EDEF43FCE.description: When a wave moves from one medium into another, the wave may refract due to a change in speed. The angle of refraction (measured with respect to the normal) depends on the angle of incidence and the properties of the media (indices of refraction).*

61BB06439314472495B3294917DFA35F.description: When a wave strikes a boundary between two media, reflection*, transmission, and absorption occur. A transmitted wave may be refracted.

B3BBB0C053974E9CB8AE0A595DF0A286.description: Electromagnetic radiation exhibits wave characteristics. Electromagnetic waves can propagate through a vacuum.

DE3C3E604E834A12AC50C2EAEDD8299A.description: Resonance occurs when energy is transferred to a system at its natural frequency.

4A46C40CA3884F1ABFDA8C816BFEC0C2.description: Waves are categorized by the direction in which particles in a medium vibrate about an equilibrium position relative to the direction of propagation of the wave, such as transverse and longitudinal waves.

0205A5EC37784B32A5AEF17E7BEFB307.description: Mechanical waves require a material medium through which to travel.

A3D31D7B10304A59BADE6C7B0E49DFE8.description: The model of a wave incorporates the characteristics of amplitude, wavelength,* frequency*, period*, wave speed*, and phase.

DD7B5BD413A84D5EBEF809FF55BA01FA.description: Waves carry energy and information without transferring mass. This energy may be carried by pulses or periodic waves.

29BCED93B14247AE81B562BF9FA01512.description: An oscillating system produces waves. The nature of the system determines the type of wave produced.

55D3EBCA856844B3B68A17684F0A1467.description:
Performance Indicator 4.3: Students can explain variations in wavelength and frequency in terms of the source of the
vibrations that produce them, e.g., molecules, electrons, and nuclear particles.

6D591344138D444DA76CBDE45A390752.description: Electrical power* and energy* can be determined for electric circuits.

C3A87B2B8CF14FB7AB1826A402F59F69.description: Circuit components may be connected in series* or in parallel*. Schematic diagrams are used to represent circuits and circuit elements.

CAC0D4051E0143409CB222F95D4453B4.description: A circuit is a closed path in which a current* can exist. (Note: Use conventional current.)

F412FEBF37414E028E7031D8B9856CD1.description: The factors affecting resistance in a conductor are length, cross-sectional area, temperature, and resistivity.*

A101105CA856415E9076FB23EBF7442E.description: All materials display a range of conductivity. At constant temperature, common metallic conductors obey Ohm’s Law*.

83CA97884BF844D19D68AD33B701D7C3.description: Moving electric charges produce magnetic fields. The relative motion between a conductor and a magnetic field may produce a potential difference in the conductor.

96D5BB990CF44EF89EFD72F35E5E619C.description: Energy may be stored in electric* or magnetic fields. This energy may be transferred through conductors or space and may be converted to other forms of energy.

A380D3D6327441299CA217ED186D5E22.description: Power* is the time-rate at which work is done or energy is expended.

350C2B4BEB034E01AA0F836A7F2279E2.description: Work done against friction results in an increase in the internal energy of the system.

AA4B224E2079442ABDE8F153B07C3EBD.description: When work* is done on or by a system, there is a change in the total energy* of the system.

A7247A0C74D64FD5B15093BBD70A601D.description: In a nonideal mechanical system, as mechanical energy decreases there is a corresponding increase in other energies such as internal energy.*

C182EB63D8A64C3DB4F6473BF4F78027.description: In an ideal mechanical system, the sum of the macroscopic kinetic and potential energies (mechanical energy) is constant.*

7EB075D583BC45F8BEDC9D2C78BC2407.description: Kinetic energy* is the energy an object possesses by virtue of its motion.

AD861E966DED4BFAB438CED2B65D5C1E.description: Potential energy is the energy an object possesses by virtue of its position or condition. Types of potential energy include gravitational* and elastic*.

51BCBCC8CE7A4249909F11D0CAB004C6.description: Energy may be converted among mechanical, electromagnetic, nuclear, and thermal forms.

6A1832F713C8442897590EF808157DA6.description: All energy transfers are governed by the law of conservation of energy.

FA5EC872F93A4F4CB3453E55816241B9.description: Performance Indicator 4.1: Students can observe and describe transmission of various forms of energy.

AF948198115A4B86AE0CC02E580F90E5.description:
Standard 4: The Physical Setting (Students will understand and apply scientific concepts, principles, and theories pertaining to the physical setting
and living environment and recognize the historical development of ideas in science.)

ECE6768AA7A940048459EC222AAAC005.description:
Key Idea 2: Solving interdisciplinary problems involves a variety of skills and strategies, including
effective work habits; gathering and processing information; generating and analyzing
ideas; realizing ideas; making connections among the common themes of mathematics,
science, and technology; and presenting results.

Recognize consumer protections provided by federal legislation
  • Issuers must give card account holders "a reasonable amount of time" to make payments on monthly bills
  • Credit card bills must arrive at least 21 days before the end of the grace period
  • Fees charged must be reasonable and proportional
  • Over-limit fees must be addressed
  • Interest rates on new transactions (not pre-existing balances) can increase only after the first year
  • Significant changes require 45 days of advance notice
  • Holders must be at least 21 years old unless they have adult co-sign
  • Credit card companies must stay at least 1,000 feet from college campuses if they are offering gifts to entice students to apply
  • Card issuers cannot raise the APR (annual percentage rate) automatically when the cardholder fails to make a payment on another card
  • Issuers need to clearly disclose all information and rates

22E3E9BBA3CF4ADBA2238A24EDAC8736.description: Professional development evaluation results are reported to key stakeholder groups in a manner that promotes effective use of the evaluation data for improving both individual educator practice and building- and district-wide professional development plans.

F3EBD2663818403EA15C2791AD476248.description: Professional development evaluation includes the use of multiple methods and techniques that provide information to ensure ongoing improvements in the quality of the professional development experience (such as participant reactions, surveys, focus groups, interviews, reflective journals, portfolios, or information about student behavior or performance).

B026DCD9DC3545EEABE5F0E0F7F0D031.description: Professional development evaluation uses multiple measures to assess effectiveness of the knowledge and skill acquired in improving professional practice and student learning (such as the use of new learning in instructional planning, the use of student data for the development and adaptation of teaching strategies, or the enhanced student performance following the application of a different teaching strategy).

733E617B7F8F47D4A091CF571E48D784.description: Resources are provided to plan and conduct ongoing evaluation of professional development.

F6AC0135CB5A4CB8A7FC52BB2CFC2ED0.description: Demonstrates competency in a variety of motor skills and movement patterns.
