6CCA4D2A4F7442BE8BBD147AF1047495.description: Use knowledge of classical languages to identify, describe, and explain the practices and products of the cultures studied as well as the cultural perspectives they suggest.

62CD49A178714DF6908CB51AB126FF0A.description: Learners use knowledge of classical languages to identify, describe, compare, and explain the practices, products and perspectives of ancient and other cultures.

3CDCCD77D89E4B37B5980DC2172637C3.description: Interact and negotiate meaning in spoken or written conversations to exchange information and express feelings, preferences, and opinions.

2261A392E7124145821441FC718DF9CA.description: Present information and ideas on a variety of topics adapted to various audiences of listeners, readers, or viewers to describe, inform, narrate, explain, and persuade.

4A9B0EAE38E344598A1A6A86F31CE7A0.description: Understand, interpret, and analyze what is heard, read, or viewed on a variety of topics, drawing on a range of diverse texts, including authentic resources.

3662817890774BDC8E970C7AC2DF8CEE.description: Learners communicate effectively in classical languages by using a variety of texts and resources for multiple purposes, while making interdisciplinary language connections.

CC45D64F1D9D4AF4980783A8DC4310A1.description: Use the target language to compare the products and practices of the cultures studied and their own.

2DFAB87B231345E9990C3E1830871586.description: Use the target language to identify, describe, and explain the practices and products of the cultures studied as well as the cultural perspectives they suggest.

232FB663260C409E91EB35CBF15282E8.description: Learners use the target language to identify, describe, compare, and explain the practices, products, and perspectives of the cultures studied.

7098A462143A4CC1B2F3A6F725C99744.description: Present information and ideas on a variety of topics adapted to various audiences of listeners, readers, or viewers to describe, inform, narrate, explain, or persuade.

A52062471BD34D6DA2B3E0B10D615927.description: Interact and negotiate meaning in spontaneous, spoken, visual, or written communication to exchange information and express feelings, preferences, and opinions.

098793A1ABFA4DE2A2E4B61A974AAF59.description: Understand, interpret, and analyze what is heard, read, received, or viewed on a variety of topics, using a range of diverse texts, including authentic resources.

48B9E4E62DC84620852B45C27F281C7A.description: Learners communicate effectively in the target language in order to function in a variety of contexts and for multiple purposes.

document.title: New York State P-12 Science Learning Standards

C83C16EADDE64EE4AF104C404ED74066.description: Develop a model to generate data for iterative testing and modification of a proposed object, tool, or process such that an optimal design can be achieved.

0925B089F8E44917B6765C2EBFAE58C1.description: Analyze data from tests to determine similarities and differences among several design solutions to identify the best characteristics of each that can be combined into a new solution to better meet the criteria for success.

1F1BF49B52BD48DCB3DCFEB223FA62EC.description: Evaluate competing design solutions using a systematic process to determine how well they meet the criteria and constraints of the problem.

4B2F2E0E66CD44BC80F615C6934D89A8.description: Define the criteria and constraints of a design problem with sufficient precision to ensure a successful solution, taking into account relevant scientific principles and potential impacts on people and the natural environment that may limit possible solutions.

8FDBDE9CB399441088703C483149FA2B.description: Construct an argument supported by evidence for how increases in human population and per-capita consumption of natural resources impact Earth's systems.

ACF45CEB8C6B4E16ABF77697ED134523.description: Apply scientific principles to design a method for monitoring and minimizing a human impact on the environment.

BD47E257C99F41CCA2187577C3624519.description: Analyze and interpret data on natural hazards to forecast future catastrophic events and inform the development of technologies to mitigate their effects.

DC857AF95691410787678C58C45AE1BD.description: Ask questions to clarify evidence of the factors that have caused the rise in global temperatures over the past century.

237BB9F68F2C4B11A9B2E35FD66638EE.description: Develop and use a model to describe how unequal heating and rotation of Earth cause patterns of atmospheric and oceanic circulation that determine regional climates.

C7829CC5775B46E195A920049DBC8383.description: Collect data to provide evidence for how the motions and complex interactions of air masses results in changes in weather conditions.

603BAA857C574B21A470931783BC6B34.description: Construct a scientific explanation based on evidence for how the uneven distributions of Earth's mineral, energy, and groundwater resources are the result of past and current geologic processes.

989ABAC3C892454593AE46387257C99B.description: Develop a model to describe the cycling of water through Earth's systems driven by energy from the Sun and the force of gravity.

9EBD4FB824BB45ACB56ED97E05E3DD84.description: Develop a model to describe the cycling of Earth's materials and the flow of energy that drives this process.

F79376FE12F641299542E07CD262543A.description: Analyze and interpret data on the distribution of fossils and rocks, continental shapes, and seafloor structures to provide evidence of the past plate motions.

A3E58AE226AE4225B165FD77A2ECDE60.description: Construct an explanation based on evidence for how geoscience processes have changed Earth's surface at varying temporal and spatial scales.

462367B89B09470EB27CB54B2F287B04.description: Construct a scientific explanation based on evidence from rock strata for how the geologic time scale is used to organize Earth's 4.6-billion-year-old history.

0AC6CBD0434C4D788BE69BCD8E6400DA.description: Analyze and interpret data to determine scale properties of objects in the solar system.

7591C4F80EFC49618DF2CC805A025A37.description: Develop and use a model to describe the role of gravity in the motions within galaxies and the solar system.

552C4D9FB6E648FC995157AFEDD3B063.description: Develop and use a model of the Earth-Sun-moon system to describe the cyclic patterns of lunar phases, eclipses of the Sun and moon, and seasons.

E9C543517C624BE3AC872E9E823EF70D.description: Use mathematical representations to support explanations of how natural selection may lead to increases and decreases of specific traits in populations over time.

09476B2A9DF647D68353BD9D5612BB66.description: Construct an explanation based on evidence that describes how genetic variations of traits in a population increase some individuals' probability of surviving and reproducing in a specific environment.

FE6C21C50AC5475C8CA64C5BFFFCE51F.description: Analyze displays of pictorial data to compare patterns of similarities in the embryological development across multiple species to identify relationships not evident in the fully formed anatomy.

701BF58E92E94D49BBCC685621666A60.description: Apply scientific ideas to construct an explanation for the anatomical similarities and differences among modern organisms and between modern and fossil organisms to infer evolutionary relationships.

A396CAAA5BA04AA580EADA78ACEFEA48.description: Analyze and interpret data for patterns in the fossil record that document the existence, diversity, extinction, and change of life forms throughout the history of life on Earth under the assumption that natural laws operate today as in the past.

5E76735D7BD84F838C1232058C4FC77C.description: Gather and synthesize information about the technologies that have changed the way humans influence the inheritance of desired traits in organisms.

97D9AF944D5341EEB46B0635BB879B44.description: Develop and use a model to describe how asexual reproduction results in offspring with identical genetic information and sexual reproduction results in offspring with genetic variation.

9FD6FCDF29B4479991ED1D39DCBE51BC.description: Develop and use a model to explain why structural changes to genes (mutations) located on chromosomes may affect proteins and may result in harmful, beneficial, or neutral effects to the structure and function of the organism.

7B9FD550210F4D8996182B067C492D04.description: Construct a scientific explanation based on evidence for how environmental and genetic factors influence the growth of organisms.

3BB084CEE23943ED93808871BB6F2C44.description: Use argument based on empirical evidence and scientific reasoning to support an explanation for how characteristic animal behaviors and specialized plant structures affect the probability of successful reproduction of animals and plants, respectively.

540E66EEE2024DDDBF1DA42C17F5442D.description: Growth, Development, and Reproduction of Organisms

6D7D73F690FB42229400ECE80AF0FE90.description: Evaluate competing design solutions for maintaining biodiversity and protecting ecosystem stability.

185C483D0BC64EF29EDC3B2150173202.description: Construct an explanation that predicts patterns of interactions among organisms in a variety of ecosystems.

9861C119CDC64B76A238E36A30314EE7.description: Construct an argument supported by empirical evidence that changes to physical or biological components of an ecosystem affect populations.

FE96DDA3528144C49B13E888B162AFA2.description: Develop a model to describe the cycling of matter and flow of energy among living and non-living parts of an ecosystem.

13F40C4BFD6C417E9BC2818BCAB091E8.description: Analyze and interpret data to provide evidence for the effects of resource availability on organisms and populations of organisms in an ecosystem.

F76334E9A4134C76946F4ACCCC59BBA0.description: Develop a model to describe how food molecules are rearranged through chemical reactions to release energy during cellular respiration and/or form new molecules that support growth as this matter moves through an organism.

7E61D7ECB2D0441FAFE2E3E6FCF391BB.description: Construct a scientific explanation based on evidence for the role of photosynthesis in the cycling of matter and flow of energy into and out of organisms.

759F2164520E4D0BBC7E481BFFC72534.description: Matter and Energy in Organisms and Ecosystems

8C692D3397B84D82A8AA57B449AC7945.description: Gather and synthesize information that sensory receptors respond to stimuli, resulting in immediate behavior and/or storage as memories.

C73681B86F124B859133242B4A924F74.description: Construct an explanation supported by evidence for how the body is composed of interacting systems consisting of cells, tissues, and organs working together to maintain homeostasis.

ECB9FC4D4FFD40A5BDC6513EC92D54AD.description: Develop and use a model to describe the function of a cell as a whole and ways parts of cells contribute to the function.

C53FAD02CFE2404B8917389F0B2A671A.description: Plan and conduct an investigation to provide evidence that living things are made of cells; either one cell or many different numbers and types of cells.

F520C8723AA9459EA326EE1051302B3F.description: Integrate qualitative scientific and technical information to support the claim that digitized signals are a more reliable way to encode and transmit information than analog signals.

C0AB226968EB46378A322A75BF3E0A1C.description: Develop and use a model to describe that waves are reflected, absorbed, or transmitted through various materials.

6587A77E2E5E478A9B9CC4615A437B01.description: Develop a model and use mathematical representations to describe waves that includes frequency, wavelength, and how the amplitude of a wave is related to the energy in a wave.

1E308C64D75B44869AC6640BC7EDCF79.description: Make observations to provide evidence that energy can be transferred by electric currents.

EDDCD94E7AEA47C280C24F57F23B448F.description: Construct, use, and present an argument to support the claim that when work is done on or by a system, the energy of the system changes as energy is transferred to or from the system.

FE988C38EAA641179DD572EE07202F04.description: Plan and conduct an investigation to determine the relationships among the energy transferred, the type of matter, the mass, and the change in the temperature of the sample of matter.

46387E2284124CFB94E1EBC91AEB3FFD.description: Apply scientific principles to design, construct, and test a device that either minimizes or maximizes thermal energy transfer.

6C8AD848E68C4420AFB88088646E509B.description: Develop a model to describe that when the arrangement of objects interacting at a distance changes, different amounts of potential energy are stored in the system.

0660CA3C9FB84207A5A7DC333B3656DE.description: Construct and interpret graphical displays of data to describe the relationships of kinetic energy to the mass of an object and to the speed of an object.

E6E4BF118242475AADF35C4F2F5DE376.description: Conduct an investigation and evaluate the experimental design to provide evidence that fields exist between objects exerting forces on each other even though the objects are not in contact.

F5DD9EDC652D445C88DBB5E791E18340.description: Construct and present arguments using evidence to support the claim that gravitational interactions are attractive and depend on the masses of interacting objects and the distance between them.

3A1C265F9F194F46B04B5B5E5073B0E2.description: Ask questions about data to determine the factors that affect the strength of electric and magnetic forces.

46055A5476A64E25BBDAFA150569EF60.description: Plan and conduct an investigation to provide evidence that the change in an object's motion depends on the sum of the forces on the object and the mass of the object.

1D8B05DCE738466B9986735C2D2D53AC.description: Apply Newton's Third Law to design a solution to a problem involving the motion of two colliding objects.

2E6BBAA2FD794EF8B8E5F1B7169858EA.description: Undertake a design project to construct, test, and modify a device that either releases or absorbs thermal energy during a chemical and/or physical process.

03ACB640571649608F9CD545C4F7DD9E.description: Develop and use a model to describe how the total number of atoms does not change in a chemical reaction and thus mass is conserved.

B886E8FC02544267A0346CF86F618B7C.description: Analyze and interpret data on the properties of substances before and after the substances interact to determine if a chemical reaction has occurred.

D88BD8EA60E34C77B4756647E6736316.description: Plan and conduct an investigation to demonstrate that mixtures are combinations of substances.

80D143398DBC44F69C5A3F9EE5B03A8A.description: Use evidence to illustrate that density is a property that can be used to identify samples of matter.

2E14B149881F4E06A3FB802D92DCFB9C.description: Develop a model that predicts and describes changes in particle motion, temperature, and phase (state) of a substance when thermal energy is added or removed.

C269A95665F2455386764C4AEE986AE3.description: Gather and make sense of information to describe that synthetic materials come from natural resources and impact society.

5FAD12331D9D4CF08B13CC503D30DDE5.description: Develop models to describe the atomic composition of simple molecules and extended structures.

document.title: New York State P-12 Science Learning Standards

176706AD1F2B47069712D831FEBF3031.description:
Developing Possible Solutions - Both physical models and computers can be used in

various ways to aid in the engineering design process.

Computers are useful for a variety of purposes, such as

running simulations to test different ways of solving a

problem or to see which one is most efficient or

economical; and in making a persuasive presentation to a

client about how a given design will meet his or her

needs. (HS-ETS1-4)

6B5EF435F870412D9FC09E9288BBE459.description: Use a computer simulation to model the impact of proposed solutions to a complex real-world problem with numerous criteria and constraints on interactions within and between systems relevant to the problem.

086E2A6624244B4ABFC2DF3B8D4FC5C7.description:
Developing Possible Solutions

▪

When evaluating solutions, it is important to take into

account a range of constraints, including cost, safety,

reliability, and aesthetics, and to consider social, cultural,

and environmental impacts. (HS-ETS1-3)

360B684B436F413598C4A139C1948292.description: Evaluate a solution to a complex real-world problem based on prioritized criteria and trade-offs that account for a range of constraints, including cost, safety, reliability, and aesthetics, as well as possible social, cultural, and environmental impacts.

15F40D2CEAF149998DD186CD2F2A0880.description:
Optimizing the Design Solution

Criteria may need to be broken down into simpler ones

that can be approached systematically, and decisions

about the priority of certain criteria over others (trade-

offs) may be needed. (HS-ETS1-2)

E17199A2B3454661B2E2D18E4A71430B.description: Design a solution to a complex real-world problem by breaking it down into smaller, more manageable problems that can be solved through engineering.

6CDB62A91A624CF19167DBB000A0F19D.description:
Defining and Delimiting Engineering Problems - Humanity faces major global challenges today, such as

the need for supplies of clean water and food or for

energy sources that minimize pollution, which can be

addressed through engineering. These global challenges

also may have manifestations in local communities. (HS-

ETS1-1)

5E7B448839ED44A5AB41ED70B26D88A8.description:
Defining and Delimiting Engineering

Problems

▪

Criteria and constraints also include satisfying any

requirements set by society, such as taking issues of risk

mitigation into account, and they should be quantified to

the extent possible and stated in such a way that one can

tell if a given design meets them. (HS-ETS1-1)

BD8BF0D2C5CB46339501E71047E7CE72.description: Analyze a major global challenge to specify qualitative and quantitative criteria and constraints for solutions that account for societal needs and wants.

87EF7F4F9BA047F596631B8AC7C275C5.description:
Global Climate Change

▪

Through computer simulations and other studies,

important discoveries are still being made about how

the ocean, the atmosphere, and the biosphere interact

and are modified in response to human activities. (HS-

ESS3-6)

C2DDD516BD4A4B06B098127C0EB3A01D.description:
Weather and Climate

▪

Current models predict that, although future regional

climate changes will be complex and varied, average

global temperatures will continue to rise. The

outcomes predicted by global climate models strongly

depend on the amounts of human-generated

greenhouse gases added to the atmosphere each year

and by the ways in which these gases are absorbed

by the ocean and biosphere. (secondary to HS-ESS3-

6)

2E033605949C4006AB61F91775D24250.description: Use a computational representation to illustrate the relationships among Earth systems and how those relationships are being modified due to human activity.

64E45F38B2C5457CABBD70C1CEBBB1BF.description:
Scientists and engineers can make major contributions

by developing technologies that produce less pollution

and waste and that preclude ecosystem degradation.

(HS-ESS3-4)

4B106A87338C41E680462435601EC71A.description: Evaluate or refine a technological solution that reduces impacts of human activities on natural systems.

CDCFC596AE5B4B91B1C7CE9540C0998D.description:
Human Impacts on Earth Systems

▪

The sustainability of human societies and the

biodiversity that supports them requires responsible

management of natural resources. (HS-ESS3-3)

74A6E511022C41DB9BFB131990F77073.description: Create a computational simulation to illustrate the relationships among management of natural resources, the sustainability of human populations, and biodiversity.

66A02909F91648B488FED6F934F2CF89.description:
Developing Possible Solutions ▪ When evaluating solutions, it is important to take into account a range of constraints, including cost, safety,

reliability, and aesthetics, and to consider social,

cultural, and environmental impacts. (secondary to

HS-ESS3-2),(secondary to HS-ESS3-4)

D6D0BB731D28423FA05A472C688FFAA4.description:
Natural Resources ▪

All forms of energy production and other resource

extraction have associated economic, social,

environmental, and geopolitical costs and risks as well

as benefits. New technologies and social regulations

can change the balance of these factors. (HS-ESS3-2)

6BF1E9A27C0B47B8B9C8A3DAB1E3351C.description: Evaluate competing design solutions for developing, managing, and utilizing energy and mineral resources based on cost-benefit ratios.

E38711DFA9E349DC8331550111C94068.description:
Natural Hazards

▪

Natural hazards and other geologic events have

shaped the course of human history; [they] have

significantly altered the sizes of human populations

and have driven human migrations. (HS-ESS3-1)

B340CDA89A3C4D65BFA6A52ADF877865.description:
Natural Resources

▪

Resource availability has guided the development of

human society. (HS-ESS3-1)

851F553C1C964415910519EC8EAC6BEF.description: Construct an explanation based on evidence for how the availability of natural resources, occurrence of natural hazards, and changes in climate have influenced human activity.

DBE3AF5ED1694DFD80C5DDCB847D402F.description:
Weather and Climate ▪

(NYSED) Concepts of density and heat energy can be

used to explain observations of weather patterns (HS-

ESS2-8).

03A72CC065484C7C9FB96E29812DE85D.description: Evaluate data and communicate information to explain how the movement and interactions of air masses result in changes in weather conditions.

C9E8B8ED6D8B4F16A3AB0DEB6D200243.description:
Global Climate Change

Though the magnitudes of human impacts are greater

than they have ever been, so too are human abilities to

model, predict, and manage current and future impacts.

(HS-ESS3-5)

2B4A1D0E475A413BA5AB2D51D8E7670B.description: Analyze geoscience data and the results from global climate models to make an evidence-based forecast of the current rate of global or regional climate change and associated future impacts to Earth systems.

572A6AFDA180426BAE66A0C55DB39337.description:
Weather and Climate - Changes in the atmosphere due to human activity have

increased carbon dioxide concentrations and thus affect

climate. (HS-ESS2-4)

334E7E9C4E884F32B12BE75830D0BFC8.description:
Earth Materials and Systems

▪

The geological record shows that changes to global and

regional climate can be caused by interactions among

changes in the sun’s energy output or Earth’s orbit,

tectonic events, ocean circulation, volcanic activity,

glaciers, vegetation, and human activities. These changes

can occur on a variety of time scales from sudden (e.g.,

volcanic ash clouds) to intermediate (ice ages) to very

long-term tectonic cycles. (HS-ESS2-4)

EE691D4D9A89423EA41AA99AB68EB2E5.description:
Earth and the Solar System

▪

Cyclical changes in the shape of Earth’s orbit around the

sun, together with changes in the tilt of the planet’s axis

of rotation, both occurring over hundreds of thousands of

years, have altered the intensity and distribution of

sunlight falling on the earth. These phenomena cause a

cycle of ice ages and other gradual climate changes.

(secondary to HS-ESS2-4)

FACCAD0DE1E845D687620078CC1BFE19.description: Use a model to describe how variations in the flow of energy into and out of Earth's systems result in changes in climate.

664A239034564B7DB3E7283475BC5DE1.description:
Biogeology ▪

The many dynamic and delicate feedbacks between the

biosphere and other Earth systems cause a continual co-

evolution of Earth’s surface and the life that exists on it.

(HS-ESS2-7)

335E74A1E8F743F185D4BF2A421A05C9.description: Construct an argument based on evidence about the coevolution of Earth's systems and life on Earth.

322026082CFD4B76B27FAEB214A98485.description: Changes in the atmosphere due to human activity have increased carbon dioxide concentrations and thus affect climate. (HS-ESS2-6)

570BB2764AB34F53B929E88D0924BC21.description:
Weather and Climate ▪

Gradual atmospheric changes were due to plants and

other organisms that captured carbon dioxide and

released oxygen. (HS-ESS2-6),(HS-ESS2-7)

753244B76442439C9C1AF9AD4CBFDAA5.description: Develop a quantitative model to describe the cycling of carbon among the hydrosphere, atmosphere, geosphere, and biosphere.

2735485F24054780903ED64A56D21B2C.description:
The Roles of Water in Earth’s Surface

Processes -The abundance of liquid water on Earth’s surface and its

unique combination of physical and chemical properties

are central to the planet’s dynamics. These properties

include water’s exceptional capacity to absorb, store, and

release large amounts of energy, transmit sunlight,

expand upon freezing, dissolve and transport materials,

and lower the viscosities and melting points of rocks.

(HS-ESS2-5)

02BE27DE0B4443DBBBE3D3E1718D996A.description: Plan and conduct an investigation of the properties of water and its effects on Earth materials and surface processes.

0A0BB3C5302F47F186133D0DF7F76148.description:
Wave Properties ▪

Geologists use seismic waves and their reflection at

interfaces between layers to probe structures deep in the

planet. (secondary to HS-ESS2-3)

9DE7AE5AF88142328E3C77592B0F8DAA.description:
Plate Tectonics and Large-Scale System

Interactions ▪

(NYSED) Minerals are the building blocks of igneous,

metamorphic, and sedimentary rocks and can be

identified using physical and chemical characteristics.

These rock types are evidence of stages of constant

recycling of Earth material by surface processes and

convection currents in the mantle. (HS-ESS2-3)

FABFF39350C041D8A979E05840E0C1F9.description:
Plate Tectonics and Large-Scale System

Interactions

▪

(NYSED) Residual heat from Earth’s formation and the

radioactive decay of unstable isotopes in Earth’s interior

continually generate energy that is absorbed by Earth’s

mantle and crust, driving mantle convection. Plate

tectonics can be viewed as the surface expression of

mantle convection. (HS-ESS2-3)

31F9D223E0FB40DC8E764F791D2F274E.description: Earth Materials and Systems ▪ Evidence from deep probes and seismic waves, reconstructions of historical changes in Earth’s surface and its magnetic field, and an understanding of physical and chemical processes lead to a model of Earth with a hot but solid inner core, a liquid outer core, a solid mantle and crust. Motions of the mantle and its plates occur primarily through thermal convection, which involves the cycling of matter due to the outward flow of energy from Earth’s interior and gravitational movement of denser materials toward the interior. (HS-ESS2-3)

C5A355CF5F434EB9AD1610E0A40ABD59.description: Develop a model based on evidence of Earth's interior to describe the cycling of matter by thermal convection.

6A65785F03B04B10A3022D93AD8AC827.description:
Weather and Climate

▪

The foundation for Earth’s global climate systems is the

electromagnetic radiation from the sun, as well as its

reflection, absorption, storage, and redistribution among

the atmosphere, ocean, and land systems, and this

energy’s re-radiation into space. (HS-ESS2-4),(secondary

to HS-ESS2-2)

269A8166688942B19ABA8D47E588D8A0.description:
Weather and Climate ▪

The foundation for Earth’s global climate systems is the

electromagnetic radiation from the sun, as well as its

reflection, absorption, storage, and redistribution among

the atmosphere, ocean, and land systems, and this

energy’s re-radiation into space. (HS-ESS2-2)

A3E384DDE16645C08025B7049FA74A5A.description:
Earth Materials and Systems

▪

Earth’s systems, being dynamic and interacting, cause

feedback effects that can increase or decrease the

original changes (HS-ESS2-2)

6C886FC586F1439090AF55CD42916CFB.description: Analyze geoscience data to make the claim that one change to Earth's surface can create feedbacks that cause changes to Earth's systems.

3FE02C453CA241C0A94D57C0128861A1.description:
Plate movements are responsible for most continental

and ocean-floor features and for the distribution of most

rocks and minerals within Earth’s crust. (ESS2.B Grade 8

GBE) (HS-ESS2-1)

C788512B65DB4CCBA1ECED6B1F557B13.description:
Plate Tectonics and Large-Scale System

Interactions

▪

Plate tectonics is the unifying theory that explains the

past and current movements of the rocks at Earth’s

surface and provides a framework for understanding its

geologic history. (ESS2.B Grade 8 GBE) (secondary to

HS-ESS1-5),(HS-ESS2-1)

4506834D2B044A22A2C711C0B1EE8D4C.description:
Earth Materials and Systems

▪

Earth’s systems, being dynamic and interacting, cause

feedback effects that can increase or decrease the

original changes. (HS-ESS2-1) (Note: This Disciplinary

Core Idea is also addressed by HS-ESS2-2)

3F71A7B47B1845F998A0533D4AEA35A3.description: Develop a model to illustrate how Earth's internal and surface processes operate at different spatial and temporal scales to form continental and ocean-floor features.

037219DBA8F942B2A01FEBB82486F95F.description:
The History of Planet Earth ▪ Although active geologic processes, such as plate

tectonics and erosion, have destroyed or altered most of

the very early rock record on Earth, other objects in the

solar system, such as lunar rocks, asteroids, and

meteorites, have changed little over billions of years.

Studying these objects can provide information about

Earth’s formation and early history. (HS-ESS1-6)

3F54EB61E9E142D79C128C2BF78E0798.description: Apply scientific reasoning and evidence from ancient Earth materials, meteorites, and other planetary surfaces to construct an account of Earth's formation and early history.

66D8D0E6ED194DEFB1DFC6F979B3A691.description:
Nuclear Processes

▪

(NYSED) Spontaneous radioactive decay follows a

characteristic exponential decay law allowing an

element’s half-life to be used for radiometric dating of

rocks and other materials. (secondary to HS-ESS1-

5),(secondary to HS-ESS1-6)

266B4E80D97E49B9893D4ADDA3BF15A8.description:
The History of Planet Earth

▪

Continental rocks, which can be older than 4 billion

years, are generally much older than the rocks of the

ocean floor, which are less than 200 million years old.

(HS-ESS1-5)

CC07097DC2AF410EA910C974FC245D95.description: Evaluate evidence of the past and current movements of continental and oceanic crust and the theory of plate tectonics to explain the ages of crustal rocks.

30E11E8F842D4D4585C56F1B5149E7E3.description: (NYSED) Earth and celestial phenomena can be described by principles of relative motion and perspective. (HS-ESS1-7)

A7C7861A27FE4DCF98931C62AB947F65.description: Construct an explanation using evidence to support the claim that the phases of the moon, eclipses, tides and seasons change cyclically.

04A5E102F789470CAFEBAF72A95C1FFE.description: Use mathematical or computational representations to predict the motion of orbiting objects in the solar system.

B9F6DE71CA094D4098A1660D3CB72F30.description:
The Universe and Its Stars  ▪

Other than the hydrogen and helium formed at

the time of the Big Bang, nuclear fusion within

stars produces all atomic nuclei lighter than and

including iron, and the process releases

electromagnetic energy. Heavier elements are

produced when certain massive stars achieve a

supernova stage and explode. (HS-ESS1-2),(HS-

ESS1-3)

6E3790CBFF3E4847BB18D237CB09D9B5.description: Communicate scientific ideas about the way stars, over their life cycle, produce elements.

DC5064FCCB524A028F31E16A7BEC39CD.description:
Earth and the Solar System

▪

Kepler’s laws describe common features of the

motions of orbiting objects, including their

elliptical paths around the sun. Orbits may

change due to the gravitational effects from, or

collisions with, other objects in the solar system.

(HS-ESS1-4)

9EA8F4B17DCE4B14AD9B53C90386C71E.description: The Universe and Its Stars ▪ The study of stars’ light spectra and brightness is used to identify compositional elements of stars, their movements, and their distances from Earth. (HS-ESS1-2) (HS-ESS1-3)

CF38CB5B0DA746579436BF9ADF97523F.description: The Universe and Its Stars  ▪ The Big Bang theory is supported by observations of distant galaxies receding from our own, of the measured composition of stars and non-stellar gases, and of the maps of spectra of the primordial radiation (cosmic microwave background) that still fills the universe. (HS-ESS1- 2)

37D96F9010144C2D9ECB3C7DA819E39E.description:
Electromagnetic Radiation

▪

Atoms of each element emit and absorb

characteristic frequencies of light. These

characteristics allow identification of the presence

of an element, even in microscopic quantities.

(secondary to HS-ESS1-2)

5D10769D06FE41638409DAB524F2501B.description: Construct an explanation of the Big Bang theory based on astronomical evidence of light spectra, motion of distant galaxies, and composition of matter in the universe.

BF5D8BCFD2274E628683440706FE6F38.description: The Universe and Its Stars ▪ The star called the sun is changing and will burn out over a lifespan of approximately 10 billion years. (HS-ESS1-1)

C5AEB3CDC2F643FFB265FD579FE1F388.description:
Energy in Chemical Processes and

Everyday Life

▪

Nuclear Fusion processes in the center of the

sun release the energy that ultimately reaches

Earth as radiation. (secondary to HS-ESS1-1)

document.title: New York State 9-12 Social Studies Framework

F0C4ACFC5E5F4CF3B200A33C69E11979.description: Students will examine the development of European maritime empires and mercantilism.

ED6EC065CD9C48FAA5E9FDDBEDA61A42.description: Students will explore how shifts in the global trade networks and the use of gunpowder affected the Ottoman Empire.

4B0AECAD13D248A68F13EE7CD1A96B58.description: Students will explore how new transoceanic routes shifted trade networks (e.g., Indian Ocean, the Silk Road, Trans-Saharan) in the Eastern Hemisphere.

414F660B7DC74CCB8EFF68CB91468258.description: The Eastern Hemisphere trade networks were disrupted by the European development of new transoceanic trade across the Indian, Pacific, and Atlantic Oceans. Shifts in global trade networks and the use of gunpowder had positive and negative effects on Asian and European empires.

BAF8BF82E8C344ADA226625B4E15A3B1.description: Students will examine the social, political, and economic impact of the Atlantic slave trade on Africa, including the development of the kingdoms of the Ashanti and Dahomey.

7248912BAB904EF488871E14AAC448AD.description: Students will investigate the different degrees of social and racial integration and assimilation that occurred under colonizing powers, laying the foundations for complex and varying social hierarchies in the Americas.

0C03ECC37F8C4D45A23E3CFA758A784C.description: Students will examine the political, economic, cultural, and geographic impacts of Spanish colonization on the Aztec and Inca societies.

62FD1DD2366545A7A17BA88361AF6A64.description: European colonization in the Americas and trade interactions with Africa led to instability, decline, and near destruction of once-stable political and cultural systems.

9BF74E32EF82442295E0AC8F1DC12286.description: Students will investigate European and African roles in the development of the slave trade, and investigate the conditions and treatment of enslaved Africans during the Middle Passage and in the Americas.

7C4701357B10464AA1FA71C3BD26AE7C.description: Students will examine how the demand for labor, primarily for sugar cultivation and silver mining, influenced the growth of the trade of enslaved African peoples.

E22B62594D2647749DB35D9DB5A042CF.description: The decimation of indigenous populations in the Americas influenced the growth of the Atlantic slave trade. The trade of enslaved peoples resulted in exploitation, death, and the creation of wealth.

4269F5A263C84962BF87597440F846C4.description: Students will contrast the demographic impacts on Europe and China after the introduction of new crops with demographic effects on the Americas resulting from the Columbian exchange.

DED170BD605E4C97A2431F05E515466C.description: Students will investigate the population of the Americas before the Encounter and evaluate the impact of the arrival of the Europeans on the indigenous populations.

EF572AF19E7343C5910F9BA48CD04F87.description: Students will map the exchange of crops and animals and the spread of diseases across the world during the Columbian exchange.

7DA0FFD662524955A49CE7F01C4BDE8D.description: Transatlantic exploration led to the Encounter, colonization of the Americas, and the Columbian exchange.

8CD654A43D70466788B3FF1B66987856.description: Students will trace major motivations for European interest in exploration and oceanic trade, including the influence of Isabella and Ferdinand.

A48C646EA1EA4CE9B86C80D7D6540A9C.description: Students will explore the relationship between knowledge and technological innovations, focusing on how knowledge of wind and current patterns, combined with technological innovations, influenced exploration and transoceanic travel.

60DEB42CA1EE471ABBA9F9447C8CF45E.description: Various motives, new knowledge, and technological innovations influenced exploration and the development of European transoceanic trade routes.

6E41B141CDC6490FB4D2D0931517477D.description: Interactions And Disruptions: Efforts to reach the Indies resulted in the encounter between the people of Western Europe, Africa, and the Americas. This encounter led to a devastating impact on populations in the Americas, the rise of the transatlantic slave trade, and the reorientation of trade networks.

D9FAB639DC4B44338888648922559618.description: Students will investigate the context and challenge to authority in the English Civil War and Glorious Revolution.

B69E98755A0A4CF8B2FDE2D7D3D215E6.description: Students will investigate the Enlightenment by comparing and contrasting the ideas expressed in The Leviathan and The Second Treatise on Government.

A993E27BF2EC4043B2A974AF70909B96.description: The Enlightenment challenged views of political authority and how power and authority were conceptualized.

BDC31AD3B9504E16BE9E2406FDA106C9.description: Students will examine the Scientific Revolution, including the influence of Galileo and Newton.

E3B7ACB93D60444894362E558402251B.description: The development of the Scientific Revolution challenged traditional authorities and beliefs.

C5AFCBDE4D1C478C8F7DC0E2ACD5408A.description: Students will investigate autocratic and absolutist rule by comparing and contrasting the reigns of Louis XIV and Peter the Great.

2E9A45B0429143BB85377DD4DAA04E18.description: Students will investigate Russian efforts to remove Mongol and Islamic influence and to expand and transform their society.

B1F34696E2F0442F830EC18B6836849D.description: Absolutist governments emerged as Western European and Russian monarchs consolidated power and wealth.

2E619BB66BCA414BA3CDD5F50F95E13C.description: Students will trace the discrimination against and persecution of Jews.

40CFD86FCF54491BB05E7E5E03FDAEA0.description: Students will explore the roles of key individuals, including Martin Luther, John Calvin, Elizabeth I, and Ignatius Loyola, and the impacts that they had on the religious and political unity of Europe.

7491E33B37F94CE68210675796B74F9E.description: The Reformation challenged traditional religious authority, which prompted a counter reformation that led to a religiously fragmented Western Europe and political conflicts. This religious upheaval continued the marginalization of Jews in European society.

4A71DD523C4D4191A9C04CD8B9E7404B.description: Students will examine political ideas developed during the Renaissance, including those of Machiavelli.

350AC040623D48798D99FE707965ACA7.description: Students will explore shifts in the Western European Medieval view of itself and the world as well as key Greco-Roman legacies that influenced Renaissance thinkers and artists.

0E7811438A2A4EC3A841C5D0A9BB7DB8.description: Students will investigate technologies and ideas, including printing and paper, navigational tools, and mathematics and medical science that diffused to Europe, noting the role of the Islamic caliphates.

36094DEA6B6644FE87D941BBBF5826F6.description: The Renaissance was influenced by the diffusion of technology and ideas. The Islamic caliphates played an important role in this diffusion.

DC9CC32AB3C84CE7840C3EBAB4CC62FF.description: Transformation Of Western Europe And Russia: Western Europe and Russia transformed politically, economically, and culturally ca. 1400–1750. This transformation included state building, conflicts, shifts in power and authority, and new ways of understanding their world.

63A5243E6E3D403E941F6E6A5C0E38AB.description: Students will investigate the achievements and contributions of the Aztec, Inca, and Songhai empires.

7D3C3A2FD36346BAB4BFE6D4EFE415E5.description: Complex societies and civilizations made unique cultural achievements and contributions.

EF78290686924A198E47C0DF0FA6B127.description: Students will explore the relationships between religious beliefs and political power in the Aztec and Inca empires.

9A0B70A4B373467DA4CF82729949232A.description: Students will examine the role of nature and the traditional religious beliefs in the Americas and Africa (e.g., animism) during this period.

15484FD2DA9F4404851F6C0A11D3007B.description: Local traditional religions influenced the development of complex societies and civilizations in Africa and the Americas ca. 1325–1600.

4B2479FCC8FA49339ECD719D47BB2879.description: Students will examine the influence of Islam on the growth of trade networks and power relations in the Songhai Empire and in East African city-states.

DD566654490F4E45BBCA901BB2CF1DFC.description: Students will examine the relationships with neighboring peoples in the region considering warfare, tribute, and trade.

64FA59FF05AC42AB9FC37A466E64048E.description: Students will locate the extent of the Songhai and East African states in Africa and the Aztec and Incan empires in the Americas using an Atlantic Ocean-centered map. Students will examine the adaptations made to the environment by the Aztecs and Incas.

D4C9C77972C547D989742D50F49C8A11.description: Complex societies and civilizations continued to develop in Africa and the Americas. The environment, the availability of resources, and the use of trade networks shaped the growth of the Aztec, Inca, and Songhai empires and East African city-states. This growth also influenced their economies and relationships with others.

DE9116013C3B489F81E9640A0339D6A8.description: Africa And The Americas Pre-1600: The environment, trade networks, and belief systems influenced the development of complex societies and civilizations in Africa and the Americas ca. 1325–1600.

C922D72DF02F4E3983BCDF0819550DED.description: Students will examine how the Ottomans interacted with Europeans noting the role of Suleiman the Magnificent.

E22BBCD84A224E348D9CF0F6E4D91CA7.description: Students will examine Ming interactions with European traders and Christian missionaries.

936F129A8EED45CB8F4C71AC60AD4631.description: The Ottoman Empire and the Ming Dynasty had different views of the world and their place in it. Islam under the Ottoman Empire and Neo-Confucianism under the Ming Dynasty influenced the political, economic, military, and diplomatic interactions with others outside of their realm.

6B4CC962C7364D4D8097CA60651F0745.description: Students will analyze how the ethnic and religious compositions of the Ottoman Empire and the Ming Dynasty were reflected in their political and societal organizations.

E8B058B7FE554B2597647EB23FF48C3F.description: The dominant belief systems and the ethnic and religious compositions of the Ottoman Empire and the Ming Dynasty affected their social, political, and economic structures and organizations.

23A9EAA6227046FF8943154767D4175B.description: Students will map the extent of the Ottoman Empire and the Ming Dynasty at the height of their power.

CA831F871B364AC18F8DBE13C8B05B8B.description: Students will map the extent of the Muslim, Neo-Confucian, and Christian realms and compare the relative size and power of these realms ca. 1400.

6803E9975AB2412F973D5B2686B96877.description: Three belief systems influenced numerous, powerful states and empires across the Eastern Hemisphere.

19606CD3360049FDBEA61AB2150E1EBC.description: The Ottoman Empire And The Ming Dynasty Pre-1600: Islam, Neo-Confucianism, and Christianity each influenced the development of regions and shaped key centers of power in the world between 1368 and 1683. The Ottoman Empire and the Ming Dynasty were two powerful states, each with a view of itself and its place in the world.

7A96C7B1543242CB9C13BF232E94BF3B.description: Students will evaluate the effects of the Black Death on these regions.

F71BBA92983A43449C4D6F29716DB1A7.description: Students will map the spread of the Black Death (Bubonic Plague) as it was carried westward from Asia to Africa and Europe.

734C58D05C6C410E9FC7A8851D07A197.description: Networks of exchange facilitated the spread of disease, which affected social, cultural, economic, and demographic development.

E6DD8FA76AE245308A3C04D359DFC55D.description: Students will examine the development of Sikhism in South Asia during this time period.

07A9F249D0D146EEB0E1C6187D10295C.description: Students will investigate the Crusades and the Delhi Sultanate from multiple perspectives.

ECDBD155163C4688A91ADC0E07F7B7D9.description: Students will investigate the divisions within Islam (Sunni-Shia) and the Great Schism between Roman Catholic Christianity and Orthodox Christianity and their impacts.

6C6E4E2C563944EB980B086806907724.description: Internal tensions and challenges grew as disputes over authority and power arose between and among religious and political leaders.

4FA2B167DF6347E48614D970D95913AF.description: Social And Cultural Growth And Conflict: During the postclassical era, the growth of transregional empires and the use of trade networks influenced religions and spread disease. These cross-cultural interactions also led to conflict and affected demographic development.

4CFAC19C6AB843B3BE036245A0E26876.description: Students will examine feudal Japan, tracing the previous arrival of elements of Chinese culture (e.g., Buddhism, writing, poetry, art) and how those elements were adopted in and adapted to Japanese society.

DDB26EEC49AB4A2A90F8418900566540.description: Students will explore the spread and evolution of technology and learning from East Asia to Western Europe via the Middle East (e.g., gunpowder, ship technology, navigation, printing, paper).

1F985931C6CE4FE1BABCEC6ACD07FD5E.description: Students will compare and contrast the achievements and innovations of the Tang and Song dynasties with the Abbasid Caliphate.

F9001D0A4E9D42ADA72135E6F95E2F90.description: Periods of stability and prosperity enabled cultural, technological, and scientific achievements and innovations that built on or blended with available knowledge, and often led to cultural diffusion.

80AA4A701B7546869C2C05D30826D18B.description: Students will compare and contrast the empire-building processes of the Mongols and the Islamic caliphates, noting important disruptions in other regions.

5DB065F1B9E64A84ABEF5E5942FCBFCC.description: Students will examine the locations and relative sizes of postclassical states and empires at the heights of their power, including the Abbasid Caliphate, Byzantine Empire, Mongol Empire, and Song and Tang dynasties, noting relative position, power within their regions and the areas they influenced.

9104DF8268CF49B0AEB49B3594131DC9.description: Political states and empires employed a variety of techniques for expanding and maintaining control, and sometimes disrupted state-building in other regions.

753EA3F8431042629E92DACB7095ACF2.description: Students will compare and contrast the institutions in feudal Western Europe and the Byzantine Empire ca. 500 to ca. 1200.

D201B56B37B74DFDA7A5917255C6131A.description: Students will examine the political, economic, and social institutions of feudal Western Europe and the Byzantine Empire, including the role of Justinian and Theodora during the Middle Ages.

9C49F48F112B486692C89CEE0264CB8E.description: Following the fall of the Roman Empire, divergent societies emerged in Europe.

CB471566A234442A863D9D7F176DDD91.description: Political Powers And Achievements: New power arrangements emerged across Eurasia. Political states and empires employed a variety of techniques for expanding and maintaining control. Periods of relative stability allowed for significant cultural, technological, and scientific innovations.

CF47649377F54D49A4B3660BF738F05D.description: Students will examine the emergence and expansion of political states along the Mediterranean Sea complex (the Byzantine Empire and rise of the Ottoman Empire) and Trans-Saharan routes (Ghana and Mali).

1208DDEA129A493E886409549F7516C0.description: Control of transregional trade and economic growth contributed to the emergence and expansion of political states.

34EA8524241F4DDC8B00A0DB855F739C.description: Students will examine the travels of Zheng He, Ibn Battuta, and Marco Polo and the influence of their journeys.

11E1F5EA1E784FA7A28E72CD49503EA7.description: Students will examine the diffusion of religious ideas along the Indian Ocean complex, Silk Roads, and Trans-Saharan routes.

D9F3C27BBB5B492992DB6E833B29E2C1.description: Students will identify trade networks involved in the exchange of enslaved people and explore the nature of slavery during this time period.

06700DF8EBC44D20B2B69AB377F7E428.description: Students will identify and explain the importance of at least two key resources and/or products and/or luxury items vital to exchanges along the Indian Ocean complex, Mediterranean Sea complex, Silk Roads, and Trans-Saharan routes.

2C8A6F0902084A6E9934B92C46A07B00.description: Interregional travelers, traders, missionaries, and nomads carried products and natural resources, and brought with them enslaved people and ideas that led to cultural diffusion.

2045085F40D64EA683BBE62ED6DE34B5.description: Students will examine the technologies that facilitated and improved interregional travel along the Indian Ocean and Trans-Saharan networks of exchange.

36247AB0614E4D63A89BD66B3296729A.description: New technologies facilitated and improved interregional travel during this era by allowing people to traverse previously prohibitive physical landscapes and waterways.

71685B16C21A434FA3956A3ECA5701E9.description: Students will identify the location of the transregional trade networks noting regional connections between the Indian Ocean complex, Mediterranean Sea complex, Silk Roads, and Trans-Saharan routes.

5C0DEFB6C28A4E76BC7FCA6114F31387.description: Afro-Eurasian transregional trade networks grew across land and bodies of water.

D0017FE3713841B38319F2A3257CB68B.description: Rise Of Transregional Trade Networks: During the classical and postclassical eras, transregional trade networks emerged and/or expanded. These networks of exchange influenced the economic and political development of states and empires.

9CEB3BA4D56044B4879E889B87233804.description: Students will compare and contrast the forces that led to the fall of the Han Dynasty, the Mayan civilization, and the Roman Empire.

F7083EB1FEDE46AA80179693557881F8.description: Political, socioeconomic, and environmental issues, external conflicts, and nomadic invasions led to the decline and fall of Classical empires.

DBEC326843934347B5D94A099D337D63.description: Students will examine the achievements of Greece, Gupta, Han Dynasty, Maya, and Rome to determine if the civilizations experienced a Golden Age.

EF566CD21FB6456495C4FBB05B927952.description: A period of peace, prosperity, and cultural achievements can be designated as a Golden Age.

F3B1F3856B974669B55021807FFA94A2.description: Students will compare and contrast how the Mauryan, Qin, and Roman civilizations consolidated and increased power.

8DB64265D5BC43618AA57D13508E89A1.description: Empires used belief systems, systems of law, forms of government, military forces, and social hierarchies to consolidate and expand power.

D6A352FB6C794296AB7C69190F2AEBBA.description: Students will investigate how geographic factors encouraged or hindered expansion and interactions within the Greek, Roman, and Mayan civilizations.

B7A0EF4A93114FE9B8D667AD91D94BE7.description: Students will examine the locations and relative sizes of classical political entities (Greece, Gupta, Han, Maurya, Maya, Qin, Rome) noting the location and size of each in relation to the amount of power each held within a region.

EA34F5E4ED9C416AA72F9A566C80C466.description: Geographic factors encouraged and hindered a state's/empire's expansion and interactions.

3B680F8ADA9F4023A901B3C3E6FB1999.description: Classical Civilizations: Expansion, Achievement, Decline: Classical civilizations in Eurasia and Mesoamerica employed a variety of methods to expand and maintain control over vast territories. They developed lasting cultural achievements. Both internal and external forces led to the eventual decline of these empires.

62DDEAE3CC6A4C14BD4C168E19DAA392.description: Students will examine similarities and differences between Hinduism, Buddhism, Judaism, Christianity, Islam, and Confucianism regarding their effects on social order and gender roles.

B931B3EA9D7E4152A9D2373A89FC6FB6.description: Belief systems were often used to unify groups of people, and affected social order and gender roles.

474B695A0FB6466AB706ED04A73E7B80.description: Students will identify the place of origin, compare and contrast the core beliefs and practices, and explore the sacred texts and ethical codes for Hinduism, Buddhism, Judaism, Christianity, Islam, Confucianism, and Daoism.

C621F3C76F8B4B0BB2B3ECAAF5436AA2.description: Belief systems developed beliefs and practices to address questions of origin, the requirements to live a good life, and the nature of the afterlife.

6B203D919DF24938A618CAA6FC79396F.description: Belief Systems: Rise And Impact: The emergence and spread of belief systems influenced and shaped the development of cultures, as well as their traditions and identities. Important similarities and differences between these belief systems are found in their core beliefs, ethical codes, practices, and social relationships.

5B2EA989F0844657A84A47C6B139BBB0.description: Students will explore the Mesopotamian, Shang, and Indus River valley civilizations by examining archaeological and historical evidence to compare and contrast characteristics and note their unique contributions.

7CC4EBEA979E4EEE84150717A5FE84EE.description: Complex societies and civilizations shared common characteristics of religion, job specialization, cities, government, language/writing systems, technology, and social hierarchy, and they made unique contributions.

2BEF3A257FD84F77B9E66886B5A22665.description: Students will explore how the Mesopotamian, Shang, and Indus River valley civilizations adapted to and modified their environments to meet their need for food, clothing, and shelter.

CFACD8B10AC749258FFCCA52129168C2.description: Complex societies and civilizations adapted to and modified their environment to meet the needs of their population.

41DEB34CE1E1423F903415E2CE582D12.description: Students will analyze the political, social, and economic differences in human lives before and after the Neolithic Revolution, including the shift in roles of men and women.

ECA8F64408E64861AD164B0B9AF1FB4F.description: The Paleolithic Era was characterized by non-sedentary hunting and gathering lifestyles, whereas the Neolithic Era was characterized by a turn to agriculture, herding, and semi-sedentary lifestyles.

7A910C6AF8754AA0AD0A4B641B14A1A0.description: Development Of Civilization: The development of agriculture enabled the rise of the first civilizations, located primarily along river valleys; these complex societies were influenced by geographic conditions, and shared a number of defining political, social, and economic characteristics.

8BD3946817D04D6C82EF8936717A5120.description: Fulfill social and political responsibilities associated with citizenship in a democratic society and interdependent global community by developing awareness of and/or engaging in the political process.

78FD3856A4A84A5889A47D928EBB1250.description: Work to influence those in positions of power to strive for extensions of freedom, social justice, and human rights.

83AA654119184E49995179B3EAD3AEC8.description: Identify situations in which social actions are required and determine an appropriate course of action.

4BEF79AB121A40BDBDABD2A7D3582C95.description: Participate in persuading, debating, negotiating, and compromising in the resolution of conflicts and differences.

F2611761244B4BE58F38F2BEF17D4C52.description: Identify, describe, and contrast the roles of the individual in opportunities for social and political participation in different societies.

AED6A6976AB544FFAF024304B0D5F498.description: Explain differing philosophies of social and political participation and the role of the individual leading to group-driven philosophies.

80C65102E6F94AC9A4AB6DECE39CED22.description: Participate in activities that focus on a classroom, school, community, state, or national issue or problem.

60F077AE9B0B4E19B3D6CE988A3A29CD.description: Demonstrate respect for the rights of others in discussions and classroom debates; respectfully disagree with other viewpoints and provide evidence for a counter-argument.

E880582BC9B04430892261702BC4AB90.description: Analyze government economic policies and the effects on the national and global economy.

8AA88F1614C04A14BAE0D7382B63EC34.description: Use economic indicators to analyze the current and future state of the economy.

5E231B19DE2E45B091302B42A7EE20B4.description: Describe concepts of property rights and rule of law as they apply to a market economy.

775E30267D65470A9BB055434E15D828.description: Evaluate the extent to which competition between sellers and between buyers exists in specific markets.

3B7C7B621A674B7FA2C1799C609F9693.description: Analyze the ways in which incentives influence what is produced and distributed in a market system.

AE4E0020CE614055923E4ADBB461F1B9.description: Use marginal benefits and marginal costs to construct an argument for or against an approach or solution to an economic issue.

5B6A5854DBF043A69A986FA096010607.description: Characterize and analyze changing connections between places and regions.

325427E0AF5140BD89372B0FA727B7E3.description: Recognize and analyze how place and region influence the social, cultural, and economic characteristics of civilizations.

58F8342C26CA43EC984A4B3905851554.description: Recognize and interpret (at different scales) the relationships between patterns and processes.

033A5AF777A44CFDB7B95FAAB41E8536.description: Identify, analyze, and evaluate the relationship between the environment and human activities, how the physical environment is modified by human activities, and how human activities are also influenced by Earth's physical features and processes.

B185B2EF00A649E3B1F7703CF811997A.description: Identify, describe, and evaluate the relationships between people, places, regions, and environments by using geographic tools to place them in a spatial context.

0C9A9DD18D86466B8E740C0C17D40CDC.description: Ask geographic questions about where places are located, why their locations are important, and how their locations are related to the locations of other places and people.

9948F1BB05C34F6784873A13F5386693.description: Connect historical developments to specific circumstances of time and place and to broader regional, national, or global processes and draw connections to the present (where appropriate).

2FFEF5E4FDA84CA986630753B4DD9E12.description: Recognize the relationship between geography, economics, and history as a context for events and movements and as a matrix of time and place.

892DF96449864F679A51C4155A75A0D9.description: Describe, compare, and evaluate multiple historical developments (within societies; across and between societies; in various chronological and geographical contexts).

7D6886D565D94DE291FDD8CD89F5E883.description: Identify and compare similarities and differences between historical developments over time and in different geographical and cultural contexts.

731086B4F8FA4337ADB901EF6FE7F883.description: Identify, compare, and evaluate multiple perspectives on a given historical experience.

E29E4BF213394B649F3D9339173058A9.description: Identify similarities and differences between geographic regions across historical time periods, and relate differences in geography to different historical events and outcomes.

7FC8353DD4C84E5EA51A20F7E7F765D9.description: Describe, analyze, evaluate, and construct models of historical periodization that historians use to categorize events.

6B71658B417B4D36A5B2B28E1109DC20.description: Relate patterns of continuity and change to larger historical processes and themes.

18D690FC579842769F8AA91DAA883246.description: Recognize that choice of specific periodization favors or advantages one narrative, region, or group over another narrative, region, or group.

1630441D3F54497881F237C8CE9A33E7.description: Recognize, analyze, and evaluate dynamics of historical continuity and change over periods of time and investigate factors that caused those changes over time.

91D0CF59DF7D49528422063C441DBDC8.description: Distinguish between long-term and immediate causes and multiple effects (time, continuity, and change).

6D6E1F96FE064586AE8325DBF1F0449A.description: Identify, analyze, and evaluate the relationship between multiple causes and effects

AC5A0C683DCB44D0BA67EDA3D64A1F8E.description: Identify causes and effects using examples from different time periods and courses of study across several grade levels.

3B7E625B2D0449999258FC968C443150.description: Articulate how events are related chronologically to one another in time and explain the ways in which earlier ideas and events may influence subsequent ideas and events.

1A53F610D7DB49C7A82040A874E65CE4.description: Create meaningful and persuasive understandings of the past by fusing disparate and relevant evidence from primary and secondary sources and drawing connections to the present.

3AA4A3E80F60434191B2F4B08B528923.description: Deconstruct and construct plausible and persuasive arguments, using evidence.

8420235059874B34AFC09AAD3E03DFDD.description: Make inferences and draw conclusions from evidence.

D28835E9C895452DB2370329212C7C5F.description: Describe, analyze, and evaluate arguments of others.

AFAA2826298344928C3EE8F816FFCFCC.description: Analyze evidence in terms of content, authorship, point of view, bias, purpose, format, and audience.

89635A249DF54340A5FD6D4C818B0684.description: Identify, describe, and evaluate evidence about events from diverse sources (including written documents, works of art, photographs, charts and graphs, artifacts, oral traditions, and other primary and secondary sources).

D6456EE3BF8144939C470C75B5A55A3C.description: Define and frame questions about events and the world in which we live, form hypotheses as potential answers to these questions, use evidence to answer these questions, and consider and analyze counter-hypotheses.

standardSets.title: Grade 10: Social Studies Practices & Global History and Geography II
standardSets.subject: Social Studies (2017-)

document.title: New York State 9-12 Social Studies Framework

E7E5730B703940E0AC36CA96E1B75D77.description: Students will explore efforts to address human rights violations by individuals and groups, including the efforts of Mother Teresa, Aung San Suu Kyi, and the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo.

1FC200D4C5BA415E8FAF295FC6D9ABCF.description: Students will examine the policy of apartheid in South Africa and the growth of the anti- apartheid movements, exploring Nelson Mandela's role in these movements and in the post-apartheid period.

767FBD88C4A044A6983F0F5C5386B51A.description: Students will examine and analyze the roles of perpetrators and bystanders in human rights violations in Cambodia, Rwanda, and Darfur in light of the principles and articles within the UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

B9532CF776544A29AB43AA6E7452C045.description: Students will examine the atrocities committed under Augusto Pinochet, Deng Xiaoping, and Slobodan Milosevic in light of the principles and articles within the UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

F14486A77E844A8193A2E3B764289F7B.description: Historical and contemporary violations of human rights can be evaluated, using the principles and articles established within the UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

63006009CD694763A2D2E4B68BFEEED7.description: Students will explore international organizations that work to maintain peace, stability, and economic prosperity, and to protect nations and people from oppressive governments and political violence.

752C5DF4DE1A4FECBFA9649BCC8DD3E8.description: Students will explore multinational treaties and international court systems that bind countries to adhere to international human rights.

C2FDCEACBD194118AA4D4079FF8AE1B7.description: Governments, groups, and individuals have responded in various ways to the human atrocities committed in the 20th and 21st centuries.

AAC68C4F8888414487373059D4443A55.description: Students will examine the articles contained in the UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

308D0EA5871B4306A80D087EA48000FD.description: Students will investigate and analyze the historical context of the Holocaust, Nuremberg Trials, and Tokyo Trials and their impacts on the UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

2BF7046D302B45A98FD8C03BC9BBA3A2.description: Following World War II, the United Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) was written. This provides a set of principles to guide efforts to protect threatened groups.

863F092ECC194517824BF0D9FDB76BAD.description: Human Rights Violations: Since the Holocaust, human rights violations have generated worldwide attention and concern. The United Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights has provided a set of principles to guide efforts to protect threatened groups and has served as a lens through which historical occurrences of oppression can be evaluated.

8AFB9EB8329C49FCBBB5889836E86A82.description: Students will examine threats to global security, such as international trade in weapons (e.g., chemical, biological, and nuclear), nuclear proliferation, cyber war, and terrorism, including a discussion of the events of September 11, 2001.

F15D57725CCB47AF8A9EFD02A39AF79D.description: Students will investigate one organization and one international action that sought to provide solutions to environmental issues, including the Kyoto Protocol.

8F7A57046E05417C9577CA85B99D1C71.description: Students will examine the roles of the United Nations (UN), North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), the European Union, nongovernmental organizations (NGOs), and efforts to build coalitions to promote international cooperation to address conflicts and issues. They will also examine the extent to which these efforts were successful.

ED87738B3F82475DAC766E11F68D18B6.description: Globalization has created new possibilities for international cooperation and for international conflict.

E979BDA9422C41C3830AD008AF0C820D.description: Students will examine strains on the environment, such as threats to wildlife and degradation of the physical environment (i.e., desertification, deforestation and pollution) due to population growth, industrialization, and urbanization.

D861301C072B479EB958AF8C803B3FA0.description: Students will explore efforts to increase and intensify food production through industrial agriculture (e.g., Green Revolutions, use of fertilizers and pesticides, irrigation, and genetic modifications).

83D34E9496AB44D9A9160713D0726B2C.description: Students will examine how the world's population is growing exponentially for numerous reasons and how it is not evenly distributed.

4FF81490FF1347069A05BE7639D3CD95.description: Population pressures, industrialization, and urbanization have increased demands for limited natural resources and food resources, often straining the environment.

09CC350C82004D9A9D77C5720D56D22F.description:
Students will compare and contrast arguments supporting and criticizing globalization by examining concerns including:
  • free market, export-oriented economies vs. localized, sustainable activities
  • development of a mixed economy in China and China's role in the global economy
  • multinational corporations and cartels (e.g., Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries)
  • roles of the World Trade Organization, the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund, and microfinance institutions
  • economic growth and economic downturns (e.g., recession, depression) on a national and a global scale
  • economic development and inequality (e.g., access to water, food, education, health care, energy)
  • migration and labor
  • ethnic diversity vs. homogenization (e.g., shopping malls, fast food franchises, language, popular culture)

5D1D3EC711C6489ABE6B34586CDE1725.description: Globalization is contentious, supported by some and criticized by others.

D3BFCEA91512410D9309A49D8910B52E.description: Students will investigate the causes and effects of, and responses to, one infectious disease (e.g., malaria, HIV/AIDS).

B3B4B9684BCD4F228DF097021A528E25.description: Students will explore how information is accessed, exchanged, and controlled and how business is conducted in light of changing technology.

956FFA2A2F67417BA1DAE86B4063B409.description: Technological changes in communication and transportation systems allow for instantaneous interconnections and new networks of exchange between people and places that have lessened the effects of time and distance.

8754982F0A0F48F1BCBCF1BF4207FDE2.description: Globalization And A Changing Global Environment (1990–Present): Technological changes have resulted in a more interconnected world, affecting economic and political relations and in some cases leading to conflict and in others to efforts to cooperate. Globalization and population pressures have led to strains on the environment.

786EE23645D2460D889ADB889278BCF0.description: Students will explore how changes in technology, such as communication and transportation, have affected interactions between people and those in authority (e.g., efforts to affect change in government policy, engage people in the political process including use of social media, control access to information, and use terrorism as a tactic).

945EC1C2C8A647DCA52882ADAB744094.description: Students will investigate, compare, and contrast tensions between modernization and traditional culture in Turkey under the rule of Kemal Atatürk and in Iran under the Pahlavis and the Ayatollahs.

CC40A95E581B467098A9473688C2DCD4.description: Tensions between agents of modernization and traditional cultures have resulted in ongoing debates within affected societies regarding social norms, gender roles, and the role of authorities and institutions.

E18ACB7330E94422BC2998D43685637D.description: Students will investigate the extent to which urbanization and industrialization have modified the roles of social institutions such as family, religion, education, and government by examining one case study in each of these regions: Africa (e.g., Zimbabwe, Kenya, Nigeria, Sierra Leone), Latin America (e.g., Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Mexico), and Asia (e.g., China, India, Indonesia, South Korea).

FC35098EFBF841EB802A8F9937F614C4.description: Cultures and countries experience and view modernization differently. For some, it is a change from a traditional rural, agrarian condition to a secular, urban, industrial condition. Some see modernization as a potential threat and others as an opportunity to be met.

2FB9D39200C5420690AC3CDAC446709A.description: Tensions Between Traditional Cultures And Modernization: Tensions exist between traditional cultures and agents of modernization. Reactions for and against modernization depend on perspective and context.

09DE46946D4D4FAE975DF8AF206B6851.description: Students will investigate political, economic, and social policies under Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping and compare and contrast these policies.

09923784C2F94242A1FD7F931D9CB709.description: Students will trace the Chinese Civil War, including the role of warlords, nationalists, communists, and the world wars that resulted in the division of China into a communist- run People's Republic of China and a nationalist-run Taiwan.

D6713BA6833045D182B03887647FEA64.description: Nationalism in China influenced the removal of the imperial regime, led to numerous conflicts, and resulted in the formation of the communist People's Republic of China.

AC36037C87554CFDB9C02D45E43513CE.description: Students will examine the creation of the State of Israel and the Arab-Israeli conflict.

2618C556698A4EA486A5D7C07F14CC8F.description: Students will investigate Zionism, the mandates created at the end of World War I, and Arab nationalism.

AF1CAE1201474017A0ABABAF4E986A35.description: Nationalism in the Middle East was often influenced by factors such as religious beliefs and secularism.

14F7E751BA0C4954A260F4B7A0AC2808.description: Students will explore at least two of these three African independence movements: Ghana, Algeria, Kenya.

F8596672D52F413BBB49C3E2AC38E51C.description: African independence movements gained strength as European states struggled economically after World War II. European efforts to limit African nationalist movements were often unsuccessful.

1216D90EC6824514B5D4D908B0C9FBBC.description: Students will compare and contrast the ideologies and methodologies of Gandhi and Ho Chi Minh as nationalist leaders.

37E22C54BFEE48B495FFFC8F5F7ACA01.description: Students will explore Gandhi's nonviolent nationalist movement and nationalist efforts led by the Muslim League aimed at the masses that resulted in a British-partitioned subcontinent.

22F7633FD02647119865D6EE9E131EAE.description: Independence movements in India and Indochina developed in response to European control.

EED5AE4762254DF1B5EF177D0520E7F1.description: Decolonization And Nationalism (1900–2000): Nationalist and decolonization movements employed a variety of methods, including nonviolent resistance and armed struggle. Tensions and conflicts often continued after independence as new challenges arose.

E59223F232DE4D63929CCE3B92C9B82B.description: Students will examine the impacts of those reforms within the Soviet Union, on the Soviet communist bloc, and in the world.

D4F37A3D6EBD41CC915273D5657DD20B.description: Students will investigate the political reforms of glasnost and economic reforms of perestroika.

55743F0DD42C4C67866C5525A6FC9647.description: The end of the Cold War and the collapse of the communist bloc in Europe had a global impact.

084A8C6CA7F6463899F11205C64A6B51.description: Students will explore the era of détente from both American and Soviet perspectives.

B49FF9FC87794E2F9CCB7D0003757B83.description: Students will examine the reasons countries such as Egypt and India chose nonalignment.

235F8326AE704F0E8BAB2EE9FA8F96B0.description: Students will examine the new military alliances, nuclear proliferation, and the rise of the military-industrial complex.

222229D036AF4AA9A113621440CE5013.description: Students will investigate the efforts to expand and contain communism in Cuba, Vietnam, and Afghanistan from multiple perspectives.

6951C4C2CE7F4E3AB7595D9FBEA635A3.description: The Cold War was a period of confrontations and attempts at peaceful coexistence.

43116E811FDC48759CA749D76572566A.description: Students will compare and contrast how peace was conceived at Yalta and Potsdam with what happened in Europe in the four years after World War II (i.e., Soviet occupation of Eastern Europe, Truman Doctrine, Berlin blockade, NATO).

ABFA33EF6251441D809AA33DC821925C.description: The Cold War originated from tensions near the end of World War II as plans for peace were made and implemented. The Cold War was characterized by competition for power and ideological differences between the United States and the Soviet Union.

1860011C015F46F79E65A574CB743634.description: Unresolved Global Conflict (1945–1991: The Cold War): The second half of the 20th century was shaped by the Cold War, a legacy of World War II. The United States and the Soviet Union emerged as global superpowers engaged in ideological, political, economic, and military competition.

DA165515029E4C808B9BC6CA0DC211D9.description: Students will examine the atrocities against the Armenians; examine the Ukrainian Holodomor, and examine the Holocaust.

B2093FD1BDFA4F3DBAF088AC1A71C373.description: Human atrocities and mass murders occurred in this time period.

44335280790A4B1D84ABB17E6CA69D18.description: Students will investigate the causes of the Great Depression and its influence on the rise of totalitarian dictators and determine the common characteristics of these dictators.

CEC3BA8502AC4BE1A27EE42D6A3B928D.description: Students will examine the role of nationalism and militarism in Japan.

BFF77FD915A34DFF8BFCED351ABFEF20.description: Students will examine the role of nationalism and the development of the National Socialist state under Hitler in Germany.

038972658CBA4E70910BA4766C4B35DF.description: Students will examine the Russian Revolution and the development of Soviet ideology and nationalism under Lenin and Stalin.

34BB0B0009084268BB767592A26223CD.description: Nationalism and ideology played a significant role in shaping the period between the world wars.

9718B7F6841C44489DA6B7779EFFFA2B.description: Students will examine international efforts to work together to build stability and peace, including Wilson's Fourteen Points, the Treaty of Versailles, the League of Nations, and the United Nations.

12825511A7D940A39ADA0B7BC3FC0A74.description: The devastation of the world wars and use of total war led people to explore ways to prevent future world wars.

9C901239B57E458E8950D2CF5D4F1D91.description: Students will compare and contrast the technologies utilized in both World War I and World War II, noting the human and environmental devastation.

A469F353A52F4953B283A149B671CC14.description: Technological developments increased the extent of damage and casualties in both World War I and World War II.

15DD28F0501440B39CB201A7A9440219.description: Students will compare and contrast long- and short-term causes and effects of World War I and World War II.

B8A18F2C88AD4C668BA2E6482B9BEA92.description: International competition, fueled by nationalism, imperialism, and militarism along with shifts in the balance of power and alliances, led to world wars.

02C2A4BDDD9A4B68A8D298CB5C3DA34C.description: Unresolved Global Conflict (1914–1945): World War I and World War II led to geopolitical changes, human and environmental devastation, and attempts to bring stability and peace.

ABB63650895D40BB9C9BBE3DD9BB28F7.description: Students will compare and contrast maps of Africa from ca. 1800 and ca. 1914, noting the changes and continuities of ethnic groups and regions, African states, and European claims.
