7D4FFB54A560472494C55BA0D902ADDC.description: Students will identify examples of scarcity.

F3E3039CB4D7405B88D76DEA0D4AA217.description: Scarcity is the condition of not being able to have all of the goods and services that a person wants or needs.

047A832661F94714B97AE0B261DD4F67.description: Students will identify examples of goods and services.

444ECC158CDA460AB04057DAC310A8ED.description: Goods are objects that can satisfy people's needs and wants; services are activities that can satisfy people's needs and wants.

E9CD774666364600865EF975947AE824.description: Students will distinguish between a need and a want.

1B8EC9C5666B4F0A97BC51A67BA902B2.description: Students will identify basic needs (food, clothing, and shelter).

C0C2BB486F1B4AFAAF0C8C280AA79A85.description: A need is something that a person must have for health and survival, while a want is something that a person would like to have.

F8D358E9CDEE477F9A58E92722B7423D.description: People have economic needs and wants. Goods and services can satisfy people's wants. Scarcity is the condition of not being able to have all of the goods and services that a person wants or needs.

656DC3B8292340FFAA18FBBAA807114B.description: Students will retell a story and explain the value, idea, tradition, or important event that it expressed.

8BB4E4002A334808B8F7CDC4667EFEFE.description: People use folktales, legends, oral histories, and music to teach values, ideas, traditions, and important events from the past.

65DD95840EB643E8963B990E4F8816A6.description: Students will correctly use words related to chronology and time when recounting events and experiences (e.g., first, next, last; now, long ago; before, after; morning, afternoon, night; yesterday, today, tomorrow; last or next week, month, year; and present, past, and future tenses of verbs).

D6B71D83294348BCB708AABE1BC893B8.description: Specific words and phrases related to chronology and time should be used when recounting events and experiences.

51A814F827144A0BBFB9F401D56727ED.description: The past, present and future describe points in time and help us examine and understand events.

6985243278F6425D9876BDC9012C3D07.description: Students will describe and give examples of seasonal weather changes and illustrate how weather affects people and communities.

26CFF99254244F10A2999D552F864136.description: Climate, seasonal weather changes, and the physical features associated with the community and region all affect how people live.

24D5A5DCB0964704960E5E2F07486B6B.description: People and communities are affected by and adapt to their physical environment.

77F7106E073D43A28505B950EE68F6A6.description: Students will correctly use words and phrases to indicate location and direction (e.g., up, down, near, far, left, right, straight, back, behind, in front of, next to, between).

4367589DEF1246CCB37F9AC9008418A4.description: Places, physical features, and man-made structures can be located on a map or globe and described using specific geographic vocabulary.

FA8E7B19BAEE4E72871C3B5C2EEDF299.description: Students will locate on a map familiar places or buildings in the community (e.g., school, grocery store, train station, hospital).

BCF988A72D074D218ED6208ECBEB8EB8.description: Places and regions can be located on a map or globe, using geographic vocabulary

B82063998D8B437AB04A69864185FA58.description: Students will identify the differences and similarities between a globe and a map.

850105CBD2754019B947ECA7E9760552.description: A globe represents Earth, and maps can be used to represent the world as well as local places or specific regions.

5F6C1AD1F8DE484BB80521E938B931F1.description: Maps and globes are representations of Earth's surface that are used to locate and better understand places and regions.

039720F3948C40C39D1232400A9C3490.description: Students will be given an opportunity to create new rules as needed for class activities.

8E4C34C206CB4F519FCDB2A9F4DD934E.description: Children and adults have opportunities to contribute to the development of rules and/or laws.

8EB37D9DCB6D442D875396A52E9F4A54.description: Students will discuss classroom routines and rules (e.g., raise hand to ask or answer a question during circle time, walk quietly in the halls when going to specials).

6AC0DCA839EB4CE4AAD203C518089649.description: People in authority make rules and laws that provide for the health and safety of all.

DD233A061E774887B2DEE0CD53F43AF4.description: Students will discuss rules for fire, water, traffic, school, and home safety, and what would happen if rules were not followed.

108F822D0E68406D9379E46C6E23FEC3.description: Children and adults must follow rules within the home, school, and community to provide for a safe and orderly environment.

7DB8E249ED584E059F9A3BE2AF6E54CC.description: Rules affect children and adults, and people make and change rules for many reasons.

06ABA7496C674CB89722C42EE750D20E.description: Students will be given the opportunity to perform duties in the classroom (e.g., cleaning up a center, serving as line leader, straightening up the library, serving as a messenger).

3478704A2C5D4B41A6AA77E3FFDF28C6.description: Children can be responsible members of a family or classroom and can perform important duties to promote the safety and general welfare of the group.

42DB2F333D4D4C3C9DAA7A9B2F17C9FC.description: Students will identify basic rights they have (e.g., provision of food, clothing, shelter, and education, and protection from abuse, bullying, neglect, exploitation, and discrimination).

7A2C3AF0AE254BCB9804354237AF288C.description: Children have basic universal rights or protections as members of a family, school, community, nation, and the world.

B93C648E88434C7981B422FE17944A16.description: Children and adults have rights and responsibilities at home, at school, in the classroom, and in the community.

4EAA611FB093462198CD58BADD4BBAF1.description: Students will learn patriotic songs, including the national anthem, "America the Beautiful," and "America."

BD57113896B44AE7BCA88B0924EEC48E.description: Students will learn the parts of the American flag (stars and stripes) and how to show respect toward the flag.

5749DFFAD99A4D8D8BE117509B49FF4F.description: Students will learn the Pledge of Allegiance.

19058A8D309D4DD3A04E53A64E7353CE.description: Students will identify American symbols, such as the Liberty Bell and the bald eagle.

F8589498F44646AE8BD5CAD553EBFB9C.description: Students will explain when and why national holidays such as Labor Day, Constitution Day, Columbus Day, Thanksgiving, Martin Luther King Jr. Day, Presidents' Day, Law Day, and Independence Day are celebrated.

1D32680EC4D9400BA61DCB4828431ED6.description: The study of American symbols, holidays, and celebrations helps to develop a shared sense of history, community, and culture.

9FE07E28DEED48788F8FBC3CDAF66224.description: Students will compare ways diverse cultural groups within the community and nation celebrate distinct holidays.

20F823E631D449B094EF0ECBD872F5C3.description: Diverse cultural groups within the community and nation embrace unique traditions and beliefs, and celebrate distinct holidays.

D0A550C284504B529202D5BD4757B586.description: Symbols and traditions help develop a shared culture and identity within the United States.

F8FB5B04B2D94274BCFFD92F51909A90.description: Students will learn about and respect individual differences.

45E4394CE94D4DEE8D7999D2BB2CEC7E.description: Children and families from different cultures all share some common characteristics, but also have specific differences that make them unique.

C2BC6E8BBF6A40DAA5BF00924415CD1D.description: Students will explain how their families celebrate birthdays or other special days.

44EC433AB9494098ACC49086140A2649.description: Unique family activities and traditions are important parts of an individual's culture and sense of self.

3E415F2A7827497EAF01641987BFFA12.description: Students will identify characteristics of themselves that are similar to their classmates and characteristics that are different, using specific terms and descriptors such as gender, race or ethnicity, and native language.

3A1A7F6E53F848279375FAE193F98388.description: Each person is unique but also shares common characteristics with other family, school, and community members.

AE484C1FA31541288B73E48EC433F2DA.description: Children, families, and communities exhibit cultural similarities and differences.

1C1F76357F884E09972F596104ABBCC1.description: Students will create A BOOK ABOUT ME that includes information about their gender, race/ethnicity, family members, likes and dislikes, talents, and skills.

A1C9439454AE4DC5A00D85D24F8343F4.description: Personal experiences shape our sense of self and help us understand our likes, dislikes, talents, and skills, as well as our connections to others.

85BFD800D99D4830934A9B07D69D196B.description: A sense of self is developed through physical and cultural characteristics and through the development of personal likes, dislikes, talents, and skills.

B14252B07E7D4B4C84268B26294C7317.description: Children's sense of self is shaped by experiences that are unique to them and their families, and by common experiences shared by a community or nation.

62DDE670DBCE4D689F61FFAD7B3825C9.description: Identify and follow rules in the classroom and school.

CE5940A2B12040BF858DD955CBE8086F.description: Identify the school principal and his/her role within the school.

45365AC55C664D3F953487B17F2438F6.description: Identify situations in which social actions are required.

4E3A03F6C1B645A2A8BBE3BB82B2ACEF.description: Show respect in issues involving difference and conflict.

C73896EBF07F4ADFB75638AB9779E05B.description: Identify the role of the individual in classroom participation.

89D78BD586A842A79F384CC6A050DAC5.description: Participate in activities that focus on a classroom or school issue or problem.

10F902EE357449DFA50DC9CD4273790A.description: Demonstrate respect for the rights of others.

89B561762C054CE8971836B3F02E7B5F.description: Identify what money is and how it is used in society.

0679E550158644A9B7F8CDFBF5DE31CD.description: Identify examples of goods and services.

98A48857700F45DF89D2FB17E6E95D10.description: Identify examples of scarcity and choices made due to scarcity.

60916BC6E15042E5B9DD096A9EF376D8.description: Identify a human activity that changed a place.

A6AEF2012AEF412C9FD94BFE618C335C.description: Describe how environment affects his/her activities.

59A551AAA91146FCA20075F4488C925E.description: Identify natural events or physical features, such as land, water, air, and wind.

FD3457C100DD4B26A6CEF105F3A4A3C7.description: Ask geographic questions about where places are located and why they are located there, using location terms and geographic representations, such as maps, photographs, satellite images, and models.

BEEC69E836EF4178BDE9CF5869CA2E95.description: Describe an event in his/her life.

AE235EB776CB47FFAAD598812F6A3610.description: Identify similarities and/or differences between him/her and others.

E1A9AB8FFD974F969F77273A255296AC.description: Identify similarities and differences between home and school.

6970C851EBDB48A7A257720D7AC8B705.description: Identify routines and common occurrences in his/her life.

CCFEA916C5C34F8F882583398396D9BC.description: Identify events of the past, present, and future in his/her life.

0880EB175ADA48B8B10048C1DF4D72CB.description: Identify change over time in his/her life.

AC7822DC80964BD3A7543250C39455F4.description: Identify causes and effects, using an example from his/her family life.

9702B810D8974023B4B9900F8B988DD3.description: Understand the concept of time measurements, including days and weeks.

3FCE9E7545AD45CCBCE274E098A6864F.description: Retell an important life event in sequential order.

0F5C1348C5C94736B91AC01DA9DED03B.description: Identify the author or creator of a book or map.

1026CE4BE24F47E9AA125CD0A71335CC.description: Recognize forms of evidence used to make meaning in social studies.

document.title: New York State K-8 Social Studies Framework

3492D608250141A884FB2ADC1A468A42.description: Students will examine decisions that people make about spending and saving money.

5A21C09642A64AC5BED681E25D284C2E.description: People make decisions about how to spend and save the money that they earn.

3B51B1A6994B47E68F955A9844E5378B.description: Students will examine how earning money through work is related to the purchase of goods and services.

C6AAC59830B141C3B328E81BC4550699.description: People and families work to earn money to purchase goods and services that they need or want.

236846550E124966B6E60D11FE389E67.description: Students will identify examples of a producer and a consumer.

9A1689F97CD3491AB4A256CDB6E09FE4.description: A producer makes goods or provides a service, while a consumer uses or benefits from the goods or services.

1F4E4CB3C75242929F7C7297DBBD2420.description: Students will identify examples of goods and services.

7C8BC08FFAE7413C9EC72579292984E4.description: Goods are consumable, tangible products; services are actions performed by a person or group of people with a certain skill.

0FDC5986F457485C8BCA43A553DDB42E.description: People make economic choices as producers and consumers of goods and services.

5E36706E4C8C49F8A2E495F2184ABEB2.description: Students will examine how tools, technology, and other resources can be used to meet needs and wants.

6D7E073E478C4817B092E64EF0AAB19D.description: People use tools, technologies, and other resources to meet their needs and wants.

EEB894C8473647B39D95C969CA12CB5A.description: Students will examine choices that families make due to scarcity, and identify costs associated with these choices.

3FEBD235C6AB4CC484092FC2BEBEC604.description: Families and communities must make choices due to unlimited needs and wants, and scarce resources; these choices involve costs.

0904FB27A6264D0C9FE0183A90E4C408.description: Students will provide examples of scarcity by identifying wants that exceed resources.

E9A1774FEA49439D940F8361CECC1B09.description: Scarcity means that people's wants exceed their limited resources.

CB4553EC1E97419FA53BDED64978537E.description: People have many economic wants and needs, but limited resources with which to obtain them.

42B57A6CBFEB4A2AB158168F778F4203.description: Students will describe the main characters and qualities after listening to biographies and legends.

4265AA6A725642B290FB5A3D91F56380.description: Students will interview family members to learn about their family histories. Students will develop a family time line as an extension of their personal time line.

66805F9AC57E483299B28A9AC3D10508.description: Oral histories, biographies, and family time lines relate family histories.

B9AF34839A234B5584C8425295E043AB.description: Students will be exposed to various historical sources, including artifacts, letters, maps, photographs, and newspapers.

B7CD9FE1466843B2BA176259402CF855.description: Various historical sources exist to inform people about life in the past, including artifacts, letters, maps, photographs, and newspapers.

A8093D990BE14806BDED4A8C0EB7584F.description: Historical sources reveal information about how life in the past differs from the present.

63A3D49642CD4C93BD8EFC2AC81915FD.description: Students will use sequence and chronological terms when describing family events.

1C46A124ECEC400699E96C372425EFF0.description: Sequence and chronology can be identified in terms of days, weeks, months, years, and seasons when describing family events and histories.

75524D855C58407CB441DFC3DDE36C2B.description: Students will examine families of the past and compare them with their family. They will identify characteristics that have been passed on through the generations.

0291F89FD839496381FBC71FEB1A97BC.description: Families of long ago have similarities and differences with families today.

A6CB6483195343F08289696E0EC87418.description: Students will examine the changes in their family over time and how the family growth and change could be documented and recorded.

469D1F10E6224E0F8FC686A58FCB9002.description: Families change over time, and family growth and change can be documented and recorded.

8610792EDCA5411BB0510F141FF441B6.description: Students will create personal time lines of their life, school year, and family events with the help of family members. Students will demonstrate an understanding of sequence and chronology and share their time lines with each other.

6B8F21E96D7046A3AA8043B9863F54A8.description: Personal and family history is a source of information for individuals about the people and places around them.

53ACCBA2FF794E7BB0A2E017A24B18A8.description: Families have a past and change over time. There are different types of documents that relate family histories. (NOTE: Teachers will use their professional judgment and demonstrate sensitivity regarding the varied family structures of their students and availability of information.)

7BC26D2F621540D89E9E44A23B779184.description: Students will identify positive and negative effects that human interaction can have on the physical environment.

94F7A4FBAE8E435594BD6D8BA7DB0BA0.description: People interact with their physical environment in ways that may have a positive or a negative effect.

17A562AA9C154DED8D59C1992514CFDC.description: Students will identify how the physical environment of their community has been modified to meet needs and wants.

E562872D36D04972A440FCEBCC7E33CB.description: Roads, dams, bridges, farms, parks, and dwellings are all examples of how people modify the physical environment to meet needs and wants.

2E207852B53C4FDB9B2E2378EFFFA6B8.description: Students will identify natural resources required to meet basic needs.

074701BA570D43D18883245A385ED7D9.description: People and communities depend on the physical environment for natural resources.

12EE2A3CB053448AB0896ED6AC8AC73F.description: People and communities depend on and modify their physical environment in order to meet basic needs.

0CDF80CFBA4D49C2980430E6973939FE.description: Students will closely read maps making use of the legends to understand symbols and what they represent.

D880161B88B146B1BC28F2E5DAB41420.description: Symbols are used to represent physical features and man-made structures on maps and globes.

0C9874217711419E9A0D87FF44DF1BCF.description: Students will use a map of the community and provide directions to another student on how to get from the school to another place identified on the map.

5F58336C35A24D2982F074FBEC7B2661.description: Maps are used to locate important places in the community, state, and nation, such as capitals, monuments, hospitals, museums, schools, and cultural centers.

6BF70E4051F74AC4A45F80711ACEF5D7.description: Students will use cardinal directions within the classroom to describe the locations of objects (e.g., desks, bookcases) and create a map of the classroom by using symbols to represent objects.

46066AB8298845A692A2C2A5F6AA20E0.description: Maps and map tools, such as legends and cardinal directions, can help us navigate from one place to the next, provide directions, or trace important routes.

3010DEC4EB95493289444528C2F6CD03.description: The location and place of physical features and man-made structures can be described and interpreted by using symbols and geographic vocabulary.

A2A9A82644CA4DD185893027DF173EFE.description: Students will be given opportunities to solve problems, make decisions, and resolve conflicts.

B6E79C0FC9A24E079852D53F80C45B75.description: Children can participate in problem solving, decision making, and conflict resolution within their home, school, and community.

EE6F68AC24E64997AA8A8A80130940C8.description: Students will begin to understand that there are local, state, and national levels of government and will identify some actions that the government takes.

64A848D3A6F441D4BC9FD2E98D0049D5.description: Governments exist at the local, state, and national levels to represent the needs of the people, create and enforce laws, and help resolve conflicts.

326E258A7B4C4B1CBAFC3C370F377019.description: Students will discuss the difference between rules and laws, and determine why school rules were developed and what the consequences are of not following the rules.

DAF1DCADA6B949A1A5533002B3D37EFF.description: Rules and laws are developed to protect people's rights and for the safety and welfare of the community.

F8ED9279715843938875E4F4998601DC.description: People create governments in order to create peace and establish order. Laws are created to protect the rights and define the responsibilities of individuals and groups.

427788571EAE48289F3405A98FABBFD0.description: Students will discuss ways that they can protect and respect our world and its people.

9F18A02C2D854D0486E40096F97F4BF6.description: As global citizens, we are connected to people and cultures beyond our own community and nation, and we have a shared responsibility to protect and respect our world.

2B93A52665794B89863623AA3F631F03.description: Students will explain the traits of a responsible citizen and model actions of responsible citizens.

D64DE65274074F94AA5F5FAF26A5EFE7.description: Traits of a responsible citizen include respecting others, behaving honestly, helping others, obeying rules and laws, being informed, and sharing needed resources.

F25467B14D954A4C9734B1FF9E85261E.description: Students will participate in group activities and contribute to the work of the group.

6AEFDF8D523345629E0297EEA3BF0D53.description: An engaged and active citizen participates in the activities of the group or community and makes positive contributions.

E4D4D326A0AF40A1BADCA463596AF8DD.description: A citizen is a member of a community or group. Students are citizens of their local and global communities.

6BAA1EA683D94FACAECE801BC0F3BB8E.description: Students will be able to recite the Pledge of Allegiance, to begin to understand its purpose and its general meaning, and to sing patriotic songs such as America the Beautiful, America ("My Country 'Tis of Thee"), and The Star Spangled Banner and begin to understand the general meaning of the lyrics.

5A4E0BF0867544028C85FA1C554D7C97.description: The Pledge of Allegiance and patriotic songs play an important role in understanding and examining the nation's history, values, and beliefs.

2E3CB09724494A26BDB571293F823107.description: Students will explain when and why celebrate national holidays such as Labor Day, Constitution Day, Columbus Day, Thanksgiving, Martin Luther King Jr. Day, Presidents' Day, Law Day, and Independence Day are celebrated.

43E2B53169B54C8BA31A670D74831387.description: Students will listen to stories about historical events, folklore, and popular historical figures and identify the significance of the event or person.

AC7863BA4BC345B3BA04EEA3236857E9.description: The study of historical events, historical figures, and folklore enables Americans with diverse cultural backgrounds to feel connected to a common national heritage.

D187078AA4C4406EA853B8793F068DE8.description: There are significant individuals, historical events, and symbols that are important to American cultural identity.

D57C55C88FE343219BC9B0B5A8D5A8B9.description: Students will compare the cultural similarities and differences between various ethnic and cultural groups found in New York State.

221B9E80F7DC4BE4A18FF2EC6AE9DD1E.description: Awareness of America's rich diversity fosters intercultural understanding.

A836FC9A37AE4E3DBD3CFD34F3F39C44.description: Students will identify traditions that are associated with their families, and tell why the tradition is important.

0BF7E5FF748F45BEBCDCA7FF4695FFA1.description: People and families of diverse racial, religious, national, and ethnic groups share their beliefs, customs, and traditions, which creates a multicultural community.

5DBD0B9D95304DA69A29874ACE4D413B.description: Students will listen to stories about different families and will identify characteristics that are the same and different.

941D74FEC2334176B61116F4CE63E493.description: Families are a basic unit of all societies, and different people define family differently.

8CBD905BA4D44B45BDCEE5FB17FB0998.description: Language, beliefs, customs, and traditions help shape the identity and culture of a family and a community.

F93B0DC0493547D39D1E2C5D2F4B9D01.description: My Family and Other Families, Now and Long Ago

8E8131F0EE9245CFABC15DD6BF4372F5.description: Identify rights and responsibilities in the classroom and school.

E210ED36EBC74FF59B4637CBADFCDC28.description: Identify the president of the United States and the school principal and their leadership responsibilities.

E47192A5319E48139803FE0E409E0B05.description: Identify situations in which social actions are required.

D430A8FA7C4A4AD5B46E8AEEA6CB4DF6.description: Show respect in issues involving difference and conflict; participate in the resolution of differences and conflict.

747FDA92751045DFA8DB648904910B20.description: Identify the role of the individual in classroom and school participation.

85BA0E00D3464D52BBD29A1350066971.description: Participate in activities that focus on a classroom or school issue or problem.

98AA4FF5F6934AB6A3E2A675FC050EBF.description: Demonstrate respect for the rights of others in discussions, regardless of whether one agrees with the other viewpoints.

91A9FA00ED104A7F8589DD8B747CD739.description: Explain how people earn money and explain other ways that people receive money.

A1528813389D4F3EA257F456A3A39E61.description: Distinguish between a consumer and a producer and their relationship to goods and services.

74CA8DB2A8A34CA9937DA0FB471AB79A.description: Explain how scarcity affects choices made by families and communities, and identify costs and benefits associated with these choices.

F998DAF6B3084D35AFFBAA2C6140E16E.description: Describe how human activities alter places.

4EAFA5D8A7B04D379761D918808A52A6.description: Identify a pattern and a process.

A1F7B55F0B3A4A38A6675768C90ABFB3.description: Describe how environment affects his/her and other people's activities.

885EBBA47710444FA6DAF32C364AF2DA.description: Identify human activities and human-made features; identify natural events or physical features.

763E59FE50F744AA98BAA8F163DACB11.description: Ask geographic questions about where places are located and why they are located there, using location terms and geographic representations, such as maps, photographs, satellite images, and models. Describe where places are in relation to each other.

A59A7DD4B5654D41A524EDA291BB3CE5.description: Understand the concepts of geography, economics, and history that apply to his/her family.

D2D59EB53A5C45E79C02A5FEDDA66E6D.description: Describe an event in his/her family.

485FDC1482B64C0EB293EBAD83532C1A.description: Identify similarities and/or differences between him/her and others with detail.

2DD7F3D59F9340E980F563E0B3EE9367.description: Identify similarities and differences between neighborhoods.

2973BFDFB7F64700809DB791B393C74C.description: Recognize and identify patterns of continuity in his/her family.

8DC66AA91D4842C3895350036B8A41CD.description: Identify events of the past, present, and future in his/her family life.

DE240D5998874305A1A14D3EB17CE4C5.description: Identify change over time in his/her family.

3965C364CF2E4755B93C76BE844FE9BB.description: Identify causes and effects, using examples from his/her family life.

7409E7EA97624990BD93CA1BF81243B8.description: Understand the concept of time measurements, including days, weeks, months and years.

896975BAA10A4A99AA735E63F892720F.description: Retell a real-life family event in sequential order.

9E3D174875BA44FB8619EADDCCF4298D.description: Create understanding of the past by using primary and secondary sources.

812E4C128CD54DA7AA5EFE2643CB775A.description: Identify the creator and/or author of different forms of evidence.

02B93AAEF7174BA8938EF67F04BBA0C0.description: Recognize different forms of evidence used to make meaning in social studies (including sources such as art and photographs, artifacts, oral histories, maps, and graphs).

standardSets.title: Grade 2: Social Studies Practices & My Community and Other Communities

document.title: New York State K-8 Social Studies Framework

F1D6AB042CB849BAAB2A0FED027C2E0C.description: Students will explore how communities share resources and services with other communities.

5795F658C51D4A2EA775AD8C609167B8.description: At times, neighboring communities share resources and workers to support multiple communities.

74C54D6A5C5A4691BEC7201E9736D5F2.description: Students will explain the services provided by community workers.

6C4E9DBBFB3A48A8BB553A491499341A.description: Students will identify different types of jobs performed in their community.

2D6A46987E5F46B980976E4EEF6A5B87.description: Members of a community specialize in different types of jobs that provide goods and/or services to the community. Community workers such as teachers, firefighters, sanitation workers, and police officers provide services.

313EE96F8B4044A3BF5232DF8DA0E5CD.description: Students will distinguish between goods and services and identify goods produced in their community.

EE62212E9766456AA35913125523EC35.description: Goods are the products a person or group of people makes. Services are actions performed by a person or group of people with a certain skill.

F104DD4B82A242A3AD00E9EEE6E1FA84.description: A community requires the interdependence of many people performing a variety of jobs and services to provide basic needs and wants.

4CCCE64CA5E34C6FAEFABABFA68909F4.description: Students will explore the purpose of taxes and how they are collected in their communities.

DEE96363D34B4443A103AAC89D991D67.description: Taxes are collected to provide communities with goods and services.

6575CF23059A4A758FD6785570B2963E.description: Students will examine how consumers react to changes in the prices of goods.

06221B1200B54FDD9ABB25B91A0634DB.description: Scarcity, the price of goods and services, and choice all influence economic decisions made by individuals and communities.

C5B64CC0CE044044B6231233D8B2C79A.description: Students will explore economic decision making and the use of money.

1EA8F3D145AB4D1E947693543325A492.description: People make decisions to buy, sell, and use money based on their needs, wants, and the availability of resources.

A9EC862ED45645E7AFB68859AFB24F3C.description: Students will examine how available resources differ in communities (e.g., home-grown food available in rural farm areas vs. shopping in supermarkets).

4E5732A851C44F6094790F37F5C954D5.description: Students will investigate what resources are available in their community and what resources are obtained from neighboring communities.

C9B2FDFF400D48138886B817945564B1.description: The availability of resources to meet basic needs varies across urban, suburban, and rural communities.

4CA1172881CC43C886A0A12B6A3036F0.description: Communities face different challenges in meeting their needs and wants.

8173EDA105A84C3F84EAEE1373E7AB17.description: Students will distinguish between cause and effect and will examine changes in their community in terms of cause and effect (e.g., automobiles and the growth of suburbs, growing population in suburban areas, and reduction of farms).

C233755125104CCDAB938705AC7BF0B8.description: Cause-and-effect relationships help us to understand the changes in communities.

B9E9961165824F3582448BAE1A010849.description: Cause-and-effect relationships help us recount events and understand historical development.

1E6836D4FEE74509A9CA673A518356C2.description: Students will develop a time line for their community, including important events, such as when the school was built.

072317108D4E45CFB552013018CB9825.description: Students will examine continuities and changes over time in their community, using evidence such as maps, population charts, photographs, newspapers, biographies, artifacts, and other historical materials.

FB9C62CC3D1746EC8EC3A594E8F90530.description: Continuities and changes over time in communities can be examined by interpreting evidence such as maps, population charts, photographs, newspapers, biographies, artifacts, and other historical materials.

DC8B551F49B44EA5AF315D8F392FED1A.description: Continuities and changes over time in communities can be described using historical thinking, vocabulary, and tools such as time lines.

09FA797B25984701BEC3A6AC655D070F.description: Identifying continuities and changes over time can help understand historical developments.

936ABECC26A145FC94B6BF373469B8F9.description: Students will use maps and legends to identify major physical features, such as mountains, rivers, lakes, and oceans of the local community, New York State, and the nation.

EE80BF4DA72E4A8B952FBFD26F766C85.description: Students will locate the equator, northern and southern hemispheres, and poles on a globe.

B4AC40CD1DCD44229B183796AD5BD1AF.description: Students will use a compass rose to identify cardinal (North, South, East, West) and intermediate (Northeast, Southeast, Southwest, Northwest) directions on maps and in their community.

616E4837E75F40C5A5D4A37B748337F3.description: The location and place of physical features and man-made structures can be described using symbols and specific geography vocabulary.

3BC674BC8B0F47EC97492304419267B7.description: Students will describe the means people create for moving people, goods, and ideas in their communities.

157C46D94ED54C0F8DD74F159D141072.description: Students will explore how humans have positively and negatively affected the environment of their community though such features as roads, highways, buildings, bridges, shopping malls, railroads, and parks.

3087BC03F5E84B7CB62ABD7D9239FDB9.description: Humans modify the environment of their communities through housing, transportation systems, schools, marketplaces, and recreation areas.

0D74F78D17224B3BA7F8A9E18F8EECBF.description: Students will compare how different communities in their state or nation have developed, and explain how physical features of the community affect the people living there.

7F3F343AF8194633BD1B1E5F59713B95.description: The location of physical features and natural resources often affects where people settle and may affect how those people sustain themselves.

137E90C97C7E46918770546A4DC1DD6F.description: Students will create maps including maps that represent their classroom, school, or community, and maps that illustrate places in stories.

5D72BAC14305418AA8056CDBB606F07E.description: Students will examine how land within a community is used and classify land use as "residential" (used for housing), "industrial" (used to make things), "commercial" (used to provide services), and "recreational" (where people play or do sports).

17DF13595DA345B3BA6D27BA7292F1B7.description: Students will locate their communities on maps and/or globes.

511B4166F1414C4ABB59DCBDD2391FB2.description: Urban, suburban, and rural communities can be located on maps, and the geographic characteristics of these communities can be described by using symbols, map legends, and geographic vocabulary.

E7DCC5BD00934DC8BB9CC546434DAC8C.description: Geography and natural resources shape where and how urban, suburban, and rural communities develop and how they sustain themselves.

0F517C27467747F2AE8847C5F7E9B6B6.description: Students will identify how adults can provide service to the school and the community at large.

06818E72AFF849F19EBE2DBA3F28D05E.description: Students will explore opportunities to provide service to their school community and the community at large (e.g., beautifying school grounds, writing thank-you notes to helpers).

C56E247017E745448291F92251B57C18.description: Citizens provide service to their community in a variety of ways.

5BB7C819DA3F4E75A92D963AE6074502.description: Students will identify who makes and enforces the rules and laws in their community. They will also explore how leaders make and enforce these rules and laws.

A7FCA2AD92514F28A8C1C366159E1BA5.description: Communities have leaders who are responsible for making laws and enforcing laws.

1CEB602C7639405CBD2A42797B87B657.description: Students will explain the importance of making fair laws and rules, the benefits of following them, and the consequences of violating them.

E9204BAEC02347B488D13A5AEB103BA7.description: Communities have the responsibility to make and enforce fair laws and rules that provide for the common good.

63D4B8346D9F45AEB8A62A9B3EAAFA4D.description: Communities have rules and laws that affect how they function. Citizens contribute to a community's government through leadership and service.

BA61BE47921F4B1FA5B8656D47E54B07.description: Students will examine the symbols of the country, including the eagle, American flag, the Statue of Liberty, the White House, and Mount Rushmore.

1047F04A96F84707AE7720167E5D7E92.description: Symbols of American democracy serve to unite community members.

20E667D4DC9F4BF2ACE59F6A8CDCB72D.description: Students will participate in voting within the classroom and in school, as appropriate.

36CC416657B14E27A629DD99CF435573.description: Students will learn about the process of voting and what opportunities adults in the community have for participation.

BF415EA9899D4E6B9073C49CF8E79583.description: The process of holding elections and voting is an example of democracy in action in schools, communities, New York State, and the nation.

9BF48B10589E4869A294D95E09DCEA53.description: Students will examine the ways in which the government in their community provides order and keeps people safe, and how citizens can demonstrate respect for authority.

7FC5DA7666EF460A865863826FB12B9D.description: Government is established to maintain order and keep people safe. Citizens demonstrate respect for authority by obeying rules and laws.

4C9BCA6B6A84432784B655313D1CC6AF.description: Students will explore democratic principles, such as dignity for all, equality, fairness, and respect for authority and rules, and how those principles are applied to their community.

61A6B92B00D240F786A674BCBB328C2B.description: The United States is founded on the democratic principles of equality, fairness, and respect for authority and rules.

4D0024FFAF6A482EAD459F748FFBA1CC.description: The United States is founded on the principles of democracy, and these principles are reflected in all types of communities.

E280E6B0742043B39A8368CF282E98F1.description: Students will explore how different ideas, talents, perspectives, and culture are shared across their community.

721365F5C81A42EBB0816AFB9E648948.description: A community is strengthened by the diversity of its members, with ideas, talents, perspectives, and cultures that can be shared across the community.

892EADAAE0464F5B9922BD927054978F.description: Students will identify community events that help promote a common community identity.

44971BE37DE949F9A0FB538868939957.description: Students will explore the cultural diversity of their local community by identifying activities that have been introduced by different cultural groups.

57BF626224EF475BB5AB3B9626BBA766.description: Students will examine the ethnic and/or cultural groups represented in their classroom.

010CACD11CFD4D938E84E98441512005.description: People living in urban, suburban, and rural communities embrace traditions and celebrate holidays that reflect both diverse cultures and a common community identity.

BA5F3E4FED904526BC24E7E91C1202FE.description: People share similarities and differences with others in their own community and with other communities.

4DF1F10BF44E42CFAB1A690CC99EC190.description: Students will identify activities that are available in each type of community, and discuss how those activities affect the people living in that community.

14AB32CB1BC74DDB829DFFAC9E623FF6.description: Activities available for people living in urban, suburban, and rural communities are different. The type of community a person grows up in will affect a person's development and identity.

2253E2404E07438B8FE19AB0891233C7.description: By discussing different types of housing (apartment, single-family house, etc.) and the proximity of houses to each other, students will understand the term "population density" and how it applies to different communities.

D0131244712141B1B151428A9DEF862E.description: Students will identify the characteristics of urban, suburban, and rural communities and determine in which type of community they live.

B8DAC6369B6C4DF5955E788A81900BB9.description: Rural communities are characterized by large expanses of open land and significantly lower populations than urban or suburban areas.

32A0D2F08EAA499FAFBDF0BD37446524.description: Suburban communities are on the outskirts of cities, where human population is less dense, and buildings and homes are spaced farther apart.

10F108F948CF40859CF74C80B7AE4B79.description: An urban community, or city, is characterized by dense population and land occupied primarily by buildings and structures that are used for residential and business purposes.

8E2B1D505782419598C534EF2483DFB1.description: A community is a population of various individuals in a common location. It can be characterized as urban, suburban, or rural. Population density and use of the land are some characteristics that define and distinguish types of communities.

ADEACB168D4446EFB55457E4964F9D99.description: Identify rights and responsibilities in the classroom, school, and community.

0049EC37F15C46CDB12720EE09A555C3.description:
Identify the governor of New York, the president of the United States, and the school principal and their
leadership responsibilities.

BCEA6603AAC8458D9683637CB549176C.description: Identify situations in which social actions are required.

A2B805F459A4454BB9113B41274296EC.description: Show respect in issues involving difference and conflict; participate in negotiating and compromising in the resolution of differences and conflict.

F05D584BCA0441D3AAE8EA467C897F73.description: Identify the role of the individual in classroom, school, and local community participation.

470932D7DACC4A3BB3A3E7615241AE49.description: Participate in activities that focus on a classroom, school, or local community issue or problem.

4C96AA73214640E38428BDAE893B3A98.description: Demonstrate respect for the rights of others in discussions and classroom debates, regardless of whether one agrees with the other viewpoints.

E7E12798FAE94BDEAFAC8539567E57F0.description: Identify goods and services that government provides and the role of taxes.

2C0FD2CCF7454087BB45787BCBE58EA8.description: Describe the goods and services that people in the local community produce and those that are produced in other communities.

323145E62EDE47158B1F3B94A1760FAC.description: Describe the role of banks, saving, and borrowing in the economy.

11EF91EEF6D54D72A11D6C5D230B67D3.description: Describe the resources used to produce goods and provide services in the local community.

B861B9106570435A9A19246B3D46A3B4.description: Explain how scarcity necessitates decision making; identify the benefits and costs of decisions.

721901E6E44F434280DC8291F9B1AC88.description: Describe how human activities alter places in a community.

737D0CDF530942379A7E25798CC1CEE2.description: Recognize a process that applies to population, and a resulting pattern.

2FA7C15F57DB4EB8927A10383DF9AC15.description: Describe how his/her actions affect the environment of the community; describe how the environment of the community affects human activities.

4A2C2A309A484E43A25D01A4BFDB9EAF.description: Distinguish human activities and human-made features from natural events or physical features.

5B99963F664D4BD1BBE6F6E28016EFD8.description: Ask geographic questions about where places are located and why they are located there, using location terms and geographic representations, such as maps, photographs, satellite images, and models. Describe where places are in relation to each other and describe connections between places.

EF4D04CB33494ACE97B924F890D21C0E.description: Describe a historical development in his/her community with specific details, including time and place.

2670591FB8C84F888C91B1C8C4D58FDE.description: Recognize the relationship between geography, economics, and history in his/her community.

739EC72350A64BDC82EB858961EBB500.description: Describe an event in his/her community.

D724707F66734BEA94F69DFD9A7ECBE1.description: Identify similarities and/or differences between his/her community and other communities.

8FE9E7E77BBE4B239FC463DEEBAC7D3F.description: Identify similarities and differences between communities.

B16DE5449C674DB7955DA6134404F4B2.description: Recognize and identify patterns of continuity and change in communities.

28382913CF3E486189653A73062B5C05.description: Identify events of the past, present, and future in his/her community life.

EA1BC33189614E32A46AD9C4AFDF51CC.description: Identify changes over time in his/her community.

93AFD18F66414718BA33F9E88FFD2F52.description: Identify causes and effects, using examples from his/her family life or from the community.

9C899B5B4F2A46A6A13E44E3343914C2.description: Understand the concept of time measurements, including minutes, hours, days, weeks, months, years.

3BE1B5C22C17401AAEE2F7022EE33D27.description: Retell a community event in sequential order.

662CF664DD2748EA892210A3DFFE179F.description: Create understanding of the past by using primary and secondary sources.

42E22B72688045B58A66D618AAE2108E.description: Identify and explain creation and/or authorship, purpose, and format of evidence.

1524F7DB9724469887A1E8B94218B584.description: Recognize different forms of evidence used to make meaning in social studies (including primary and secondary sources, such as art and photographs, artifacts, oral histories, maps, and graphs).

standardSets.title: Grade 3: Social Studies Practices & Communities Around the World
standardSets.subject: Social Studies (2017-)

document.title: New York State K-8 Social Studies Framework

C2B6131B48424F31B6348BC61D943701.description: Students will examine how technological developments in transportation and communication have influenced trade over time.

76AD05AC088C4201B071159474EB5F43.description: Students will explore the basic economic concepts of supply and demand and how they influence prices and trade.

9E3946493F10459EBA300D93158A5277.description: Students will examine each selected world community in terms of what products and/or services it imports from other communities.

1F09F46737D04EFA857D7D2D16030EC7.description: Students will examine each selected world community in terms of what products and/or services it exports to other communities.

5680C5ABA19640C9A0E136AA10514407.description: World communities have needs, wants, and limited resources. To meet their needs and wants, communities trade with others. Technological developments in transportation and communication have influenced trade.

966F19A270004995B015DB69E1D5F858.description: Students will investigate who receives the goods that are produced in each selected world community.

DB482BCF39064D9B942BE91CE0F48771.description: Students will examine how the goods are produced within each selected world community.

04F6E72E873D4091A2AA05B76341606F.description: Students will determine what goods are produced and services are provided in each selected world community.

B59180C19CEB4D778FA10E7D1E13DFE4.description: Communities around the world produce goods and provide services.

E55A17F58CB94F1DA2CE29BA4895F2B8.description: Each community develops an economic system that addresses three questions: what will be produced, how will it be produced, and who will get what is produced?

81DFF704B9954C358A01E3E5D907D6D5.description: Students will examine the various ways people earn a living and how this has changed, if at all, over time in each selected world community.

574CE374283C4B4D93F3A2FFC2EEFAFD.description: Students will investigate how each selected world community meets its basic needs of food, clothing, and shelter, and compare that to their own community.

873A6C4322F84868BB741041ABE81938.description: People in communities have various ways of meeting their basic needs and earning a living.

8FBD2A78F1BF4B9FA26615C62ABEAAB8.description: Students will explore the concepts of surplus and scarcity in relation to resources for each selected world community.

5B55BC27E8A04649BDF99FC174E7D5ED.description: Students will investigate available resources for each selected world community and how these resources are used to meet basic needs and wants.

1985C8800C334B14BE75D070F9C199B6.description: World communities use human and natural resources in different ways.

DAF10133FF3340CDB286F9B1F699E12B.description: Communities meet their needs and wants in a variety of ways, forming the basis for their economy.

05FEDAA227F94938B198B0376E2F1CDE.description: Students will investigate steps people can take to support social action and change.

70248D224BA8417AB17C7A44BFB5121D.description: When faced with prejudice and discrimination, people can take steps to support social action and change.

BDAA580985FD48E89B7B3BA3DC940A72.description: Students will examine prejudice and discrimination and how they serve as barriers to justice and equality for all people.

D5854A994E48456DB12505635B04E245.description: Across time and place, communities and cultures have struggled with prejudice and discrimination as barriers to justice and equality for all people.

B0B5EC7BEC7C4AF3A4A0CA9BC9336EFD.description: Students will examine the extent to which governments and citizens have protected human rights and treated others fairly for each world community.

02CB0706269F416E98E1B49A20051689.description: Across global communities, governments and citizens alike have a responsibility to protect human rights and to treat others fairly.

F1C27A55772B49DFA2E46367D4651100.description: The concept of universal human rights suggests that all people should be treated fairly and should have the opportunity to meet their basic needs.

6DA9465484F64554B6E78F6F023D94DD.description: Students will examine the role of the citizen in each selected world community and how this role is similar to or different from the role a citizen plays in the United States, as well in as other selected world communities.

0FFBF2B806AD46839F7A750384F59600.description: The definition of citizenship and the role of the citizen vary across different types of political systems, and citizens play a greater role in the political process in some countries than in others.

56D2ADF921B041FEB52BF6B0A96C9B52.description: Students will examine how the government maintains order, keeps people safe, and makes and enforces rules and laws in each selected world community and compare and contrast it with the process in the United States, as well as in selected world communities.

A5FC0E2644274E29AA6B2140A2344CDF.description: Different governments have different ways of maintaining order and keeping people safe. This includes making rules and laws and enforcing these rules and laws.

953E85566938488C92797EDD616CBFA1.description: Students will examine different processes of selecting leaders, solving problems, and making decisions in nations and communities and compare and contrast them to the process used in the United States.

BE77AFB12EFC46F5B8D7B95221EAADAD.description: The process of selecting leaders, solving problems, and making decisions differs across governments in nations and communities around the world.

A6AD099C29134235BD5418E99D9C54E5.description: Students will examine the type of government is found in each selected world community and compare and contrast it with United States government, as well as with the types of governments found in other selected world communities.

AF065089480046E5AE8A33F939D8AFD7.description: The United States government is based on democratic principles. The fundamental principles of other governments may be similar to or different from those of the United States government.

C4A65A149FAE4F19B98913DEF8E2231B.description: Governments in communities and countries around the world have the authority to make and the power to enforce laws. The role of the citizen within these communities or countries varies across different types of governments.

B666CBFDB08644459E4220CB68C4460A.description: Students will examine people, goods, and ideas from each selected world community that have diffused into other communities and their effects on those communities.

37F688236D4E4A1AB8199D48DC880078.description: Students will examine people, goods, and ideas that have diffused from other communities into each selected world community and the effects of the people, goods, and ideas on these communities.

E8CEDCDD6E594A38B7EBE5CFF88E8D51.description: Cultural diffusion is the process by which cultures exchange and transmit ideas, beliefs, technologies, and goods over time.

33C2EB8B64F54BC6A9ACA350A6A8FBFC.description: Communities from around the world interact with other people and communities and exchange cultural ideas and practices.

992A2F8FB1EE4ADE93CA4277D8F2021C.description: Students will learn about the holidays and festivals celebrated in each selected world community and compare them to the holidays and festivals celebrated in their own community.

A815C8EE4F974C93A6537D884B467CE1.description: Students will examine each selected world community in terms of its members, languages spoken, customs and traditions, and religious beliefs and practices.

DE27F6251FF74317A4FDA603B3D13683.description: Communities around the world can be diverse in terms of their members, languages spoken, customs and traditions, and religious beliefs and practices. People in world communities celebrate various holidays and festivals.

9046DFA6CB5E42CC860CAD699800B3C8.description: Students will compare and contrast the structure and activities of families and schools in each selected community with their own.

D4D894E374204FD2ABF1CF69B6FCAAD1.description: The structure and activities of families and schools share similarities and differences across world communities.

448C0FDF90284631BB16BC79A8103556.description: Communities share cultural similarities and differences across the world.

FCE7D0F1E9424892A78F3D6E90B497C6.description: Students will explore the arts, music, dance, and literature of each selected world community.

0D0BE4D77CBD4C4E8D3D54195564F3EB.description: Arts, music, dance, and literature develop through a community's history.

C3C9FE9C2CDB4BC0858C9369689FDD9F.description: Students will examine symbols of each selected world community.

6C0E2810B3154DC4ADACC944A9C64447.description: Students will examine legends, folktales, oral histories, biographies, and historical narratives to learn about the important individuals and events of each selected world community.

E52911D4DB924D5EA93C4C035FFE775A.description: People in world communities use legends, folktales, oral histories, biographies, and historical narratives to transmit cultural histories from one generation to the next.

541EEA4751D04A87B94CD45593169018.description: Each community or culture has a unique history, including heroic figures, traditions, and holidays.

656E8B78746B4FADA3BE85C0B5EA4989.description: Students will explore actions that are being taken to protect the environment in the selected world communities and in their own community.

A6E80CC6E90A4A8395BB1CF01B4FC46B.description: Students will investigate how human activities and the use of technology have altered the environment, bringing about unintended consequences for each of the selected world communities and their own community.

6733C9DD2ED84ABB99916DF3040C5AEE.description: Students will examine how each selected world community has adapted to and/or modified its environment to meet its needs.

1C67F5475FD64D1089958AEBD2DC4FC2.description: People make adaptations and modifications to the environment. Advancements in science, technology, and industry can bring about modifications to the environment and can have unintended consequences on the environment. People have attempted to take actions to protect the environment.

2A16E5843DE3423A9C9106DA001972E6.description: Students will investigate the lifestyle of the people who live in each selected world community and how the lifestyle has been influenced by the geographic factors.

EBDEBF02B3B74B66A805423E97DEC040.description: Students will examine the geographic factors of each selected world community, including physical features and climate, noting how certain factors are likely to support settlement and larger populations.

59A3A815E66244F4AF072681B75EE628.description: Geographic factors influence where people settle and their lifestyle. Some geographic factors make a location more suitable for settlement, while others act as deterrents.

B03F8E44462943C58AACD7BDADCDEB3C.description: Geographic factors often influence where people settle and form communities. People adapt to and modify their environment in different ways to meet their needs.

862BDEDF8B934BF9A134DF9C427924E6.description: Students will examine the location of each selected world community relative to the United States and other selected world communities. Students will locate each selected world community in relationship to principal parallels (equator, Tropic of Cancer, Tropic of Capricorn, Arctic Circle, and Antarctic Circle) and meridians (Prime Meridian) using cardinal and intermediate directions.

01B64ACD351746F0B282DD3069F5AABF.description: World communities can be located in relation to each other and to principle parallels and meridians.

F8CD3A8D89EE4CBD95D6C58F439C4C29.description: Students will examine where each selected world community is located.

4BB5FB464A9043A3B9C5B14EE4AD8BB1.description: World communities can be located on globes and maps.

3EF9E1E3EA894207B35C0386EC7724E7.description: The location of world communities can be described using geographic tools and vocabulary.

DA7AD066871E4AD88F6AF81DBC7D03E9.description: Students will compare geographic information found in photographs and satellite images with other representations of the same area and identify differences for at least one of the selected world communities

F41008AE704F4C8CB8BE8A4118EF49AB.description: Students will examine a variety of maps for at least two of the selected world communities, looking for structural features of the map such as title, legend or key, compass orientation, author, date, grid, and scale. These should include political, physical, vegetation, and resource maps. A variety of scale should be represented (e.g., continent vs. country, country vs. city).

A6CE2170D33C4CFB8F2EDBF7FFAD77BD.description: Students will identify the differences between a globe and a map.

7E603065548B4F818839D45B362FB60B.description: Globes, maps, photographs, and satellite images contain geographic information. Maps often have a title, legend or key, compass orientation, author, date, grid, and scale.

49D8A629DA6A4824AE0972B49A021B2A.description: Students will locate the selected world communities in relation to oceans and continents.

ECB3F2C9DF0F4C698530750B50F4EBED.description: Students will identify the continents and oceans, by using globes and maps.

212BE84D10DB4911AE87721A05DBA874.description: Earth is comprised of water and large land masses that can be divided into distinct regions.

B57EC774047D4BD387C0C8B04F99D0EB.description: Geographic regions have unifying characteristics and can be studied using a variety of tools.

C1A0F020DFBE45C19BA269B5A61CF5DA.description: Identify rights and responsibilities of citizens in the local community and compare them to those in world communities.

3DFE0C4516CF46BFBF436CDA7A1D1376.description: Identify leaders of world communities and the president of the United States; identify similarities and differences in their roles.

38ED0120FA2B4B4BB72788C6899BCFC2.description: Identify situations in which social actions are required and suggest actions.

343686844E834085BFAD71E0691D1840.description: Show respect in issues involving difference and conflict; participate in negotiating and compromising in the resolution of differences and conflict.

F52EFD02B80C4397ABB07F976FAEB84F.description: Identify opportunities for and the role of the individual in social and political participation in the school, local community, or world community.

D0ACFCD940FC44AB93CCBD880EF5F6DF.description: Identify different types of political systems found in world communities.

1197EF8A665B43B1BDE3C1192D0813D5.description: Participate in activities that focus on a classroom, school, or world community issue or problem.

E76292DF095D4CDD9221BDB0979931ED.description: Demonstrate respect for the rights of others in discussions and classroom debates, regardless of whether one agrees with the other viewpoints.

C65F40FBCB634B28A6527FC3DE038636.description: Explore the types of governments in world communities and the services that they provide to citizens.

03713379BB944F99B68594944D868C0D.description: Examine the goods and services provided by world communities; describe what goods and services a world community trades with other world communities.

1F98999503B04B7E89C539A23D989B21.description: Identify products found in world communities and the various ways that people in those communities pay for products.

3296A75AAC154E88A6658D12A5BD0E37.description: Identify the variety of resources available in a particular world community used to produce goods and/or provide services.

9E35A0F078C545CA9515647A577FDE72.description: Examine how scarcity affects the decisions about the use of resources by people and governments; examine the costs and benefits of economic decisions.

EFA9248287EE45A78C8D69F2BF9AE488.description: Describe how human activities alter places and regions.

A4780BA517684C9CA20B6A69FECFF9E7.description: Recognize a process that applies to population, and a resulting pattern.

C9D589629E93404CB3029EBEE4B601CF.description: Describe how human activities affect the environment of a world community; describe how the environment of a specific world community affects the human activities in that community.

6D5353D447844CB2A384D583C621336B.description: Distinguish human activities and human-made features from "environments" (natural events or physical features—land, air, and water— that are not directly made by humans).

20D5382F6F25407FBC43B21363395666.description: Ask geographic questions about where places are located and why they are located there, using location terms and geographic representations, such as maps, photographs, satellite images, and models. Describe where places are in relation to each other and describe connections between places.

0A1805432ED74A0B90406AB9636B4BAE.description: Describe a historical development in a world community with specific details, including time and place.

473ADA6A560841149388DDC4941C70F9.description: Recognize the relationship between geography, economics, and history in world communities.

1C6E38F2EA3844F2B1EF368D58559B25.description: Describe a historical event in a world community.

3975DB7E0FE74064A587DF264E34A612.description: Identify multiple perspectives by comparing and contrasting points of view in differing world communities.

C4778A219F8340E7ACEB573480FD4D74.description: Identify a world region by describing a characteristic that places within it have in common.

C6BC0CA282AE4C0797AEB24A568E448C.description: Recognize and identify patterns of continuity and change in world communities.

83D279D214C84BCBA436000B52DB4FDE.description: Recognize periods of time, such as decades and centuries.

03DB0C80A424455A8A48033CE3927D6B.description: Recognize continuity and change over periods of time.

E3899C7707674CA9B742F98AC35AEB68.description:
Distinguish between long-term and immediate causes and effects of an event from his/her life or current events
or history.

6CE5E06817AA42B496E1BF4E8BC624BC.description: Identify causes and effects, using examples from his/her life or from a current event or history.

9E0FA4B218224809A789834066A04562.description: Employ mathematical skills to measure time in years and centuries

CEA3B87B8E38465795B6806EE90DD965.description: Explain how three or more events are related to one another.

ECDDE2CF056F46D3BC0CF458035D3A42.description: Create understanding of the past by using and analyzing primary and secondary sources.

D1DF6D55045B4B7B8C45E0AA99C2D227.description: Identify and explain creation and/or authorship, purpose, and format of evidence. Where appropriate, identify point of view.

7873332154974F25865E42A69BDAAC6D.description: Recognize and use different forms of evidence to make meaning in social studies (including primary and secondary sources, such as art and photographs, artifacts, oral histories, maps, and graphs).

2769828EFC4D4278A4E8F442823FB1DD.description: Develop questions about a world community.

document.title: New York State K-8 Social Studies Framework

D48145FC7A59486EA0CDB4F74C91B1C4.description: Students will investigate artists, writers, and musicians associated with the Harlem Renaissance.

3C85602310DF4AD8BCB8A58B4F273835.description: Students will investigate the reasons that African Americans moved into northern cities.

33F155EABE454C6FB427D0F11EDD00A2.description: Beginning in the 1890s, large numbers of African Americans migrated to New York City and other northern cities to work in factories.

4A3EBC9466974F82A108049847760862.description: Students will research an immigrant group in their local community or nearest city in terms of where that group settled, what types of jobs they held, and what services were available to them, such as ethnic social clubs and fraternal support organizations.

57D8A6ED81024B8DA47A86A4E2FD392D.description: Students will investigate the requirements for becoming a United States citizen.

508048486DB84102A0181A4EB8360192.description: Students will investigate factory conditions experienced by immigrants by examining sweatshops, the Triangle Shirtwaist Fire, the use child labor, and the formation of labor unions.

DF4EE2EA64FD452187ABA6629AA876B4.description: Students will explore the experiences of immigrants being processed at Ellis Island and what challenges immigrants faced.

3452B7EFB32F403297D10A4D97F88B24.description: Students will trace the arrival of various immigrant groups to New York State in the mid-1800s, 1890s, 1920s, mid-1900s, 1990s, and today; examining why they came and where they settled, noting the role of the Irish potato famine.

0A71145B859A45EBBBA49C62B1F9E01C.description: Immigrants came to New York State for a variety of reasons. Many immigrants arriving in New York City were greeted by the sight of the Statue of Liberty and were processed through Ellis Island.

702403E377FC413A88E0E4708B3A63EC.description: Immigration And Migration From The Early 1800s To The Present: Many people have immigrated and migrated to New York State contributing to its cultural growth and development.

B8727C4F6DEA451385329DC9E5C1F331.description: Students will investigate major economic activities in regions of New York State and create a map showing the major economic activities in Long Island, New York City, Lower Hudson Valley, Mid- Hudson Valley, Capital District, Adirondacks/North Country, Mohawk Valley/Central New York, Mid-West/Finger Lakes, Catskills, Southern Tier, and Western New York.

CD5308741BED4FEBB13F91DB94348FDA.description: Students will examine how the economic activities in their local community have changed over the last 50 years.

2823C5B229914E58A04864020DFDD4DB.description: As manufacturing moved out of New York State, service industries and high-technology industries have grown.

04EDD8F319814E80B0CE13F056168052.description: Students will trace manufacturing and industrial development in New York State and in their local community in terms of what major products were produced, who produced them, and for whom they were produced from the 1800s to today.

664E8EB6523F4A33BAA11600DB4E917E.description: Between 1865 and 1915, rapid industrialization occurred in New York State. Over time, industries and manufacturing continued to grow.

F00B994492AE4CBC92C72E4EA77838C3.description: Students will research several people who made important contributions to business, technology, and New York State communities. Some people to consider include Thomas Jennings, Thomas Edison, Henry Steinway, John Jacob Bausch, Henry Lomb, Cornelius Vanderbilt, Lewis H. Latimer, Jacob Schoellkopf, Nikola Tesla, George Westinghouse, George Eastman, Amory Houghton, Willis Carrier, John D. Rockefeller, Edward H. Harriman, J.P. Morgan, Hetty Green, Emily Roebling, and Elisha Otis, and others, as locally appropriate.

3E41EAA4365942B08A9E58E03BAD235A.description: Entrepreneurs and inventors associated with New York State have made important contributions to business and technology.

A459876A0FF846F38F6865B12642AD83.description: Students will examine the importance of New York City in the development of banking and finance in New York State and the United States.

06579815A37845FA951B6019A8BD181D.description: Students will explore which resources were extracted in New York State over time, the location of those resources, and the economic activities associated with those resources.

DDBE29D8E90A40F887D530B62EC26D5A.description: Students will examine New York State's key agricultural products during the 1800s and compare these to the key agricultural products of today.

501BEBA63EF14C99BE50A56B7A883491.description: Farming, mining, lumbering, and finance are important economic activities associated with New York State.

F29357CBEDF34A9097A348D532D958BA.description: Students will trace developments in transportation and communication technology from the 1800s to the present, noting the effects that these changes had on their communities, the State, and the world.

00508A3D85274F02BE2B29544780606F.description: Students will investigate which early means of transportation were used in their local community and to which communities they were linked, noting why they were linked to those communities.

08611F984BD3436293AE16DD2164986E.description: Improved technology such, as the steam engine and the telegraph made transportation and communication faster and easier. Later developments in transportation and communication technology had an effect on communities, the State, and the world.

0ACC365AC0F847DF98F82E499F28522C.description: Students will locate and name at least five towns and four cities along the canal, and identify major products shipped using the canal.

7D94F3D9510C4DAB9EC429CDD598A3DD.description: Students will examine how the development of the canal affected the Haudenosaunee nations.

66B343BB153B48A8B5F8935DB9F31BC6.description: Students will examine the physical features of New York State and determine where it might be easiest to build a canal, and form a hypothesis about the best location. Students will compare their hypothesis with the actual location of the Erie Canal.

8EA8ED0C84CB434AB585BABA1DC4BB07.description: In order to connect the Great Lakes with the Atlantic Ocean, the Erie Canal was built. Existing towns expanded and new towns grew along the canal. New York City became the busiest port in the country.

41E45E8E1A6E4D548B790C1EF50775CC.description: Students will examine the difficulties of traveling west at this time and methods used to improve travel on roads, including corduroy roads and turnpikes.

F1BE1054746942ADA88C4AF0384A3F32.description: Students will examine why people began to move west in New York State.

FD7B47B50AE0441C8F786550EF6C0CDC.description: After the Revolution, New Yorkers began to move and settle farther west, using roads many of which had begun as Native American trails.

6F10541D991F4B519C81135210AC7DB3.description: Westward Movement And Industrialization: New York State played an important role in the growth of the United States. During the 1800s, people traveled west looking for opportunities. Economic activities in New York State are varied and have changed over time, with improvements in transportation and technology.

985BA4DA8FF64C6DA0FA74260EA12F70.description: Students will research a local community's contribution to the Civil War effort, using resources such as war memorials, a local library, reenactments, historical associations, and museum artifacts.

51C250877452478EADA0D3C79DD7B975.description: Students will explore how New York State supported the Union during the Civil War; providing soldiers, equipment, and food.

BFDD6B4F1B5C4AD1B677DD1DB357FF6E.description: The United States became divided over several issues, including slavery, resulting in the Civil War. New York State supported the Union and played an important role in this war.

7A702199AED84A7595A51C6D5D588AD7.description: Students will investigate people who took action to bring about change, such as Amelia Bloomer, Sojourner Truth, Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Lucretia Mott, Susan B. Anthony, Matilda Joslyn Gage, and Elizabeth Blackwell. Students will explore what happened at the convention of women in Seneca Falls.

F4FA9F6A60F8465BA05B1220F1BDC544.description: Students will examine the rights denied to women during the 1800s.

E25A3D4E46104BB2BA06B2544A82D482.description: Women have not always had the same rights as men in the United States and New York State. They sought to expand their rights and bring about change.

5CBFD2DAF9164E53BFC8EBF66BCB2DE6.description: Students will investigate people who took action to abolish slavery, including Samuel Cornish, Fredrick Douglass, William Lloyd Garrison, and Harriet Tubman.

7B2A62E69D84454582CF263244D313DE.description: Students will examine life as a slave in New York State.

CF3CF356F2CD4757849BE050E365A3FE.description: There were slaves in New York State. People worked to fight against slavery and for change.

3902EFE18AD745C4BED136C9D6C2E931.description: In Search Of Freedom And A Call For Change: Different groups of people did not have equal rights and freedoms. People worked to bring about change. The struggle for rights and freedoms was one factor in the division of the United States that resulted in the Civil War.

03EE20904944452FB83A30054CA99628.description: Students will discuss active citizenship and adults' responsibility to vote, to understand important issues, and to serve on a jury.

E17F425C1663475F91B4AAFB72199032.description: Students will learn their responsibilities as citizens, such as obeying rules and laws (e.g., traffic safety, see something–say something, anti-bullying).

762314B8585642C19F6BF50B13EC89A8.description: Citizens of the State of New York have responsibilities that help their nation, their state, and their local communities function. Some responsibilities are stated in laws.

693EBB76E65D486A903E6E8503A9BC4C.description: Students will examine the rights and freedoms guaranteed to citizens.

30225E7192864EC8BB1136D4DBAA8108.description: New Yorkers have rights and freedoms that are guaranteed in the United States Constitution, in the New York State Constitution, and by state laws.

AB12CF43E55541999D06FF326B486E28.description: Students will examine the structure of their local government and its relationship to state government. Students will be able to identify the elected leaders of their community.

28730B1A96944721BBBF90302B6B3569.description: Students will identify the borough of New York City in which they live, and in which county the borough is located.

4B453F3C244D4266A9BE62ABA235CE3F.description: Students will identify the county in which they live, noting where their city, town or village is within that county.

C9CC1B99A5D9466CBCDE5D765D1ECC67.description: Government in New York State is organized into counties, cities, towns, and villages.

1D2FF15F1C6946B1A44DF555F2772992.description: Students will investigate the steps necessary for a bill to become a law in New York State.

CB5BB390EA7944728BE203B6F1B91F83.description: Students will use a graphic organizer to show the different branches of state government and the roles and responsibilities of each. The present governor, the local senator, and the local assemblyperson should be identified.

5D68CC01001E4CABA9BAFB416A1ADE50.description: Students will examine the elements of the New York State Seal adopted in 1777 and the New York State flag and explain the symbols used.

B40592A34D584595B8A15510FCDAA994.description: The New York State Constitution establishes the basic structure of government for the state. The government of New York creates laws to protect the people and interests of the state.

99DA3813E0274F908828CAA210B906A0.description: Students will explore ways that the federal, state, and local governments meet the needs of citizens, looking for similarities and differences between the different levels of government.

0B097659D65746679EE29ED072FB9903.description: Students will examine the basic structure of the federal government, including the president, Congress, and the courts.

D58229E81C9B4B79B8B683C691662A2A.description: After the Revolution, the United States of America established a federal government; colonies established state governments.

6A367BC90CBD412A8D07D19ED95A43F0.description: Government: There are different levels of government within the United States and New York State. The purpose of government is to protect the rights of citizens and to promote the common good. The government of New York State establishes rights, freedoms, and responsibilities for its citizens.

43D53630E8604419B242C511C4CAC0C2.description: Students will investigate the strategically important battles of Long Island and Saratoga and why the Battle of Saratoga is considered by many to be a turning point. A turning point can be an event in history that brought about significant change.

9CD3D6CF858D4C99A49A5322E58115A9.description: Students will explore why African Americans volunteered to fight with the British during the war.

EC5192275FEA43468CCEF610FF7D7160.description: Students will examine which Native Americans supported the British and which Native Americans supported the Patriot cause.

EA9F344B00174AB9B2FE7E912A04142E.description: Students will examine New York's geographic location relative to the other colonies, locate centers of Loyalist support, and examine the extent of the British occupation.

9D86D55159F447DEBB96CFC911406D85.description: Students will examine issues of political and economic rights that led to the American Revolution.

8B05613E8C8D475884131B773226F5FD.description: Growing conflicts between England and the 13 colonies over issues of political and economic rights led to the American Revolution. New York played a significant role during the Revolution, in part due to its geographic location.

1D73DBA9ECF843CD82FEDD3B8541E29C.description: Students will examine the alliances between Native Americans and the English and between Native Americans and the French.

778098B555FA42F38CAB069EE954271D.description: Students will locate some of the major battles fought in New York State during the French and Indian War, noting why they were important.

4E2672E797E14D16AE16CEF75FA52B16.description: In the mid-1700s, England and France competed against each other for control of the land and wealth in North America. The English, French, and their Native American allies fought the French and Indian War. Several major battles were fought in New York.

639225C5FF494036928F67659C8DEADF.description: Students will examine the colonial experience of African Americans, comparing and contrasting life under the Dutch and under the British.
