7E8A537FAC8A4F95B86832EE445860E3.description: Student will investigate colonial life under the Dutch and the English, examining the diverse origins of the people living in the colony.

0A6AEC3D34BB49FFA7CC9C448E679CF2.description: Students will trace colonial history from the Dutch colony of New Netherland to the English colony of New York, making note of lasting Dutch contributions.

A30F3857A113495C80D3D764EB42DD35.description: Colonial New York became home to many different peoples, including European immigrants, and free and enslaved Africans. Colonists developed different lifestyles.

264FA790D9874FD79D3D30EB60181D31.description: Students will investigate the interactions and relationships between Native American groups, Dutch and French fur traders, French missionaries, and early settlers, noting the different perspectives toward land ownership and use of resources.

41B34E053099425B9A7137D1F4F6C8C9.description: Students will map the voyages of Verrazano, Hudson, and Champlain and will determine which Native American peoples encountered these explorers.

99E26DC5F7C54490B184DCA1953A8499.description: Europeans in search of a route to Asia explored New York's waterways. Early settlements began as trading posts or missions.

22DC48275A0A437A8C9D271865DA4D18.description: Colonial And Revolutionary Period In New York: European exploration led to the colonization of the region that became New York State. Beginning in the early 1600s, colonial New York was home to people from many different countries. Colonial New York was important during the Revolutionary Period.

5514216061BD4E77969BB7CC28EFEF43.description: Students will examine contributions of Native Americans that are evident today.

A5CAB89EB3BD47F195525AEC3C7B23D5.description: Students will examine Native American traditions; work specialization and the roles of men, women, and children in their society; transportation systems; and technology.

B339A18570E64CAE9650579E4871CE42.description: Each Native American group developed a unique way of life with a shared set of customs, beliefs, and values.

C6627CBF213A483598CDDAF7C6D60EF3.description: Students will compare and contrast the patterns of organization and governance of Native American groups such as the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) and Munsees, including matrilineal clan structure, decision-making processes, and record keeping, with a focus on local Native American groups.

C4128328675648B3B342F3AD59B984CA.description: Native American groups developed specific patterns of organization and governance to manage their societies.

8DB0B235D6D94EA8A536525DBA4CD60F.description: Students will investigate how Native Americans such as the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) and the Algonquian-speaking peoples adapted to and modified their environment to meet their needs and wants.

7AA55544EE84425AA52C7663341297ED.description: Students will examine the locations of early Native American groups in relation to geographic features, noting how certain physical features are more likely to support settlement and larger populations.

071CC21A6E8B4E42B4411E7333BF92D0.description: Geographic factors often influenced locations of early settlements. People made use of the resources and the lands around them to meet their basic needs of food, clothing, and shelter.

D68C3D61508140EC912F94BDE102AC6D.description: Native American Groups And The Environment: Native American groups, chiefly the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) and Algonquian-speaking groups, inhabited the region that became New York State. These people interacted with the environment and developed unique cultures.

93F3930961D14E50B408FFD31BD70A6F.description: Students will use maps of a variety of scales including a map of the United States and the world to identify and locate the country and states that border New York State.

2F12F2109C1D4A119063CAB0F6E9AC2D.description: Students will examine the location of the capital of New York State and the major cities of New York State in relation to their home community, using directionality, and latitude and longitude coordinates.

09403722F4144634B56D02CEA3A15EC6.description: Students will create a map of the political features of New York State that includes the capital city and the five most populous cities, as well as their own community.

C7A63D0C631E44EAB166D55C1B7577DE.description: New York State can be represented using a political map that shows cities, capitals, and boundaries.

53659B3B89264FF691463B6B11419BAB.description: Students will examine New York State climate and vegetation maps in relation to a New York State physical map, exploring the relationship between physical features and vegetation grown, and between physical features and climate.

CBC5EA19DFAE4A56AF338F6A408BF6E1.description: Students will be able to identify and map New York State's major physical features, including mountains, plateaus, rivers, lakes, and large bodies of water, such as the Atlantic Ocean and Long Island Sound.

9E6832D81A304A3DB2F5401A5C251AA2.description: Physical and thematic maps can be used to explore New York State's diverse geography.

6E8018E97E754675A9CC1B5F2DF25A1F.description: Geography Of New York State: New York State has a diverse geography. Various maps can be used to represent and examine the geography of New York State.

E63E2DEFC5A249E3BB41E65A20A72B7E.description: New York State and Local History and Government

59A15CECD95F40FDAF4133027EBE1A46.description: Identify rights and responsibilities as a citizen of the community and the state.

1D4A15F19F954C3087FD40DFC2CB358B.description: Identify people in positions of power and how they can influence people's rights and freedom.

34A0B74EEB974B16A456F74427DC3946.description: Identify situations in which social actions are required and suggest actions.

D594AF6A9DFC40B182B03E27EF527332.description: Show respect in issues involving difference and conflict; participate in negotiating and compromising in the resolution of differences and conflict.

E2BB2BD1D42B48298DE69FAB2EC245E6.description: Identify opportunities for and the role of the individual in social and political participation in the school, local, and/or state community.

BFD047AF00B343A4B608F411DE1A8E7C.description: Identify different types of political systems used at various times in New York State history and, where appropriate, in United States history.

B4A73ACE78A940F98FF035449F61ABCB.description: Participate in activities that focus on a classroom, school, community, state, or national issue or problem.

00DE030A0F874BE5AAD226559BA14BB7.description: Demonstrate respect for the rights of others in discussions and classroom debates, regardless of whether one agrees with the other viewpoints.

20EB50A67BB54EEE9C915EDECB8E6DA7.description: Explain the ways that the government pays for the goods and services that it provides, including tax revenue.

9FD56A054DBD45D0AC06CEA8C4BA0368.description: Explain why individuals and businesses specialize and trade.

63FC12E1528E4964B791C4100F11A551.description: Explain the role of money in making exchange easier; examine the role of corporations and labor unions in an economy.

D9BCF1643E36435AA1FA5036EA483985.description: Distinguish between the various types of resources (human capital, physical capital, and natural resources) required to produce goods and services.

BDF164B893684BC089251E25D3014A44.description: Explain how scarcity necessitates decision making; compare the costs and benefits of individual and economic decisions.

560A5DE0085F435493582BE8E663F799.description: Describe how human activities alter places and regions.

41D9C8DC67A14B50AB59B5FC35DD6687.description: Recognize relationships between patterns and processes.

AE25296A32C84660B82945689A45BF44.description: Identify how environments affect human activities and how human activities affect physical environments.

75033EFAEEA6470FAF3C9740E9968841.description: Distinguish human activities and human-made features from "environments" (natural events or physical features—land, air, and water—that are not directly made by humans).

B1931B44F33D4CB3A4499088D556029B.description: Use location terms and geographic representations, such as maps, photographs, satellite images, and models, to describe where places are in relation to each other, to describe connections between places, and to evaluate the benefits of particular places for purposeful activities.

327E84B2EA0B44A99C912C2A46D044E5.description: Describe historical developments in New York State with specific details, including time and place.

FFA8E38FB79F4DD7821ABDA185A77D5D.description: Recognize the relationship between geography, economics, and history in social studies.

6D62C4A544324D41BACCC4FA391A13D0.description: Describe and compare New York State historical events.

83A73CBEB60E4DB1906AB7272CDA9783.description: Identify multiple perspectives from a historical event.

ECF091F68A59491AA8238F51EB49432A.description: Identify a region in New York State by describing a characteristic that places within it have in common, and then compare it to other regions.

39EA80F1CB5E4DE1AED60B697B92252D.description: Recognize and identify patterns of continuity and change in New York State.

A36FEED197C544369B78E80C8B5B3C5D.description: Use periods of time, such as decades and centuries to put events into chronological order.

499CBE341EB9440AAEE721E5EA0CC619.description: Recognize dynamics of historical continuity and change over periods of time.

377056F0C756488ABA5646021D9253ED.description: Distinguish between long-term and immediate causes and effects of an event from his/her life or current events or history.

4F6B917B14E94722BE6C76FAF301ED71.description: Identify the relationship between multiple causes and multiple effects, using examples from his/her life and from a current event or history.

9DA0FACE1FFB4F919F55F9D9EC4FAF82.description: Employ mathematical skills to measure time in years and centuries. Understand the difference between B.C.E. and C.E. Identify the chronological significance of data presented in time lines, with teacher support.

D27F1034D9D74C3DBA0FAEC30C5C5AB5.description: Explain how events are related chronologically to one another.

7A89EE9B23A24B62BE35C475D8BFDECE.description: Create understanding of the past by using and analyzing primary and secondary sources.

9AE59955C77C4C9AB15A422548B0480B.description: Identify and explain creation and /or authorship, purpose, and format of evidence. Where appropriate identify point of view and bias.

77DE92B4C86B4F6C8013723161FA5229.description: Recognize, use, and analyze different forms of evidence to make meaning in social studies (including primary and secondary sources, such as art and photographs, artifacts, oral histories, maps, and graphs).

3513889B9E594B729AA853040A58AC51.description: Develop questions about New York State and its history, geography, economics, and/or government.

document.title: New York State K-8 Social Studies Framework

46D003565B6D47C4A73787CAF410C8B8.description: Students will examine products that are exported from the United States to other markets in the Western Hemisphere, noting how this affects the United States economy.

7C8A855AD61E4787800C39A5F7675043.description: Students will examine products that are imported into markets within the United States based on demand for these products, noting how this affects the United States economy.

B68A908847BB4577BA5C442DE6F3BAC5.description: Countries trade with other countries to meet economic needs and wants. They are interdependent.

D9DD0FB437204367825451AC47AF2637.description: Students will examine why certain products are manufactured in particular places, taking into account the weight, transportation availability, and costs and markets (e.g., soda pop).

49B2FD18913A4C3F873A30595583B30E.description: Students will identify the major natural resources of the United States, Canada, Mexico, and one Caribbean or one South American country to determine the major industries of those countries in relation to available resources.

C60A918B5A644DB0A370B95719D64D29.description: Peoples of the Western Hemisphere have engaged in a variety of economic activities to meet their needs and wants.

62CB51D8AE8E4FE8811307D99607A5E3.description: Students will explore the characteristics of a traditional economy used by the Inuit, the market economy of the United States or Canada, and the command economy of Cuba, noting similarities and differences.

3A5AEAE01B984FBE888AF83036913DB7.description: Different types of economic systems have developed across time and place within the Western Hemisphere. These economic systems, including traditional, market, and command, address the three economic questions: what will be produced, how it will be produced, and who will get what is produced?

5526798B9CA44E569E3616DAC7C6E185.description: Economics: The peoples of the Western Hemisphere have developed various ways to meet their needs and wants. Many of the countries of the Western Hemisphere trade with each other, as well as with other countries around the world.

418D468CF37F4496A780EE61C0429EF9.description: Students will examine multinational organizations and nongovernmental organizations and their roles in promoting cooperation, peace, and cultural understanding.

14F50CA3E75C4F338013E5C617609E68.description: Multinational organizations and nongovernmental organizations in the Western Hemisphere seek to encourage cooperation between nations, protect human rights, support economic development, and provide assistance in challenging situations.

BBC0B8E000344F5E85B3C7CA25537AD5.description: Students will examine at least one group of people, such as Native Americans, African Americans, women, or another cultural, ethnic, or racial minority in the Western Hemisphere, who have struggled or are struggling for equality and civil rights or sovereignty.

8F79F93E8C07473B9CA22C98E73484B8.description: Across time and place, different groups of people in the Western Hemisphere have struggled and fought for equality and civil rights or sovereignty.

8B362657E32E458A82902C807E2C9564.description: Students will examine the Declaration of Independence, the United States Constitution and Bill of Rights, the British North America Act, and the Canadian Bill of Rights in terms of key values, beliefs, and principles of constitutional democracy.

06A849A7505D40CB8E2CB28AA97EC4EC.description: Legal, political, and historic documents define the values, beliefs, and principles of constitutional democracy.

C4AF636928904505A0FD6C6F77307B1D.description: Students will compare and contrast the government structures and functions of the United States government with those of Canada, Mexico, and one other country in either the Caribbean or South America.

37254A3DFC9B4E3C8891ED4B63495C8A.description: Students will examine the foundational documents of the United States government for evidence of the country's beliefs, values, and principles.

581C3786CC8C4E239FAE476595A2B738.description: Students will examine the basic structure of the United States federal government, including the president, Congress, and the courts.

71B540A8B0B341C4BFD0538567A3B21D.description: Government structures, functions, and founding documents vary from place to place in the countries of the Western Hemisphere.

95D796A7B863420487BF3C94AF018081.description: Government: The political systems of the Western Hemisphere vary in structure and organization across time and place.

C61083EEAB514FB784939662BCAC44BE.description: Students will investigate a current issue that two or more Western Hemisphere countries are facing together. Some examples include environmental issues, immigration, and trade.

7CC3D7C9ECC446788CD03E45CE846F36.description: Countries in the Western Hemisphere face a variety of concerns and issues specific to the region.

1A73B5093B3F452F85EE91DD409463F6.description: Students will compare and contrast key cultural characteristics and contributions associated with the United States with those associated with Canada, Mexico, and a country in either the Caribbean or South America.

423EE518E001490CB53CE7B930890B6B.description: Students will explore key cultural characteristics, such as the languages, religions and contributions, of the United States, Canada, Mexico, and one Caribbean or one South American country.

3F55CC59D13044AFAA61836AF95BC894.description: The countries of the Western Hemisphere have varied characteristics and contributions that distinguish them from other countries.

A39C2FFE71C249A7AAB060AB340B4313.description: Comparative Cultures: The countries of the Western Hemisphere are diverse and the cultures of these countries are rich and varied. Due to their proximity to each other, the countries of the Western Hemisphere share some of the same concerns and issues.

E42F461752EB43E6A8ABEBCFF1A3BB9F.description: Students will use physical, climate, and vegetation maps in combination with population density, land use, and resource distribution maps to discern patterns in human settlement and types of economic activity.

22AA57A88274460C9ED1A2CF2B056C4D.description: Students will create a political map of the Western Hemisphere, noting which countries are in which region, and a political map of the United States showing the location of the states.

51AE4BAF0628440CB1D1761DB5335DEB.description: Students will map the regions within the Western Hemisphere and locate major physical features within each region.

7F64270DA65747CFB471F90EA5B4CD6D.description: The physical environment influences human population distribution, land use, and other forms of economic activity.

FE152217E0FC4A0B9818560BB47E9E91.description: The Western Hemisphere can be divided into regions. Regions are areas that share common, identifiable characteristics such as physical, political, economic, or cultural features. Regions within the Western Hemisphere include:North America (Canada and the United States), Mesoamerica (Mexico and Central America), Caribbean, and South America

DEE52A1C51A2470AB1980EBC8D4ECBE8.description: Physical maps reflect the varied climate zones, landforms, bodies of water, and natural resources of the Western Hemisphere.

7D2FF0CC28404F1FAEC9205AC458FE42.description: Geography In The Western Hemisphere: The diverse geography of the Western Hemisphere has influenced human culture and settlement in distinct ways. Human communities in the Western Hemisphere have modified the physical environment.

01E13224C28B4DBBBB28A9984DEEB6DE.description: Students will examine the conditions experienced by enslaved Africans during the Middle Passage.

4A70534BAFCC47E3A861AA507CD4805D.description: Students will investigate why sugar was brought to the Americas, noting where it was grown and why, and the role of supply and demand.

A835F455D7294556881808FD90CC183C.description: Africans were captured, brought to the Americas, and sold as slaves. Their transport across the Atlantic was known as the Middle Passage.

D8ADD6CC968E4A6897115A4027716BAC.description: Students will examine the effect of diseases introduced to the Western Hemisphere.

91E749C428E94FC3B60BAF71FE567AE5.description: Students will map the movements of people, plants, animals, and disease between Europe, the Americas, and Africa.

893E29F747EA465C8DD861133DAA5526.description: The transatlantic trade of goods, movement of people, and spread of ideas and diseases resulted in cultural diffusion. This cultural diffusion became known as the Columbian Exchange which reshaped the lives and influenced the beliefs of people.

E77B924E0C5942C289B658CC58E4874C.description: French in Canada and the fur trade

028FE28BC9F6403AB8951EBFB5C363AA.description: Conquests by Cortez and Pizarro and the resulting demographic change

BD0C35DD98B243C88F6686BDF914814A.description: Students will examine European interactions with Native Americans, using these examples:

5524A1BD91CB4965BAB6FE447924D22B.description: Students will examine how Native Americans viewed the newcomers.

6F249E248DD24AD5A666ADC48FB38849.description: Europeans encountered and interacted with Native Americans in a variety of ways.

A3B71449B1874D3F8A78710FE26825FD.description: Students will map the key areas of the Western Hemisphere that were colonized by the English, Dutch, French, Portuguese, and Spanish, comparing the locations, relative sizes, and key resources of these regions.

087FEE707B9A44C3B63269653833CEE5.description: Students will investigate explorers from different European countries and map the areas of the Western Hemisphere where they explored, including Christopher Columbus, John Cabot, Jacques Cartier, Pedro Cabral, and Vasco Nunez de Balboa.

3C6B5337472241D584BF4EE8CC98B721.description: Europeans traveled to the Americas in search of new trade routes, including a northwest passage, and resources. They hoped to gain wealth, power, and glory.

CB5D8F32252A46FCBA5B3A86DED869A2.description: European Exploration And Its Effects: Various European powers explored and eventually colonized the Western Hemisphere. This had a profound effect on Native Americans and led to the transatlantic slave trade.

D05B3BD8189543EFA2CD90BDB14B695C.description: Students will compare and contrast political states of the Maya and the Aztec, noting the territories that they controlled, the type of rule each had, and how the ruler attempted to unify the people.

4494DC1F7D424EA1A1B9D0539487518B.description: Political states can take different forms, such as city-states and empires. A city-state is comprised of a city with a government that controls the surrounding territory, while an empire is a political organization developed when a single, supreme authority conquers other geographic and/or cultural regions beyond its initial settlements.

5D73501AD0D941FC98E36982CC3D1A5A.description: Students will compare how the Mayas, Aztecs, and Incas adapted to and modified their environment to meet the needs of the people, examining the clothing, farming, shelter, and transportation systems for each.

71AD0E9F59724A76AED8A8E1F97612B7.description: Complex societies and civilizations adapted to and modified their environment to meet the needs of their people.

E7E1BF0040D94335819569931F95AFDD.description: Students will investigate the characteristics of the Mayas, Aztecs, and Incas, noting similarities and differences.

B56DAB8626224768852AD66A2CFEDCA3.description: Students will locate the complex societies and civilizations of the Mayas, Aztecs, and Incas on a map, and students will determine when these societies and civilizations occurred.

C84725011E33484B81A5D7D966EF4A61.description: Civilizations share certain common characteristics of religion, job specialization, cities, government, language and writing systems, technology, and social hierarchy.

D128CB27C9964C969B160ABF388C7352.description: Complex Societies And Civilizations: Between 1100 B.C.E. and 1500 C.E, complex societies and civilizations developed in the Western Hemisphere. Although these complex societies and civilizations have certain defining characteristics in common, each is also known for unique cultural achievements and contributions.

914FBB6031A742068569CD42DFBA1E52.description: Students will select one Native American culture group from the United States, one from Canada, and one from the Caribbean region and compare and contrast them by examining how each of these groups adapted to and used the environment and its resources to meet their basic needs, and by examining elements of their culture, including customs, beliefs, values, languages, and patterns of organization and governance.

3AF617BF3D554700AAC34074A89A0F07.description: Students will examine maps that show the variety of different Native American∗ groups located in the Western Hemisphere, noting that there are many different culture groups in many different types of physical, climate, and vegetative regions.

719CF326091840A49AD20459CD1A05A3.description: Early peoples living together in settlements developed shared cultures with customs, beliefs, values, and languages that give identity to the group. These early peoples also developed patterns of organization and governance to manage their societies.

E0D712CC33D346C58C3CA3D8FBFD124D.description: Human populations that settled along rivers, in rainforests, along oceans, in deserts, on plains, in mountains, and in cold climates adapted to and made use of the resources and environment around them in developing distinct ways of life.

C3551E81C71E45108BCB60B27291B153.description: Students will examine the various theories of the migration routes by which the first humans may have arrived, including the Bering land bridge, using maps and archaeological evidence.

80BF4EBD537B4DC98E11AD4972E129D3.description: Various forms of scientific evidence suggest that humans came to North America approximately 25,000 to 14,000 years ago and spread southward to South America.

ADEE59E9B0AC41D8952BF40F447D25CE.description: Early Peoples Of The Americas: The first humans in the Western Hemisphere modified their physical environment as well as adapted to their environment. Their interactions with their environment led to various innovations and to the development of unique cultures.

F410817288ED4C369F6A6F07B1C2E052.description: Develop an understanding of the interdependence of individuals and groups in communities in the Western Hemisphere

F6A7463340314D62AD06E7BE8DEE01D7.description: Identify rights and responsibilities of citizens within societies in the Western Hemisphere.

EA22E096E59F410BA0D48967BC8640B9.description: Describe the roles of people in power in the Western Hemisphere, both historically and currently. Identify ways that current figures can influence people’s rights and freedom.

B6EBA8FEEDD149818B0455F8A4E3E9CE.description: Identify situations with a global focus in which social actions are required and suggest solutions.

A11C5AED2379447DBC338F1AA2ED9E76.description: Participate in negotiating and compromising in the resolution of differences and conflict.

AAD03FF00515421899E26CF1E98311EA.description: Identify opportunities for and the role of the individual in social and political participation at various times and in various locations in the Western Hemisphere outside the United States.

5DC336B508AE4C39A92230C268F6BFE2.description: Identify different types of political systems and ideologies used at various times and in various locations in the Western Hemisphere, and identify the roles of individuals and key groups in those political and social systems.

2AC5FEBBFA8B436F9D262E1AF42D158B.description: Participate in activities that focus on a localized issue or problem in a country other than the United States in the Western Hemisphere.

ACD4FC609AB54FEFA0F6EB47774966CE.description: Demonstrate respect for the rights of others in discussion and classroom debates, regardless of whether one agrees with the other viewpoint. Consider alternate views in discussion, with teacher support.

DEC7B14B795A472EB4A8C5286C77F0B2.description: Describe government decisions that affect economies in case studies from the Western Hemisphere.

4CEEC1AA284943A2921019B97630B3AF.description: Explain the meaning of unemployment, inflation, income, and economic growth in the economy.

0A7C46205A9442BA89D2FAFC5BE54F3C.description: Examine the role of job specialization and trade historically and during contemporary times in the Western Hemisphere.

56CD69CFE4AD4301922B0F18BE6A6299.description: Provide examples of how currency makes exchange easier by comparing a barter economy to a currency-based economy; examine why corporations and labor unions have a role in a market economy.

097B2FC2C5DC415EA015F37F91E5FEBF.description: Show examples of various types of resources (human capital, physical capital, and natural resources) required to provide goods and services.

8E48827DF2294A63907507934D08A296.description: Explain how scarcity necessitates decision making; employ examples from the Western Hemisphere to illustrate the role of scarcity historically and in current events.

C5726DC5449B48699CFC399ADBE81EC9.description: Describe how human activities alter places and regions in the Western Hemisphere. 6. Recognize that boundaries and definition of location are historically constructed.

AC683A90129C485A82EB07CD2CC6EB52.description: Recognize and explain how characteristics (cultural, economic, and physical-environmental) of regions affect the history of societies in the Western Hemisphere.

11645F47C3864B17A4212E7CB667ADCE.description: Identify and describe how environments affect human activities and how human activities affect physical environments through the study of cases in the Western Hemisphere.

8A12A91287B3464B92FD4DECE506EF34.description: Distinguish human activities and human-made features from “environments” (natural events or physical features—land, air, and water—that are not directly made by humans) in the Western Hemisphere.

098451FDDA7C41B18F7400BFE69D9457.description: Use location terms and geographic representations such as maps, photographs, satellite images, and models to describe where places in the Western Hemisphere are in relation to each other, to describe connections among places, and to evaluate the benefits of particular places for purposeful activities.

BCB76E18CA4145B998B6EBB5AD3CFEBD.description: Describe historical developments in the history of the Western Hemisphere with specific references to circumstances of time and place and to connections to broader regional or global processes, with teacher support.

AA47D0DE3C734A69B2EA4306593A2FFD.description: Identify how the relationship between geography, economics, and history helps to define a context for events in the study of the Western Hemisphere.

AC353706C45949A28C4ACC104D2514D4.description: Describe and compare events in the history of the Western Hemisphere in societies in similar chronological contexts and in various geographical contexts.

B19FF118714F41A281D3FA1CC2E17FA3.description: Categorize divergent perspectives of an individual historical event.

DAF4DC5F4581463282558D3807A1F518.description:
Identify a region in the Western Hemisphere by describing a characteristic that places within it have in
common, and then compare it to other regions. Understand how regions can be defined as sharing common
characteristics in contrast with other regions.

6CE34968116D42A19C916AF83ABCF9F2.description: Understand the role of periodization as a practice in history and social studies.

A826FE53A9D84E9F8109DAE4AE658117.description: Recognize and identify patterns of continuity and change in history.

3ACBF0DAF5C94D6FA8BCE40F7E980DD1.description: Use periods of time such as decades and centuries to organize a historical narrative; compare histories in different places in the Western Hemisphere utilizing timelines.

9C0DFC0051084D16A54C93C6474EA7BC.description: Recognize the dynamics of historical continuity and change over periods of time. Identify important turning points in history.

0A015532B2264010B285EA2E7B724CD5.description: Distinguish between long-term and immediate causes and effects of an event from current events or history.

DA87700FA0C0408AAE4A880650C84EB3.description: Identify and classify the relationship between multiple causes and multiple effects.

D8E3B78D29FF4F6DBF4AF7A99AFC6C73.description: Identify causes and effects using examples from current events or grade-level content and historical events

75C81EA4914841528C3B15C48400607F.description: Employ mathematical skills to measure time in years and centuries. Understand the difference between B.C.E. and C.E. Identify the chronological significance of data presented in time lines.

CB6192CABFF0438FA1816E50E387DC32.description: Explain how events are related chronologically to one another in time.

CB24DCE9F1644E8B81F5FC52909943C2.description: Recognize arguments on specific social studies topics and identify evidence supporting the argument.

439C17B3EE7F47A2993301BDD050003E.description: Identify implicit ideas to draw inference, with support.

B69D4333C63A4AF8ADABE31E2015525C.description: Identify evidence and explain content, authorship, purpose, and format; identify bias; explain the role of bias and potential audience, with teacher support.

8D6F7157A9834E18870ED34A44CDA284.description: Recognize and effectively select different forms of evidence used to make meaning in social studies (including primary and secondary sources such as art and photographs, artifacts, oral histories, maps, and graphs).

E963776DDFC949D8A391A6C99FDB7B98.description:
Develop questions to help identify evidence about topics related to the historical events occurring in the
Western Hemisphere that can be answered by gathering, interpreting, and using evidence.

document.title: New York State K-8 Social Studies Framework

0503FA43F4BB4D08BD63EE4D36680A8B.description: Students will examine how various technologies affected trade and exchanges. Some examples are types of ships, including junks and caravels; improvements to ships, such as sails and rudders; navigation tools, such as the compass and astrolabe; and gunpowder.

236044BEF25745EE99C34F1B9E6C826B.description: Complex societies and civilizations adapted and designed technologies for transportation that allowed them to cross challenging landscapes and move people and goods efficiently.

0BB7ED9D776B469099CAA358BA134A0F.description: Students will examine the spread of the Black Death (Bubonic Plague) as a result of interregional exchange and its effects on various regions within Afro-Eurasia, using a variety of sources, such as maps, poetry, and other primary source documents.

DBA029AD7C1240218A31DA96F7E1FD41.description: Students will examine the methods used by the Mongols to enable them to rule over a diverse population, noting how Mongol rule expanded trade.

3F88EB3B788345AA8DC681FF08EC6B80.description: Students will map the extent of the Mongol Empire at the height of its power.

4AC3F0C68F41446F8E500DE29816EADB.description: The Mongol conquests in Eurasia fostered connections between the East and the West, and the Mongols served as important agents of change and cultural diffusion.

BB56A5CD35054987A7DF83711F6ED977.description: Students will study interregional travelers such as Marco Polo, Ibn Battuta, Mansa Musa, and Zheng He and examine why they traveled, the places visited, what was learned, and what was exchanged as a result of their travel.

0F40AE65F07D47D99035B68DED4EF15A.description: Students will examine how the location of resources helped determine the location of trade routes and the economic impact of the exchange of resources.

C5E4A9B7E0CC4FC6A88B4C427281B1A3.description: Students will create maps that illustrate items exchanged and ideas spread along the Silk Roads, across the Indian Ocean, and on the Trans-Saharan trade routes.

D17DABDCD5174B17ACC38C641E01EF5F.description: The Silk Roads, the Indian Ocean, and the Trans-Saharan routes formed the major Afro-Eurasian trade networks connecting the East and the West. Ideas, people, technologies, products, and diseases moved along these routes.

50A3CD18011448D3815A54B24D28680E.description: Interactions Across The Eastern Hemisphere (ca. 600 C.E. – ca. 1450): Trade networks promoted the exchange and diffusion of language, belief systems, tools, intellectual ideas, inventions, and diseases.

44B3107D627242E58FEE8D4A7FD83876.description: Students will examine the conflict of the Crusades from three different perspectives: feudal Europe, Byzantine, and Islamic.

0DC93A6B090041BF87FC7E103BEAC98C.description: Students will examine the three distinct cultural regions of the Mediterranean world in terms of their location, the extent of each region at the height of its power, and the political, economic, and social interactions between these regions.

78342550FA9340F48C0E718D46E309AE.description: Competition and rivalry over religious, economic, and political control over holy lands led to conflict such as the Crusades.

F38E83F6E9974025990CA953FDF3417C.description: Students will examine the Umayyad and Abbasid caliphates, noting how the introduction of Islam changed the societies and cultures each conquered, blending with those societies and cultures and creating dynamic new Islamic societies and cultures.

CD602077A70A4A17A183BC7E417E0A93.description: Islam spread within the Mediterranean region from southwest Asia to northern Africa and the Iberian Peninsula.

85E48A08F07E46F0B6CE8DED68C30D4F.description: Students will examine how the Byzantine Empire preserved elements of the Roman Empire by blending Roman traditions with Greek culture, and developed a Christian faith, known as Orthodox Christianity, which united Church and state authority in the person of the emperor.

6BE73AE6CC9F47BCAC6294E42D4B8C6A.description: The Byzantine Empire preserved elements of the Roman Empire, controlled lands within the Mediterranean basin, and began to develop Orthodox Christianity.

B6440C477558415EB2779C34D789BD98.description: Students will examine reasons for the fall of the Roman Empire and the development of feudalism in Western Europe, including efforts to restore the empire, the decentralization of political authority, and the role of the Christian Church in providing some measure of central authority.

F8DDFC26237B445BBA5F2AA8409A441A.description: Overexpansion, corruption, invasions, civil wars, and discord led to the fall of Rome. Feudalism developed in Western Europe in reaction to a need for order and to meet basic needs.

A8DF137EFCE247599F5090BE9C1D1ADB.description: Mediterranean World: Feudal Western Europe, The Byzantine Empire, And The Islamic Caliphates (ca. 600 C.E. – ca. 1450): The Mediterranean world was reshaped with the fall of the Roman Empire. Three distinct cultural regions developed: feudal Western Europe, the Byzantine Empire, and the Islamic caliphates. These regions interacted with each other and clashed over control of holy lands.

861F7347CD7E4DDB9CC26E0DEE3FDB90.description: Students will examine how cultural achievements of these civilizations have influenced contemporary societies.

B232940C95774461A4B254E5951962FE.description: Students will examine evidence related to the Qin, Han, and Greco-Roman (Athens and Roman Empire) civilizations and determine if these civilizations have experienced a golden age.

EEBEAEA5D09543A1B87A34AF606842CF.description: A period of peace, prosperity, and cultural achievements may be indicative of a golden age.

61D42EE7DB2F404DB88B5B605EC8D3E4.description: Students will examine the similarities and differences between the political systems of Chinese (Qin, Han) and Greco-Roman (Athens, Sparta, Roman Republic, Roman Empire) classical civilizations.

01251339451F4546977671E5E3C49176.description: Political structures were developed to establish order, to create and enforce laws, and to enable decision making.

0CD6CEBD1DF64641B608AB1B21E9F681.description: Students will compare and contrast the similarities and differences between the Chinese (Qin, Han) and Greco-Roman classical civilizations by examining religion, job specialization, cities, government, language/record keeping system, technology, and social hierarchy.

9D7626A6F03146AF98E6B99530883851.description: Students will locate the classical civilizations on a map and identify geographic factors that influenced the extent of their boundaries, locate their cities on a map, and identify their political structures.

1CE5CAAB124E4B63A86F4956EF820EC4.description: Geographic factors influence the development of classical civilizations and their political structures.

1545086206F1479D851DC84DACF06272.description: Comparative Classical Civilizations In The Eastern Hemisphere (ca. 600 B.C.E. – ca. 500 C.E.): As complex societies and civilizations change over time, their political and economic structures evolve. A golden age may be indicated when there is an extended period of time that is peaceful, prosperous, and demonstrates great cultural achievements.

3E856CCE2DD84400889C400F84777058.description: Students will explore the influence of various belief systems on contemporary cultures and events.

68F0DB06DE4B423FB198F9F766B698FD.description: Students will be able to identify similarities and differences across belief systems, including their effect on social order and gender roles.

6FEC7825B47D4AF79FF8E86AE35D1755.description: Belief systems and religions often are used to unify groups of people, and may affect social order and gender roles.

A84E4B5F2DFD4FFCB9F38668AFD8E6B6.description: Students will study the belief systems of Judaism, Christianity, Islam, Buddhism, Hinduism, and Confucianism by looking at where the belief system originated, when it originated, founder(s) if any, and the major tenets, practices, and sacred writings or holy texts for each. (Note: Although not within this historic period, students may also study Sikhism and other major belief systems at this point.)

264477BF1203491EACEAF181E6BC5612.description: Belief systems and religions are based on sets of mutually held values.

E3E2EE011E744B978227C7BF63910B25.description: Civilizations and complex societies developed belief systems and religions that have similar, as well as different, characteristics.

3412693CB228485CB72F0C330E9BA7C6.description: Comparative World Religions (ca. 2000 B.C.E – ca. 630 C.E): Major religions and belief systems developed in the Eastern Hemisphere. There were important similarities and differences between these belief systems.

1730107E1ED84815A04C2942BAA75DD0.description: Students will examine the unique achievements of each of the selected complex societies and civilizations that served as lasting contributions.

C44B480FEC1B4EF8A7482063A377BAFB.description: Students will compare and contrast the gender roles, access to wealth and power, and division of labor within the political and social structures of the selected river valley societies and civilizations.

AF7738FC0B55467DA759D96257334DB8.description: Political and social hierarchies influenced the access that groups and individuals had to power, wealth, and jobs and influenced their roles within a society.

1E80785D405544ECBCBCEB7DC05B1F5C.description: Students will explore how the selected complex societies and civilizations adapted to and modified their environment to meet their basic needs of food, clothing, and shelter.

CD4C088C628B48DBA56E6397EFA7A474.description: Mesopotamia, Yellow River valley, Indus River valley, and Nile River valley complex societies and civilizations adapted to and modified their environment to meet the needs of their population.

61DD6AB2F26644D6A2EAD60D1D763709.description: Students will explore at least two river valley societies and civilizations: one in the Middle East (Mesopotamia or Nile river valley), one in South Asia (Indus River valley), or one in East Asia (Yellow River valley) by examining archaeological and historical evidence to compare and contrast characteristics of these complex societies and civilizations.

E41F64D6066047B8ADC983065934C402.description: Complex societies and civilizations share the common characteristics of religion, job specialization, cities, government, language/record keeping system, technology, and social hierarchy. People in Mesopotamia, the Yellow River valley, the Indus River valley, and the Nile River valley developed complex societies and civilizations.

DDD8DDABA52A4DB5B876FF9C4B4A39E7.description: Humans living together in settlements develop shared customs, beliefs, ideas, and languages that give identity to the group.

5BDA88FF62774989A7C7DECD05B277FE.description: Early River Valley Civilizations In The Eastern Hemisphere (ca. 3500 B.C.E. – ca. 500 B.C.E.): Complex societies and civilizations developed in the Eastern Hemisphere. Although these complex societies and civilizations have certain defining characteristics in common, each is also known for unique cultural achievements and contributions. Early human communities in the Eastern Hemisphere adapted to and modified the physical environment.

510BDFB3B7FF49EDB886A112AD9ACD17.description: Students will determine if the Neolithic Revolution is a turning point in world history, using various forms of evidence.

E6723A10ACD14370B4FB566FE3DC905F.description: Historians use archaeological and other types of evidence to investigate patterns in history and identify turning points. A turning point can be an event, era, and/or development in history that has brought about significant social, cultural, ecological, political, or economic change.

B1A273CB13924507B2C2AC75088A690E.description: Students will compare the use of tools and animals, types of dwellings, art, and social organizations of early peoples, and distinguish between the Paleolithic Age and Neolithic Age.

CAF26B6835BA41EE8F67B72FB4FDD00E.description: Students will be introduced to pastoral nomadic peoples as a culture type that existed throughout history.

58539A3F8FB24A259A40598A611345C1.description: Students will explore early human migration patterns and settlements through the use of multiple maps and the examination of various forms of archaeological evidence.

931EC99427824B70BD7D1FBAB84FD653.description: The Neolithic Revolution was marked by technological advances in agriculture and domestication of animals that allowed people to form semi-sedentary and sedentary settlements.

7C1A09F3E99C4C3092469C4C8F05FCAF.description: Early peoples in the Eastern Hemisphere are often studied by analyzing artifacts and archaeological features. Archaeologists engage in digs and study artifacts and features in a particular location to gather evidence about a group of people and how they lived at a particular time.

5E3DB011943F4D398C4B36A0B0EEFEA4.description: Human populations that settled along rivers, in rainforests, along coastlines, in deserts, and in mountains made use of the resources and the environment around them in developing distinct ways of life.

C8B5B6E2C06244DA80DD3090A9B69D79.description: The First Humans Through The Neolithic Revolution In The Eastern Hemisphere: The first humans modified their physical environment as well as adapted to their environment.

92A1198DEAA94A12B2C8FEE74AFF3EAB.description: Students will examine current political and environmental issues in a region or country of the Eastern Hemisphere being studied.

6D72D6E281334735B5A5AB79A075ACC9.description: Issues and problems experienced in the regions of the Eastern Hemisphere have roots in the past.

809E61B629F84AE1BC23583BA770AE91.description: To understand scale, students will work with maps at a variety of scales so they can compare patterns in population density and land use, economic activity, and political connections across the present-day Eastern Hemisphere, within a region of the Eastern Hemisphere, and in a specific country. In doing so, students will examine maps of the hemisphere, three regions within the present-day Eastern Hemisphere, and one specific country within each region.

50EBD227B6C54ADDAF5C257D52D4DDCE.description: Students will use physical, climate, and vegetation maps in combination with population density, land use, and resource distribution maps in order to discern patterns in human settlement, economic activity, and the relationship to scarcity of resources in the present-day Eastern Hemisphere.

567DC7E9B4E64B7DADB13A3184101CDC.description: The physical environment influences human population distribution, land use, economic activities, and political connections.

785BA3861BAB47BF96C6B25DEFCB9725.description: The Eastern Hemisphere can be divided into regions. Regions are areas that share common identifiable characteristics, such as physical, political, economic, or cultural features. Regions within the Eastern Hemisphere include:Middle East (North Africa and Southwest Asia), Sub-Saharan Africa, Europe (West, North, South, Central, and Southeast), Russia and the Independent States (Russia, Caucasia, Central Asia, the region of Belarus, Moldova, and Ukraine), East Asia (People's Republic of China, North Korea, South Korea, Japan, and Taiwan), Southeast Asia (Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, Thailand, Myanmar [Burma], Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Brunei, Philippines), South Asia (Afghanistan, Pakistan, India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan), and Oceania (Australia, New Zealand, the Pacific)

DF59E7892A0244CC9E3D4875BE0F269A.description: Maps can be used to represent varied climate zones, landforms, bodies of water, and resources of the Eastern Hemisphere.

A1B8E626F18F48578F48B343D48AB669.description: Present-Day Eastern Hemisphere Geography: The diverse geography of the Eastern Hemisphere has influenced human culture and settlement patterns in distinct ways. Human communities in the Eastern Hemisphere have adapted to or modified the physical environment.

61649D8A62574C46817A500C287BA4C8.description: 9. Develop an understanding of an interdependent global community by developing awareness and/or engaging in the political process as it relates to a global context.

9A170E873C064AA18E941EF130E26772.description: 8. Identify rights and responsibilities of citizens within societies in the Eastern Hemisphere.

2A21D019FA3D416AA12B2B850C6710CD.description: 7. Describe the roles of people in power in the Eastern Hemisphere both historically and currently. Identify ways that current figures can influence people’s rights and freedom.

37670F29FF334016A744EDED4B292029.description: 6. Identify situations with a global focus in which social actions are required and suggest solutions.

608A2E5202FB4C8FA8F25C5FC1F627BD.description: 5. Participate in negotiating and compromising in the resolution of differences and conflict; introduce and examine the role of conflict resolution.

34340F4A15D945809E676B6D09C83281.description: 4. Identify and describe opportunities for and the role of the individual in social and political participation at various times and in various locations in the Eastern Hemisphere.

7B274C16BEEE47C281CDEE87C68CBD95.description: 3. Identify and explore different types of political systems and ideologies used at various times and in various locations in the Eastern Hemisphere and identify the role of individuals and key groups in those political and social systems.

E66DAB5FC0AB4F0EB60D33E822F0CA9F.description: 2. Participate in activities that focus on a local issue or problem in a country in the Eastern Hemisphere.

4A9C8F6595AB473F8F1F8F7931B039AD.description: 1. Demonstrate respect for the rights of others in discussion and classroom debates, regardless of whether one agrees with the other viewpoint. Consider alternate views in discussion.

709B1DA6C8B5439786D6C91EF8CCEBF4.description: Describe government decisions that affect economies in case studies from the Eastern Hemisphere.

51E7F0B925344CA2AF95B34767A25879.description: Provide examples of unemployment, inflation, total production, income, and economic growth in economies in the Eastern Hemisphere.

54E575E9A3144CBCA8EDD24E7D63FD15.description: Examine the role of job specialization and trade historically and during contemporary times in the Eastern Hemisphere.

6536A31A11F24052BAE69C70A9B26D77.description: Compare market economies to other economic systems in the Eastern Hemisphere.

3DFC858ED0C0403CB15203FFB7B4C413.description: Examine the role that various types of resources (human capital, physical capital, and natural resources) have in providing goods and services.

A598CE16D6DC480C9C7D9B9D03B58F42.description: Explain how scarcity necessitates decision making; employ examples from the Eastern Hemisphere to illustrate the role of scarcity historically and in current events; compare through historical examples the costs and benefits of economic decisions.

3AAA459266DD4274B8ED984EDFDFA9E3.description: Describe the spatial organization of place, considering the historical, social, political, and economic implication of that organization. Recognize that boundaries and definitions of location are historically constructed.

CD0CE9142B334D4AAB9D9872D8DC1421.description: Describe how human activities alter places and regions in the Eastern Hemisphere.

9640538361214D41B44384D6A9FD708E.description: Recognize and explain how characteristics (cultural, economic, and physical-environmental) of regions affect the history of societies in the Eastern Hemisphere.

FBCE2CA5215B4CDFBA59B4FD2CAED710.description: Identify and describe how environments affect human activities and how human activities affect physical environments through the study of cases in the Eastern Hemisphere. Grades K-8 Page 80

6C514E9542DA481E8A2AE7CE0FCDFC9E.description: Distinguish human activities and human-made features from “environments” (natural events or physical features—land, air, and water—that are not directly made by humans) in the Eastern Hemisphere; identify the relationship between human activities and the environment.

CDE27A1975BA435AB05C6E1E0374A33C.description: Use location terms and geographic representations such as maps, photographs, satellite images, and models to describe where places in the Eastern Hemisphere are in relation to each other, to describe connections between places, and to evaluate the benefits of particular places for purposeful activities.

7D515DF261224EA39347B4ABAD3A4A74.description: Understand the roles that periodization and region play in developing the comparison of historical civilizations. Identify general characteristics that can be employed to conduct comparative analysis of case studies in the Eastern Hemisphere in the same historical period, with teacher support.

189F48D60A804EA5ABDD07F7F9073FC5.description: Describe historical developments in the history of the Eastern Hemisphere, with specific references to circumstances of time and place and to connections to broader regional or global processes.

FEE86C5991FB40B5AD591118F7515A2B.description: Identify how the relationship between geography, economics, and history helps to define a context for events in the study of the Eastern Hemisphere.

D5173D18798E4801A132322F5C246B19.description: Describe and compare multiple events in the history of the Eastern Hemisphere in societies in similar chronological contexts and in various geographical contexts.

0F52459D1F0049B496453CE08D0BB51F.description: Categorize and evaluate divergent perspectives on an individual historical event.

FE9BE66D29D1429290327CDD47C69026.description: Identify a region in the Eastern Hemisphere by describing a characteristic that places within it have in common, and then compare it to other regions.

7248837E3E94442E9BA79D2BD0936B2E.description: Understand that historians use periodization to categorize events. Describe general models of periodization in history.

3041FD59AD144F23A08AC0A975AB510D.description: Identify the relationships of patterns of continuity and change to larger historical processes and themes.

74CC9EE484874CCC8D75CA16846499EA.description: Compare histories in different places in the Eastern Hemisphere, utilizing time lines. Identify ways that changing periodization affects the historical narrative.

45E7B7371A9C49D7B54ED20993198B33.description: Recognize and analyze the dynamics of historical continuity and change over periods of time. Identify the role of turning points as an important dynamic in historical change.

79E85DD2ABF84F0595E8A3E02C92435C.description: Distinguish between long-term and immediate causes and effects of an event from current events or history.

938ED944AAFF4BD9963507528FE2F40D.description: Identify and classify the relationship between multiple causes and multiple effects.

4556AD52EB2749548E4C944DD70448CC.description: Identify causes and effects from current events, grade-level content, and historical events.

23E1B98C86834F9F831D1731B50BC665.description: Employ mathematical skills to measure time by years, decades, centuries, and millennia; to calculate time from the fixed points of the calendar system (B.C.E. and C.E.); and to interpret the data presented in time lines, with teacher support.

4C4E3D7169B44C1B83112901CDE7D5FB.description: Identify ways that events are related chronologically to one another in time.

626FF4E749DE4AF78A2AD411D4F02A2D.description: Recognize arguments on specific social studies topics and identify evidence to support the arguments. Examine arguments related to a specific social studies topic from multiple perspectives.

AB9832C1429B4B35B6540EAAB27FE793.description: Identify implicit ideas and draw inferences, with support.

6E54ED3FCB234962A65934E8B76EE1D8.description: Identify evidence and explain content, authorship, point of view, purpose, and format; identify bias; explain the role of bias and potential audience.

CB34547B59B04FFAB63D39F6327CC5CC.description: Identify, effectively select, and analyze different forms of evidence used to make meaning in social studies (including primary and secondary sources such as art and photographs, artifacts, oral histories, maps, and graphs).

7141FCC50DEA480593572B42C5604CD6.description: Develop and frame questions about topics related to historical events occurring in the Eastern Hemisphere that can be answered by gathering, interpreting, and using evidence.

standardSets.title: Grade 7: History of the United States and New York State I
standardSets.subject: Social Studies (2017-)

document.title: New York State K-8 Social Studies Framework

AA804D56EB9845989E80A418510175C8.description: Students will explain how events of the Civil War led to the establishment of federal supremacy.

5327059C15A14579AEBCDF1C76C885C4.description: Students will examine the aftermath of the war in terms of destruction, effect on population, and economic capacity by comparing effects of the war on New York State and Georgia.

F0A16DC5426D41D0A357D5FF13C5115C.description: Students will examine the roles of women, civilians, and free African Americans during the Civil War.

DB70A0A93DC54A7EBB7F72D0C6ADE3B6.description: The Civil War affected human lives, physical infrastructure, economic capacity, and governance of the United States.

023D286B5AFB4B9088CC5A777DBC2452.description: Students will examine the topography and geographic conditions at Gettysburg and Antietam, and analyze the military strategies employed by the North and the South at Gettysburg or Antietam.

EBF748D03F014985BC38A8CF633D8C24.description: Students will examine the enlistment of freed slaves and how this helped to change the course of the Civil War.

598549110CFE444BB4F0AF90A88A5DFB.description: Students will examine how the use of various technologies affected the conduct and outcome of the Civil War.

7AB7E028194A47198E5A81B6C773B6DC.description: Students will examine the goals and content of Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation.

DBE7515FD19946D9AEC42B1B97377FB4.description: Students will compare the advantages and disadvantages of the North and the South at the outset of the Civil War.

0C52072061DA469A9AC068ECBD116A07.description: The course and outcome of the Civil War were influenced by strategic leaders from both the North and South, decisive battles, and military strategy and technology that utilized the region's geography.

C9D3BAFAD8B143F7A791D1FF9FB7B846.description: Students will examine the role of New York State in the Civil War, including its contributions to the war effort and the controversy over the draft.

48D64DA35F0E4DA9A7E7F6BCDBF685F2.description: Students will identify which states seceded to form the Confederate States of America and will explore the reasons presented for secession. Students will also identify the states that remained in the Union.

9DFB27B99C59431880ECA63D12D850B2.description: Students will examine both long- and short-term causes of the Civil War.

182B60C76806407F979F7C566EBF7E3A.description: Perspectives on the causes of the Civil War varied based on geographic region, but the election of a Republican president was one of the immediate causes for the secession of the Southern states.

A6F0258B8E2241CEBA23A5374857304B.description: Students will examine growing sectional tensions, including the decision in Dred Scott v. Sanford (1857) and the founding of the Republican Party.

8772737C9F684B23872FA23F4278CEA2.description: Students will examine attempts at resolving conflicts over whether new territories would permit slavery, including the Missouri Compromise, the Compromise of 1850, and the Kansas-Nebraska Act.

E79D9D3233B545FAB8ABC9503C85EAC8.description: As the nation expanded geographically, the question of slavery in new territories and states led to increased sectional tensions. Attempts at compromise ended in failure.

CD66C99837E0437C8FF18769EC16CFDC.description: Students will examine regional economic differences as they related to industrialization.

0BAA393A6A8E41ECA3082EF04AE52418.description: Early United States industrialization affected different parts of the country in different ways. Regional economic differences and values, as well as different conceptions of the Constitution, laid the basis for tensions between states' rights advocates and supporters of a strong federal government.

401912343DA74C1C9CA14E021ABF4903.description: A Nation Divided: Westward expansion, the industrialization of the North, and the increase of slavery in the South contributed to the growth of sectionalism. Constitutional conflicts between advocates of states' rights and supporters of federal power increased tensions in the nation; attempts to compromise ultimately failed to keep the nation together, leading to the Civil War.

C89A73ED82AE4429B7E8E5FE1F6D8745.description: Students will trace the Anti-Rent movement in New York State.

D185A3CDFEC14BA1A6C119DA67509B9E.description: The Anti-Rent movement in New York State was an attempt by tenant farmers to protest the landownership system.

EAB55DBCD7A443F4A0F22D6C33758807.description: Students will explain the significance of the Seneca Falls Convention and the Declaration of Sentiments.

C2624AB840E343E690C289A311BF49FC.description: Students will examine the efforts of women to acquire more rights. These women include Sojourner Truth, Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Matilda Joslyn Gage, and Susan B. Anthony.

763596203ADB4911BE894C130AE5A222.description: Women joined the movements for abolition and temperance and organized to advocate for women's property rights, fair wages, education, and political equality.

6A3C7E63FBCC4D2293D9C134151BB3AC.description: Students will examine the seizure of the ship, La Amistad, carrying enslaved Africans, off the coast of Long Island and the resulting Supreme Court decision in United States v. The Amistad (1841).

9D9DC18259FC4220AA64578CA6E17214.description: Students will investigate New York State and its role in the abolition movement, including the locations of Underground Railroad stations.

D7DC33A243A642F3A7E78F3E0E11A29D.description: Students will examine the effects of Uncle Tom's Cabin on the public perception of slavery.

C72B2AABB380481BA212D803CF8E0750.description: Students will explore the efforts of William Lloyd Garrison, Frederick Douglass, and Harriet Tubman to abolish slavery.

1F344CDB473347D4B3D708593BD69466.description: Students will examine ways in which enslaved Africans organized and resisted their conditions.

D68FF11D1D15452F844E3D70C4A0A8AD.description: Enslaved African Americans resisted slavery in various ways in the 19th century. The abolitionist movement also worked to raise awareness of and generate resistance to the institution of slavery.

07A9DD6809C04D1F9E38EC92D83EC4F2.description: Students will investigate examples of early 19th-century reform movements, such as education, prisons, temperance, and mental health care, and examine the circumstances that led to the need for reform.

C82D1A10CA2B49BD9ECACF443D257D3A.description: The Second Great Awakening, which had a strong showing in New York State, inspired reform movements.

0F585C33B5714142BE19AC28D233A656.description: Reform Movements: Social, political, and economic inequalities sparked various reform movements and resistance efforts. Influenced by the Second Great Awakening, New York State played a key role in major reform efforts.

5D8DE31633F94CF3878B59D8B98B853A.description: Students will examine the policies of New York State toward Native Americans at this time, and its efforts to take tribal lands, particularly those of the Oneidas, and exercise jurisdiction over those communities.

DE09021DFF3C46C5BCBD3C105BC198BD.description: Students will examine the ways westward movement affected the lives of women and African Americans.

843AB86CEB734CE486AB7D16D012545B.description: Students will examine examples of Native American resistance to western encroachment, including the Seminole Wars and Cherokee judicial efforts.

C388EEB909644F1B8735AEB39F2ACADA.description: Students will examine the conditions faced on the Trail of Tears by the Cherokee and the effect that the removal had on their people and culture.

4563F28612954EE287F6FF1C121E13A9.description: Students will examine the growth of suffrage for white men during Andrew Jackson's administration.

8A65361219E7451C9A09D4A834DEB80D.description: Students will examine the Erie Canal as a gateway to westward expansion that resulted in economic growth for New York State, economic opportunities for Irish immigrants working on its construction, and its use by religious groups, such as the Mormons, to move westward.

53621C30B7D44443A2E7055EF1381C7B.description: Westward expansion provided opportunities for some groups while harming others.

74EB9AB65B15434ABBBF8E16D633F0FA.description: Students will compare and evaluate the ways in which Florida, Texas, and territories from the Mexican Cession were acquired by the United States.

C883889C4BD84A8B86AD6E12C7C94E70.description: Conflict and compromise with foreign nations occurred regarding the physical expansion of the United States during the 19th century. American values and beliefs, such as Manifest Destiny and the need for resources, increased westward expansion and settlement.

AD636187C47046298B39E3387892FB92.description: Some Native Americans who aligned with the British during the American Revolution lost land and were forced to move.

E75D5003FB2043ADBFC257DE859790BE.description: Westward Expansion: Driven by political and economic motives, the United States expanded its physical boundaries to the Pacific Ocean between 1800 and 1860. This settlement displaced Native Americans as the frontier was pushed westward.

F5365212C5FD4BEC8649AE9464195DA1.description: Students will examine the Monroe Doctrine and its effects on foreign policy.

33755FB5D1E54F0A93D19D8E426761B6.description: Students will examine events of the early nation including Hamilton's economic plan, the Louisiana Purchase, the Supreme Court decision in Marbury v. Madison, and the War of 1812 in terms of testing the strength of the Constitution.

59562C79608C421E9DC75A101C6FAD09.description: Foreign and domestic disputes tested the strength of the Constitution, particularly the separation of powers, the system of checks and balances, and the issue of States rights. The United States sought to implement isolationism while protecting the Western Hemisphere from European interference.

88F989B5BFDE4AC9A305766DECEAF5DD.description: Students will examine the changes to the New York State Constitution and how they were made during the 19th century.

DB49BCC642F34CB8AECE7F4B9BB0F951.description: Students will examine the evolution of the unwritten constitution, such as Washington's creation of the presidential cabinet and the development of political parties.

5654AB22EC404BA2954B475BE4DFE1E3.description: Students will examine the process for amending the constitution.

D709940163F04EA4A204DFAD47681824.description: While the Constitution provides a formal process for change through amendments, the Constitution can respond to change in other ways. The New York State Constitution changed over time, with changes in the early 19th century that made it more democratic.

630ECCC8640242859C04EE63C90CB4BF.description: Students will identify the individual rights of citizens that are protected by the Bill of Rights.

6ECFBCA306B049129DE7B4642C2D4484.description: Students will examine how checks and balances work by tracing how a bill becomes a law.

F68D76ABF85C4F249FE35FDEF7C4A627.description: Students will compare and contrast the powers granted to Congress, the president, and the Supreme Court by the Constitution.

B5FF81105D5049DCAF682881784D8E76.description: The Constitution established three branches of government as well as a system of checks and balances that guides the relationship between the branches. Individual rights of citizens are addressed in the Bill of Rights.

493FA0330C114382BD0ED8231AEB76FF.description: Students will identify powers granted to the federal government and examine the language used to grant powers to the states.

8C1D060F9FF6413398DA54D01484A548.description: The Constitution outlined a federalist system of government that shares powers between the federal, state, and local governments.

010863E7CE72401E96FA4A7F402BF435.description: The Constitution In Practice: The United States Constitution serves as the foundation of the United States government and outlines the rights of citizens. The Constitution is considered a living document that can respond to political and social changes. The New York State Constitution also has been changed over time.

25A8EDA2ECED459BBE741085847B8BD1.description: Students will examine the role of New York State residents Alexander Hamilton and John Jay as leading advocates for the new Constitution.

87A395FC040D412CBE4DCC1F8C7AF70D.description: Students will examine how key issues were resolved during the Constitutional Convention, including: state representation in Congress (Great Compromise or bicameral legislature), the balance of power between the federal and state governments (establishment of the system of federalism), the prevention of parts of government becoming too powerful (the establishment of the three branches), and the counting of the enslaved African American community for purposes of congressional representation and taxation (the Three-Fifths Compromise)

ACA7EB2B5AC440AB959546C4D9B76F93.description: Students will examine from multiple perspectives arguments regarding the balance of power between the federal and state governments, the power of government, and the rights of individuals.

6B2BE6B00E3A4A32A1B5DF9B2FAFFA42.description: Advocates for and against a strong central government were divided on issues of States rights, role/limits of federal power, and guarantees of individual freedoms. Compromises were needed between the states in order to ratify the Constitution.

B4A8BF931F044769890E2459776417B1.description: Students will examine the New York State Constitution, its main ideas and provisions, and its influence on the formation of the United States Constitution.

EC3D05F7109442A5BD082700EEED8683.description: Students will investigate the successes and failures of the Articles of Confederation, determine why many felt a new plan of government was needed, and explain how the United States Constitution attempted to address the weaknesses of the Articles.

EE3DAFCFE5E64E81A8382C0BC44C7AE0.description: The lack of a strong central government under the Articles of Confederation presented numerous challenges. A convention was held to revise the Articles, the result of which was the Constitution. The Constitution established a democratic republic with a stronger central government.

D56342A65207453D97CEF798DDDE8F09.description: Throughout the American Revolution, the colonies struggled to address their differing social, political, and economic interests and to establish unity. The Articles of Confederation created a form of government that loosely united the states, but allowed states to maintain a large degree of sovereignty.

F1CE1731DEF74109B87297038DD3E7F4.description: Historical Development Of The Constitution: The newly independent states faced political and economic struggles under the Articles of Confederation. These challenges resulted in a Constitutional Convention, a debate over ratification, and the eventual adoption of the Bill of Rights.

66A2AA6BD2F3448382FBE01651B99DAA.description: Students will examine the terms of the Treaty of Paris, determine what boundary was set for the United States, and illustrate this on a map.

4EB69B995FED4A13A01DF2C97FB2107C.description: Students will examine the strategic importance of the New York colony. Students will examine the American victory at the Battle of Saratoga in terms of its effects on American and British morale and on European views on American prospects for victory in the Revolution.

CC541C323B1F4022B3DB25926470DA17.description: Students will explore the different military strategies used by the Americans and their allies, including various Native American groups, during the American Revolution.

760F59676B36453EA1C934272A677DC3.description: The outcome of the American Revolution was influenced by military strategies, geographic considerations, the involvement of the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) and other Native American groups in the war, and aid from other nations. The Treaty of Paris (1783) established the terms of peace.

952715FB6EB943DBA0F46B74B182FD5D.description: Students will examine the Declaration of Independence and the arguments for independence stated within it.

6876EB93788E4BD98E51D829BDEF483E.description: Students will examine the influence Enlightenment ideas such as natural rights and social contract and ideas expressed in Thomas Paine's Common Sense had on colonial leaders in their debates on independence.

C480D2E73D434F30A766D4C34A47B2D1.description: Influenced by Enlightenment ideas and their rights as Englishmen, American colonial leaders outlined their grievances against British policies and actions in the Declaration of Independence.

6DEE9EE571B843C89967516E357A3E20.description: Students will examine the events at Lexington and Concord as the triggering events for the Revolutionary War.

06E420E501EE4893AFDA8B9768801DBA.description: Students will compare the proportions of loyalists and patriots in different regions of the New York colony.

A689E13832E54B29AC39C974C0F0BE06.description: Students will compare British and colonial patriot portrayals of the Boston Massacre, using historical evidence.

ECF7A30FDBF5489689BDECF38E154ED6.description: Students will examine actions taken by the British, including the Proclamation of 1763, the Quartering Act, the Stamp Act, the Tea Act, and the Coercive Acts, and colonial responses to those actions.

6C1CA763BB8742358A7BB7B049430E5D.description: Students will investigate the Albany Congress and the Albany Plan of Union as a plan for colonial unification.

EC71772C71684A889CD0E19F443A9A8A.description: Stemming from the French and Indian War, the British government enacted and attempted to enforce new political and economic policies in the colonies. These policies triggered varied colonial responses, including protests and dissent.

DC9716D34EB1470E8EF889C0142FC3E7.description: Students will identify the issues stemming from the Zenger Trial that affected the development of individual rights in colonial America.

49D0A86703F14AA1B743B9D68D45CB6E.description: Students will examine the changing economic relationship between the colonies and Great Britain, including mercantilism and the practice of salutary neglect.

CAD06458BB734B37BADD01A24E3E9955.description: Students will examine how Native Americans attempted to maintain a diplomatic balance between themselves and the French and the English settlers.

59EB52B588314D91BB44E4CDDE4D4784.description: Students will locate battles fought between France and Great Britain during the 17th and 18th centuries, and how this led to the importance of British troops in the area of New York.

B710474484B44E689931D00A6097EBC4.description: Conflicts between France and Great Britain in the 17th and 18th centuries in North America altered the relationship between the colonies and Great Britain.

DE3990C78C1C4B31A71249F0EABB73EF.description: American Independence: Growing tensions over political power and economic issues sparked a movement for independence from Great Britain. New York played a critical role in the course and outcome of the American Revolution.

EB0F1403F301435880B7CD4A961F75D9.description: Within the context of New York State history, students will distinguish between indentured servitude and slavery.

DC595D0E218C4BF285058B0A32DD4E35.description: Students will investigate different methods enslaved Africans used to survive and resist their conditions, including slave revolts in New York State.

EBD6B0DECF4D4999BCACC67C5E8CAB21.description: Students will explain why and where slavery grew over time in the United States and students will examine the living conditions of slaves, including those in New York State.

1AB821E36C1F4FD28DE256FEF5A72885.description: Students will describe the conditions of the Middle Passage.

72727F129FE9482DA1840F7C4A83C21B.description: Over the course of the 17th and 18th centuries, slavery grew in the colonies. Enslaved Africans utilized a variety of strategies to both survive and resist their conditions.

AE213CBBF77D4474ABFB12C091906BB0.description: Student will examine Dutch contributions to American society, including acceptance of a diverse population, a degree of religious toleration and right to petition. Students will examine Dutch relations with Native Americans.

DF5260F5456D4396810769EBA458344B.description: Students will examine the changing status and role of African Americans under the Dutch and English colonial systems.

878D7E9F549947699B67F6D0233FB42B.description: Students will compare and contrast the early Dutch settlements with French settlements and with those in the subsequent British colony of New York in terms of political, economic, and social characteristics, including an examination of the patroon system.

CE2491BF07AE4A499B1568A5C62E6DC3.description: In New York, the Dutch established settlements along the Hudson River and the French established settlements in the Champlain Valley. Dutch contributions to American society were long-lasting.

4D3DFF2651C944CC982C0EBBFF1955DF.description: Students will examine the economic, social, and political characteristics of each colonial region.

4744DE40A49A4F02AAE6415AF3929202.description: Students will investigate the reasons for colonization and the role of geography in the development of each colonial region.

0DE401CE8DB14518A074CD785AE7D3B6.description: European nations established colonies in North America for economic, religious, and political reasons. Differences in climate, physical features, access to water, and sources of labor contributed to the development of different economies in the New England, Middle, and Southern Colonies.

852DC2AA11AC4109A069759EE3034378.description: Students will examine the major reasons why Native American societies declined in population and lost land to the Europeans.

D3613BE004E248A19EC2DCB919A8C9FA.description: Students will investigate other Native American societies found in their locality and their interactions with European groups.

F253F6342E6B4F68B1D86AF699E16269.description: Students will compare and contrast British interactions with southern New England Algonquians, Dutch and French interactions with the Algonquians and Iroquoians, and Spanish interactions with Muscogee.

3655DCE7617C43D1A6D46238F83C7C88.description: Different European groups had varied interactions and relationships with the Native American societies they encountered. Native American societies suffered from loss of life due to disease and conflict and loss of land due to encroachment of European settlers and differing conceptions of property and land ownership.
