B7B3AC31D2344781994423037B9DE706.description: Students will examine the voyage of Columbus, leading to the Columbian Exchange and the voyages of other explorers such as Champlain, Hudson, and Verrazano.

94C485955FFB42769218B388C50F4C04.description: Students will explain the significance of the technological developments and scientific understandings that improved European exploration such as the caravel, magnetic compass, astrolabe, and Mercator projection.

6248C079CD474CF5B404A492113EF18E.description: Social, economic, and scientific improvements helped European nations launch an Age of Exploration.

EAAA59B7CE6742E697F26C89094E85F8.description: Colonial Developments: European exploration of the New World resulted in various interactions with Native Americans and in colonization. The American colonies were established for a variety of reasons and developed differently based on economic, social, and geographic factors. Colonial America had a variety of social structures under which not all people were treated equally.

C47C5161444B43FA9D2A85253EF84890.description: Students will examine various groups of Native Americans located within what became New York State and the influence geographic factors had on their development.

57F79DA8C8EA499C8D0E7FCFDDE3E34B.description: Students will compare and contrast different Native American culture groups of North America, with a focus on the influence geographic factors had on their development.

51541675BD524054A58533345F60DA3D.description: Students will examine theories of human settlement of the Americas.

161BF68B61D544C5944464EE0606D336.description: Geography and climate influenced the migration and cultural development of Native Americans. Native Americans in North America settled into different regions and developed distinct cultures.

4F4F973B218142F5B480EDC8C391DF75.description: Native Americans: The physical environment and natural resources of North America influenced the development of the first human settlements and the culture of Native Americans. Native American societies varied across North America.

62DDE1C7F82D4D96A13AAC8679194DAD.description: History of the United States and New York State I

DC3D988033844524BF16FC7B3076DF8F.description: Develop the connections of an interdependent community by engaging in the political process as it relates to a local context.

E402C9014D744244B934EBBBCDBEA7F9.description: Identify how social and political responsibilities developed in American society.

0F2165907D8343169F54AAF46581C772.description: Identify how people in power have acted to extend the concept of freedom, the practice of social justice, and the protection of human rights in United States history.

C5904281BDB64436AD3107ED0E4C85FB.description: Identify situations in which social actions are required and determine an appropriate course of action.

411BB4A107BB4EB7A3745DAAE91FE793.description: Participate in negotiating and compromising in the resolution of differences and conflict; introduce and examine the role of conflict resolution.

8FC768D8EAE846B68472CDC5F1A9A795.description: Identify, describe, and compare the role of the individual in social and political participation in, and as an agent of, historical change at various times and in various locations in colonial North America and in the early history of the United States.

5A854A07CE384D24A7CEFB409E0376F1.description: Identify and explain different types of political systems and ideologies used at various times in colonial history and the early history of the United States and explain the role of individuals and key groups in those political and social systems.

FEE595AE518B46E08B73C650EA79E2D9.description: Participate in activities that focus on a classroom, school, community, state, or national issue or problem.

8BE9884E058840E5843F87E6A60FE9AE.description: Demonstrate respect for the rights of others in discussions and classroom debates; respectfully disagree with other viewpoints. Use techniques and strategies to be an active and engaged member of class discussions of fellow classmates’ views and statements, with teacher support.

560B29783EF3446C9252F0D96AAA8568.description: Explain how government policies affected the economies in colonial and early United States history

0CF3279FD8E742B289BED69AA467BE07.description: Examine data on the state of employment, unemployment, inflation, total production, income, and economic growth in the economy.

4A4F9589C0CA415CBF6AFB50FD752AFA.description: Examine the roles of institutions, such as joint stock companies, banks, and the government in the development of the United States economy before the Civil War.

5B3F31D5FA5C4661B45785757DA298ED.description: Describe the role that competition has in the determination of prices and wages; identify other factors that help to determine prices.

D2E8AC49694547AA9E1DABFF209C3344.description: Identify examples of buyers and sellers in product, labor, and financial markets.

A3B6739A24AC4B7E9EDCD7F4267475EC.description: Explain how economic decisions affect the well-being of individuals, businesses, and society; evaluate alternative approaches or solutions to economic issues in terms of benefits and costs for different groups of people.

CE9E0E39490B4760A9F0F6431BEC9BF0.description: Describe the spatial organization of place, considering the historical, social, political, and economic implication of that organization. Describe how boundaries and definition of location are historically constructed.

6D738658F099448EA9106F1AE14D9793.description: Characterize and analyze changing interconnections between places and regions.

A0C18EDE99234988A4CFDE52548BC1CC.description: Recognize and analyze how characteristics (cultural, economic, and physical-environmental) of regions affect the history of the United States.

BFB94CA6B7084F139C2B74B4A8E62725.description: Identify and analyze how environments affect human activities and how human activities affect physical environments in the United States.

C0C847D106CB4527A2739B3DFB88B93C.description: Distinguish human activities and human-made features from “environments” (natural events or physical features—land, air, and water—that are not directly made by humans) and describe the relationship between human activities and the environment.

A2A32128BDFF411E90A73707C7FB34F4.description: Use location terms and geographic representations, such as maps, photographs, satellite images, and models to describe where places in early United States history were in relation to each other, to describe connections among places, and to evaluate effectively the benefits of particular places for purposeful activities.

4BDF9C5A099A4E84A4F213876168A86E.description: Understand the roles that periodization and region play in developing the comparison of colonial settlements in North America. Identify general characteristics that can be employed to conduct comparative analyses of case studies in the early history of the United States.

EE98732B67CD48EDA0A87B49DCF04B20.description: Connect historical developments to specific circumstances of time and place and to broader regional, national, or global processes.

3A94952430734E15BF0CFB7D4AFE6B65.description: Identify how the relationship between geography, economics, and history helps to define a context for events in the study of the United States.

1E52139A5AB9421FBA1167CFA40FC912.description: Describe, compare, and evaluate multiple historical developments within the United States in various chronological and geographical contexts.

3356CB572C394C1994EDAB1A3D0ABCA0.description: Identify and categorize multiple perspectives on a given historical experience.

7D14D81A732344E9B20B38BD6041D850.description: Identify a region of colonial North America or the early United States by describing multiple characteristics common to places within it, and then identify other similar regions (inside or outside the continental United States) with similar characteristics.

7A3B351AF7814F338CEDFCAC9B8F867F.description: Identify models of historical periodization that historians use to categorize events.

B5399975B1EF4D7CB63C21CCD86D1D0F.description: Identify patterns of continuity and change as they relate to larger historical process and themes.

C26323B9B6F045DF83635037FE9BBD50.description: Recognize that changing the periodization affects the historical narrative.

14CDD7374B524444A71F8B3191959A7C.description: Recognize, analyze, and evaluate dynamics of historical continuity and change over periods of time.

2CB4719C898042FFBBC06C80A480F3D9.description: Distinguish between long-term and immediate causes and effects of an event from current events or history.

BF3A612F2F7F4BDCA782243AD3E979A7.description: Identify and analyze the relationship between multiple causes and multiple effects.

F059580E8E6E40518CF10F9704A32770.description: Identify causes and effects, using examples from current events, grade-level content, and historical events.

A64E0040AEA04B66915F4348BE957C03.description: Employ mathematical skills to measure time by years, decades, centuries, and millennia; to calculate time from the fixed points of the calendar system (B.C.E. and C.E.); and to interpret the data presented in time lines.

1DD1B1C98F254656B0BB9E78EAEA6C49.description: Identify how events are related chronologically to one another in time, and explain the ways in which earlier ideas and events may influence subsequent ideas and events.

5C5ECAFFC28D41EB8C8B3B523A01DFA0.description: Recognize an argument and identify supporting evidence related to a specific social studies topic. Examine arguments related to a specific social studies topic from multiple perspectives. Recognize that the perspective of the argument’s author shapes the selection of evidence used to support it.

EAED954E681B4635B89EC8A9A6C4AD2F.description: Make inferences and draw general conclusions from evidence.

8194F7B575524A68BED0E8EEBF736AA2.description: Describe and analyze arguments of others, with support.

716605BE09D74C6CB9DBFA31E3E9BD4E.description: Analyze evidence in terms of historical context, content, authorship, point of view, purpose, and format; identify bias; explain the role of bias and audience in presenting arguments or evidence.

49E09FBF8E9146D0B50FE5C9C654214C.description: Identify, select, and evaluate evidence about events from diverse sources (including written documents, works of art, photographs, charts and graphs, artifacts, oral traditions, and other primary and secondary sources).

88D3006411554F10AD18BE6C42CD6175.description: Define and frame questions about the United States that can be answered by gathering, interpreting, and using evidence.

standardSets.title: Grade 8: History of the United States and New York State II
standardSets.subject: Social Studies (2017-)

document.title: New York State K-8 Social Studies Framework

50F72E5C8B074054B4A79FE79EFDE828.description: Students will examine state and federal responses to gun violence, cyber-bullying, and electronic surveillance.

FB223972F8DB4B6081196436CA64ECA3.description: Constitutional issues involving the violation of civil liberties and the role of the federal government are a source of debate in American society.

34F051D277E8451C90D432A9A362EC7D.description: George H. W. Bush's cuts to social programs and taxes in an attempt to stimulate the economy.

671326B1184C4058BA57C1810294BD19.description: Economic recession during the 1970s and concerns about the growth and size of the federal government encouraged fiscal conservatives to push for changes in regulation and policy.

448967BC5D804F139E7247B6E5F550A9.description: Students will examine the connection between the Vietnam War, especially the draft, and the growth of a counterculture and peace movement.

61CB642406A64DC38821E9996FA316F8.description: Students will explain the difference between Medicare and Medicaid.

EABFF54CF8E041EA8E711E960210DA24.description: The Great Society programs of President Lyndon Johnson strengthened efforts aimed at reducing poverty and providing health care for the elderly, but the Vietnam War drained resources and divided society.

7AD9C740058249058BE606DBA82C3E7C.description: Students will examine judicial actions taken to protect individual rights, such as Miranda v. Arizona (1966) and Tinker v. Des Moines School District (1969).

A0138BA9C9C940AEB8D9351035D5B3BC.description: Students will examine struggles for equality and factors that enabled or limited success on behalf of women, farm workers, Native Americans, the disabled, and the LGBT community.

2A8A3C35EEC64A3CBE54D81D1BE66C78.description: The civil rights movement prompted renewed efforts for equality by women and other groups.

03223B40881D41FEB6EDCC1C346EAD51.description: Students will examine the extent to which the economic situation of African Americans improved as a result of the civil rights movement.

013A7C2674AE4CD681A3C239305DA73D.description: Students will explain the significance of key civil rights victories, including President Truman's desegregation of the military, Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka (1954), the Civil Rights Act of 1964, and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

7916AB1DD21445289284682E03AFBB07.description: Students will compare and contrast the strategies used by civil rights activists, such as Thurgood Marshall, Rosa Parks, Martin Luther King, Jr., and Malcolm X.

8DF62CE6A5E441598142D57D04BADCBE.description: The civil rights movement began in the postwar era in response to long-standing inequalities in American society, and eventually brought about equality under the law, but slower progress on economic improvements.

FB230924EE0E4CB19C7C4FDCB58581E6.description: Domestic Politics And Reform: The civil rights movement and the Great Society were attempts by people and the government to address major social, legal, economic, and environmental problems. Subsequent economic recession called for a new economic program.

E4FF7707180443BC9132091F3D874035.description: Students will explore the effects of pollution, industrialization, and population growth on the environment, including urban areas (Love Canal), plant and animal life (Adirondack Park) and energy sources (Three Mile Island).

81271A2F8CD64B58AB5FF4C3FAEF7AA4.description: Pollution, population growth, the consumption of natural resources, clearing of land for human sustenance, and large-scale industrialization have put added stress on the global environment.

DD3295CC3A004CEAA51A38510EC3BBBD.description: Students will examine the effects of immigration legislation and policy, including recent debates over immigration policy.

210E543274B14D819065489E293F119B.description: Students will examine migration and immigration trends in New York State and New York City such as the increase in Spanish-speaking, South Asian, East Asian, Middle Eastern, and African populations and the contributions of these groups.

849B067F1E9F4C78A1EC6B32FB64C428.description: The postwar United States experienced increasing immigration, debates over immigration policy, and an increase in cultural diversity.

5BE7265F0A6E48FD90A7915852731E03.description: Students will examine the population shift from the Midwest and northern industrial states to the Sun Belt, including its effect on political power.

77184B42D8034E0AB281E5BAE8E0F4C8.description: Students will examine the effects of suburbanization, including urban decay, suburban growth, and the diminished availability of farmland both nationally and within New York State.

FB76890BEF9F465BAEFEF6AA9B3885C0.description: Students will explore the short-term and long-term effects of the baby boom generation on the economy, including increases in the construction of homes and schools and increased demands on both Social Security and health care.

E4624E543A0E4F53A97EF418BFCA95D8.description: After World War II, the United States experienced various shifts in population and demographics that resulted in social, political, and economic consequences.

665B96D0CEC94C2FA5FBA00719E3A07C.description: Demographic Change: After World War II, the population of the United States rose sharply as a result of both natural increases and immigration. Population movements have resulted in changes to the American landscape and shifting political power. An aging population is affecting the economy and straining public resources.

6481C5D73A214242BA9664C51373ED8B.description: Students will examine the roles of multinational corporations and their influence on the world economy.

D480E32F841142F09E2D8C5B9C489B58.description: Students will examine the increased economic interdependence in terms of globalization and its impact on the United States and New York State economy, including the workforce.

957A234AF16B4B1CA200A778CF3C919F.description: Increased globalization has led to increased economic interdependence and competition.

B1607BD7C141492E9E385655F7AFF120.description: Students will examine the terrorist attack of September 11, 2001, its effects on national security and the United States responses to it, including the USA Patriot Act, the formation of the Department of Homeland Security, the War on Terror, and military attacks on suspected terrorist locations.

8435E6671D1B406193CCF18EAFAD0E46.description: Terrorist groups not representing any nation entered and reshaped global military and political alliances and conflicts. American foreign and domestic policies responded to terrorism in a variety of ways.

62A2A2653B9C4BCC8B218C5D026EDCD4.description: Students will examine the changing relationships between the United States and foreign countries such as: China beginning in 1950, Afghanistan beginning in the 1980s, Russia beginning in 1990, Middle East (Israel, Palestine, Iran, Kuwait, Iraq), Countries in the Western Hemisphere, focusing on NAFTA, Cuba and Mexico, and European Union countries

B983F12863FE429DAECA3A67DD7E12C4.description: Following the end of the Cold War, the United States sought to define a new role in global affairs, but the legacies of Cold War actions continue to affect United States foreign policy today.

60A3A1984B104924AF11355712C850DD.description: Students will examine the policy of containment and its application in the postwar period, including the Marshall Plan, the Korean War, the Cuban missile crisis, and the Vietnam War.

2066E96A32C246638A6EE85949F05308.description: The United States based its military and diplomatic policies from 1945 to 1990 on a policy of containment of communism.

C96073112D5545C98B6C5B752A089104.description: Students will examine the term nuclear superpower and the threat of nuclear weapons as a cause and as an effect of the arms race between the United States and the Soviet Union.

437836932BAE4B9A94F2D2CDCE4A3328.description: Students will locate on a map the nations that were aligned with the United States, those aligned with the Soviet Union, and the non-aligned nations.

0F77FB51E28C4114941501285FB233C4.description: The Cold War was an ongoing struggle between the two nuclear superpowers, the United States and the Soviet Union. The Cold War shaped the reconstruction of national boundaries and political alliances across the globe.

D6FB6B8D894C4806AADEF39ADD720B75.description: Foreign Policy: The period after World War II has been characterized by an ideological and political struggle, first between the United States and communism during the Cold War, then between the United States and forces of instability in the Middle East. Increased economic interdependence and competition, as well as environmental concerns, are challenges faced by the United States.

78BD19CDEA5F4BAC90C2613431F82342.description: Students will examine the structure and work of the United Nations.

6AB3E1AF2A404A9282BD2318C0C9AAB2.description: Students will investigate the Holocaust and explain the historical significance of the Nuremberg trials.

56764B897C4745BB97A3D7953DD21283.description: Students will examine the role of air power by the allies, including the use of the atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

B50EC7AD92EF47C98F86DEA6F90DF0B3.description: The nature and consequences of warfare during World War II transformed the United States and the global community. The damage from total warfare and human atrocities, including the Holocaust, led to a call for an international organization to prevent future wars and the protection of human rights.

8664D86BDCA142D4AFB054AE83D37DA2.description: Student will examine the role of New Yorkers in World War II, focusing on local institutions, such as the Fort Ontario Refugee Center or the Brooklyn Navy Yard.

223B6C8A4EE0425EBF61EE7502F7AEC7.description: Students will examine the internment of Japanese Americans in light of perceived national security concerns versus constitutional rights, including the decision in Korematsu v. United States (1944).

9C183B76949D4607BF1C8DAC57124DF4.description: Students will investigate the effects of the war on the American economy and day-to-day life.

658C900E49CF4631BF0545B43AF91EA7.description: Students will examine the role of the Tuskegee Airmen within the segregated military during World War II.

F5AEB7DBAF8646B19BD5ADA892FE6F00.description: Students will examine American involvement in World War II, including the American strategy in the Pacific and the invasion of Normandy on D-Day.

D4B9B51A192840CF8D5551590B759D25.description: From 1939 to 1941, the United States government tried to maintain neutrality while providing aid to Britain but was drawn into the war by the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor. The United States fought a war on multiple fronts. At home, the economy was converted to war production, and essential resources were rationed to ensure adequate supplies for military use.

A0F4F1B22FB2427CB4923A5E6A93D70B.description: Students will examine how the worldwide economic depression and militant nationalism resulted in the rise of totalitarian rule.

63CA32CD4969493B880FFC27E4EB3915.description: Worldwide economic depression, militant nationalism, the rise of totalitarian rule, and the unsuccessful efforts of the League of Nations to preserve peace contributed to the outbreak of war in Europe and Asia.

CADBF085173B496DB51FD970579FBAB8.description: World War II: The aggression of the Axis powers threatened United States security and led to its entry into World War II. The nature and consequences of warfare during World War II transformed the United States and the global community. The damage from total warfare and atrocities such as the Holocaust led to a call for international efforts to protect human rights and prevent future wars.

CCCC7B233D774E648B48FFFD40567666.description: Students will identify key programs adopted under the New Deal, including the creation of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and the Securities and Exchange Commission, and the adoption of the Social Security Act.

EF1053060DC44A1CB3182392145BC0CB.description: President Roosevelt issued the New Deal in an attempt to revive the economy and help Americans deal with the hardships of the Great Depression. These New Deal reforms had a long-lasting effect on the role of government in American society and its economic life, but did not resolve all of the hardships Americans faced.

656F20A3ED5948A7910E6EDAF296BB56.description: Students will explore the man-made and environmental conditions that led to the Dust Bowl, the economic as well as cultural consequences of the Dust Bowl, and federal government efforts to address the problem.

56E9698E41014693AD0FC46F39AB824A.description: Students will examine the effects of the Great Depression on American families in terms of the loss of jobs, wealth, and homes, noting varying effects based on class, race, and gender. Students will explore the conditions in New York City and other communities within New York State during the Great Depression.

4CE9790BA1C847499F02A13160A65490.description: The Great Depression and the Dust Bowl affected American businesses and families.

01CC775BC82C42F38B893CFE2BB07CD8.description: Students will examine how the economic practices of the 1920s contributed to the coming of the Great Depression.

FEA6F1BCD60C48AB94538A25709450EF.description: Risky investing, protectionism, and overproduction led to the collapse of the stock market, a wave of bank failures, and a long and severe downturn in the economy called the Great Depression.

42C8044FC00240AAB92C3D4C055098CF.description: Great Depression: Economic and environmental disasters in the 1930s created hardships for many Americans. Amidst much debate about the appropriate role of government, President Franklin D. Roosevelt helped to create intensive government interventions in the United States economy and society.

5C21D2682A1C454DBA426C6FC255CC1C.description: Students will explore the changes in American culture after World War I, including an examination of the Harlem Renaissance and other changes in New York City.

B488F44EC57148299A7CAC7F49742F62.description: Students will examine examples of World War I and postwar race relations, such as the East St. Louis riots, the Silent March, and the Tulsa riots.

99F508927E154F3C8210C9CA8BA1C181.description: Students will examine the reasons for and effects of prohibition on American society.

ABF139C45E6B420A973CFDC72BE2F81A.description: Students will investigate the efforts of women suffragists and explain the historical significance of the 19th amendment.

6CC4FD4CC3C9422D9F665A1D54B342F0.description: After World War I, the United States entered a period of economic prosperity and cultural change. This period is known as the Roaring Twenties. During this time, new opportunities for women were gained, and African Americans engaged in various efforts to distinguish themselves and celebrate their culture.

447AA35788B145F48DCAAFD3E3637C60.description: Students will examine Wilson's Fourteen Points and investigate reasons why the United States Senate refused to support the Treaty of Versailles, focusing on opposition to the League of Nations.

701D8A5FB2EF443CAA290C1DABC0D01B.description: Following extensive political debate, the United States refused to ratify the Treaty of Versailles. The United States then sought to return to prewar policies by focusing on domestic rather than international matters.

AD57BB15891F4A5A80D1D0644A59AAAF.description: Students will examine the effects of the changes in military technologies used during World War I, including trench warfare, chemical weapons, machine guns, and aircraft.

C0267CD78E7A409D8F31654E202E24D0.description: New military technologies changed military strategy in World War I and resulted in an unprecedented number of casualties.

A0FBF00DE44B42909A29EAE098B56962.description: Students will examine the restrictions placed on citizens after United States entry into the war, including the Espionage Act (1917) and the Sedition Act (1918).

D655ABFB764A4CCE9310E6208A0FAC77.description: Students will examine examples of war propaganda and its effects on support for United States involvement in the war.

DB630204A9DC47B7A01985C573BBCBA1.description: Students will examine an overview of the causes of World War I, focusing on the factors leading to United States entry into the war.

D4FCCA12480B48379AF9FEF8D3EE263E.description: International, economic, and military developments swayed opinion in favor of the United States siding with the Allies and entering World War I. Domestic responses to World War I limited civil liberties within the United States.

B9099C3EBA8646D6AC546C071C621C2B.description: European militarism, the alliance system, imperialism, and nationalism were all factors that contributed to the start of World War I.

5C1962A6239C4851B3630610277E54B1.description: World War I And The Roaring Twenties: Various diplomatic, economic, and ideological factors contributed to the United States decision to enter World War I. Involvement in the war significantly altered the lives of Americans. Postwar America was characterized by economic prosperity, technological innovations, and changes in the workplace.

8BEF02694C244201844929BA072A9F64.description: Students will evaluate the United States actions taken under the Roosevelt Corollary and their effects on relationships between the United States and Latin American nations, including the building of the Panama Canal.

C3971A68469142D5B11E9FACFD20C8F0.description: The Roosevelt Corollary expanded the Monroe Doctrine and increased United States involvement in the affairs of Latin America. This led to resentment of the United States among many in Latin America.

DB54A88351AA40D99A6637E9A9124365.description: Students will examine the purpose and effects of the Open Door Policy.

107FA4B25B1A4A78A25AD0BE466728FF.description: Students will assess the events surrounding the annexation of Hawaii.

28FBCBA4A61D432CB25D788048F7CD7F.description: Interest in Pacific trade contributed to an increase in United States foreign interactions.

F098CDF4D3DC4F7586155204C871FBE7.description: Students will explain how the events and outcomes of the Spanish-American War contributed to the shift to imperialism in United States foreign policy.

5CE98259FA7D4F488213657DE6BFD2C2.description: Students will examine examples of yellow journalism that contributed to United States entry into the Spanish-American War, including the portrayal of the sinking of the USS Maine.

35AFF6854C1B487197DD3FC08E1A4490.description: The Spanish-American War contributed to the rise of the United States as an imperial power.

172CE383344F4B2FAC5DFAEDA8756E66.description: Students will examine United States and New York State policies toward Native Americans, such as the displacement of Native Americans from traditional lands, creation of reservations, efforts to assimilate Native Americans through the creation of boarding schools, the Dawes Act, and the Indian Reorganization Act and the Native Americans' various responses to these policies.

4334C3B8D07047AC979AB41DB30F1136.description: Students will examine examples of Native American resistance to the western encroachment, including the Sioux Wars and the flight and surrender of Chief Joseph and the Nez Perce.

08B5D8F53D864443B8736098025CC489.description: Students will examine the effects of the transcontinental railroad on the movement toward westward expansion.

2FBD5C0DB8014C6B9FE105FF797511C9.description: Continued westward expansion contributed to increased conflicts with Native Americans.

C7799C4DED5D4465A6CCE4F10220739E.description: Expansion And Imperialism: Beginning in the second half of the 19th century, economic, political, and cultural factors contributed to a push for westward expansion and more aggressive United States foreign policy.

9C2AF989ED904F1DB41934939ADFEEB7.description: Students will examine state and federal government responses to reform efforts, including the passage of the 17th amendment, child labor and minimum wage laws, antitrust legislation, and food and drug regulations.

8531506A0C9F4E0DA6C37E2769044C2D.description: Students will investigate the Triangle Shirtwaist Fire and the legislative response.

D87771BCCD964EA99389105CA6C36597.description: Students will explore leaders and activities of the temperance and woman's suffrage movements.

115591705AD24E5EBE6F2EAD8DD884A3.description: Students will investigate reformers and muckrakers such as Jane Addams, Florence Kelley, W. E. B. du Bois, Marcus Garvey, Ida Tarbell, Eugene V. Debs, Jacob Riis, Booker T. Washington, and Upton Sinclair. Student investigations should include the key issues in the individual's work and the actions that individual took or recommended to address those issues.

B3D9E74CCE864DAA8D46CFCBABB17617.description: Students will examine the Populist Party as a reform effort by farmers in response to industrialization.

BAF350610E8544E7BC1AFFE1BFB8D564.description: Progressive reformers sought to address political and social issues at the local, state, and federal levels of government between 1890 and 1920. These efforts brought renewed attention to women's rights and the suffrage movement and spurred the creation of government reform policies.

ED4910310EB044C3AECDAED7BB9F31D5.description: Students will examine key labor events including the Haymarket affair, the Pullman Strike and the International Ladies Garment Workers' Union strike.

533EC0957B5B45CE87F7E225BCBD66F6.description: Students will examine the goals and tactics of specific labor unions including the Knights of Labor, the American Federation of Labor, and the Industrial Workers of the World.

AB9EE0485FEE47B1897082B5A7369423.description: In response to shifts in working conditions, laborers organized and employed a variety of strategies in an attempt to improve their conditions.

ADB188FD6E044375B46E0E086E4DC556.description: Students will explore the development of political machines, including Boss Tweed and Tammany Hall.

74E6BAA49FF9478B994F3A8699FB2C57.description: Students will explore the growth and effects of child labor and sweatshops.

DA48FE8EC8AA4E9FAB1FE89BE7E74318.description: Students will examine nativism and anti-immigration policies, including the Chinese Exclusion Act, the Gentlemen's Agreement, and immigration legislation of the 1920s.

41C5560F16754B47A87159F626268B92.description: Increased urbanization and industrialization contributed to increasing conflicts over immigration, influenced changes in labor conditions, and led to political corruption.

A5E1852D9FCF458789DDD005B6635193.description: Students will examine the living conditions in urban areas with a focus on increasing population density and the effects that this growth had on the social, cultural, and economic lives of people.

AF348A0C2CFA4F57B05C4FCC1EBB8C59.description: Students will examine the population growth of New York City and other New York cities and the technologies and industries which encouraged this growth.

7A97767AECA34986AA2A0BDC4FACA2E7.description: Population density, diversity, technologies, and industry in urban areas shaped the social, cultural, and economic lives of people.

7867C44A69854B1A858FB042DC8679CD.description: Students will compare and contrast immigrant experiences in locations such as ethnic neighborhoods in cities, rural settlements in the Midwest, Chinese communities in the Far West, and Mexican communities in the Southwest.

0FC2EFAB5ABC4924987E41EBB39AF213.description: Students will identify groups of people who moved into urban areas, and examine where they came from and the reasons for their migration into the cities. Students will explore the immigrant experience at Ellis Island.

9B3CD9959C2149A28602F6C311BBFC81.description: Technological developments changed the modes of production, and access to natural resources facilitated increased industrialization. The demand for labor in urban industrial areas resulted in increased migration from rural areas and a rapid increase in immigration to the United States. New York City became the nation's largest city, and other cities in New York State also experienced growth at this time.

C77DD415B53D4B59BDA927926FF1C729.description: A Changing Society: Industrialization and immigration contributed to the urbanization of America. Problems resulting from these changes sparked the Progressive movement and increased calls for reform.

5D39BF5DB5A843A8AC9F87CBAB1D7EFC.description: Students will examine the effects of the Plessy v. Ferguson ruling.

6F7BCDB3DC234E8593D93652CA14A5C1.description: Students will examine the ways in which the federal government failed to follow up on its promises to freed African Americans.

D57E65C6B0D746378C4BFE89EE810025.description: Students will explore the responses of some Southerners to the increased rights of African Americans, noting the development of organizations such as the Ku Klux Klan and White Leagues.

5E75C044437C432EAA93EC84B27DE028.description: Students will explore methods used by Southern state governments to affect the lives of African Americans, including the passage of Black Codes, poll taxes, and Jim Crow laws.

86A9CCD2752B421BB4389D7E36BBDD05.description: Federal initiatives begun during Reconstruction were challenged on many levels, leading to negative impacts on the lives of African Americans.

94EB7BC8871A4D6DAAD2B02F98473154.description: Students will examine the rise of African Americans in government.

A40271C5ACE840AF91DC40E6D19C2B8C.description: Students will examine the reasons for the migration of African Americans to the North.

987C97D7DAB341F4933D13FE0DF75F33.description: Students will examine the effects of the sharecropping system on African Americans.

92C405BC645B4F719D0D18499D3C66F2.description: Students will examine the Freedmen's Bureau's purpose, successes, and the extent of its success.

83890B36A4F44A16A421900A2BAA40C5.description: Students will examine the Reconstruction amendments (13th, 14th, and 15th) in terms of the rights and protections provided to African Americans.

5381EE25CD0743058AFEAF1381AE71C4.description: Freed African Americans created new lives for themselves in the absence of slavery. Constitutional amendments and federal legislation sought to expand the rights and protect the citizenship of African Americans.

D5A69EC874054A10B4C199DB1A0AC46D.description: Students will compare and contrast the differences between Reconstruction under Lincoln's plan, Johnson's plan, and congressional (Radical) Reconstruction.

B8D9EDF776734CDC975EE7CF365D2220.description: Different approaches toward and policies for Reconstruction highlight the challenges faced in reunifying the nation.

C5BBA735E4B141768E4310AE635B0D75.description: Reconstruction: Regional tensions following the Civil War complicated efforts to heal the nation and to redefine the status of African Americans.

DD847B12CA4B464B838315204C818982.description: History of the United States and New York State II

AD2D4A9E52C9493C97ACA67A3D6C78A4.description: Develop the connections of an interdependent global community by engaging in the political process as it relates to a global context

F64837DD7E5A47DDA883F6AB4E5EE9EE.description: Fulfill social and political responsibilities associated with citizenship in a democratic society.

E1D539A04D5A4309B187F8E10FE10C57.description: Work to influence those in positions of power to strive for extensions of freedom, social justice, and human rights.

907FE054EC6C43609654EECA6FBE4F87.description: Identify situations in which social actions are required and determine an appropriate course of action.

20F198DB05AD42B7B9F28C33C810CD33.description: Participate in persuading, negotiating, and compromising in the resolution of conflicts and differences; introduce and examine the elements of debate.

748212FD5C6C4F1FB979D713B95496A1.description: Identify, describe, and contrast the role of the individual in opportunities for social and political participation as an agent of historical change in different societies and communities, as well as at different times, in the United States.

C4A4B8922BBF43F185CA1DCA9CF06534.description: Identify and explain different types of political systems and ideologies used at various times in United States history and explain the roles of individuals and key groups in those political and social systems.

2EEF0B0F30D84E88BD283BC85C86DB59.description: Participate in activities that focus on a classroom, school, community, state, or national issue or problem.

76013D44643041888F28BA800F526588.description: Demonstrate respect for the rights of others in discussions and classroom debates; respectfully disagree with other viewpoints. Use techniques and strategies to be an active and engaged member of class discussions of fellow classmates’ views and statements.

5D5FDAF1A85A4079B2EAB5D849F62B1B.description: Explain how government policies affect the economy.

EDDE474B608E4BADA6126223263AF791.description: Use appropriate data to evaluate the state of employment, unemployment, inflation, total production, income, and economic growth in the economy.

D293B4D9B6294A9589B4B43E3CF11580.description: Examine the roles of institutions such as corporations, non-profit organizations, and labor unions in a market economy in the United States.

947741F158B846BE835A64AD43291A91.description: Describe the role of competition in the determination of prices and wages in a market economy.

4D3F7C3DF29F45E79AE76F63EEB48BFF.description: Explain the roles of buyers and sellers in product, labor, and financial markets.

A219BEDB40294316AD0F68FFCCBF3C9F.description: Explain how economic decisions affect the well-being of individuals, businesses, and society; evaluate alternative approaches or solutions to economic issues in terms of benefits and costs for different groups of people.

B6735C5C9EE4446E8F0B30E82D18F924.description: Describe the spatial organization of place, considering the historical, social, political, and economic implication of that organization. Identify and describe examples of how boundaries and definition of location are historically constructed.

936970CA9D714771A1C1AF1C763A91B2.description: Characterize and analyze changing interconnections between places and regions.

A465D7EE3C3240F59EDEBEF0108F4160.description: Recognize and analyze how characteristics (cultural, economic, and physical-environmental) of regions affect the history of the United States.

B911B51B368F4EE8A689D1288865629F.description: Identify and analyze how environments affect human activities and how human activities affect physical environments in the United States.

8760D47DDDDC4036BBC3BA6874B95BCF.description: Distinguish human activities and human-made features from “environments” (natural events or physical features—land, air, and water—that are not directly made by humans) and describe the relationship between human activities and the environment.

B3A16779355A484187A58C6BBFF52A3E.description: Use location terms and geographic representations, such as maps, photographs, satellite images, and models to describe where places are in relation to each other and connections between places; evaluate the benefits of particular places for purposeful activities.

54D14B742BB64021B22F51A66FD5996F.description: Analyze case studies in United States history in a comparative framework, attending to the role of chronology and sequence, as well as categories of comparison or socio-political components.

15840E3F71084B6B9BDCDCCA26A8FB97.description: Connect historical developments to specific circumstances of time and place and to broader regional, national, or global processes.

555F9F17D46C488DBC301139C78A2FA4.description: Describe the relationship between geography, economics, and history as a context for events and movements in the United States.

995F9D26ED7249F393D271AF8D3DBED1.description: Describe, compare, and evaluate multiple historical developments (within societies; across and between societies; in various chronological and geographical contexts).

3B84B5DB6EC64E57A9EFF44E5DBEB540.description: Identify and compare multiple perspectives on a given historical experience.

4108B6D3A3BC4B8DA4F0DFA7ACC091FA.description: Identify a region of the United States by describing multiple characteristics common to places within it, and then identify other similar regions inside the United States.

EA29C88075D94B1D9FF8F8C9FE7F9617.description: Identify and describe models of historical periodization that historians use to categorize events

522CEF9EF33D415C990FCACCEC2CDF32.description: Relate patterns of continuity and change to larger historical processes and themes.

33EEEBC2D4AC41D58020875116BD70C1.description: Recognize that changing the periodization affects the historical narrative.

291CC7538CB1413E93DCC696D1BD7086.description: Recognize, analyze, and evaluate dynamics of historical continuity and change over periods of time.

53F34633B9574CF6A48E721C17E0E733.description: Distinguish between long-term and immediate causes and effects of an event from current events or history.

8CD2B985F26E4D8AA5AF17E2150F1A29.description: Identify, analyze, and evaluate the relationship between multiple causes and effects.

947D5100095B478AA6C5AF7E629FBC35.description: Identify causes and effects, using examples from current events, grade-level content, and historical events.

93B6E5B7692F4D719CD8B4C2A8082103.description: Employ mathematical skills to measure time by years, decades, centuries, and millennia; to calculate time from the fixed points of the calendar system (B.C. or B.C.E. and A.D. or C.E.); and to interpret the data presented in time lines.

BE8C2827646B48A4A23B6E9F2C6DAC08.description: Articulate how events are related chronologically to one another in time, and explain the ways in which earlier ideas and events may influence subsequent ideas and events.

0CF4A8F7A527418BA87D05B9CA3038AC.description: Recognize an argument and identify evidence that supports the argument; examine arguments related to a specific social studies topic from multiple perspectives; deconstruct arguments, recognizing the perspective of the argument and identifying evidence used to support that perspective.

7AE598CC461A40F983F89D99D753D71C.description: Make inferences and draw conclusions from evidence.

F253802653B84BE2A2D72381677B27C4.description: Describe and analyze arguments of others, considering historical context.

0BFD2F657CF94B478131A4B233139542.description: Analyze evidence in terms of historical and/or social context, content, authorship, point of view, purpose, and format; identify bias; explain the role of bias, context and audience in presenting arguments or evidence.

C0D0276FEC83496E8D7005005F6C80B8.description: Identify, describe, and evaluate evidence about events from diverse sources (including written documents, works of art, photographs, charts and graphs, artifacts, oral traditions, and other primary and secondary sources).

05F76A5CC985478D9F57E9AB723A074C.description: Define and frame questions about the United States and answer them by gathering, interpreting, and using evidence.

56C334FA76464C7C9412F3BA071AA933.description:

appropriate, positive,
and responsible online
behavior and identify
strategies to combat
negative online
behavior.

5E760AB69714457D99241592B5343469.description:

between the persistence
of data on the Internet,
personal online identity,
and personal privacy.

A986318F0606433FA2B5955EF9D0242B.description:
Transfer knowledge of
technology in order to
explore new
technologies.

ADCD4660A97941A5A4E4607A003F78D6.description:

743B5681925240AB8162CE7015A8D920.description:

for effectiveness and

124DAC152AB147898721DEB7A6B40EEC.description:

89FF65644D664346A35BC9454EA9DCA0.description:

security safeguards.

10A98D93F3B5416EA0A89C520DAB200F.description:

digital, and behavioral
safeguards that can be
employed in different
situations.

AC46362C32A9406FA0CF1AB428F17CA6.description:
Determine the types of
personal information

needs to be protected

4A9FAE15BC4243E1AD33692EEB9B4954.description:

9457198001B74ECDA60B089CE20AB5D7.description:

6F573F24730047FB85F83738227184F1.description:

with computing devices
and their components
using a systematic
troubleshooting method or

F799F0153F8B4C93AE2C8F4D5D746D3B.description:
Design a project that
combines hardware and
software components.

3CA88C1B6FE2490F876BEFEE9108B34B.description:
Design a user interface
for a computing
technology that
considers usability,
accessibility, and

6CA1C41F0D304A18B1D7D54D7C83B39E.description:
Document the iterative

that incorporates user

8337051A146A44098054E11C99DE7E39.description:
Read and interpret code to
predict the outcome of
various programs that
involve conditionals and
repetition for the purposes

EA288B30A9FE4200A22B3C9C762CA593.description:

variable to maintain the

piece of information.

86D16AB47F8F495298C6F32AA2D33534.description:

A85B956372BB4696ACEF40C03953C5BC.description:

D4DCA4BD643C403BB18946617E16E5B3.description:

D4C05256755A42B0A057E41276CECAD2.description:

D3F0D754F2194AA29A619A6C419F69BF.description:
Explore a range of
computer sciencerelated career paths.

74C2759D4BAB4F55AF58A1F52E8142EF.description:
Assess the accessibility

or software application
in terms of user needs.

580AB02B74174C0CA9B4CE2FF4D5E7D6.description:
Analyze potential sources

biases on individuals.

E55B560E6216434D9059F846E6BD15B2.description:

6A7EAC051C3548F89DE4D1A4170447E2.description:

6FD734F05E744781B9E2B295CEC570A6.description:

document.title: The New York State Physical Education Learning Standards (2020)

04BD7BF3B1F24E08AD480B2AEF879CE0.description:
Explains how to get help in emergency situations (e.g., communicates their guardian’s
name).

832BBC53ADE744B8BC837AFFAB447B15.description:
Participates in fire evacuation drills, understands what the alarm bell is and the need
to go to a safe location, etc.

F577CC7613D74E36AEA36445D8B176A8.description:
Understands and communicates that some practices could be unsafe (e.g., playing
with matches, playing near a busy street, not wearing a bike helmet, etc.).

6D4442A3F27D414B82278099D01F160E.description:
Verbalizes and demonstrates safety rules (e.g., bus safety, holding an adult’s hand
when walking on sidewalks or near a street).

3C0936309CBD44A9825865FB41E08624.description: Demonstrates awareness and understanding of safety rules.

5602AB704C454EA88A56146A3FED6D4D.description:
Relates healthy behaviors to good personal health (e.g., eating a balanced diet,
exercising, etc.).

8A0A4C2CBE914D51BB6F45E08FA83FE5.description: Talks about food choices in relationship to personal allergies and overall health.

685C9162EC5B49328D518FA64BD28B08.description: Demonstrates ways to self-soothe during times of stress.

FBDBF0D4081047B193108FFE3154EED5.description: Recognizes the importance of good nutrition, water, rest, and sleep to be healthy.

827FAB9BFD88447EBA78316B2BAE400E.description: Demonstrates awareness and understanding of healthy habits.

474205BF03F44F19B37B16570C0CD3A6.description:
Recognizes and communicates the need to use the restroom or when experiencing
symptoms of hunger or illness.

E4351324B0DB4116AE0232A5109E6C8A.description: Exhibits self-help when dressing, cleaning up, participating in meals, etc.

AE24849DFB264D068E5422A3505374DF.description: Demonstrates growing independence in using personal hygiene skills.

B587C9B7BC1848AE9D0D7BD886CD8BC3.description: Demonstrates personal care and hygiene skills.

A0DF4782DF684EC585CF3403DB120A61.description: Participates in activities to promote balance and flexibility.

9C7F7E6ADCD54B23984950940D3EF609.description: Participates in activities designed to strengthen major muscle groups.

AFAC7431598E40EE9F71FC01E3136340.description:
Engages in rigorous large motor activities (e.g., walking, marching, hopping, running,
jumping, dancing) in increasingly longer periods of time as skill and endurance
develops.

document.title: New York State Next Generation English Language Arts Learning Standards

89DBB7E5258F4477B27362F3B0F0A955.description:
Acquire and accurately use general academic and content-specific words and phrases,
sufficient for reading, writing, speaking, and listening; demonstrate independence in applying
vocabulary knowledge when considering a word or phrase important to comprehension or
expression.

B094F2F1DA6841E8917B62D71EF22E61.description: Analyze nuances in the meaning of words with similar denotations.

22D15F4217CF4D99BAF1A66016FF6AE8.description:
Interpret figures of speech, including euphemism and oxymoron, in context
and analyze their role in the text.

94E104B6F41A44668166B763D20D14AC.description:
Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in
word meanings.

00E7BDB578A24F16BEF44E93BB1635D9.description:
Verify the preliminary determination of the meaning of a word or phrase (e.g.,
by checking the inferred meaning in context or in a dictionary).

09B56D151EF44324BD35664621D275CB.description:
Consult general and specialized reference materials (e.g., dictionaries,
glossaries, thesauruses) to find the pronunciation of a word or determine or clarify its
precise meaning, its part of speech, or its etymology.

E0364DEBCB5D4C86BC2B35D5281DAA38.description:
Identify and correctly use patterns of word changes that indicate different
meanings or parts of speech (e.g., analyze, analysis, analytical; advocate, advocacy).

47AB8E98A9FA48E3BDC0746E024DD5E5.description:
Use context (e.g., the overall meaning of a sentence, paragraph, or text; a
word’s position or function in a sentence) as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.

C8B7014EB9B043C0B24C6D57EE65B9E0.description:
Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and
phrases, choosing flexibly from a range of strategies.

903963CFD9EE44B697422CDDC02094DF.description:
Write and edit work so that it conforms to the guidelines in a professionally
recognized style manual appropriate for the discipline and writing type.

00660879B3BC4A3D816AFADB20E0938F.description:
Apply knowledge of language to understand how language functions in different
contexts, to make effective choices for meaning or style, and to comprehend more fully when
reading or listening.

5322DF8BBC5D40F9A44A0593333D13DB.description:
Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and tasks, demonstrating command of formal
English when indicated or appropriate.

3BE6076F99AE4A0F81EDFF0CF4469622.description:
Make strategic use of digital media and/or visual displays in presentations to enhance
understanding of findings, reasoning, and evidence, and to add elements of interest to engage
the audience.

08010C0ACDAF4198B41188AFD69DD7A6.description:
Evaluate a speaker’s point of view, reasoning, and use of evidence and rhetoric;
identify any fallacious reasoning or exaggerated or distorted evidence.

D15F7D00F124449E80D019F3FDC2D761.description:
Integrate multiple sources of information presented in diverse formats (e.g., including
visual, quantitative, and oral), evaluating the credibility, accuracy, and relevance of each source.

339DACDB3FBD4A08932CC261E49C38BD.description:
Respond thoughtfully to diverse perspectives, summarize points of
agreement and disagreement, and, when warranted, qualify or justify personal views
and understanding and make new connections in light of the evidence and reasoning
presented.

88C86B7F3D694765BCD0260D69D86956.description:
Pose and respond to questions that relate the discussion to broader themes
or ideas; actively incorporate others into the discussion; and clarify, verify, or challenge
ideas and conclusions.

B3DAE9BD9C154335BC82C6F2793E9B1C.description:
Work with peers to set norms for collegial discussions and decision-making,
establish clear goals, deadlines, and individual roles as needed.

E2AD3D788CDE46BA811B9D45D6A655B7.description:
Come to discussions prepared, having read and researched material under
study; draw on that preparation by referring to evidence to stimulate a thoughtful, wellreasoned exchange of ideas.

CD39C3C0A4A045AEA89CB588E837A366.description:
Initiate and participate effectively in a range of collaborative discussions with diverse
partners on complex topics, texts, and issues; express ideas clearly and persuasively, and build
on those of others.

820AEF2BF3E74C72BD4A12492B9E7075.description:
Gather relevant information from multiple sources, using advanced searches
effectively; assess the usefulness of each source in answering the research question; integrate
information into the text selectively to maintain the flow of ideas; avoid plagiarism and follow a
standard format for citation.

44D98B40E52A4930BEFF7BC4C834C4F3.description:

problem; narrow or broaden the inquiry when appropriate. Synthesize multiple sources,
demonstrating understanding of the subject under investigation.

43F8B72963CE4BCAA8B777728D7DBA3F.description: Research to Build and Present Knowledge

5F1CBA4D94444B9782C05CEACE9ADBF1.description:

677B4D8DEAD749438C71E74125AF7B86.description:

A3E9A41898BF482DA10FD7CF28D0B753.description:

5F2B2F96DC244D848E02FC0F1E7B6146.description: Establish and maintain a style appropriate to the writing task.

appropriate complexity of a topic.

DD6E5864D92645AEA72F5A39866B007F.description:
Introduce and organize complex ideas, concepts, and information to make
important connections and distinctions.

01559731299A4420A659B48ED3E4596D.description:

analysis of content.

4B009B550D58424CAD92617547542080.description: Maintain a style and tone appropriate to the writing task.

B2AB127E1AD94D688FE5BFD6705AC1AF.description:
Provide a concluding statement or section that explains the significance of the
argument presented.

C1A7E15898C4406C8ADE9ECB77ED405A.description:
Use appropriate and varied transitions to make critical connections and
distinctions, create cohesion, and clarify the relationships among complex ideas and
concepts.

2509BC0FE2A44332984A2521C894DB9C.description:
Use precise language and content-specific vocabulary to express the
appropriate complexity of the topic.

61E9D09ABCAB40708CCB7E16FBC3AD2E.description:
Develop claim(s) and counterclaims in a balanced manner, supplying evidence
for each while pointing out the strengths and limitations of both, anticipating the
audience’s knowledge level and concerns.

276435372C3747A7A8953811C43C543E.description:

evidence.

BA1CF86F172F4986B4BB56C8D335CF27.description:

2CB794E334574129B85A34EE2E2C525B.description:

CBF74B09500342EB975061DBD9E8114D.description:

sufficient. (RI&RL)

5FCC0A9E033944D3AA924CE218BBD2C7.description:

8D5F464B513248A0BC613EC3B5B8C038.description:

(RI&RL)

B49676A1674B40C6A517441476F4A3B8.description:

4A3665080CAD4147B08BF537591AE8E4.description:

2AF7BCEA4BAF44C498FB826448CE8760.description:

problem (issue)

events are related chronologically.

recommended by a historical figure, a group, or a government.

stakeholder or a stakeholder’s issue.

action/belief)

6C9B92837D7B4F33B3A51AFBCA18B02D.description: Use mathematical and/or computational representations to support explanations of biotic and abiotic factors that affect carrying capacity of ecosystems at different scales.

171003F4815A4A7289FA7E5FACF2C946.description: Science and engineering are influenced by society and society is influenced by science and engineering. (HS-LS3-2), (HS-LS3-3),(HS-LS1-8)

483762FC0CBB497A8BE6177EB0149D66.description: Technological advances have influenced the progress of science and science has influenced advances in technology. (HS-LS3-2),(HS-LS3- 3),(New NYSED PE)

E66B963D204B4A6DBCFA740111F7D3C9.description: Models (e.g., physical, mathematical, computer models) can be used to simulate systems and interactions— including energy, matter, and information flows—within and between systems at different scales. (HS-LS1- 4),(HS-LS1-8)

F2CCC6A812604BDB8B118EB2D1CDE8D7.description: Algebraic thinking is used to examine scientific data and predict the effect of a change in one variable on another (e.g., linear growth vs. exponential growth). (HS-LS3-3)

169ADAED28FF43A285DBA47E3C7FA835.description: Empirical evidence is required to differentiate between cause and correlation and make claims about specific causes and effects. (HS-LS3- 1),(HS-LS3-2)

644E0223AD2F479A84BF6429004602E9.description: Environmental factors also affect expression of traits, and hence affect the probability of occurrences of traits in a population. Thus the variation and distribution of traits observed depends on both genetic and environmental factors. (HS-LS3-2),(HS-LS3-3)

5E2BBAF1FE5F43809877C5BC21A1BFF1.description: (NYSED) Advances in biotechnology have allowed organisms to be modified genetically. (HS-LS3-2)

58CA98D3FE46448FB71C65D88DFC1A66.description: (NYSED) Environmental factors can cause mutations in genes. Only mutations in sex cells can be inherited. (HS-LS3-2)

0347D20573E94C22AC272859A9E019A5.description: In sexual reproduction, chromosomes can sometimes swap sections during the process of meiosis (cell division), thereby creating new genetic combinations and thus more genetic variation. Although DNA replication is tightly regulated and remarkably accurate, errors do occur and result in mutations, which are also a source of genetic variation. (HS-LS3-2)

7084C33BFE17492C9EEEC9DF55534816.description: Each chromosome consists of a single very long DNA molecule, and each gene on the chromosome is a particular segment of that DNA. The instructions for forming species’ characteristics are carried in DNA. All cells in an organism have the same genetic content, but the genes used (expressed) by the cell may be regulated in different ways. Not all DNA codes for a protein; some segments of DNA are involved in regulatory or structural functions, and some have no as-yet known function. (HS-LS3-1)

B555888345AF4CFCB9F7292028782596.description: (NYSED) The continuity of life is sustained through reproduction and development. Human development, birth, and aging should be viewed as a predictable pattern of events influenced by factors such as gene expression, hormones, and the environment. (HS-LS1- 8)

3CC4F923BB8448399D7D35368933B533.description: In multicellular organisms individual cells grow and then divide via a process called mitosis, thereby allowing the organism to grow. The organism begins as a single cell (fertilized egg) that divides successively to produce many cells, with each parent cell passing identical genetic material (two variants of each chromosome pair) to both daughter cells. Cellular division and differentiation produce and maintain a complex organism, composed of systems of tissues and organs that work together to meet the needs of the whole organism. (HS-LS1-4)

A4E8F5D9E5154174A78DEBC19318DEAD.description: LS1.B: Growth and Development of Organisms

065B0B25E06D4F21A8C8A2B5D945F6F1.description: (NYSED) The structures and functions of the human female reproductive system produce gametes in ovaries, allow for internal fertilization, support the internal development of the embryo and fetus in the uterus, and provide essential materials through the placenta, and nutrition through milk for the newborn. The structures and functions of the human male reproductive system produce gametes in testes and make possible the delivery of these gametes for fertilization. (HS-LS1-8)

07738CF9054E421E830497F3BAC0FB25.description: All cells contain genetic information in the form of DNA molecules. Genes are regions in the DNA that contain the instructions that code for the formation of proteins. (secondary to HS-LS3-1) (Note: Disciplinary Core Idea is also addressed by HS-LS1-1.)

F7AB84A30D074C649C3E003B5F4CDDD0.description: Make and defend a claim based on evidence about the natural world that reflects scientific knowledge, and studentgenerated evidence. (HS-LS3-2)

963CE9B3E42142D499D04C8B595FC0ED.description: Apply concepts of statistics and probability (including determining function fits to data, slope, intercept, and correlation coefficient for linear fits) to scientific and engineering questions and problems, using digital tools when feasible. (HS-LS3-3)

74FD4A9761B443198DD19A373E78D8C3.description: Use a model based on evidence to illustrate the relationships between systems or between components of a system. (HS-LS1-4),(HS-LS1-8)

AB49E631E0EE497B8654552B82DEFC5C.description: Ask questions that arise from examining models or a theory to clarify relationships. (HS-LS3-1)

E6761795FE1142E7887F29A1D4C9982E.description: HS-LS1-8. Use models to illustrate how human reproduction and development maintains continuity of life.

14D72A80FB2B468BB2CCBA6F864FA9AA.description: HS-LS3-3. Apply concepts of statistics and probability to explain the variation and distribution of expressed traits in a population.

FFF034FF570745429FB27468ABCD9E48.description: HS-LS3-2. Make and defend a claim based on evidence that inheritable genetic variations may result from: (1) new genetic combinations through meiosis, (2) viable errors occurring during replication, (3) mutations caused by environmental factors and/or (4) genetic engineering.

7959697AD8F54BD8AC92717656764DBB.description: HS-LS3-1. Ask questions to clarify relationships about the role of DNA and chromosomes in coding the instructions for characteristic traits passed from parents to offspring.

4F5504C0BB754D17B2EECB1C35C77B24.description: HS-LS1-4. Use a model to illustrate cellular division (mitosis) and differentiation.

89BC2A2121AA4DAFA937F5CAA5EB745F.description: Energy drives the cycling of matter within and between systems. (HSLS2-3)

7A603FD6F5864F3E819DEEB6E9FE35A8.description: Energy can be transferred between one place and another place, between objects and/or fields, or between systems. (HS-LS1-7),(HS-LS2-4)

B9DBC5758CDB430CA6F3B244F84D916A.description: Changes of energy and matter in a system can be described in terms of energy and matter flows into, out of, and within that system. (HS-LS1-5), (HS-LS1-6)

CF1F2698DA1D4B94A814D11260636F60.description: Models (e.g., physical, mathematical, computer models) can be used to simulate systems and interactions— including energy, matter, and information flows—within and between systems at different scales. (HS-LS2-5)

430F752CEEBC4FCBA74F5D02B93DE8AF.description: The main way that solar energy is captured and stored on Earth is through the complex chemical process known as photosynthesis. (secondary to HS-LS2-5)

ECEB4FBB0D854C55AED61074A338CA7A.description: (NYSED) Photosynthesis and cellular respiration are important components of the carbon cycle, in which carbon is exchanged among the biosphere, atmosphere, hydrosphere, and geosphere through chemical, physical, geological, and biological processes. (HS-LS2-5)

55F58A250D454B098CB39DF04AB39B1C.description: (NYSED) When matter is cycled through organisms and ecosystems, some of the matter reacts to release energy for life functions, some is stored in newly made structures, and some is eliminated as waste. (HS-LS2-4)

B23F79F8907A4528BA16381C263A70BD.description: Plants or algae form the lowest level of the food web. At each link upward in a food web, only a small fraction of the matter consumed at the lower level is transferred upward, to produce growth and release energy in cellular respiration at the higher level. Given this inefficiency, there are generally fewer organisms at higher levels of a food web. The chemical elements that make up the molecules of organisms pass through food webs and into and out of the atmosphere and soil, and they are combined and recombined in different ways. At each link in an ecosystem, matter and energy are conserved. (HS-LS2-4)

8C029A3C146D40CCA7F3704482B2A850.description: Photosynthesis and cellular respiration (including anaerobic processes) provide most of the energy for life processes. (HS- LS2-3)

50C976AB1D7F4438A16DA99AE9167FFA.description: LS2.B: Cycles of Matter and Energy Transfer in Ecosystems

AC52649AD51E49DF8280AFEF007FFF79.description: (NYSED) Cellular respiration is a chemical process in which the bonds of food molecules and oxygen molecules are broken and new compounds are formed. In this process ATP is produced, which is used to carry out life processes. (HS-LS1-7)

3F70D9BF20FC4FB7A23B39929A327380.description: (NYSED) Sugar molecules contain carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen. Their hydrocarbon backbones combine with other elements to make amino acids and other carbon-based molecules that can be assembled into larger molecules, such as proteins or DNA. (HS-LS1-6)

58F77D0CC9794684BB2E3375312C4136.description: As matter and energy flow through different organizational levels of living systems, chemical elements are recombined in different ways to form different products. As a result of these chemical reactions, energy is transferred from one system of interacting molecules to another. (HS-LS1-6),(HS-LS1- 7)

94F1C17EF9614AFF9B8052950DBEF87E.description: The process of photosynthesis converts light energy to stored chemical energy by converting carbon dioxide plus water into sugars plus released oxygen. (HSLS1-5)

9D3F022953DA4FB99ED5B2FFB8EA963F.description: LS1.C: Organization for Matter and Energy Flow in Organisms

7A75239EF8764B17BCD12759069D2CE6.description: Most scientific knowledge is quite durable, but is, in principle, subject to change based on new evidence and/or reinterpretation of existing evidence. (HS-LS2-3)

29E9ED1211CC41ACB7D0CF93FBF66A46.description: Scientific Knowledge is Open to Revision in Light of New Evidence

C271FE5CD8924F4491EF14216434170B.description: Construct and revise an explanation based on valid and reliable evidence obtained from a variety of sources (including students’ own investigations, models, theories, simulations, peer review) and the assumption that theories and laws that describe the natural world operate today as they did in the past and will continue to do so in the future. (HS-LS1-6),(HS-LS2-3)

6205F296B28F46169B0A84651A086D00.description: Use mathematical representations of phenomena or design solutions to support claims. (HS-LS2-4)

CFCAEDB849A44F9784E5B1036A70DCFE.description: Develop a model based on evidence to illustrate the relationships between systems or components of a system. (HS-LS2-5)

E262D7FCCA3040FDA279D92C3CB089F3.description: Use a model based on evidence to illustrate the relationships between systems or between components of a system. (HS-LS1-5),(HS-LS1-7)

C2BE69F7BA69457FADE7F2160FAADB85.description: Develop a model to illustrate the role of various processes in the cycling of carbon among the biosphere, atmosphere, hydrosphere, and geosphere.

4AD582C37A05440DBC37D6E6309F2938.description: Use mathematical representations to support claims for the cycling of matter and flow of energy among organisms in an ecosystem.

C8F2F267DD1A417197AD61DDD89FDD24.description: Construct and revise an explanation based on evidence for the cycling of matter and flow of energy in ecosystems.

2134A22AF5CE4409BE27AFE905FE2645.description: Use a model to illustrate that aerobic cellular respiration is a chemical process whereby the bonds of food molecules and oxygen molecules are broken and the bonds in new compounds are formed resulting in a net transfer of energy.

9173A49EAD0F47C2AA95F07747BEDF89.description: Construct and revise an explanation based on evidence for how carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen from sugar molecules may combine with other elements such as nitrogen, sulfur, and phosphorus to form amino acids and other carbon-based molecules.

583DD62B54F341EDB9056BA2B0B31AA8.description: Use a model to illustrate how photosynthesis transforms light energy into stored chemical energy.

18B4EEA623F840128360988E1C15549E.description: New technologies can have deep impacts on society and the environment, including some that were not anticipated. Analysis of costs and benefits is a critical aspect of decisions about technology. (HS-ESS2-2)

529CC717784D4A68A6D4DD8B9FEDC0DB.description: Influence of Engineering, Technology, and Science on Society and the Natural World

E8A8A05B43A146A49F2DECC10F005AEF.description: Science and engineering complement each other in the cycle known as research and development (R&D). Many R&D projects may involve scientists, engineers, and others with wide ranges of expertise. (HS-ESS2-3)

9B997E73619544DFB205F5A4C11074E3.description: Interdependence of Science, Engineering, and Technology

5E165CA4FBBF4C66B091B7981CDFC17D.description: Feedback (negative or positive) can stabilize or destabilize a system. (HSESS2-2)

CE9E7A8DA3CA426B928DC768E7CB8AB8.description: Much of science deals with constructing explanations of how things change and how they remain stable. (HS-ESS2-7)

A18303E4CC104470B9391902639F3801.description: The functions and properties of natural and designed objects and systems can be inferred from their overall structure, the way their components are shaped and used, and the molecular substructures of its various materials. (HS-ESS2-5)

AAF57FEA6A5843469212CF360B607AD8.description: Energy drives the cycling of matter within and between systems. (HS-ESS2- 3)

45E9EE8748ED478487C02EEA8EF8227B.description: The total amount of energy and matter in closed systems is conserved. (HSESS2-6)

328B32E71DBB4883874D3168571DF307.description: Geologists use seismic waves and their reflection at interfaces between layers to probe structures deep in the planet. (secondary to HS-ESS2-3)

AE2A0475EAE248729892665A2312CCA5.description: The many dynamic and delicate feedbacks between the biosphere and other Earth systems cause a continual coevolution of Earth’s surface and the life that exists on it. (HS-ESS2-7)

AB53DE575FB643A6B8AAA52A4C9174A0.description: Changes in the atmosphere due to human activity have increased carbon dioxide concentrations and thus affect climate. (HS-ESS2-6)

61578E3C951A4DD39F7AAF5F852FCEA7.description: Gradual atmospheric changes were due to plants and other organisms that captured carbon dioxide and released oxygen. (HS-ESS2-6),(HS-ESS2-7)

4412161F2CA24CEAAE8DE3382E503567.description: The foundation for Earth’s global climate systems is the electromagnetic radiation from the sun, as well as its reflection, absorption, storage, and redistribution among the atmosphere, ocean, and land systems, and this energy’s re-radiation into space. (HS-ESS2-2)

865EF8060FD94078A1F5F80461DE0A6A.description: The abundance of liquid water on Earth’s surface and its unique combination of physical and chemical properties are central to the planet’s dynamics. These properties include water’s exceptional capacity to absorb, store, and release large amounts of energy, transmit sunlight, expand upon freezing, dissolve and transport materials, and lower the viscosities and melting points of rocks. (HS-ESS2-5)

5F89240531C144BF9AEC784815F7C146.description: ESS2.C: The Roles of Water in Earth’s Surface Processes

AB03285F2B574061BCBA089271576BAA.description: (NYSED) Minerals are the building blocks of igneous, metamorphic, and sedimentary rocks and can be identified using physical and chemical characteristics. These rock types are evidence of stages of constant recycling of Earth material by surface processes and convection currents in the mantle. (HS-ESS2-3)

4C25CF85E9C446B7B9E598C84D08CBC6.description: (NYSED) Residual heat from Earth’s formation and the radioactive decay of unstable isotopes in Earth’s interior continually generate energy that is absorbed by Earth’s mantle and crust, driving mantle convection. Plate tectonics can be viewed as the surface expression of mantle convection. (HS-ESS2-3)

744608658A984290B3C5EF3902DA4D94.description: ESS2.B: Plate Tectonics and Large-Scale System Interactions

D21FE099601F472A94E7C3B836AF3C48.description: Evidence from deep probes and seismic waves, reconstructions of historical changes in Earth’s surface and its magnetic field, and an understanding of physical and chemical processes lead to a model of Earth with a hot but solid inner core, a liquid outer core, a solid mantle and crust. Motions of the mantle and its plates occur primarily through thermal convection, which involves the cycling of matter due to the outward flow of energy from Earth’s interior and gravitational movement of denser materials toward the interior. (HS-ESS2-3)

990E009F3A204832A917C2D71D82EC89.description: Earth’s systems, being dynamic and interacting, cause feedback effects that can increase or decrease the original changes (HS-ESS2-2)

9C981C89C4EB4DCBB31BFC1C48FBE67C.description: Science disciplines share common rules of evidence used to evaluate explanations about natural systems. (HS-ESS2-3) Science includes the process of coordinating patterns of evidence with current theory. (HS-ESS2-3)

7E5520D7510147558116FB607473EEF1.description: Science knowledge is based on empirical evidence. (HSESS2-3)

A41F1C56EFB347638163F69F92DA07CB.description: Scientific Knowledge is Based on Empirical Evidence

8C3F2094B3C24AF3A1788A29BC71CEA0.description: Construct an oral and written argument or counterarguments based on data and evidence. (HS-ESS2-7)

6D011E7AB6404930A5C4729A9F74BC50.description: Analyze data using tools, technologies, and/or models (e.g., computational, mathematical) in order to make valid and reliable scientific claims or determine an optimal design solution. (HS-ESS2-2)

58A2A9174E314A8D8EA84833FC5E997A.description: Plan and conduct an investigation individually and collaboratively to produce data to serve as the basis for evidence, and in the design: decide on types, how much, and accuracy of data needed to produce reliable measurements and consider limitations on the precision of the data (e.g., number of trials, cost, risk, time), and refine the design accordingly. (HS-ESS2-5)

F910774789C44A548197FD96CC5A8B80.description: Develop a model based on evidence to illustrate the relationships between systems or between components of a system. (HS-ESS2-3),(HS-ESS2-6)

72BE071D8CAE4501A0C8FEACECF53715.description: Construct an argument based on evidence about the coevolution of Earth’s systems and life on Earth.

496EE0BF7A4644CD8B4E0BCD6F0A29DE.description: Develop a quantitative model to describe the cycling of carbon among the hydrosphere, atmosphere, geosphere, and biosphere.

363171E5E41644D8AD0F903AAA20B49B.description: Plan and conduct an investigation of the properties of water and its effects on Earth materials and surface processes.

8FFC6C0D467047FA81C4F772253DE3E0.description: Develop a model based on evidence of Earth’s interior to describe the cycling of matter by thermal convection.

069A50204C284F5B887F3EDAD259445E.description: Analyze geoscience data to make the claim that one change to Earth’s surface can create feedbacks that cause changes to Earth’s systems.

A6414F70D8664639845E2080DFA10CF8.description: Investigating or designing new systems or structures requires a detailed examination of the properties of different materials, the structures of different components, and connections of components to reveal its function and/or solve a problem. (HS-LS1-1)

8FB7D7602CF24A53976D82B762225A25.description: Models (e.g., physical, mathematical, computer models) can be used to simulate systems and interactions— including energy, matter, and information flows—within and between systems at different scales. (HS-LS1-2)

7B517EAE12C34672921A6ED0DF3663FE.description: (NYSED) Disease is a failure of homeostasis. Organisms have a variety of mechanisms to prevent and combat disease. Technological advances including vaccinations and antibiotics have contributed to the prevention and treatment of disease. (HS-LS1-2),(HS-LS1-3)

D71136B1085143C9A990062C075C8981.description: Feedback mechanisms maintain a living system’s internal conditions within certain limits and mediate behaviors, allowing it to remain alive and functional even as external conditions change within some range. Feedback mechanisms can encourage (through positive feedback) or discourage (negative feedback) what is going on inside the living system. (HS-LS1-3)

0C00E588B926465A8D8D1D47C46133B2.description: Multicellular organisms have a hierarchical structural organization, in which any one system is made up of numerous parts and is itself a component of the next level. (HS-LS1-2)

6B6476C947D6437D81704F977657DF26.description: All cells contain genetic information in the form of DNA molecules. Genes are regions in the DNA that contain the instructions that code for the formation of proteins, which carry out most of the work of cells. (HS-LS1-1) (Note: This Disciplinary Core Idea is also addressed by HS-LS3-1.)

9C2645CEE0594A198A6AE45C844717B4.description: Systems of specialized cells within organisms help them perform the essential functions of life. (HS-LS1-1)

D7F1B353F6C94133BD1527FF0CB0D190.description: Scientific inquiry is characterized by a common set of values that include: logical thinking, precision, open-mindedness, objectivity, skepticism, replicability of results, and honest and ethical reporting of findings. (HS-LS1-3)
