E1D03C8EFEFA472A94BB1205E8E26D09.description: Construct an explanation based on valid and reliable evidence obtained from a variety of sources (including students’ own investigations, models, theories, simulations, peer review) and the assumption that theories and laws that describe the natural world operate today as they did in the past and will continue to do so in the future. (HSLS1-1)

FADD2D339858476CB988FDA7F1DDBAE0.description: Plan and conduct an investigation individually and collaboratively to produce data to serve as the basis for evidence, and in the design: decide on types, how much, and accuracy of data needed to produce reliable measurements and consider limitations on the precision of the data (e.g., number of trials, cost, risk, time), and refine the design accordingly. (HS-LS1-3)

AFCE2D1E75E74575BFDCB36983CE6942.description: Develop and use a model to illustrate the hierarchical organization of interacting systems that provide specific functions within multicellular organisms.

20A7173E9C9C476891768A062A054968.description: Construct an explanation based on evidence for how the structure of DNA determines the structure of proteins which carry out the essential functions of life through systems of specialized cells.

E55DAAFBCCDE45039B50DC2F72EF4512.description: When investigating or describing a system, the boundaries and initial conditions of the system need to be defined. (HS-PS2-2)

387AD73733A7433398FDD4B0A13D1CF3.description: Systems can be designed to cause a desired effect. (HSPS2-3)

7FCE68988D7746C3958F2311FCF7AB80.description: Empirical evidence is required to differentiate between cause and correlation and make claims about specific causes and effects. (HS-PS2- 1),(HSPS2-5)

D346C6C2DEAC4F85BA04793D487452AB.description: Different patterns may be observed at each of the scales at which a system is studied and can provide evidence for causality in explanations of phenomena. (HS-PS2-4)

21B8FFCE1D2B43708C2B9E19886CC5F8.description: Criteria may need to be broken down into simpler ones that can be approached systematically, and decisions about the priority of certain criteria over others (trade- offs) may be needed. (secondary to HS-PS2-3)

FDA3779C10B5477DAF1761AF34F28F60.description: Criteria and constraints also include satisfying any requirements set by society, such as taking issues of risk mitigation into account, and they should be quantified to the extent possible and stated in such a way that one can tell if a given design meets them. (secondary to HS-PS2- 3)

9BFDE9ED136D4EB59A38C2B1AFB45F56.description: ETS1.A: Defining and Delimiting Engineering Problems

Magnets or electric currents cause magnetic fields; electric charges or changing magnetic fields cause electric fields. (HS-PS2-4),(HS-PS2-5)

B01717EA166944BE829549895F74051A.description: Newton’s law of universal gravitation and Coulomb’s law provide the mathematical models to describe and predict the effects of gravitational and electrostatic forces between distant objects. (HS-PS2-4)

EAB60D215D5744A881F4DEE522789C99.description: If a system interacts with objects outside itself, the total momentum of the system can change; however, any such change is balanced by changes in the momentum of objects outside the system. (HS-PS2-2),(HS-PS2-3)

CC29970D1DCD42EFA713BB9800E8AE16.description: Momentum is defined for a particular frame of reference; it is the mass times the velocity of the object. (HS-PS2-2)

CEC65D264906486CBD42B784C4EBFBEA.description: Newton’s second law accurately predicts changes in the motion of macroscopic objects. (HS-PS2-1)

81897D161EC049348CED45532ED38169.description: Theories and laws provide explanations in science. (HS-PS2- 1),(HS-PS2-4)

C4104D612E8A4B8BBBA88C60F88BCEE9.description: Apply scientific ideas to solve a design problem, taking into account possible unanticipated effects. (HS-PS2-3)

BA5F333EAF9B4B5485983570CEDE7C01.description: Use mathematical representations of phenomena to describe explanations. (HS-PS2-2),(HS-PS2-4)

12E0DA201DD44C9390FF3BDD683E6484.description: Analyzing data in 9–12 builds on K–8 and progresses to introducing more detailed statistical analysis, the comparison of data sets for consistency, and the use of models to generate and analyze data. ▪ Analyze data using tools, technologies, and/or models (e.g., computational, mathematical) in order to make valid and reliable scientific claims or determine an optimal design solution. A6B111A3FE5842BEB96839B4C5C5EBAB.description: Plan and conduct an investigation to provide evidence that an electric current can produce a magnetic field and that a changing magnetic field can produce an electric current.

9ABEA36CDD304EA99B83FFC2BF4EE019.description: Use mathematical representations of Newton’s Law of Gravitation and Coulomb’s Law to describe and predict the gravitational and electrostatic forces between objects.

0B0EA6AF1FE84CA7A8D0AF457D83CD59.description: Apply scientific and engineering ideas to design, evaluate, and refine a device that minimizes the force on a macroscopic object during a collision.

81C2960AF9D54FA894209891F85264E7.description: Analyze data to support the claim that Newton’s Second Law of Motion describes the mathematical relationship among the net force on a macroscopic object, its mass, and its acceleration.

document.title: New York State High School Science Learning Standards

72C3F93CFFC14ADDBB12D9CB02511279.description: Scientific knowledge is based on the assumption that natural laws operate today as they did in the past and they will continue to do so in the future. (HS-LS4-1),(HSLS4-4)

9B842BA359474E328D77AF2AF7DB22CC.description: Scientific Knowledge Assumes an Order and Consistency in Natural Systems

5FB835465E584E108535193354C108C3.description: Empirical evidence is required to differentiate between cause and correlation and make claims about specific causes and effects. (HSLS4-2),(HS-LS4-4),(HS-LS4-5)

F79553FC048B47C7A522E4F072B0CF02.description: Different patterns may be observed at each of the scales at which a system is studied and can provide evidence for causality in explanations of phenomena. (HSLS4-1),(HS-LS4-3)

2583D8D83D5044D0BD85A8A48624716A.description: Species become extinct because they can no longer survive and reproduce in their altered environment. If members cannot adjust to change that is too fast or drastic, the opportunity for the species’ evolution is lost. (HS-LS4-5)

BCFD1CC0B587478BACB165F612CD17FF.description: Changes in the physical environment, whether naturally occurring or human induced, have thus contributed to the expansion of some species, the emergence of new distinct species as populations diverge under different conditions, and the decline–and sometimes the extinction–of some species. (HS-LS4-5)

5BB10D1CB90A464AAFCE0572749C35A3.description: Adaptation also means that the distribution of traits in a population can change when conditions change. (HS-LS4-3)

7E99D7BC4ACA4CAB8CF7F9CC034B1231.description: Natural selection leads to adaptation that is, to a population dominated by organisms that are anatomically, behaviorally, and physiologically well suited to survive and reproduce in a specific environment. That is, the differential survival and reproduction of organisms in a population that have an advantageous heritable trait leads to an increase in the proportion of individuals in future generations that have the trait and to a decrease in the proportion of individuals that do not. (HS-LS4-3),(HS-LS4-4)

AE7D8FC14A1D42B4960A16C7622ADD31.description: Evolution is a consequence of the interaction of four factors: (1) the potential for a species to increase in number, (2) the genetic variation of individuals in a species due to mutation and sexual reproduction, (3) competition for an environment’s limited supply of the resources that individuals need in order to survive and reproduce, and (4) the ensuing proliferation of those organisms that are better able to survive and reproduce in that environment. (HS-LS4-2)

2165AAA6A68D416AAF7D1272E9A990B5.description: The traits that positively affect survival are more likely to be reproduced, and thus are more common in the population. (HS-LS4-3)

B78941C9A59A45F8B8697829574A5914.description: Natural selection occurs only if there is both (1) variation in the genetic information between organisms in a population and (2) variation in the expression of that genetic information—that is, trait variation—that leads to differences in performance among individuals. (HS-LS4-2),(HS-LS4-3)

249C1CC3F14E444BB948EDA445B95248.description: Genetic information provides evidence of evolution. DNA sequences vary among species, but there are many overlaps; in fact, the ongoing branching that produces multiple lines of descent can be inferred by comparing the DNA sequences of different organisms. Such information is also derivable from the similarities and differences in amino acid sequences and from anatomical and embryological evidence. (HS-LS4-1)

71A5BCFA1E734CEBBD1AF063D0118FAB.description: LS4.A: Evidence of Common Ancestry and Diversity

F2A3C05B78144F929C6B68C8D6BECB04.description: A scientific theory is a substantiated explanation of some aspect of the natural world, based on a body of facts that have been repeatedly confirmed through observation and experiment and the science community validates each theory before it is accepted. If new evidence is discovered that the theory does not accommodate, the theory is generally modified in light of this new evidence. (HS-LS4-1)

7887C61A87284BF599B4CFA0A1CC9982.description: Science Models, Laws, Mechanisms, and Theories Explain Natural Phenomena

9F144B75721C42ABBD653B89F9D306EC.description: Communicate scientific information (e.g., about phenomena and/or the process of development and the design and performance of a proposed process or system) in multiple formats (including orally, graphically, textually, and mathematically). (HS-LS4-1)

29CD6FFCDAE444A3ABD2412ECCE48D1C.description: Evaluate the evidence behind currently accepted explanations or solutions to determine the merits of arguments. (HS-LS4-5)

5088D55F7A2C41268B01449D912BBA9A.description: Construct an explanation based on valid and reliable evidence obtained from a variety of sources (including students’ own investigations, models, theories, simulations, peer review) and the assumption that theories and laws that describe the natural world operate today as they did in the past and will continue to do so in the future. (HS-LS4-2),(HS-LS4-4)

2C601F67F1D048279C559D78CC4F4B99.description: Apply concepts of statistics and probability (including determining function fits to data, slope, intercept, and correlation coefficient for linear fits) to scientific and engineering questions and problems, using digital tools when feasible. (HS-LS4-3)

21484B55BF2749B598B07A951C63DB6F.description: Evaluate the evidence supporting claims that changes in environmental conditions may result in: (1) increases in the number of individuals of some species, (2) the emergence of new species over time, and (3) the extinction of other species.

DBCCB9DEE57E4086BD7CE7AB9CE25C74.description: Construct an explanation based on evidence for how natural selection leads to adaptation of populations.

AA3CC3413B1B48BC9DB21D06C1ABE24E.description: Apply concepts of statistics and probability to support explanations that organisms with an advantageous heritable trait tend to increase in proportion to organisms lacking this trait.

7F95A1FD39F74E37B387D85620ACBCC1.description: Construct an explanation based on evidence that the process of evolution primarily results from four factors: (1) the potential for a species to increase in number, (2) the heritable genetic variation of individuals in a species due to mutation and sexual reproduction, (3) competition for limited resources, and (4) the proliferation of those organisms that are better able to survive and reproduce in the environment.

60B8F8B9F29648409EF65FA54775A2F1.description: Communicate scientific information that common ancestry and biological evolution are supported by multiple lines of empirical evidence.

Demonstrate respect for the rights of others in discussions and classroom debates; respectfully disagree with
other viewpoints. Use techniques and strategies to be an active and engaged member of class discussions of
fellow classmates’ views and statements.

86030D7422AC4574B307133BD7E3D449.description: Explain how government policies affect the economy.

6D6F8EC7D1C048C7960C1F79061C2ACB.description:
Use appropriate data to evaluate the state of employment, unemployment, inflation, total production, income,
and economic growth in the economy.

5C9948A28CEC41879DEE3B5FAA0DD4CC.description:
Examine the roles of institutions such as corporations, non-profit organizations, and labor unions in a market
economy in the United States.

04A4C7A6841F48858C8318BD5DF00710.description: Describe the role of competition in the determination of prices and wages in a market economy.

B9AD0B564D7449E3B72B702B8EA3A02D.description: Explain the roles of buyers and sellers in product, labor, and financial markets.

B82B68F018AE4DA4B7675A76068688B0.description:
Explain how economic decisions affect the well-being of individuals, businesses, and society; evaluate
alternative approaches or solutions to economic issues in terms of benefits and costs for different groups of
people.

15F024B3E6D34478925033C6BD4F161E.description:
Describe the spatial organization of place, considering the historical, social, political, and economic implication
of that organization. Identify and describe examples of how boundaries and definition of location are
historically constructed.

6ACA48F6098C46979ED49F0BBB376847.description: Characterize and analyze changing interconnections between places and regions.

1DEAA6FD5705458E91BB27ECF96B6E76.description:
Recognize and analyze how characteristics (cultural, economic, and physical-environmental) of regions affect
the history of the United States.

8F2D4E6A0C3743D5B02EEB2EF2FDA4B0.description:
Identify and analyze how environments affect human activities and how human activities affect physical
environments in the United States.

BE95DCCDECD545ADBB69A99986374249.description:
Distinguish human activities and human-made features from “environments” (natural events or physical
features—land, air, and water—that are not directly made by humans) and describe the relationship between
human activities and the environment.

80A93C74E8A845E18211701D48EB3228.description:
Use location terms and geographic representations, such as maps, photographs, satellite images, and models to
describe where places are in relation to each other and connections between places; evaluate the benefits of
particular places for purposeful activities

A0C3B1237D27446C8C6FBCC152AD41EC.description:
Analyze case studies in United States history in a comparative framework, attending to the role of chronology
and sequence, as well as categories of comparison or socio-political components.

2616BCB5DAC84F798452D12A89F58989.description:
Connect historical developments to specific circumstances of time and place and to broader regional, national,
or global processes.

A24160920E58463FB3F5138C2B2A3797.description:
Describe the relationship between geography, economics, and history as a context for events and movements in
the United States.

708E4A6B8B4047D18154B911229BF2DA.description:
Describe, compare, and evaluate multiple historical developments (within societies; across and between
societies; in various chronological and geographical contexts).

DCB644590B97480FAA37476DA82AAB09.description: Identify and compare multiple perspectives on a given historical experience

8EB7D73651094942B1E44D9B74E7D17F.description:
Identify a region of the United States by describing multiple characteristics common to places within it, and
then identify other similar regions inside the United States.

27A4400249CF45EEABECFE1B5E5D150A.description: Identify and describe models of historical periodization that historians use to categorize events.

C8749252EED540B8A487D3FF77C3ADEF.description: Relate patterns of continuity and change to larger historical processes and themes

D0FA79EC45F74C8089FA77D5E81DB218.description: Recognize that changing the periodization affects the historical narrative.

95B50DE088844B3295721987B2520E5C.description: Recognize, analyze, and evaluate dynamics of historical continuity and change over periods of time.

2C1E4F415E9B4B3BB25CEA273EE83E95.description: Distinguish between long-term and immediate causes and effects of an event from current events or history.

C8E9A187FE084AA8BFD538027BD2217B.description: Identify, analyze, and evaluate the relationship between multiple causes and effects.

B20049D2FCC44899BC9F3B0933492F88.description: Identify causes and effects, using examples from current events, grade-level content, and historical events

E73847825FD347F99541365CEF9CB368.description:
Employ mathematical skills to measure time by years, decades, centuries, and millennia; to calculate time from
the fixed points of the calendar system (B.C. or B.C.E. and A.D. or C.E.); and to interpret the data presented in
time lines.

9EED64A1CD80450B8FBE511ADE8FD6AB.description:
Articulate how events are related chronologically to one another in time, and explain the ways in which earlier
ideas and events may influence subsequent ideas and events.

22CC9BADF7E846F889E12A9B6A0D9AC2.description:
Recognize an argument and identify evidence that supports the argument; examine arguments related to a
specific social studies topic from multiple perspectives; deconstruct arguments, recognizing the perspective of
the argument and identifying evidence used to support that perspective.

2B3EE181F0CE403B9273A29614043BA8.description: Make inferences and draw conclusions from evidence.

CE9541020FAD4D8096509AA1C4A617D7.description: Describe and analyze arguments of others, considering historical context.

CC3E58E61E71462CAC0F8EE34358A6E3.description:
Analyze evidence in terms of historical and/or social context, content, authorship, point of view, purpose, and
format; identify bias; explain the role of bias, context and audience in presenting arguments or evidence.

4A9A1984835F4546A524182D0EC2BA54.description:
Identify, describe, and evaluate evidence about events from diverse sources (including written documents,
works of art, photographs, charts and graphs, artifacts, oral traditions, and other primary and secondary
sources).

D8CA2E485D1848829EBAF4544BF0233B.description:
Define and frame questions about the United States and answer them by gathering, interpreting, and using
evidence.

05EF5E7C9F2B467088063628D87D0B40.description: The food of almost any kind of animal can be traced back to plants. Organisms can survive only in environments in which their particular needs are met. A healthy ecosystem is one in which multiple species of different types are each able to meet their needs in a relatively stable web of life. 08F59DC78D6C45199F7E261C4B1CD137.description: Make observations and measurements to produce data to serve as the basis for evidence for an explanation of a phenomenon. (5-PS1-3)

83DBACF409B742D899D68D748BA08974.description: Conduct an investigation collaboratively to produce data to serve as the basis for evidence, using fair tests in which variables are controlled and the number of trials considered. (5-PS1-4)

2333725D648240F6AFAB29D14DA20DBC.description: Develop a model to describe phenomena. (5- PS1-1)

BE704018C48F4833B089296538CA19CF.description: Conduct an investigation to determine whether the mixing of two or more substances results in new substances

0217D7D75CA04416A4E8A4060144F3E5.description: Make observations and measurements to identify materials based on their properties.

185C2AE998294427A34F5919DC557BA0.description: Measure and graph quantities to provide evidence that regardless of the type of change that occurs when heating, cooling, or mixing substances the total amount of matter is conserved.

BDFE6B60C3E0453EAF95783AE227378D.description: Develop a model to describe that matter is made of particles too small to be seen.

3A452D7F19FF4D3D8861497E042E3A4D.description: Engineers improve existing technologies or develop new ones to increase their benefits, decrease known risks, and meet societal demands. (3-5-ETS1-2)

FAFD6F7AA8D74304A3E330A11502502D.description: People’s needs and wants change over time, as do their demands for new and improved technologies. (3-5-ETS1-1)

9D0E3B4E039645C78D9A6DD65ED58A67.description: Influence of Science, Engineering, and Technology on Society and the Natural World

D6B84E78020045C884B7E8D6ADBFCE7D.description: Different solutions need to be tested in order to determine which of them best solves the problem, given the criteria and the constraints. (3-5-ETS1-3)

D27603A691E24277A756B394D0C148D3.description: Tests are often designed to identify failure points or difficulties, which suggest the elements of the design that need to be improved. (3-5-ETS1-3)

9A8BBE05971E4CD18DDEF58F1C3611F1.description: At whatever stage, communicating with peers about proposed solutions is an important part of the design process, and shared ideas can lead to improved designs. (3-5-ETS1-2)

D9EF4A977030415695A959550BA4DF87.description: Research on a problem should be carried out before beginning to design a solution. Testing a solution involves investigating how well it performs under a range of likely conditions. (3-5-ETS1-2)

80E5C833768C468BA2E4F619EE581BDD.description: Possible solutions to a problem are limited by available materials and resources (constraints). The success of a designed solution is determined by considering the desired features of a solution (criteria). Different proposals for solutions can be compared on the basis of how well each one meets the specified criteria for success or how well each takes the constraints into account. (3-5-ETS1-1)

0E5240AFE6384F3EA64BDDFC57ECF976.description: ETS1.A: Defining and Delimiting Engineering Problems

ECF2BE5612A347ED8082CC1535F7712C.description: Generate and compare multiple solutions to a problem based on how well they meet the criteria and constraints of the design problem. (3-5-ETS1- 2)

DD1C05B8877445B9B6D615089D1F4986.description: Plan and conduct an investigation collaboratively to produce data to serve as the basis for evidence, using fair tests in which variables are controlled and the number of trials considered. (3-5-ETS1-3)

D14E2700156E4A678EBD5893695C0DB9.description: Define a simple design problem that can be solved through the development of an object, tool, process, or system and includes several criteria for success and constraints on materials, time, or cost. (3-5- ETS1-1)

B440442AEEF1469BBD024375AE6A4EE4.description: Plan and carry out fair tests in which variables are controlled and failure points are considered to identify aspects of a model or prototype that can be improved.

25181A19B7CF4018BDDA4A100F274818.description: Generate and compare multiple possible solutions to a problem based on how well each is likely to meet the criteria and constraints of the problem.

5247A15AADB34B7EA8CDDA1158C9F1CE.description: Define a simple design problem reflecting a need or a want that includes specified criteria for success and constraints on materials, time, or cost.

document.title: New York State K-8 Social Studies Framework

212EE5B4E28F4C1599132929F863689D.description:
Develop the connections of an interdependent community by engaging in the political process as it relates to a
local context.

B03DAF8A87AE4660AB112ABF52746CB4.description: Identify how social and political responsibilities developed in American society.

32D96CC19C90465589466341D33F557D.description:
Identify how people in power have acted to extend the concept of freedom, the practice of social justice, and the
protection of human rights in United States history.

4A6BF11C479540F78B015C2E5DA64416.description: Identify situations in which social actions are required and determine an appropriate course of action

D8A59F8F3EC844D89E43C291C9E16A38.description:
Participate in negotiating and compromising in the resolution of differences and conflict; introduce and examine
the role of conflict resolution.

207A9C07DA5B4252BA9CED2A470F281E.description:
Identify, describe, and compare the role of the individual in social and political participation in, and as an agent
of, historical change at various times and in various locations in colonial North America and in the early history
of the United States

99B08144799245A09B585BEF04709621.description:
Identify and explain different types of political systems and ideologies used at various times in colonial history
and the early history of the United States and explain the role of individuals and key groups in those political
and social systems.

1DAAC5B51FBC4C61BD63466686297852.description: Participate in activities that focus on a classroom, school, community, state, or national issue or problem

800E5B3BE3E947C49AC8FC947EC9C05D.description:
Demonstrate respect for the rights of others in discussions and classroom debates; respectfully disagree with
other viewpoints. Use techniques and strategies to be an active and engaged member of class discussions of
fellow classmates’ views and statements, with teacher support.

4BC83BAAE3F0482992F63DE2A1E8D39D.description: Explain how government policies affected the economies in colonial and early United States history

1A880D41036C4C49AAD65295F7B33681.description:
Examine data on the state of employment, unemployment, inflation, total production, income, and economic
growth in the economy.

130DF7098785453AACB58E830F56A0E9.description:
Examine the roles of institutions, such as joint stock companies, banks, and the government in the development
of the United States economy before the Civil War

717685648A434F2EAE4074461BF79774.description:
Describe the role that competition has in the determination of prices and wages; identify other factors that help
to determine prices.

B716BE005CEA47E1BD08F824A0C32AF1.description: Identify examples of buyers and sellers in product, labor, and financial markets.

F787AEC7D36B47728B87E6ED8D980DAF.description:
Explain how economic decisions affect the well-being of individuals, businesses, and society; evaluate
alternative approaches or solutions to economic issues in terms of benefits and costs for different groups of
people.

580DCB7A2876473D892BADED3B254986.description:
Describe the spatial organization of place, considering the historical, social, political, and economic implication
of that organization. Describe how boundaries and definition of location are historically constructed.

786FF7A49AD34F92BD12AB88138B6BEE.description: Characterize and analyze changing interconnections between places and regions.

4D442759229E4B53A9F12BD1D3AE2A86.description:
Recognize and analyze how characteristics (cultural, economic, and physical-environmental) of regions affect
the history of the United States.

D3A69427B6B54CE0B26BC7D77800F23D.description:
Identify and analyze how environments affect human activities and how human activities affect physical
environments in the United States.

E35886C4D5614932835B7F9FF8B5D62B.description:
Distinguish human activities and human-made features from “environments” (natural events or physical
features—land, air, and water—that are not directly made by humans) and describe the relationship between
human activities and the environment.

08731D38D61F43B681689BFD1A228ED0.description:
Use location terms and geographic representations, such as maps, photographs, satellite images, and models to
describe where places in early United States history were in relation to each other, to describe connections
among places, and to evaluate effectively the benefits of particular places for purposeful activities.

8207D7C36EF04C5699B54CEABF41E9D4.description:
Understand the roles that periodization and region play in developing the comparison of colonial settlements in
North America. Identify general characteristics that can be employed to conduct comparative analyses of case
studies in the early history of the United States.

4D16E5B76107442C830CD445A0F2FB2F.description:
Connect historical developments to specific circumstances of time and place and to broader regional, national,
or global processes.

16158C78A4FC4DD58399CD56BA745B59.description:
Identify how the relationship between geography, economics, and history helps to define a context for events in
the study of the United States

571891F62009418BB2DFBA1CE757CAB7.description:
Describe, compare, and evaluate multiple historical developments within the United States in various
chronological and geographical contexts.

7B63355A46EB476D8986F3A11FF03511.description: Identify and categorize multiple perspectives on a given historical experience.

69DF462B1258488DB43317925EBA9E7D.description:
Identify a region of colonial North America or the early United States by describing multiple characteristics
common to places within it, and then identify other similar regions (inside or outside the continental United
States) with similar characteristics.

AB8ED10184D44F8187CD8970CBFA297B.description: Identify models of historical periodization that historians use to categorize events.

36901906BE6D4DE286C957D8AF38A5D8.description: Identify patterns of continuity and change as they relate to larger historical process and themes

71291EEDED38429381805157C5BD2CAF.description: Recognize that changing the periodization affects the historical narrative.

58F8DC0D498244F3BDA8F5F5E3E05653.description: Recognize, analyze, and evaluate dynamics of historical continuity and change over periods of time.

F5E09C84C03A4824806BFCC2D4E4431B.description: Distinguish between long-term and immediate causes and effects of an event from current events or history

F3DE7893E79848B7A3AF18B5B79693E1.description: Identify and analyze the relationship between multiple causes and multiple effects.

0330E8539D2E48938E162B7F3BEE4D8E.description: Identify causes and effects, using examples from current events, grade-level content, and historical events

C87CF1616ECD48C8974FD5EBB67B493C.description:
Employ mathematical skills to measure time by years, decades, centuries, and millennia; to calculate time from
the fixed points of the calendar system (B.C.E. and C.E.); and to interpret the data presented in time lines

AD1078C6500E4D63B8F1B24F0DAA8C11.description:
Identify how events are related chronologically to one another in time, and explain the ways in which earlier
ideas and events may influence subsequent ideas and events.

0FF9E184AF424BC68E1F1CA7C1DF0FD6.description:
Recognize an argument and identify supporting evidence related to a specific social studies topic. Examine
arguments related to a specific social studies topic from multiple perspectives. Recognize that the perspective of
the argument’s author shapes the selection of evidence used to support it.

6131C4358D044899BDD18861E855F243.description: Make inferences and draw general conclusions from evidence.

EA3860450FCF468D8A2E0E2E7DEECA19.description: Describe and analyze arguments of others, with support.

9F251A2291504D389A6A8E0CCE2D65E3.description:
Analyze evidence in terms of historical context, content, authorship, point of view, purpose, and format;
identify bias; explain the role of bias and audience in presenting arguments or evidence.

B5BD82F5D4E9464CA2012939FFE9B0E0.description:
Identify, select, and evaluate evidence about events from diverse sources (including written documents, works
of art, photographs, charts and graphs, artifacts, oral traditions, and other primary and secondary sources).

943F72DE24534C5888249A09DE183A82.description:
Define and frame questions about the United States that can be answered by gathering, interpreting, and using
evidence

document.title: New York State K-8 Social Studies Framework

B04707AC19AC43BFA0420AD4A8079F6A.description:
Develop an understanding of an interdependent global community by developing awareness and/or engaging in
the political process as it relates to a global context.

6021B91ADAD843D882BEBDDC9EBAB5F9.description: Identify rights and responsibilities of citizens within societies in the Eastern Hemisphere.

2C87BB7A1E644BD1A9CA461C44C48E06.description:
Describe the roles of people in power in the Eastern Hemisphere both historically and currently. Identify ways
that current figures can influence people’s rights and freedom

42F111E632214026A83BDF00AF1D1F4F.description: Identify situations with a global focus in which social actions are required and suggest solutions

157470928B3C42F9887FDFB0BA2B3AA1.description:
Participate in negotiating and compromising in the resolution of differences and conflict; introduce and examine
the role of conflict resolution.

12AB051F60B54AFEA28DD86805875A58.description:
Identify and describe opportunities for and the role of the individual in social and political participation at
various times and in various locations in the Eastern Hemisphere.

5AC07A0A1C2A4A0DBEA9B4662230A5D7.description:
Identify and explore different types of political systems and ideologies used at various times and in various
locations in the Eastern Hemisphere and identify the role of individuals and key groups in those political and
social systems.

7A67174611C24BBF8947E5201B7D1270.description: Participate in activities that focus on a local issue or problem in a country in the Eastern Hemisphere

DED7BA7DB02343AB9774B95F01E25FB2.description:
Demonstrate respect for the rights of others in discussion and classroom debates, regardless of whether one
agrees with the other viewpoint. Consider alternate views in discussion.

21B3B0A92DAB42EF96EAAEE4D9F9F03B.description: Describe government decisions that affect economies in case studies from the Eastern Hemisphere.

3618781751FC4BE5B6A6FB8232FB21A6.description:
Provide examples of unemployment, inflation, total production, income, and economic growth in economies in
the Eastern Hemisphere.

2C690C0F21E04658AF7125A0D60DFB99.description:
Examine the role of job specialization and trade historically and during contemporary times in the Eastern
Hemisphere.

245B1E59E4B94CEF919C079F8953F7D3.description: Compare market economies to other economic systems in the Eastern Hemisphere.

CE38EF2B70884359901A9D0803FF27B3.description:
Examine the role that various types of resources (human capital, physical capital, and natural resources) have in
providing goods and services.

1EE34C40CE9F48FCB48F4027BB5C1C02.description:
Explain how scarcity necessitates decision making; employ examples from the Eastern Hemisphere to illustrate
the role of scarcity historically and in current events; compare through historical examples the costs and benefits
of economic decisions.

326A521E88BF4CD687733AA5CF74176A.description:
Describe the spatial organization of place, considering the historical, social, political, and economic implication
of that organization. Recognize that boundaries and definitions of location are historically constructed.

C5E7E91D1FBA4FA5BBAA922C399FD198.description: Describe how human activities alter places and regions in the Eastern Hemisphere

CB92FFEC361545DBB16BEA1596B38D83.description:
Recognize and explain how characteristics (cultural, economic, and physical-environmental) of regions affect
the history of societies in the Eastern Hemisphere

B3F82E6085234E2D815B78308665DF23.description:
Identify and describe how environments affect human activities and how human activities affect physical
environments through the study of cases in the Eastern Hemisphere.

C5BD91F455DC4F1FAC3213742BA36842.description:
Distinguish human activities and human-made features from “environments” (natural events or physical
features—land, air, and water—that are not directly made by humans) in the Eastern Hemisphere; identify the
relationship between human activities and the environment.

DF0E11D6FDCA40AE93896F864A8AFA10.description:
Use location terms and geographic representations such as maps, photographs, satellite images, and models to
describe where places in the Eastern Hemisphere are in relation to each other, to describe connections between
places, and to evaluate the benefits of particular places for purposeful activities

33D653E068874FE4A6C6940A650DAA34.description:
Understand the roles that periodization and region play in developing the comparison of historical civilizations.
Identify general characteristics that can be employed to conduct comparative analysis of case studies in the
Eastern Hemisphere in the same historical period, with teacher support.

B07D58DCC9474FDC847E13DD5A0FFADE.description:
Describe historical developments in the history of the Eastern Hemisphere, with specific references to
circumstances of time and place and to connections to broader regional or global processes.

E53548722035436E864703D7A7A05E51.description:
Identify how the relationship between geography, economics, and history helps to define a context for events in
the study of the Eastern Hemisphere.

9D05913E2658416094EB2296B1BC152A.description:
Describe and compare multiple events in the history of the Eastern Hemisphere in societies in similar
chronological contexts and in various geographical contexts.

C8C5A7619B634B638B1F245AC8D57436.description: Categorize and evaluate divergent perspectives on an individual historical event

A6732289444145A986388AE35BB6FF5D.description:
Identify a region in the Eastern Hemisphere by describing a characteristic that places within it have in common,
and then compare it to other regions.

AFE33683C1494A48A14D3249F9F92208.description:
Understand that historians use periodization to categorize events. Describe general models of periodization in
history.

F04743AC2FCD4F96B18745B2215C87D0.description: Identify the relationships of patterns of continuity and change to larger historical processes and themes.

6F7FE8C1FF734874BE6D1449812D8494.description:
Compare histories in different places in the Eastern Hemisphere, utilizing time lines. Identify ways that
changing periodization affects the historical narrative.

89A89108D54B4BCC99B218F87E783CE5.description:
Recognize and analyze the dynamics of historical continuity and change over periods of time. Identify the role
of turning points as an important dynamic in historical change

910FB3736DE142CCBB114AC42FA0BB35.description: Distinguish between long-term and immediate causes and effects of an event from current events or history.

AED6200901C24EC7BF92E5C1DAAD610F.description: Identify and classify the relationship between multiple causes and multiple effects.

A052DF9E24DA4140ACB5DB4F89A2042C.description: Identify causes and effects from current events, grade-level content, and historical events

EF7963BC372B4C038A07F7E994D050D8.description:
Employ mathematical skills to measure time by years, decades, centuries, and millennia; to calculate time from
the fixed points of the calendar system (B.C.E. and C.E.); and to interpret the data presented in time lines, with
teacher support.

A659583B360144F4B1B9589DD4A29981.description: Identify ways that events are related chronologically to one another in time.

C1D471ECC1124A33B6531F6C4D0F2256.description:
Recognize arguments on specific social studies topics and identify evidence to support the arguments. Examine
arguments related to a specific social studies topic from multiple perspectives.

EBBE6ED5B4D34C869C4E516F623ED836.description: Identify implicit ideas and draw inferences, with support.

08A7D59AF40B4673B58C8C8A52008C42.description:
Identify evidence and explain content, authorship, point of view, purpose, and format; identify bias; explain the
role of bias and potential audience.

9DA304DDFE864388A5EDAEFD485B4519.description:
Identify, effectively select, and analyze different forms of evidence used to make meaning in social studies
(including primary and secondary sources such as art and photographs, artifacts, oral histories, maps, and
graphs).

1D791250A8CA40D1991FB83B7A1EF258.description:
Develop and frame questions about topics related to historical events occurring in the Eastern Hemisphere that
can be answered by gathering, interpreting, and using evidence.

document.title: New York State P-12 Science Learning Standards

04FBF37BC2F74C368BC946ACEC342812.description: Change and rates of change can be quantified and modeled over very short or very long periods of time. Some system changes are irreversible. (HSESS3-5)

CEF4E469727F4CEE8EC6C11F6053915C.description: Empirical evidence is required to differentiate between cause and correlation and make claims about specific causes and effects. (HS-ESS2- 4)

E813AB95C5EB45DAA513B2E834AFE86C.description: Empirical evidence is needed to identify patterns. (HS-ESS2-8)

B198E9976E2E446882CE7066DD47351B.description: Different patterns may be observed at each of the scales at which a system is studied and can provide evidence for causality in explanations of phenomena. (HS-ESS2-8)

37E12BCB6D5D4234A7636F40C2DBA4BD.description: Though the magnitudes of human impacts are greater than they have ever been, so too are human abilities to model, predict, and manage current and future impacts. (HS-ESS3-5)

4F8BDCF265D94A8EA8123C27EAFF45D8.description: (NYSED) Concepts of density and heat energy can be used to explain observations of weather patterns (HSESS2-8).

C5E1FCF68D6F48AAA4A2D54B07F764D3.description: Changes in the atmosphere due to human activity have increased carbon dioxide concentrations and thus affect climate. (HS-ESS2-4)

896FD10AB1704205B0F7EEC5721AAD85.description: The foundation for Earth’s global climate systems is the electromagnetic radiation from the sun, as well as its reflection, absorption, storage, and redistribution among the atmosphere, ocean, and land systems, and this energy’s re-radiation into space. (HS-ESS2-4),(secondary to HS-ESS2-2)

8DF8AC7D3419479F8E648DDC97915FBA.description: The geological record shows that changes to global and regional climate can be caused by interactions among changes in the sun’s energy output or Earth’s orbit, tectonic events, ocean circulation, volcanic activity, glaciers, vegetation, and human activities. These changes can occur on a variety of time scales from sudden (e.g., volcanic ash clouds) to intermediate (ice ages) to very long-term tectonic cycles. (HS-ESS2-4)

7DB9EB8DAFFE4DF78050026B899949F5.description: Cyclical changes in the shape of Earth’s orbit around the sun, together with changes in the tilt of the planet’s axis of rotation, both occurring over hundreds of thousands of years, have altered the intensity and distribution of sunlight falling on the earth. These phenomena cause a cycle of ice ages and other gradual climate changes. (secondary to HS-ESS2-4)

D0B91761EED946058D5A55B01F27FBCF.description: ESS1.B: Earth and the Solar System

EEA73204EAE9434A8097F62F9AA6089A.description: Science arguments are strengthened by multiple lines of evidence supporting a single explanation. (HS-ESS2-4), (HSESS3-5)

D51AE79DE3F84FD0A1264DC67624B114.description: Science knowledge is based on empirical evidence. (HSESS3-5)

8870CB63E94F4818BF3932F7BADF3808.description: Scientific Knowledge is Based on Empirical Evidence

2AD06DD21FF442B395B6111AFFC3F4B5.description: Science investigations use diverse methods and do not always use the same set of procedures to obtain data. (HSESS3-5)

C974C703628A4713916BB7E58650669E.description: Scientific Investigations Use a Variety of Methods

6F6B312B0E3C4BDB98E5886CF4758394.description: Communicate scientific ideas (e.g., about phenomena and/or the process of development and the design and performance of a proposed process or system) in multiple formats (including orally, graphically, textually, and mathematically). (HS-ESS2-8)

077E49DD900A45CD92DE721E34D70582.description: Analyze data using tools, technologies and/or models (e.g., computational or mathematical) in order to make valid and reliable scientific claims or determine optimal design solution. (HS-ESS3-5)

EDA291EEDF3441CF8CEC62CC9DF7F1BC.description: Use a model to provide mechanistic accounts of phenomena. (HS-ESS2-4)

7976BF1A66C54B659CE98E97D591D7BA.description: Evaluate data and communicate information to explain how the movement and interactions of air masses result in changes in weather conditions.

36A0EDCE4BE14076BC5D04ABA3C82133.description: Analyze geoscience data and the results from global climate models to make an evidence-based forecast of the current rate of global or regional climate change and associated future impacts to Earth systems.

BF48C22866F14AB982CBD8FF66B0AD59.description: Use a model to describe how variations in the flow of energy into and out of Earth’s systems result in changes in climate.

226C631F555B43ED9D7C98AF4CAAB7E8.description: Science assumes the universe is a vast single system in which basic laws are consistent. (HS-ESS1-2)

7CF0582E291141A7BFF19898B97591E4.description: Scientific knowledge is based on the assumption that natural laws operate today as they did in the past and they will continue to do so in the future. (HS-ESS1-2)

E89B3BA62A2246B6B8807FB007106912.description: Scientific Knowledge Assumes an Order and Consistency in Natural Systems

E4AF1C4B20284DBE903BF9A439AE1249.description: Science and engineering complement each other in the cycle known as research and development (R&D). Many R&D projects may involve scientists, engineers, and others with wide ranges of expertise. (HS-ESS1- 2),(HS-ESS1-4)

1A1DEC02593F45319C19ED15536DF4B0.description: Interdependence of Science, Engineering, and Technology

84A86524A70748C181F0EE6DB780EAAC.description: In nuclear processes, atoms are not conserved, but the total number of protons plus neutrons is conserved. (HS-ESS1-3)

A704E188D57B45D6AD97F44F478C9DA8.description: Energy cannot be created or destroyed– only moved between one place and another place, between objects and/or fields, or between systems. (HS-ESS1- 2)

935EADCDEBFB4F85BDFA5758E48D68A3.description: Algebraic thinking is used to examine scientific data and predict the effect of a change in one variable on another (e.g., linear growth vs. exponential growth). (HS-ESS1-4)

44B9F700FBC14CE6AB7403E77A46FCE1.description: The significance of a phenomenon is dependent on the scale, proportion, and quantity at which it occurs. (HS-ESS1-1)

CD00CCB04F564E0CB62983E4DEF55CA7.description: Different patterns may be observed at each of the scales at which a system is studied and can provide evidence for causality in explanations of phenomena. (HS-ESS1-7)

929F86C82A3443DD983A7199AAA207CE.description: Atoms of each element emit and absorb characteristic frequencies of light. These characteristics allow identification of the presence of an element, even in microscopic quantities. (secondarytoHS-ESS1-2)

A7F1E994825C4137A88FA2EAC871118C.description: Nuclear Fusion processes in the center of the sun release the energy that ultimately reaches Earth as radiation. (secondary to HS-ESS1-1)

5AA50F4290C0407E806AC2AFF42613FA.description: PS3.D: Energy in Chemical Processes and Everyday Life

72A0D64746964C5681DBE1D1B51C8CCD.description: (NYSED) Earth and celestial phenomena can be described by principles of relative motion and perspective. (HS-ESS1-7)

A64CE6A0036246F1AA46AB3A53823752.description: Kepler’s laws describe common features of the motions of orbiting objects, including their elliptical paths around the sun. Orbits may change due to the gravitational effects from, or collisions with, other objects in the solar system. (HS-ESS1-4)

66468136D62C4A2588152A4C45319337.description: ESS1.B: Earth and the Solar System

924926BC9A10476481F8E58CEB1944A3.description: Other than the hydrogen and helium formed at the time of the Big Bang, nuclear fusion within stars produces all atomic nuclei lighter than and including iron, and the process releases electromagnetic energy. document.title: New York State K-8 Social Studies Framework

BEFC1B8764C94301AA00E2E6F07FF376.description:
Develop an understanding of the interdependence of individuals and groups in communities in the Western
Hemisphere

75E7737C396F4B809F5A2E51A1FC1D9D.description: Identify rights and responsibilities of citizens within societies in the Western Hemisphere.

9AF945044FD040E5A22A19F8344E523B.description:
Describe the roles of people in power in the Western Hemisphere, both historically and currently. Identify ways
that current figures can influence people’s rights and freedom.

24C34517FDB647E2B7475083999C9697.description: Identify situations with a global focus in which social actions are required and suggest solutions.

839497B4355641A6A56AF4EFEA0970FB.description: Participate in negotiating and compromising in the resolution of differences and conflict.

E83AFB3BB4A64FCF82890CAADED07695.description:
Identify opportunities for and the role of the individual in social and political participation at various times and
in various locations in the Western Hemisphere outside the United States.

0445FE61A99E4526A9932CE8A26B026E.description:
Identify different types of political systems and ideologies used at various times and in various locations in the
Western Hemisphere, and identify the roles of individuals and key groups in those political and social systems.

3F6A9FBECBC142A78256413E6EDD3E80.description:
Participate in activities that focus on a localized issue or problem in a country other than the United States in the
Western Hemisphere.

EC7A6A10D63E403B9EBF276B33A788AF.description:
Demonstrate respect for the rights of others in discussion and classroom debates, regardless of whether one
agrees with the other viewpoint. Consider alternate views in discussion, with teacher support.

12202FEC25C54B26B45307C891DE9A41.description: Describe government decisions that affect economies in case studies from the Western Hemisphere.

8B7A90EA7D5047D298DA6FD8B07429F1.description: Explain the meaning of unemployment, inflation, income, and economic growth in the economy.

09B59D502BE4435F88D82D3F707E620B.description:
Examine the role of job specialization and trade historically and during contemporary times in the Western
Hemisphere.

20012F1A6DCF4F89B5AB5EC4DC234EF3.description:
Provide examples of how currency makes exchange easier by comparing a barter economy to a currency-based
economy; examine why corporations and labor unions have a role in a market economy.

B356E60C94C14FDBAFEAD1CAF8265D6A.description:
Show examples of various types of resources (human capital, physical capital, and natural resources) required to
provide goods and services.

DE6F0D4985294C80AC22AF568AF3D82F.description:
Explain how scarcity necessitates decision making; employ examples from the Western Hemisphere to illustrate
the role of scarcity historically and in current events.

7AD9AD49F887427C9D930DA3965FDE0F.description: Recognize that boundaries and definition of location are historically constructed.

9AF6A36FD76D45198FC48106FE7638C6.description: Describe how human activities alter places and regions in the Western Hemisphere.

DF65CFE659A549C7B478585E70075344.description:
Recognize and explain how characteristics (cultural, economic, and physical-environmental) of regions affect
the history of societies in the Western Hemisphere.

BEEB7663CF7E4DE2BEB8D4A80733E041.description:
Identify and describe how environments affect human activities and how human activities affect physical
environments through the study of cases in the Western Hemisphere.

C83DCF9E115D405785AA7BBD106EC541.description:
Distinguish human activities and human-made features from “environments” (natural events or physical
features—land, air, and water—that are not directly made by humans) in the Western Hemisphere.

11A89BA322E049BAB85C007B24C29432.description:
Use location terms and geographic representations such as maps, photographs, satellite images, and models to
describe where places in the Western Hemisphere are in relation to each other, to describe connections among
places, and to evaluate the benefits of particular places for purposeful activities.

B4244051421D4FE7B6D1DB5E9187AC8A.description:
Describe historical developments in the history of the Western Hemisphere with specific references to
circumstances of time and place and to connections to broader regional or global processes, with teacher
support.

1AF2B30D01A24EC2A9743564878192D3.description:
Identify how the relationship between geography, economics, and history helps to define a context for events in
the study of the Western Hemisphere.

8E755B305FDC4A6985F13FA7BF0D762D.description:
Describe and compare events in the history of the Western Hemisphere in societies in similar chronological
contexts and in various geographical contexts.

7E615E8781634A418AE4F7184DD3D1B7.description: Categorize divergent perspectives of an individual historical event.

4C5BCA94FEC946BA9C79111C13287F63.description:
Identify a region in the Western Hemisphere by describing a characteristic that places within it have in
common, and then compare it to other regions. Understand how regions can be defined as sharing common
characteristics in contrast with other regions.

F57AA3CA29594EB18BBB71B0302F12B2.description: Understand the role of periodization as a practice in history and social studies.

C15BB9799FA54D07ABEC8FCF3A61947F.description: Recognize and identify patterns of continuity and change in history.

68D2FAB061CE40E8A1FA65620355115A.description:
Use periods of time such as decades and centuries to organize a historical narrative; compare histories in
different places in the Western Hemisphere utilizing timelines.

01A59B0D117847B3B40652AFE4B0AC4B.description:
Recognize the dynamics of historical continuity and change over periods of time. Identify important turning
points in history.

985F5CF79E244249B25DADEE03136F96.description: Distinguish between long-term and immediate causes and effects of an event from current events or history.

D477F0A892304F0CA2C3EA0EEEF5A6C0.description: Identify and classify the relationship between multiple causes and multiple effects.

89F958CB22F54F47A8C354C42E514E80.description: Identify causes and effects using examples from current events or grade-level content and historical events

E5A3802DEF3F42D282FA01C65CBBE38E.description:
Employ mathematical skills to measure time in years and centuries. Understand the difference between B.C.E.
and C.E. Identify the chronological significance of data presented in time lines.

E5B68F1FDC954CEB8FC211F3FC53435A.description: Explain how events are related chronologically to one another in time.

D29CE094255046C38E0F3CDE8C47781F.description: Recognize arguments on specific social studies topics and identify evidence supporting the argument.

BA38824546B04BCD8F6520A8A561898C.description: Identify implicit ideas to draw inference, with support

A1E075ADEF1B445BAB8A730618BEC57D.description:
Identify evidence and explain content, authorship, purpose, and format; identify bias; explain the role of bias
and potential audience, with teacher support.

FF7FA6DD6894455F95844BBDBADE5AF7.description:
Recognize and effectively select different forms of evidence used to make meaning in social studies (including
primary and secondary sources such as art and photographs, artifacts, oral histories, maps, and graphs).

B5B297674A4A41A4BAB7F611E76AE249.description:
Develop questions to help identify evidence about topics related to the historical events occurring in the
Western Hemisphere that can be answered by gathering, interpreting, and using evidence.

standardSets.subject: NYS Portrait of a Graduate Attributes

document.title: New York State Education Department

6B2437E11CFF4FB5BEF09FF0FB6A0CCD.description:
Engages in self-reflection to identify strengths and
areas for growth, sets meaningful goals, uses social
awareness to maintain supportive relationships,
and demonstrates responsible decision-making
that prioritizes social, emotional, and mental wellbeing.

51F70997E047468B84CA56AEEE05120B.description:
Acts responsibly and ethically within local, global,
and digital communities, employing civic
knowledge, skills, and mindsets to promote global
sustainability and contribute positively to a
culturally diverse, democratic society.

AD32E4F845D74196888A8A53995A6A5E.description:
Articulates ideas clearly and confidently through
speaking, writing, and the use of different types of
media for various purposes, while engaging with
diverse audiences and actively listening to different
perspectives

5CA5128AA6EE4C52B688DECC07BC384B.description:
Analyzes information thoughtfully, evaluates
evidence critically, and identifies patterns and
connections between different pieces of
information (across multiple content areas) to
address complex issues and navigate the world
with insight.

A16D5A9BA890421B94C09B1EFB4F582D.description:
Utilizes imagination, curiosity, and flexible thinking
to solve problems creatively, and develop new
ideas and products, while adapting to evolving
circumstances and challenges.

04947F22445B423B97E6DD0280031E79.description:
Demonstrates a strong foundation in the NYS
learning standards and is equipped with the
knowledge and skills necessary to achieve
success in college, careers, civic engagement,
service, and life.

9EC01E1D78DD4CFEA3A4F3B1A66D03BC.description:
A New York State high school graduate who is culturally responsive builds strong, respectful relationships, valuing diverse
perspectives as essential to a rigorous, inclusive learning community. New York State students who embody cultural
responsiveness and academic readiness—demonstrating creativity, critical thinking, communication, reflection, and
global awareness—will be prepared to learn, grow, innovate, and contribute meaningfully to society. These graduates will
be equipped with the interpersonal and intellectual skills needed to thrive in an interconnected, ever-evolving world.
